corpus_definition: Something you ask to get more facts.
usage_note: a question about + noun / -ing: 'a question about the homework', 'a question about getting a visa'. Common verbs: have, ask, answer. Plural: questions about.

relations.note: A question asked to get information or to check something, common at work and in shops: 'a query about my bill'.
Formal: a question to an office or company. British English also spells it enquiry.
What you say or write back to a question: 'an answer to your question'.

context.text: Excuse me, I have a question about the bus to Samarkand. My friend also asked a question about the ticket price.

reviewer_note: Fixed noun phrase; 'about' introduces the topic. Kept as phrase, not a single word.

corpus_definition: A bad event that happens by mistake and causes damage.

forms.definition: a bad thing that happens by mistake and hurts people or breaks things
forms.example: He had a small accident with his car yesterday.
forms.note: Also in the phrase 'by accident' = by chance, without planning it.

syn.note: Related: an accident where a car, bus or plane hits something.
A small accident that is not serious; a bit formal or humorous.
Related and formal: when two moving things hit each other.
Related: a very big event with a lot of damage, like a flood or earthquake.

forms.note: There is no verb from accident. Use 'have an accident' or 'crash'.

forms.definition: happening by chance, when nobody planned or wanted it
forms.example: The police said the fire was accidental.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Not planned before; can be about good things too.
Related and easy: you did not think it would happen.

ant.note: Done on purpose, because someone wanted to do it.
Planned and wanted; a bit formal.

forms.definition: by mistake, without wanting or planning to do it
forms.example: I accidentally broke my mother's favourite cup.

syn.note: Easy and common; stresses that you did something wrong.
Same meaning, more formal.
Related: it happened without a plan, often something good: 'We met by chance.'

ant.note: Because you wanted to do it.
Easy, everyday English: 'He did it on purpose.'

context.text: There was a bad accident on the road to Fergana last night. A driver accidentally pressed the wrong pedal, but luckily nobody was hurt.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows (A2 'by mistake and causes damage', A1 'unexpectedly without planning') are the same meaning, merged. accidental/accidentally lean on the 'by chance' side of the word; kept as existing because accidental damage/death use this sense.

corpus_definition: A person who performs in plays or movies.

forms.definition: a person who performs in plays, films or TV shows
forms.example: He is a famous movie actor.
forms.note: Today actor is used for men and women; actress is only for women.

syn.note: Wider: also singers, dancers and musicians who perform for people.
Related and easy: a very famous actor or singer.
Old-fashioned for actors in a theatre; today it usually means a sports player.

forms.definition: the job or skill of performing in plays and films
forms.example: She studied acting in Tashkent for three years.

syn.note: Related: the subject of plays and performing, often at school.
Related: one show, or how well someone performs in it.

forms.definition: something that you do, especially to deal with a problem
forms.example: We need to take action before it is too late.
forms.note: Belongs to act = do something, not act = perform in a film. ('Action!' in film-making is a different, special use.)

forms.definition: to perform as a character in a play, film or TV show
forms.example: My cousin acts in a small theatre in Bukhara.
forms.note: act in a film / act the part of someone. Act also means 'do something' and 'behave'.

syn.note: Wider: also sing, dance or play music for people.
Easy, used with a role: 'He played the king.'
Related: to have the main part: 'She stars in a new film.'

forms.definition: doing a lot of things or moving around a lot
forms.example: My grandfather is still very active at seventy.
forms.note: Belongs to act = do something, not act = perform in a play or film.

forms.definition: in a way that involves doing things, not just waiting
forms.example: She actively looks for ways to improve her English.
forms.note: Belongs to act = do something, not act = perform in a play or film.

people.definition: a woman who performs in plays, films or TV shows
people.example: The actress won a prize for her first film.
people.note: Many women now prefer to be called actors.

people.definition: a person who works hard to change society or politics
people.example: Young activists planted trees in Tashkent.
people.note: Belongs to act = do something (active), not to acting in films.

context.text: My brother wants to be an actor. He goes to acting classes every Saturday, and next month he will act in a school play.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: act = perform (this map) vs act = do something (action, active, actively, activist shown as other_meaning). act is the verb the headword is made from, so relation 'derivational'.

corpus_definition: The invisible mix of gases that we breathe in.

forms.definition: the mix of gases around us that we breathe
forms.example: The air in the mountains is very fresh.
forms.note: Uncountable: 'fresh air', not 'a fresh air'. 'By air' means by plane.

syn.note: Related: the gases around the whole Earth; also the feeling in a place.
Related: the gas in the air that we need to live.
Related: a light, pleasant wind.
Related and easy: air that moves, often strongly.

forms.definition: to open the windows so that a room becomes fresh
forms.example: Mum airs the bedrooms every morning, even in winter.
forms.note: American English often says 'air out'. Air also means 'show on TV or radio' (other meaning).

syn.note: Formal and technical: let fresh air move through a place.
Related: make something clean and fresh again.

forms.definition: with a lot of space and light, and fresh to breathe in
forms.example: Our new classroom is big and airy.

syn.note: Related: having a lot of space.
Related and easy: full of daylight.
Related: full of light; says nothing about fresh air.

ant.note: A stuffy room is warm and has no fresh air.

forms.definition: with no fresh oxygen, so it is hard to breathe
forms.example: The small office was hot and airless.

syn.note: More common in everyday English.

forms.definition: in a light, careless way, as if something is not important
forms.example: 'It doesn't matter,' she said airily.
forms.note: Belongs to airy = light and careless (an airy promise), not the air we breathe. Not common.

context.text: In summer the air in Tashkent is hot and dry. My grandmother airs the house early in the morning, so the rooms stay cool and airy all day.

reviewer_note: aerial/aerate share the Latin root but are not made from English air: listed in not_family. airily belongs to airy = light/careless, so other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A living thing that can move and eat other things.

forms.definition: a living creature that can move, eat and breathe, like a dog or a bird
forms.example: The dog is a friendly animal.
forms.note: In everyday English, animal often means mammals only, not birds, fish or insects.

syn.note: Any living thing that moves; often used for strange or small animals.
Related: a large or wild animal; old-fashioned or used in stories.
Related and easy: an animal you keep at home, like a cat.
Related: wild animals and plants as a group.

forms.note: animate (make drawings move) shares an old Latin root but is not made from animal; animalize is very rare.

forms.definition: coming from or connected with living creatures, not plants
forms.example: Some soaps are made from animal fat.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: animal fat, animal products, animal rights.
There is no adverb from animal.

context.text: There are many wild animals in the Chatkal mountains. Farmers there sell milk, cheese and other animal products at the bazaar.

reviewer_note: No real affix: anim- is not an English word. animality is very rare and not shown. The adjective is a zero-change conversion used before nouns.

corpus_definition: The long body part attached to the shoulder.

forms.definition: the long part of your body between your shoulder and your hand
forms.example: She hurt her left arm.

syn.note: Related and formal: an arm or a leg.
Related and easy: the part at the end of your arm.

forms.definition: an amount that you can carry by holding it against your body
forms.example: She came in with an armful of flowers.

forms.definition: to give someone weapons to fight with
forms.example: The soldiers were armed with rifles.
forms.note: Belongs to arms = weapons, which is a different old word, not the body part.

forms.definition: carrying a gun or other weapon
forms.example: Two armed guards stood at the bank door.
forms.note: Belongs to arms = weapons, not the body part. Opposite: unarmed.
There is no adverb from arm.

people.definition: metal clothes that soldiers wore in the past to protect their bodies
people.example: The museum has a suit of armour from the Middle Ages.
people.note: Belongs to arms = weapons, not the body part. American spelling: armor.

context.text: Dilnoza broke her arm when she fell off her bike. Now her brother carries an armful of her books to school every day.

reviewer_note: Homograph trap: arm (body) and arm/arms (weapons) are different old words; the weapon family (arm verb, armed, armour) is shown as other_meaning only. army comes from Latin, not from arm.

corpus_definition: To reach a specific place after finishing a trip.
particle_note: Not separable: 'arrive at the hotel', never 'arrive the hotel at'. Use 'arrive at' for buildings and points (station, airport, school) and 'arrive in' for cities and countries (arrive in Tashkent). No preposition with home: 'arrive home'.

relations.note: Easy, everyday English: 'We got to the hotel at noon.'
Same meaning, with no preposition: 'We reached the hotel.'
Related: move to a place where the speaker is.
Go away from a place: 'We left the hotel at nine.'
Formal, used for trains and planes: 'The train departs from platform 2.'

context.text: Our train arrived at Bukhara station at nine in the morning. We arrived at the hotel an hour later and went straight to bed.

reviewer_note: Other meaning 'arrive at a decision/an answer' (= reach after thinking) is not this map. Kept as phrasal (verb + preposition, not separable).

corpus_definition: a person who creates paintings or drawings as a job.

forms.definition: a person who paints or draws pictures as a job
forms.example: The artist painted a beautiful mountain scene.
forms.note: Also used for musicians, singers and writers: 'a recording artist'.

syn.note: Easy: an artist who paints; also a worker who paints walls.
Related: draws pictures for books and magazines.
Related: plans how clothes, buildings or products will look.

forms.definition: paintings, drawings and other beautiful things that people make
forms.example: We saw some modern art at the museum in Tashkent.
forms.note: Art is uncountable here: 'a lot of art', not 'many arts'. 'The arts' = music, theatre, painting and so on.

syn.note: Related and easy: one kind of art, or one picture.

forms.definition: great skill in painting, music or other creative work
forms.example: Everyone admired the artistry of the old carpet makers in Bukhara.

syn.note: Related and easy: the ability to do something well, in any job.
Skill in making things by hand, like carpets or furniture.

forms.note: There is no verb from artist. Use paint, draw or create.

forms.definition: good at painting, drawing, music or other creative things
forms.example: My little sister is very artistic; she draws every day.
forms.note: Also means 'connected with painting and music': artistic freedom.

syn.note: Good at making new things and ideas, not only pictures.
Related and easy: having a natural ability for anything.

forms.definition: in a way that shows skill and a good eye for beauty
forms.example: The dishes were artistically arranged on the table.

syn.note: In a new and clever way.
Related and easy: in a way that looks very nice.

context.text: My uncle is an artist in Samarkand. He sells his art to tourists, and his paintings of old mosques are very artistic.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a person noun, so it sits in the noun slot as base; art (the thing) and artistry are extras. No -ly affix claimed on artistically (artistical is not a word).

corpus_definition: the season after summer, when leaves fall from trees

forms.definition: the season between summer and winter, when leaves fall from trees
forms.example: The leaves turn red and orange in autumn.
forms.note: British English. 'In (the) autumn', not 'on autumn'.

syn.note: Same meaning in American English: 'in the fall'.

ant.note: The season on the other side of the year, between winter and summer.

forms.note: There is no verb from autumn.

forms.definition: typical of the season after summer, with cool days and falling leaves
forms.example: The park looks beautiful in its autumnal colours.
forms.note: In everyday English people often just say 'autumn' before a noun: autumn colours.
There is no adverb from autumn.

context.text: Autumn in Uzbekistan is warm and sunny. In October the trees in Tashkent turn yellow, and the cool autumnal evenings are perfect for long walks.

reviewer_note: autumn (British) vs fall (American) noted. autumnal is literary; marked register.

corpus_definition: The part of your body that is behind you.

forms.definition: the part of your body between your neck and your bottom, behind you
forms.example: My back hurts after sitting all day.

syn.note: Related: the line of bones down the middle of this part of your body.

forms.definition: help or support, often money, for a person or plan
forms.example: The project has the backing of the city government.
forms.note: Belongs to back = support, not the body part.

forms.definition: to support a person or plan
forms.example: My parents backed my decision to study abroad.
forms.note: Belongs to back = support (also 'move backwards': back the car out), not the body part.

forms.definition: at or near the rear part of something
forms.example: Please use the back door.
forms.note: Belongs to back = the rear part of a thing (back seat, back garden), not the body part.

forms.definition: directed towards the place behind you
forms.example: He left without a backward look.
forms.note: Belongs to back = behind / in the other direction, not the body part.

forms.definition: to the place where someone or something was before
forms.example: Come back soon!
forms.note: Belongs to back = return, not the body part.

forms.definition: towards the direction that is behind you
forms.example: She took two steps backwards.
forms.note: Belongs to back = behind / in the other direction, not the body part. American English often says backward.

people.definition: a person who gives money or support to a plan
people.example: The new film found a rich backer.
people.note: Belongs to back = support, not the body part.

context.text: Grandpa has a bad back, so he can't lift heavy things. When his back hurts, he lies down for an hour.

reviewer_note: back has many meanings (rear part, return, support); only the body part is anchored here, all others are other_meaning. backache is a compound, not a suffix form, so no affix is claimed.

corpus_definition: To start doing something.

forms.definition: the first part of something, or the time when it starts
forms.example: The beginning of the film was a bit boring.
forms.note: Double n: beginning. Common phrase: 'at the beginning of the year'.

syn.note: Easy and very common: 'the start of the lesson'.
Formal, used in the phrase 'from the outset' = from the very first moment.
Related: the first part of a book, film or event, or the day a new place opens.

ant.note: The last part of something: 'the end of the film'.
The way a story or film finishes: 'a happy ending'.

forms.definition: to start doing something, or to start happening
forms.example: The lesson begins at nine o'clock.
forms.note: Irregular verb: begin, began, begun. Begin + -ing or begin + to do: 'It began raining / It began to rain.'

syn.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday speech.
Very formal, used in official writing: 'The meeting will commence at ten.'
Related: to start doing a job or task in an active way.
Related: to start something big and new, like a product or a project.

ant.note: To do the last part of something: 'I finished my homework.'
To stop, or to make something stop: 'The concert ended at eleven.'
To not continue doing something.

forms.note: There is no adjective from begin. Use 'first', 'early' or 'opening' ('the opening scene').
There is no adverb from begin. Use 'first' or 'at first'.

people.definition: a person who is starting to learn something and has little experience
people.example: This English course is for beginners.
people.note: Double n: beginner.

context.text: Our English course begins in September. At the beginning, it was hard for me, but the teacher is very patient with beginners.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: the n doubles before -ing and -er (beginning, beginner). No adjective or adverb exists in the family.

corpus_definition: A long seat for several people to sit on together.

forms.definition: a long seat for two or more people, often made of wood
forms.example: We sat on a bench in the park and ate ice cream.
forms.note: Plural: benches. A bench can also be a long table for working on, in a workshop.

syn.note: Related and easy: any place where you can sit, for one or more people.
Related: a long wooden seat in a church.

forms.definition: to stop a player from playing in a game for a time
forms.example: The coach decided to bench his best player for the final.
forms.note: Belongs to bench = the seat where sports players wait, not a park seat. Mostly American English.
There is no adjective from bench.
There is no adverb from bench.

context.text: In Navoi Park there are many wooden benches under the trees. Every evening my grandfather sits on the same bench and talks with his friends.

reviewer_note: Simple noun. The verb bench (sports) is listed as other_meaning, not hidden. Compounds like benchmark are left out.

corpus_definition: An animal with wings and feathers that can fly.

forms.definition: an animal with feathers, two legs and wings, which usually can fly
forms.example: A small bird was singing in the tree outside my window.

syn.note: Related: birds like chickens and ducks that people keep for meat or eggs.
Related: a baby one, just out of the egg.

forms.note: There is no common verb from bird. People say 'go birdwatching'.
There is no common adjective from bird.
There is no adverb from bird.

context.text: In spring, many birds come back to Uzbekistan from the south. My little brother likes to watch the birds in our garden and give them bread.

reviewer_note: Simple noun with no learner-level derived forms. Rare words (birder, birdie in golf) and compounds (birdwatching, birdcage) are left out.

corpus_definition: The anniversary of the day someone was born.

forms.definition: the day each year that has the same date as the day you were born
forms.example: Happy birthday! How old are you today?
forms.note: Common phrases: 'Happy birthday!', 'a birthday party', 'a birthday cake'.

syn.note: Related: the same date as an important past event, like a wedding, not the day someone was born.
Related: the full date (day, month and year) you were born, used on forms and documents.

forms.note: There is no verb from birthday. Use 'celebrate your birthday'.
There is no adjective from birthday. The noun is used before other nouns: 'a birthday present'.
There is no adverb from birthday.

context.text: Today is my sister's birthday. We are having a small party at home, and my mother has made a big birthday cake with eighteen candles.

reviewer_note: birthday is itself a compound (birth + day); birth and other compounds are not listed as forms. No derived forms exist.

corpus_definition: a thick warm cover used on a bed to keep you warm

forms.definition: a thick warm cover, often made of wool, that you use on a bed
forms.example: It was cold at night, so I asked for another blanket.

syn.note: Related and easy: anything you put over something to protect it or keep it warm.
Related: a warm bed cover filled with soft material, often with a sewn pattern.
Related: a thick soft bed cover filled with feathers, used instead of sheets and blankets. Mainly British English.
Related: a light cover you put over a sofa or chair.

forms.definition: to cover something completely with a thick layer
forms.example: Snow blanketed the mountains near Chimgan.
forms.note: Belongs to blanket = a thick layer over something (snow, fog), not a bed cover. Mostly used in writing.

forms.definition: affecting everyone or everything, with no exceptions
forms.example: The city has a blanket ban on smoking in cafes.
forms.note: Belongs to blanket = covering everything, not a bed cover. Used only before a noun: 'a blanket ban', 'a blanket rule'.
There is no adverb from blanket.

context.text: In winter, my grandmother puts two heavy blankets on every bed. When I visit her village, I sleep under a warm wool blanket and never feel cold.

reviewer_note: Same-spelling verb and adjective exist but belong to the 'complete layer / covering everything' meaning, so both are other_meaning, not no_form.

corpus_definition: The physical form of a person.

forms.definition: the whole physical form of a person or animal: head, arms, legs and so on
forms.example: Swimming is good for your whole body.
forms.note: Plural: bodies. Also means a dead person ('The police found a body') and a group or organization ('a government body').

syn.note: Related: the shape of a person's body, often a woman's: 'She has a slim figure.'
Related: the size and shape of a body, especially a strong one.
Related: how big or strong a person's body is: 'a man of medium build'.

ant.note: The part of a person that thinks and feels: 'a healthy mind in a healthy body'.

forms.definition: to show or express an idea or quality very clearly
forms.example: For many people, Amir Temur embodies the history of Uzbekistan.
forms.note: Belongs to body = something that gives an idea a real form, not a person's physical form. Formal, C1 level.

forms.definition: connected with the physical form of a person, not the mind
forms.example: The doctor checked all his bodily functions.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: 'bodily harm', 'bodily needs'. Spelling: y changes to i.

syn.note: Same meaning and much more common: 'physical health'.
Related and formal: used mainly in 'corporal punishment' (hitting someone as a punishment).

ant.note: Connected with the mind: 'mental health'.
Connected with the soul or religion, not the physical form.

forms.definition: by moving or lifting a person's whole physical form
forms.example: The guards carried him bodily out of the room.
forms.note: Same spelling as the adjective. Not common; used mostly with lift, carry, throw.

syn.note: Related: using force on the body: 'They physically removed him.'

context.text: Our sports teacher says we must take care of our body every day. Sleep, water and good food are basic bodily needs, just like exercise.

reviewer_note: Kept the 'physical form' sense only; body = dead person and body = organization are mentioned in the note. embody is other_meaning (idea given a form). Compounds (somebody, bodyguard) left out.

corpus_definition: The first meal of the day eaten in the morning.

forms.definition: the first meal of the day, eaten in the morning
forms.example: We had eggs, bread and tea for breakfast.
forms.note: Usually no 'a' or 'the': 'have breakfast', 'eat breakfast', 'for breakfast'.

syn.note: Same meaning, but people almost never say it in everyday English.
Related: a late morning meal that is both the first and the midday meal.

forms.definition: to eat the first meal of the day
forms.example: We breakfasted on bread and honey before the long drive.
forms.note: Formal and not common. In everyday English say 'have breakfast'.

syn.note: Related and formal: to eat a meal, usually in the evening.

forms.note: There is no adjective from breakfast. The noun is used before other nouns: 'breakfast time', 'a breakfast table'.
There is no adverb from breakfast.

context.text: In Uzbekistan, many families eat bread, cheese and tea for breakfast. On holidays, some people breakfast on hot samsa from the bazaar.

reviewer_note: breakfast is a historical compound (break + fast); no affix split claimed. The rare verb is kept as a formal conversion.

corpus_definition: To clean your mouth using a small tool and paste.
usage_note: Natural English uses a possessive: brush your / my / his teeth. 'Brush teeth' without one sounds like a list or a sign. Past: brushed his teeth.

relations.note: Same meaning, common in British English.
Related: to clean between your teeth with a special thin string.
Related: to wash your mouth with water, often after brushing.

context.text: Every night before bed, my little son brushes his teeth for two minutes. The dentist told us to brush our teeth after breakfast too.

reviewer_note: Corpus item drops the possessive; usage note and context use the natural 'brush your teeth'. The corpus example 'brush teeth after every meal' should ideally read 'brush your teeth'.

corpus_definition: A structure with walls and a roof used for people.

forms.definition: a structure with walls and a roof, such as a house, school or office
forms.example: My office is in that tall building next to the bank.
forms.note: Also means the work of making houses and other structures: 'building work'.

syn.note: More formal and wider: can also mean a bridge or a tower.
Related and easy: a structure where a family lives.
Related: a large tall structure with many flats or offices. Mainly British English.
Related and formal: the building and land that a business uses.

forms.definition: to make a house, road or other structure by putting parts together
forms.example: They are building a new school in our district.
forms.note: Irregular verb: build, built, built. The headword comes from this verb.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Informal and easy: 'They put up a new wall.'
Related and very easy, but more general.
Very formal, used in official writing.

ant.note: To destroy an old structure on purpose.
Easier phrasal verb: 'They knocked down the old cinema.'
To damage something so badly that it no longer exists.

forms.definition: to make something again after it was damaged or destroyed
forms.example: After the earthquake in 1966, Tashkent was rebuilt.
forms.note: Irregular like the base verb: rebuild, rebuilt, rebuilt.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Related: to repair an old structure so it looks as it did before.

forms.definition: having a particular size or shape of body
forms.example: He is a tall, heavily built man.
forms.note: Belongs to build = the size and shape of a person's body, not a structure. In 'a newly built school', built is just the past participle of the verb.
There is no adverb from building.

people.definition: a person whose job is making or repairing houses and other structures
people.example: The builders finished our new kitchen in two weeks.

context.text: Many new buildings are going up in Tashkent City. The builders work day and night, and they want to build ten more by next year.

reviewer_note: Headword is a noun made from build, so build is the existing verb (derivational). built as an adjective means body shape (other_meaning); the participle in 'newly built' is not counted.

corpus_definition: Using a bus for your travel.
usage_note: by + transport with no 'a' or 'the': go / travel / come by bus (also by car, by train, by plane). With a/the/my use on: 'on the bus', 'on the 7 bus'.

relations.note: Similar, but talks about a particular bus or being inside it: 'I read on the bus.'
Related: by a big comfortable bus for long trips between cities. Mainly British English.
Related: by bus, train or metro, not in your own car.
Related: walking, not using a bus or car. Note: 'on foot', never 'by foot' in careful English.

context.text: My sister goes to university by bus every morning. It takes forty minutes, but it is cheaper than going by taxi.

reviewer_note: Fixed prepositional phrase; trap is 'by bus' vs 'on the bus' (no article after by). No antonym: other ways to travel are related, not opposite.

corpus_definition: Using your own or another car to travel.
usage_note: go / travel / come + by car. No 'a', 'the' or 'my' after 'by': say 'by car', not 'by the car' or 'by my car'. With 'my' use 'in': 'in my car'.

relations.note: Same idea, but you can add who owns it: 'in my dad's car'.
A verb: 'We drove there' means almost the same as 'We went there by car', but you are the driver.
Another way to travel, with a paid driver.
Walking, with no car or bus.

context.text: My family usually goes to Samarkand by car. It takes about four hours. My brother prefers the train, but by car we can stop for lunch on the way.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; key trap is 'by the car / by my car', covered in usage_note.

corpus_definition: To be in time for a bus or train.

forms.definition: the act of taking and holding a ball that is thrown
forms.example: That was a great catch by the goalkeeper!
forms.note: Belongs to catch = take hold of something moving, not getting a bus. Informal 'catch' can also mean a hidden problem: 'What's the catch?'

forms.definition: to get on a bus, train or plane before it leaves
forms.example: I caught the last metro home from Chorsu.
forms.note: Irregular verb: catch, caught, caught.

syn.note: Easy everyday verb: 'I get the bus at eight.' It does not always show you were in time.
Informal: 'We just made the train' means we were only just in time.
Take is about using a bus or train to travel; catch is about getting it in time.
Formal: to get on a plane, train or ship.

ant.note: To be too late for a bus or train: 'I missed the bus.'

forms.definition: easy to remember and nice to listen to, used about songs
forms.example: The song has a very catchy tune.
forms.note: Belongs to catch = take and hold (a song 'catches' your mind), not getting a bus.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: the player behind the batter who takes the ball in baseball
people.example: The catcher threw the ball back to the pitcher.
people.note: Belongs to catch = take a ball, not getting a bus.

context.text: I woke up late, so I ran to the bus stop. I caught the bus just in time, but my friend Aziz missed it and had to catch the next one.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: only the 'in time for transport' meaning is existing; ball/song meanings (catch n., catchy, catcher) are other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Small coins given back after payment.

forms.definition: the money you get back when you pay more than the price
forms.example: The shopkeeper gave me my change and a receipt.
forms.note: Uncountable in this meaning: 'some change', not 'a change' or 'changes'. Also means small coins: 'Have you got any change for the bus?'

syn.note: Change is often coins, but it can also be small notes.
Coins of low value that you carry in your pocket.
Easy phrase, but it also means a refund when you return something.

forms.definition: to give someone smaller notes or coins for a big note
forms.example: Can you change a 100,000 som note for me?
forms.note: Also used for swapping one country's money for another: 'change dollars into som'.

syn.note: Informal, mostly American: 'Can you break a twenty?'
To give one thing and get another thing back; not only about money.

forms.definition: likely to become different often, used about weather or moods
forms.example: The weather in spring is very changeable.
forms.note: Belongs to change = become different, not money you get back.
No adverb is used in this family; 'changeably' is very rare.

context.text: I paid for the bread with a 50,000 som note, and the seller gave me my change. Then I asked her to change another big note into coins for the bus.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: map is only the money meaning (uncountable 'change'); changeable is other_meaning. 'exchange' kept out of synonyms because it is built on change.

corpus_definition: More than one young person.

forms.definition: boys and girls; more than one young person
forms.example: The children are playing football in the park.
forms.note: Irregular plural of child. Never 'childs' or 'childrens'; possessive is children's: 'the children's room'.

syn.note: Very common in everyday speech.
Young people, often older kids and teenagers.
Easy phrase, often used by teachers.

ant.note: People who are fully grown.
Informal word for adults, often used by and with young kids.

forms.definition: the time of your life when you are young
forms.example: I spent my childhood in a small village near Bukhara.

syn.note: Youth is the time when you are young, often including the teenage years.

ant.note: The time of your life when you are an adult.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: behaving in a silly way, like a very young kid
forms.example: Stop being so childish and say sorry to your sister.
forms.note: Usually negative. For a positive meaning use childlike.

syn.note: Not behaving like an adult; a bit more formal.
Informal and stronger: like a baby.
Easy word: not sensible, but not always about age.

ant.note: Behaving in a sensible, adult way.
Informal: behaving like an adult.

forms.definition: having the good qualities of a young kid, such as trust and joy
forms.example: My grandfather still has a childlike love of kites.
forms.note: Positive, unlike childish.

syn.note: Trusting and not knowing bad things about the world.

forms.definition: having no sons or daughters
forms.example: They were childless for ten years before their son was born.

forms.definition: in a silly way, like a very young kid
forms.example: He laughed childishly at the joke.

syn.note: In a stupid way, not only about age.

ant.note: In a sensible, adult way.

context.text: The children laughed and played in the garden all afternoon. Their grandmother smiled and talked about her own childhood in Fergana. 'Don't be childish,' she said when the boys started fighting.

reviewer_note: GATE? 'children' is a real noun (irregular plural of child); the gate's dictionary only lists the lemma child, and using child as base fails the headword check. Trap: childish (negative) vs childlike (positive).

corpus_definition: a show with clowns, acrobats, and trained animals

forms.definition: a show with clowns, acrobats and animals, often in a big tent
forms.example: We went to the circus in Tashkent on Saturday.
forms.note: Plural: circuses.

syn.note: Any performance people watch; a circus is one kind of show.
The large tent where a circus performs; sometimes used to mean the circus itself.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective in this family; 'circus' is used before nouns instead: 'a circus tent'.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: The circus came to our city last week. The children loved the clowns and the acrobats most of all.

reviewer_note: Leaf word with no family forms; clown and acrobat are not made from circus, so they are left out.

corpus_definition: Free from dirt or bad marks.

forms.definition: the state of being free from dirt, or the habit of keeping things so
forms.example: The hotel is famous for its cleanliness.
forms.note: Pronounced /ˈklenlinəs/: the first part sounds like 'clen', not 'clean'.

syn.note: Keeping yourself and things free from dirt to stay healthy.
Tidiness is about things being in order, not about dirt.

ant.note: The state of being covered with dirt.

forms.definition: the work of taking dirt away from a house or other place
forms.example: We do the cleaning every Saturday morning.

syn.note: All the jobs you do at home, including washing and cooking.

forms.definition: to take away the dirt from something
forms.example: I clean my room every weekend.

syn.note: To clean with water and often soap.
To clean a surface with a cloth.
To put things in order; a room can be tidy but still dirty.

ant.note: As a verb: to make something not clean: 'Don't dirty the floor.'

forms.definition: to make your skin or a cut completely free from dirt
forms.example: The nurse cleansed the cut before putting on a plaster.
forms.note: Pronounced /klenz/. Used mostly about skin and wounds.

forms.definition: not dirty; with no marks or dust
forms.example: Please put on a clean shirt for school.

syn.note: Very clean, with no dirt at all.
Made clean with water.
In good order; not the same as free from dirt.
Clean and new, often about clothes or air.

ant.note: Covered with dirt or marks.
Formal word for dirty.

forms.definition: without making dirt or smoke
forms.example: Gas burns more cleanly than coal.
forms.note: Also means 'in one smooth movement': 'The knife cut cleanly through the bread.'

people.definition: a person whose job is to take away dirt in offices or houses
people.example: The cleaner comes to our office every evening.
people.note: Also a thing: a product for cleaning, as in 'window cleaner'.

people.definition: a liquid or cream for washing your face
people.example: She uses a gentle cleanser every night.

context.text: On Saturday my mother and I do the cleaning together. We clean the kitchen first, and by lunchtime the whole flat is clean.

reviewer_note: Pronunciation traps flagged: cleanliness and cleanse use /klen/. -ness affix not claimed on cleanliness (stem 'cleanli-' is not a clean split).

corpus_definition: A device that shows what time it is.

forms.definition: a machine on a wall or table that shows the time
forms.example: Look at the clock on the wall: it's nearly nine.

syn.note: A watch is small and you wear it on your wrist; a clock is on a wall or table.
A device that measures a period of time and then rings.

forms.definition: to measure how fast someone goes or how long something takes
forms.example: The police clocked the car at 130 kilometres an hour.
forms.note: Belongs to clock = measuring speed or time, not the machine on the wall. Also 'clock in/out' = record the time you start and finish work.

forms.definition: moving in the same direction as the hands of a watch
forms.example: Walk round the table in a clockwise direction.

ant.note: The other direction; British English.
The other direction; American English.

forms.definition: in the same direction as the hands of a watch
forms.example: Turn the key clockwise to open the door.

ant.note: The other direction; British English.
The other direction; American English.

forms.definition: used after a number from 1 to 12 to give the exact hour
forms.example: The lesson starts at nine o'clock.
forms.note: Short for 'of the clock'. Only for full hours: say 'half past nine', not 'nine thirty o'clock'.

context.text: The old clock in my grandmother's kitchen says it's six o'clock. To set the right time, you turn the small key clockwise.

reviewer_note: o'clock (from 'of the clock') added as an existing adverb because every A1 learner meets it; clockwork and alarm clock are compounds and left out.

corpus_definition: Only a short distance away from a specific point.
usage_note: be close to + place or person: 'The school is close to my house.' Comparative: closer to, closest to. Here close is said /kləʊs/ with an 's' sound, not /kləʊz/ like the verb 'close the door'.

relations.note: Same meaning and very common; no 'to' is needed: 'near the store'.
Easy phrase with almost the same meaning.
Stronger: right beside something, with nothing between.
A long distance away from a place.

context.text: Our flat is close to the metro, so I get to work quickly. My sister wants to live closer to her university in Chilonzor.

reviewer_note: kind_hint 'phrasal' corrected to 'phrase': close is an adjective here, not a verb + particle.

corpus_definition: A group of people who meet to share a common hobby.

forms.definition: a group of people who meet to do a hobby or sport together
forms.example: I joined a photography club at my school.

syn.note: Used for clubs at universities and for more serious groups: 'the history society'.
A more formal word for an organized group.
Easy, general word for people together; a club is organized and meets often.
People who play a sport or work together to win or finish something.

forms.definition: going out to dance at night in places with loud music
forms.example: They went clubbing on Friday night.
forms.note: Belongs to club = nightclub, not a hobby group. Informal.

forms.definition: to share the cost of something with other people
forms.example: We clubbed together to buy our teacher a present.
forms.note: Belongs to club = people paying together; almost always 'club together', mostly British English.

forms.definition: friendly only to people who are already in the group
forms.example: The office has a clubby feel, and new workers find it hard to fit in.
forms.note: Belongs to club = a closed group of members; informal and not very common.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My brother is in a chess club at school. The club meets every Wednesday, and next month they will play against a club from Namangan.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: nightclub (clubbing) and 'club together' kept as other_meaning; clubby shown as other_meaning; clubber left out as rare; golf club / heavy stick meanings left out.

corpus_definition: A public performance of music by one or more people.

forms.definition: a show where musicians or singers perform for an audience
forms.example: We went to a loud concert at the stadium yesterday.

syn.note: Informal, usually for pop or rock music in a small place.
A classical concert, often by one musician or singer.
Any show of music, dance or theatre.
Easy, general word for something people watch.

forms.note: No verb is used by learners; 'concert' as a verb is very rare.

forms.definition: done by many people working hard together
forms.example: The school made a concerted effort to help new students.
forms.note: Belongs to concert = working together (an old meaning), not a music show. Usually in 'a concerted effort'.
There is no common adverb; 'concertedly' is very rare.

context.text: There was a big concert in Tashkent last night. Thousands of people came, and the concert ended with fireworks.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: concerted (working together) is other_meaning; concerto is a related loan word, not made from concert, so it is left out.

corpus_definition: To prepare food by using heat.

forms.definition: the activity of making food ready to eat with heat
forms.example: My grandmother's cooking is the best in Fergana.

syn.note: Related: the typical food and way of preparing it in one country or restaurant: 'Uzbek cuisine'.
Related: one kind of preparing food, in an oven, for bread and cakes.

forms.definition: the skill of preparing food, as a class or in books
forms.example: She took a cookery course in Tashkent.
forms.note: Mostly British (cookery book, cookery class). American English usually says cooking.

forms.definition: to make food ready to eat by heating it
forms.example: My father likes to cook dinner on Sundays.

syn.note: Easy everyday word: 'make dinner', 'make plov'. It can also mean food with no heat, like a salad.
A little more formal; it also includes washing and cutting food.
Related: to cook bread, cakes or meat in an oven.
Related: to cook food in hot oil in a pan.
Related: to cook food in very hot water.

forms.definition: heated and ready to eat, not raw
forms.example: Cooked carrots are softer than fresh ones.

syn.note: Related, informal: 'The meat is done' means it is cooked enough to eat.

ant.note: Raw food has not been heated: raw fish, raw onion.
Same idea as raw; often used about rice, pasta or meat.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person whose job is preparing food
people.example: My uncle works as a cook in a big restaurant.
people.note: Same spelling as the verb. A cook can be a job or anyone who makes food: 'My mum is a great cook.'

people.definition: a large kitchen machine with an oven, used for heating food
people.example: Put the pot of soup on the cooker.
people.note: British English; American English says stove. Trap: a cooker is a machine, NOT a person. The person is a cook.

context.text: My father cooks plov every Sunday. His cooking is famous in our street, and there is never any cooked rice left at the end.

reviewer_note: GATE? 'cook' (person noun) is listed in People & things as rule 8 requires; the gate fails it only because the same spelling is the base verb. Two corpus rows merged (same meaning). Traps: cooker = machine not person; cookie is not from cook.

corpus_definition: The amount of money needed to buy something.

forms.definition: the amount of money you need to buy or do something
forms.example: What is the cost of dinner for four people?

syn.note: Very close and easy. The price is what the seller asks; the cost is what you pay in the end.
More formal: money you spend on something, often regularly: 'travel expenses'.
Related: money you pay for a service: 'There is no charge for delivery.'
Related: money paid to a school, doctor or for an official service.

forms.definition: to need a particular amount of money to buy
forms.example: How much does this bag cost?
forms.note: Irregular: cost - cost - cost (past is NOT 'costed' in this meaning).

syn.note: Shop talk: 'These shoes sell for 300,000 som.'
Related: used for a total: 'The bill comes to 80,000 som.'

forms.definition: very expensive; needing a lot of money
forms.example: Repairing the old car was too costly.
forms.note: Also means 'causing loss or problems': a costly mistake. Looks like an adverb, but it is an adjective.

syn.note: The everyday word with the same meaning.
Informal: a little expensive.
British and a bit old-fashioned: 'Meat is very dear this month.'

ant.note: Not costing much money.
More polite than cheap: good value, low price.

forms.note: There is no adverb; say 'at a high cost' or 'expensively'.

context.text: How much does a taxi to the airport cost? The cost is about 50,000 som in the day, but at night it is more costly.

reviewer_note: Noun anchor; same-spelling verb is shown as conversion (irregular cost-cost-cost). costly is an -ly adjective, not an adverb.

corpus_definition: a long comfortable seat that several people can sit on

forms.definition: a long soft seat for two or more people
forms.example: He fell asleep on the couch while watching TV.

syn.note: The same thing; sofa is more common in British English, couch in American English.
British, a bit old-fashioned word for the same seat.
Related: a soft seat for only one person, with arms.

forms.definition: to say or write something in a particular style
forms.example: His answer was couched in very polite language.
forms.note: Belongs to a different, formal meaning (to express words in a certain way), not the seat. Rare, usually passive: be couched in.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: After dinner, my grandfather always sleeps on the couch. The couch in our living room is big enough for five people.

reviewer_note: Simple noun. Formal verb couch (be couched in) shown as other_meaning, not hidden. Compound couch potato left out.

corpus_definition: To move from one side of a place to the other.

forms.definition: a place where people can safely go over a road, river or border
forms.example: Wait for the green light at the crossing.
forms.note: Also means a trip over the sea: 'The crossing took two hours.' British: pedestrian or zebra crossing.

syn.note: American English for a place to walk over a road.
Related: a structure for going over a river or road.

forms.definition: a mark like x or +, or the Christian religious symbol
forms.example: Put a cross next to the wrong answers.
forms.note: Belongs to cross = the shape or mark, not moving to the other side.

forms.definition: to go from one side of something to the other
forms.example: It is safe to cross the street now.
forms.note: Other uses: cross your arms/legs, cross out a word.

syn.note: Easy phrase: 'go over the bridge'.
Formal, often about big areas: 'traverse the desert'.
Related: to go past or through a place, not always to the other side.

forms.definition: a bit angry or annoyed
forms.example: Mum was cross with me for coming home late.
forms.note: False friend: belongs to cross = angry (British, informal), nothing to do with going to the other side.

forms.definition: from one side to the other side of something
forms.example: The river is too wide to swim across.
forms.note: Also a preposition: 'walk across the road'. Made from a- + cross (old 'on cross').

syn.note: Easy and very close: 'swim over / swim across'.

forms.definition: in an angry or annoyed way
forms.example: "Where have you been?" she asked crossly.
forms.note: Goes with cross = angry, not with going to the other side.

context.text: Be careful when you cross the road near our school. Always use the crossing, and look both ways before you walk across.

reviewer_note: False friend: adjective cross = angry (and crossly) shown as other_meaning. across included as the family adverb (a- not in affix table, so no affix claimed). Compounds crossroads/crossword left out.

corpus_definition: A person who buys things at a shop.

forms.definition: a person who buys things or services from a shop or business
forms.example: The shop has many happy customers.

syn.note: A person who is shopping in a shop or market right now.
Any person who buys something, often something big like a house or car.
Used for people who pay for a service: a lawyer's or bank's client.
Related: anyone who buys and uses goods, used in economics and the news.

ant.note: The person who sells; the customer buys.
The person who owns or runs the shop.

forms.definition: a traditional way of doing something in a culture
forms.example: It is a custom in Uzbekistan to give guests tea first.
forms.note: Belongs to custom = tradition or habit. customer first meant a person with the habit of buying at one shop.

forms.definition: to change something so it fits what one person wants
forms.example: You can customize the app with your own colours.
forms.note: Comes from custom = made for one buyer. British spelling: customise. Not a verb for being a customer.

forms.definition: usual or traditional in a particular place or situation
forms.example: It is customary to take off your shoes at home.
forms.note: Belongs to custom = tradition, not to buying in a shop. Formal.

forms.definition: usually, as the tradition is
forms.example: Guests are customarily given the best seat.
forms.note: Goes with customary (custom = tradition). Formal and rare.

people.definition: the office at an airport or border that checks bags and goods
people.example: We waited an hour at customs in Tashkent airport.
people.note: Always with -s. Belongs to the old meaning custom = tax on goods, not to shop buyers.

context.text: Our bakery has many regular customers. One customer comes every morning at seven for fresh non bread.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a person noun, so it stays in the noun slot (rule 6). Root custom (tradition/tax) family shown as other_meaning: custom, customize, customary, customarily, customs.

corpus_definition: Likely to hurt or harm someone.

forms.definition: the chance that someone will be hurt or harmed
forms.example: The sign on the door said: Danger! High voltage.

syn.note: Very close: the chance that something bad will happen.
Something or someone that may cause harm.
More formal; something that can be dangerous: 'a fire hazard'.

ant.note: The state of being safe and protected from harm.

forms.definition: to put someone or something at risk of harm
forms.example: Driving too fast can endanger other people.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Close: to be likely to harm something.
Related: to actually hurt someone; endanger means it might happen.

ant.note: To keep someone or something safe.

forms.definition: likely to hurt someone or cause harm
forms.example: Driving fast on ice is very dangerous.

syn.note: Same meaning; often used about places and machines.
Close: something bad may happen, often about plans and money too.
Formal, used on signs and in rules: 'hazardous waste'.
Related: it causes damage, especially to health: 'harmful chemicals'.

ant.note: Not likely to hurt anyone.
Not able to cause any hurt or damage.

forms.definition: at risk of disappearing completely, used about animals and plants
forms.example: The snow leopard is an endangered animal.
forms.note: Used mostly about species: endangered animals, endangered languages.

forms.definition: in a way that could hurt someone
forms.example: He was driving dangerously on the wet road.
forms.note: Also 'very', before bad situations: dangerously ill, dangerously close.

syn.note: Related: without thinking about the risk.

ant.note: In a way that does not hurt anyone.

context.text: The mountain road near Chimgan is dangerous in winter. Drivers who go too fast put everyone in danger.

reviewer_note: Headword is an adjective made from danger (noun = derivational). endanger/endangered shown; endangered is about species at risk.

corpus_definition: The final meal of the day eaten in the evening.

forms.definition: the main meal of the day, usually eaten in the evening
forms.example: What are we having for dinner?
forms.note: In some parts of Britain, dinner means the main meal in the middle of the day.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little formal; clear for everyone.
Some people use it for the evening meal, often a lighter or later one.
Related: any time you eat food: breakfast, lunch or dinner.

forms.definition: to eat the evening meal, often at a restaurant
forms.example: Tonight we will dine at a restaurant in old Bukhara.
forms.note: dinner comes from the old French word for dine. Common phrases: dine out, dining room.

syn.note: The everyday way to say it.
Easy and general; dine is formal and about a proper meal.

forms.note: There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person eating a meal in a restaurant
people.example: The diners clapped when the chef came out.
people.note: In American English a diner is also a small cheap restaurant.

context.text: We usually have dinner at seven. On special days my parents dine at a restaurant in Tashkent with their friends.

reviewer_note: dinner is historically made from dine, so dine (formal) is shown as the family verb and diner as the person. Compounds dinnertime/dining room left out.

corpus_definition: A person trained to treat people who are sick.

forms.definition: a person trained to help sick people get better
forms.example: I must visit the doctor today.
forms.note: Short form in writing: Dr (British) or Dr. (American): Dr Karimova.

syn.note: Informal short form, mostly spoken.
Formal, common in American English.
Informal, often a doctor or helper in the army or at an accident.
Related, British: a family doctor who treats everyday illnesses.

forms.definition: to change something secretly in order to trick people
forms.example: Someone had doctored the photo before it was posted.
forms.note: Belongs to a different meaning: to change a document or picture dishonestly. Not 'to treat a patient'.

forms.definition: connected with the highest university degree
forms.example: She is writing her doctoral thesis on Uzbek history.
forms.note: Belongs to doctor = a person with the highest university degree (PhD), not a medical doctor.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: the highest university degree, a PhD
people.example: He has a doctorate in chemistry.
people.note: Belongs to doctor = PhD holder, not a medical doctor.

context.text: I felt ill, so I went to see a doctor. The doctor told me to drink tea and rest for three days.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun (rule 6). Verb doctor (change dishonestly) and doctoral/doctorate (PhD sense) shown as other_meaning. Cognate doctrine is not shown.

corpus_definition: To operate a car or another vehicle while it is moving.

forms.definition: a trip in a car
forms.example: Let's go for a drive in the mountains this weekend.
forms.note: Other meanings: the road up to a house, and a computer drive.

syn.note: Close, but you can be the passenger: 'He gave me a ride.'
Related: any short journey, by car, bus or train.
Related: travel from one place to another, often long.

forms.definition: the activity of controlling a car on the road
forms.example: Driving in Tashkent traffic can be stressful.

forms.definition: to control a car or other vehicle and make it move
forms.example: I learned to drive when I was eighteen.
forms.note: Irregular: drive - drove - driven.

syn.note: Related: travel in a car, but you may not be the one controlling it.
Related: to turn the wheel to choose the direction.
Related: used for bikes, horses and motorbikes: you ride a bike, you drive a car.

forms.definition: moving by itself, with no person controlling it
forms.example: Driverless cars are being tested in some cities.

forms.definition: having a very strong wish to succeed
forms.example: She is a very driven student and always studies late.
forms.note: Belongs to drive = push yourself to work hard, not to operating a car.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who controls a car, bus or other vehicle
people.example: The bus driver waited for us at the stop.

context.text: My brother is learning to drive. He wants to be a taxi driver, but first he has to pass his driving test.

reviewer_note: GATE? driverless is a real learner-dictionary adjective (Cambridge, Oxford: a driverless car) built on driver + -less; WordNet 3.1 just predates it. drift shares an old root but is not made from drive (not_family). Trap: drive a car, ride a bike/horse; driven (ambitious) is other_meaning.

gate_overrides.reason: real modern adjective (driverless car), not yet in WordNet 3.1

corpus_definition: The body part on the side of the head used for hearing sounds.

forms.definition: one of the two body parts on the sides of your head that you hear with
forms.example: She whispered a secret into my left ear.
forms.note: Idiom: 'be all ears' = listen carefully.

syn.note: Related: the sense that ears give you. 'An ear for music' means good hearing for music.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective for learners. aural looks related but is a Latin word, not made from ear.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: I have a small pain in my left ear. The doctor looked inside both of my ears and said it was nothing serious.

reviewer_note: Corpus example_en lacks the word ('into my left side'); our example uses 'ear'. Compounds earring, earphones, earache left out (rule 7).

corpus_definition: Physical activity to make your body stronger and better.

forms.definition: physical activity that you do to keep your body strong and healthy
forms.example: I try to do some exercise every morning before work.

syn.note: Very close; a workout is one session of exercise, often at a gym.
Same meaning; a bit more formal, used by doctors.
Exercise with a plan, often to get ready for a sport or a race.
Related: a game or activity with rules, like football; sport is one kind of exercise.

ant.note: Time when you stop moving and let your body relax.

forms.note: Usually uncountable: 'do exercise', 'get some exercise'. Countable for one activity: 'stretching exercises'.

forms.definition: to move your body a lot to make it strong and healthy
forms.example: I exercise at the gym three times a week.

syn.note: Very close and a little informal: 'I work out every day.'
Exercise with a plan, usually for a sport or a competition.
British English: to stay healthy by doing physical activity regularly.

ant.note: To stop moving and let your body relax.

forms.definition: very worried or upset about something
forms.example: Local people are very exercised about the new road.
forms.note: Belongs to exercise = make someone think or worry (formal, rare), not physical activity. Usually 'exercised about/over'.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: My brother exercises in the park every morning before school. He says that exercise helps him sleep well and study better.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows (noun A1, verb A2) are the same meaning, merged with lowest CEFR. Exercised = worried is other_meaning. Exercise = use a right/power is a different sense, left out.

corpus_definition: A door used for leaving a room or building.

forms.definition: a door or opening you use to leave a room or building
forms.example: Please find the nearest fire exit.

syn.note: Same meaning and very common on signs in British English.
Related: any door; an exit is a door for going out.

ant.note: The door you use to go in.
Easy phrase for the door you use to go in.

forms.note: Pronounced /ˈeksɪt/ or /ˈeɡzɪt/.

forms.definition: to go out of a room, building or vehicle
forms.example: Passengers must exit the bus through the back door.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Easy phrase: 'go out of the room'.
Common in speaking, especially for cars: 'get out of the car'.

ant.note: To go into a room or building.

forms.note: More formal than 'leave'; also used for closing a computer program.
No adjective exists in this family.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: When the concert ended, everyone walked to the main exit. We exited through a side door because it was faster.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed: 'ex-' + 'it' is not a real split in English.

corpus_definition: The organ of the body used for seeing things.

forms.definition: one of the two parts of your face that you see with
forms.example: She has big brown eyes.

syn.note: Related: sight is the ability to see, not the body part.

forms.note: Plural: eyes. Words like eyebrow, eyelash and eyesight are compounds, collected separately.

forms.definition: to look at someone or something carefully, often with interest
forms.example: The cat eyed the fish on the table.

syn.note: Watch is general; eye suggests careful looking because you want or doubt something.
Easy phrase; eye adds the idea of careful, interested looking.
Related: to look for a long time without moving your eyes away.

forms.note: Present participle: eyeing (also eying).
No common adjective is made from this word. Blue-eyed, wide-eyed etc. are compounds. Visual and optical mean 'about seeing' but are not made from eye.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Close your eyes and listen to the music. At the bazaar, my grandmother eyed every melon carefully before she chose one.

reviewer_note: Verb 'eye' kept as existing (looking with the eyes). Compounds (eyebrow, eyesight) left out per rule 7.

corpus_definition: A group consisting of parents and children.

forms.definition: a group of people made of parents and their children
forms.example: I love spending time with my family at the weekend.

syn.note: Related: all the people who live in one home, family or not.
Related: people connected to you by blood or marriage, like aunts and cousins.
Related, informal: your parents or close relatives: 'my folks'.

forms.note: Plural: families. In British English it can take a plural verb: 'My family are all tall.'
No verb exists in this family. Familiarize comes from familiar, not from family.

forms.definition: connected with or typical of parents, children and relatives
forms.example: Doctors think the illness may be familial.

syn.note: Related: passed from parents to children in the body, like an illness.
Related: about the home and home life.

forms.note: Rare, used in medicine and science. Everyday English uses 'family' before a noun: 'family car'. Don't confuse with familiar (well known).
No adverb in common use (familially is extremely rare).

context.text: My family lives in Andijan, and every Friday we eat plov together. My grandfather has a familial heart problem, so the doctor checks all of us.

reviewer_note: Familiar shares the old Latin root but is not made from family; listed in notes only. Familial is rare/formal but real, so it is shown.

corpus_definition: A long distance away from a certain spot.
usage_note: far from + place: 'The school is not far from my home.' Most common in questions and negatives: 'Is it far from here?' In positive sentences people often say 'a long way from'. Far from + adjective/-ing ('far from easy') means 'not at all' - a different meaning.

relations.note: Same meaning; more natural in positive sentences: 'It's a long way from the city.'
More formal, mostly in writing.
Related: not at a place; it can be near or far: 'two kilometres away from here'.
A short distance from a place.
Not far; a short distance from something.
Right beside something.

context.text: Our house is not far from Chorsu Bazaar, so we walk there. My university is far from the city centre, so I take the metro.

reviewer_note: Second meaning 'far from easy = not at all' is mentioned in usage_note only.

corpus_definition: One of the five thin parts at the end of the hand.

forms.definition: one of the five long thin parts at the end of your hand
forms.example: She cut her finger while cooking.

syn.note: Formal or medical word; it can also mean a toe.
Related: the short, thick one of the five; some people do not call it a finger.

forms.note: The toes are on your feet, not your hands.

forms.definition: to touch or feel something with your hand
forms.example: She fingered the silk scarf before buying it.

syn.note: Easy, general word; finger means touching gently, often again and again.
Related: to touch something to learn what it is like.
Related: to touch or hold something with your hands.

forms.note: No common adjective. Light-fingered (= likely to steal) is a compound.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Be careful with that knife, or you will cut your finger. At the market, my aunt fingered the cloth to check how soft it was.

reviewer_note: Compounds (fingerprint, fingernail, fingertip) left out per rule 7.

corpus_definition: An animal that lives in water and swims with fins.

forms.definition: an animal that lives in water and swims using fins
forms.example: I saw a bright orange fish in the tank.

syn.note: Related: fish and other sea animals that people eat.

forms.note: Plural is usually fish: 'three fish'. Fishes is used for different kinds. Fish is also the food: 'We had fish for dinner.'

forms.definition: the sport or job of catching animals from rivers, lakes or the sea
forms.example: My grandfather loves fishing on the river.

syn.note: Fishing with a rod and line, as a hobby; less common word.

forms.definition: to try to catch animals from a river, lake or the sea
forms.example: We fished all afternoon but caught nothing.

syn.note: Less common word: to fish with a rod and line.

forms.note: Often 'go fishing'. 'Fish for' can also mean try to get information: a different meaning.

forms.definition: smelling or tasting like animals from the sea
forms.example: The kitchen had a fishy smell after dinner.

syn.note: Related: having a bad smell of any kind.

forms.note: Also informal 'suspicious, not honest': 'There's something fishy about this offer.'
No adverb in common use (fishily is very rare).

people.definition: a person who catches animals from rivers, lakes or the sea
people.example: An old fisher pulled his boat onto the beach.
people.note: Less common; most people say fisherman (a compound).

people.definition: a place where people catch or raise animals from the water
people.example: The village has a small fishery near the lake.

context.text: My father likes fishing on the Chirchiq River. Last Sunday he fished all day and caught three big fish.

reviewer_note: Fisherman is a compound (rule 7), left out. Fishy covers both literal smell and the informal 'suspicious' meaning in a note.

corpus_definition: The part of a plant that is often colorful and smells nice.

forms.definition: the colourful part of a plant that often smells nice
forms.example: She gave me a beautiful flower.

syn.note: A bit literary; often used about flowers on a plant: 'roses in full bloom'.
Flowers on a fruit tree or bush: 'apple blossom'.
Related: the whole living thing, with leaves and roots.

forms.definition: to produce colourful blooms
forms.example: These roses flower in early summer.

syn.note: Same meaning; very common.
Same meaning, mostly for trees and bushes.

ant.note: To become dry and die, like an old plant.

forms.definition: covered with or decorated with pictures of blooms
forms.example: She wore a flowery dress to the party.

syn.note: Same meaning for patterns: 'a floral dress'. Floral comes from Latin, not from flower.
Related: covered with any kind of pattern.

ant.note: With no pattern; just one colour.

forms.note: Also used about speech or writing with too many fancy words: 'flowery language'.

forms.definition: producing blooms; having blooms
forms.example: We planted some flowering trees in the garden.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: In spring, the apricot trees in our garden flower in pink and white. My sister wore a flowery dress and picked a flower for our mother.

reviewer_note: Florist and floral come from Latin flos, not from flower, so they are not family forms.

corpus_definition: To put clothes on your body.
usage_note: get dressed has no object: 'I got dressed quickly.' To name the clothes, use put on: 'put on your coat'. Get dressed up = put on special, smart clothes.

relations.note: Same meaning but more formal and less common in speaking: 'I dressed quickly.'
Related: needs the name of the clothes: 'put on a jacket'.
To take your clothes off.
More formal: to take your clothes off.

context.text: Hurry up and get dressed, or you will be late for school. I usually get dressed after breakfast.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; trap is using an object (say 'put on', not 'get dressed a shirt').

corpus_definition: To exit a bus, train, or plane.
particle_note: Not separable with the vehicle: 'get off the bus' (not 'get the bus off'). Can be used without an object: 'Where do I get off?' For cars and taxis say 'get out of'.

relations.note: Very formal, used in announcements: 'Alight at the next station.'
Related: used for cars and taxis: 'get out of the taxi'.
Related: general word for going away from a place.
To go onto a bus, train or plane.
Formal: to get on a plane, train or ship.

context.text: We got off the bus at Chorsu and walked to the bazaar. Get off at the next metro station, and I will meet you there.

reviewer_note: Other meanings of get off (finish work, leave a phone line) not covered; only the vehicle sense.

corpus_definition: to rise from bed after sleeping in the morning
particle_note: Not separable in this meaning, with no object: 'I get up at seven.' 'get someone up' (separable) means to make someone leave their bed: 'Get the kids up at 7.'

relations.note: Same meaning, very easy and clear.
Formal or literary: 'He rose at dawn.'
Related: you wake up first (open your eyes), then you get up (leave the bed).
You go to bed at night and get up in the morning.

context.text: On school days I get up at half past six. My father gets up even earlier to make bread for breakfast.

reviewer_note: Kept apart from wake up: learners often mix them up; wake up is listed as related, not a synonym.

corpus_definition: To return to a place.
particle_note: Not separable: go back to + place ('go back to school', 'go back to Bukhara'). No 'to' before home, here or there: 'go back home', not 'go back to home'.

relations.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Same idea, but used when the speaker is in that place or will be there.
Related: going back to the place where you live.
You leave a place, and later you go back to it.

context.text: After the summer holidays, Malika went back to Tashkent to start university. She wants to go back to her village in Khorezm for Navruz.

reviewer_note: Corpus example 'go back to home' is ungrammatical (should be 'go back home'); flagged in particle_note and context avoids it.

corpus_definition: To visit stores to buy items you need.
usage_note: go shopping (for + thing) / go shopping at or in + place: 'go shopping for shoes', 'go shopping at Chorsu Bazaar'. Not 'go to shopping'. British English also says 'do the shopping' for food and things for the house.

relations.note: Same meaning as a verb: 'We shop on Saturdays.'
Usually buying food and things for the home, as a regular job.
Related: buy is the action of paying for one thing.
Related: to look at things in shops without buying them.

context.text: On Saturday we went shopping at the bazaar. My mother likes to go shopping for fruit early in the morning.

reviewer_note: Common learner error 'go to shopping' handled in usage_note.

corpus_definition: To lay down in a place to sleep.
usage_note: No 'the': 'go to bed', not 'go to the bed'. Often with a time: 'go to bed at ten', 'go to bed early/late'.

relations.note: Informal: 'I'm tired, I'm going to turn in.'
Very informal and friendly.
Related: you go to bed first, then you go to sleep (start sleeping).
You get up in the morning and go to bed at night.

context.text: My little brother has to go to bed at nine o'clock. Last night I went to bed late because I was watching football.

reviewer_note: Corpus definition says 'lay down'; correct grammar is 'lie down'. Copied as given; learner-facing text avoids it.

corpus_definition: Having the skill to do an activity well.
usage_note: be good at + noun / -ing: 'good at maths', 'good at drawing'. Use 'at', not 'in'. Make it stronger with very/really: 'really good at football'.

relations.note: A little more formal; often about a job or craft.
Informal and stronger: very good at something.
Related: born with a natural skill; not followed by 'at' so often.
Not able to do something well: 'I'm bad at singing.'
A little more formal than bad at.

context.text: Aziz is very good at chess, and he plays every evening with his grandfather. I'm not good at drawing, but I'm good at maths.

reviewer_note: Preposition trap (good in vs good at) handled in usage_note.

corpus_definition: The thin green plant that covers the ground.

forms.definition: a common green plant with thin leaves that covers fields and parks
forms.example: The children are sitting on the grass in the park.

syn.note: Related: an area of short, cut grass near a house or in a park.
Related: grass and the earth under it, often used on sports fields.
Related: grass that has been cut and dried to feed animals.

forms.note: Usually uncountable: 'cut the grass'. Countable 'grasses' means different kinds of this plant.

forms.definition: to cover an area of ground with green plants for a lawn
forms.example: The city grassed over the old car park and made a small garden.

syn.note: British English: to cover ground with pieces of cut lawn.

forms.note: Usually 'grass something over'. In informal British English it also means to tell the police about someone (grass on someone); that is a different meaning.

forms.definition: covered with short green plants
forms.example: We had a picnic on a grassy hill near Chimgan.

syn.note: Related and easy: green fields are often covered with plants.
Related: with a lot of leaves or trees.

ant.note: With no plants growing on it: 'bare ground'.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: In spring the grass in our garden grows very fast. On Sundays we walk to a grassy field near the river and play football.

reviewer_note: Compounds (grassland, grasshopper) left out by rule. Graze has the same old root but is not made from grass. Grass = inform on someone (BrE slang) only mentioned in a note.

corpus_definition: Several people or things that are together in one place.

forms.definition: a number of people or things that are together
forms.example: A group of tourists was standing in front of the Ark in Bukhara.

syn.note: Informal: a bunch of friends, a bunch of keys.
Related: a team works or plays together for one aim.
Related: a large number of people, often with no order.
Related: things that belong together, like a set of plates.

ant.note: One single person, not part of a larger number.

forms.definition: a set of people or things that are put together because they are similar
forms.example: The students were put into new groupings for the project.

forms.definition: to put people or things together, or to come together
forms.example: The teacher grouped the students by their level.

syn.note: Easy and common.
Related: to put things in order by type.
Related: to put things in a certain order or position.
Related and formal: to put things into types by their qualities.

ant.note: To move people or things apart.

forms.note: Regroup means to form a group again, often after a problem.
No adjective exists in this family; grouped is only a verb form.
No adverb exists in this family.

people.definition: a big fan who follows a famous band or singer everywhere
people.example: A groupie waited outside the hotel to meet the singer.
people.note: Belongs to group = a music band, not people standing together. Informal.

context.text: Our English teacher grouped us into teams of four. My group made a poster about Samarkand, and the teacher liked the new grouping.

reviewer_note: Groupie is from group = music band, so other_meaning. No adjective or adverb exists.

corpus_definition: A room or building with tools for doing physical exercise.

forms.definition: a room or building with machines and equipment for doing exercise
forms.example: I go to the gym three times a week after work.

syn.note: Same meaning. American spelling: fitness center.
A place for exercise, usually with a pool, where you pay to be a member.
Related: a big room for indoor sports like basketball.

forms.note: In American English, gym is also a sports lesson at school (gym class).

forms.definition: a large room with equipment for sports, often in a school
forms.example: The school gymnasium is used for basketball and concerts.
forms.note: Gym is the short form. False friend: in English this is NOT a type of school (Russian 'gimnaziya').
No verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: connected with exercises that show strength, balance and control of the body
forms.example: She can do amazing gymnastic moves on the beam.

syn.note: Related: about jumps, flips and other difficult body movements.
Related: about sports, or having a strong, fit body.

forms.note: No common adverb; gymnastically is extremely rare.

people.definition: a sport with exercises that show strength, balance and body control
people.example: Uzbekistan has won Olympic medals in gymnastics.

people.definition: a person who does a sport of jumps, balance and body control
people.example: The young gymnast trains every day in Tashkent.

context.text: My cousin goes to the gym every morning before university. Her little sister prefers gymnastics and trains in the big gymnasium at her school.

reviewer_note: Gym is a clipping of gymnasium; listed gymnasium as noun extra with a false-friend note for Russian speakers (gimnaziya = school).

corpus_definition: To enjoy yourself during an activity.
