usage_note: have fun (+ -ing): 'We had fun swimming.' Fun is uncountable: not 'have a fun' or 'have funs'. 'Have fun!' is a friendly wish when someone is going out.

relations.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Same meaning, very common and easy.
Very informal and stronger: to have a lot of fun.
Related: needs an object: 'enjoy the party'.
To feel tired and unhappy because nothing is interesting.
To feel unhappy during an event or trip.

context.text: We had so much fun at the wedding last night. Before my friends left for Issyk-Kul, I said, "Have fun!"

reviewer_note: Countability trap ('have a fun') handled in usage_note.

corpus_definition: The top part of the body containing the face.

forms.definition: the top part of your body, with your face, eyes, mouth and brain
forms.example: She turned her head and smiled at me.

syn.note: Related: the bone inside, around the brain.
Related: only the front part, with the eyes, nose and mouth.

ant.note: The head is the top of the body and the feet are the bottom: 'from head to foot'.

forms.definition: hitting the ball with the top of your body in football
forms.example: Ronaldo scored with a header in the last minute.
forms.note: Header also means the text at the top of a page; that is a different meaning.

forms.definition: the title at the top of a page or part of a text
forms.example: Write your name under the heading.
forms.note: Belongs to head = the top or front of something, not the body part.

forms.definition: to hit the ball with the top of your body in football
forms.example: He headed the ball into the goal.

syn.note: Related, informal football English: 'He nodded the ball in.'

forms.definition: to go or move in a certain direction
forms.example: After school we headed to the park.
forms.note: Belongs to head = go towards (head for, head home), not the body part. Also means to lead a group: 'She heads the company.'

forms.definition: having no top part of the body
forms.example: The museum has a headless statue from ancient times.

syn.note: Formal: with the top part cut off.

forms.note: No adverb made only from this word. Headfirst and headlong are compounds, collected separately.

context.text: In the football match, Bobur jumped and headed the ball into the goal. It was a great header, but he hurt his head and had to sit down.

reviewer_note: Head = leader and head = go towards are other meanings; football 'head the ball' and 'header' kept as body-part meaning. Compounds (headache, headteacher, headfirst) left out.

corpus_definition: Strong and not suffering from any illness.

forms.definition: the condition of your body and mind, and how well or ill you are
forms.example: My grandmother is 85, but she is in good health.

syn.note: Related: being strong and able to do sport; health is wider and includes illness.
Related: feeling well and happy in body and mind. A bit formal.

ant.note: Illness is being ill; good health is the opposite.
Sickness is being ill, a little less formal than illness.

forms.note: There is no verb made from health or healthy.

forms.definition: strong, well and not ill
forms.example: Eating fresh fruit is good for a healthy life.
forms.note: Also means 'good for your body': healthy food. The opposite is unhealthy.

syn.note: Easy word, used after be/feel: 'I feel well.' Not used before a noun.
Strong and healthy, usually because you do sport.
Related: having a powerful body; a healthy person is usually strong.

ant.note: Not healthy: in bad condition, or bad for your body.
Not well, having a disease. Used after be/feel.
Ill; more common in American English.

forms.definition: in a way that is good for your body
forms.example: If you eat healthily and walk every day, you will feel better.
forms.note: Most often used with eat and live. The opposite is unhealthily.

syn.note: Related: 'eat well' means eat good food, close to eat healthily.

context.text: My grandfather is 80 and still very healthy. He says his good health comes from fresh fruit and long walks. He eats healthily and never drinks cola.

reviewer_note: health -> healthy (-y); heal shares the old root but is not made from health, so it is not_family. Unhealthy kept as antonym, not a form.

corpus_definition: To assist a person to finish a task.
usage_note: help + person + with + noun: 'Can you help me with my homework?' The person comes between help and with. For an action, use help + person + (to) + verb: 'help me (to) carry the box'.

relations.note: Same meaning but formal: 'Staff will assist you with your bags.'
Informal and friendly: 'Can you give me a hand with this box?'
Related: support is often longer help, with money, advice or feelings.
To make it harder for someone to do something. Formal.

context.text: My little brother always asks me to help him with his English homework. Today my mother helped me with the heavy shopping bags.

reviewer_note: Verb pattern with an object between help and with; treated as a phrase, not a phrasal verb.

corpus_definition: A special day for celebration or rest.

forms.definition: a special day when people do not work and often celebrate
forms.example: Navruz is a public holiday in Uzbekistan.
forms.note: In British English a holiday is also a trip away from home; Americans call that a vacation.

syn.note: A day when you do not go to work or school, for any reason.
Related: a time of celebration, often with music, food and events.
Related: a party or event for a happy day.

ant.note: A normal day when people go to work.

forms.definition: to spend time away from home for rest or fun
forms.example: Every summer they holiday by the lake in Chimgan.
forms.note: Belongs to holiday = a trip away from home (British English), not a special day of celebration.
No adjective. Holiday is used before other nouns like an adjective: the holiday season.

context.text: Navruz is my favourite holiday. On March 21 nobody goes to work, and families cook sumalak together. Many people visit their relatives during the holidays.

reviewer_note: Compound holidaymaker left out (rule 7). Verb holiday belongs to the 'trip away' sense, so other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A place where sick people get medical care.

forms.definition: a large building where doctors and nurses look after sick or hurt people
forms.example: He works at the city hospital.
forms.note: British English says 'in hospital'; American English says 'in the hospital'.

syn.note: Related: a smaller place where you see a doctor but usually do not stay the night.
Related: a place with doctors for everyday health problems. American spelling: center.

forms.definition: the time when a sick person is kept in a place for medical care
forms.example: After the accident he needed two weeks of hospitalization.
forms.note: British spelling: hospitalisation.

forms.definition: to send a sick or hurt person to stay somewhere for medical care
forms.example: My uncle was hospitalized with a bad cough last winter.
forms.note: Usually passive: be hospitalized. British spelling: hospitalise.

syn.note: 'Be admitted to hospital' means the same and is very common.

ant.note: To let a patient leave and go home.

forms.note: No adjective made from hospital.

context.text: My grandmother fell and broke her leg last week. She was hospitalized for five days. We visited her at the hospital every evening.

reviewer_note: Hospitable/hospitality share an old Latin root (guest) but are not made from hospital; listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: A global network connecting computers around the world.

forms.definition: the world system that connects computers and lets people share information
forms.example: I use the internet to find information.
forms.note: Usually 'the internet'. Some people write it with a capital I: the Internet. To say 'using the internet', use online: shop online.

syn.note: Very close; strictly the web is the websites you see on the internet.
Informal short name.

forms.note: No adjective. People say online: an online shop.
No adverb. People say online: buy something online.

context.text: The internet in our village is slow, so I go to the library in Namangan. There I can watch lessons on the internet for free.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Inter- is not in the affix table, so no affix claimed.

corpus_definition: A common hard grey metal that is very strong.

forms.definition: a hard, strong grey metal used to make steel, tools and gates
forms.example: The gate is made of heavy iron.
forms.note: Pronounced /ˈaɪən/; the r is not said in British English. Iron is also in food: spinach has a lot of iron.

syn.note: Related: metal is the general word; iron is one kind of metal.
Related: steel is a stronger metal made from iron.

forms.definition: to make clothes smooth with a hot electric device
forms.example: I iron my shirt every morning before school.
forms.note: Belongs to iron = the device for clothes, not the metal.

forms.definition: made of a hard grey metal; also very strong and firm
forms.example: My grandfather kept his money in an old iron box.
forms.note: Only before a noun: an iron gate. It can also mean very strong: an iron will.

syn.note: Related: made of any metal: a metal box.
Related: in 'an iron will' it means very strong.

forms.note: No adverb. Ironic and ironically come from irony, not iron.

context.text: Iron is a strong metal, so many old gates in Bukhara are made of it. My grandfather still keeps his tools in an iron box.

reviewer_note: Row 6a6ef9b2... mixes metal + clothes device; its example is the device, so it went to the Clothes map. Ironic/irony are false friends (from irony), not family.

corpus_definition: a hard, strong metal, or a device used to smooth clothes with heat

forms.definition: an electric device that you heat to make clothes flat and smooth
forms.example: She pressed her shirt with a hot iron.

syn.note: Related: a machine that presses clothes flat, used in laundries.

forms.definition: the job of making clothes smooth with a hot device; also the clothes that need it
forms.example: I do the ironing on Sunday evenings.

forms.definition: to make clothes smooth using a hot electric device
forms.example: Can you iron my white shirt for the wedding?

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal: 'press a suit'.
Related: make something flat, with your hands or a tool.

ant.note: To make lines in cloth by folding or pressing it.
To make small lines in cloth or skin.

forms.definition: made flat and smooth with a hot device
forms.example: He wore a clean, freshly ironed shirt to the interview.

syn.note: Same meaning: 'a pressed suit'.

ant.note: Having lines in it from folding.
Having many small lines.

context.text: Before the wedding, my mother ironed all our clothes. I hate doing the ironing, but I love wearing an ironed shirt.

reviewer_note: This row's definition mixes metal + device; its example is the device, so it gets the Clothes map and the metal row gets the Metal map. Ironing board is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: a young child; informally, any young person

forms.definition: a child or a young person
forms.example: Every kid in the class got a small prize.
forms.note: Informal. Kid also means a young goat, a different meaning.

syn.note: Same meaning; child is neutral, kid is informal.
A young person, a little old-fashioned.
Related: a young person aged 13 to 19.

ant.note: A person who is fully grown.
An adult; often used by or to children.

forms.definition: to joke or say something that is not true for fun
forms.example: Are you kidding? I don't believe you!
forms.note: Belongs to kid = to joke or tease, not a child. Very common: 'Just kidding!'
No real adjective. In 'my kid sister' (= my younger sister, informal) kid is a noun used before another noun.

context.text: After school, the kids in our mahalla play football in the street. My little brother Jasur is only six, but he is the loudest kid there.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a person noun, so it stays in the noun slot. 'Kid sister/brother' treated as noun-before-noun (not in WordNet as adj). Kidnap is a compound, left out. Verb kid = joke is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Being nice, helpful, and gentle toward someone.
usage_note: be kind to + person / animal: 'Be kind to your sister.' Different pattern: 'It's kind of you to help' (kind of + you, for thanking).

relations.note: Easy and very common, same meaning.
Kind and helpful to someone, often over a long time: 'She was good to me.'
Behaving like a friend; less about helping.
Related: careful and soft, not rough.
Making someone suffer on purpose.
Informal: unkind, not nice to someone.

context.text: Our teacher is always kind to new students. She says we must be kind to animals too, especially the street cats near the school.

reviewer_note: Adjective + preposition pattern; kept apart from 'kind of you to'.

corpus_definition: To have information regarding a specific subject.
particle_note: Not separable: know about + noun / -ing / wh- clause: 'Do you know about the meeting?' Not used in the continuous form (not 'I am knowing about').

relations.note: A little more formal; you know that something exists or is happening.
You know because someone told you, but maybe not the details.
Related: you know something well because you have seen or used it.
Not knowing that something exists or is happening.

context.text: Do you know about the new bus to Chorsu? My neighbour knows about everything that happens in our street.

reviewer_note: Prepositional verb (verb + about); handled as phrasal like 'arrive at'.

corpus_definition: To get knowledge regarding a new topic.
particle_note: Not separable: learn about + noun / -ing / wh- clause: 'We learned about the Silk Road.' British past form can be learnt.

relations.note: Get information, often quickly or by asking.
Learn in a serious way, often at school or university.
Related: find something new for the first time.
Related: learn about a topic by reading a lot.
Lose knowledge you had: learning adds it, forgetting loses it.

context.text: In history class we are learning about the Silk Road. Last week we learned about Amir Temur and Samarkand.

reviewer_note: Prepositional verb (verb + about); handled as phrasal like 'arrive at'.

corpus_definition: A body part that allows humans and animals to stand and walk.

forms.definition: one of the long body parts that you stand and walk on
forms.example: She broke her leg while skiing in Chimgan.
forms.note: A table or chair also has legs. A trip can have legs too: 'the first leg of the journey'.

syn.note: A limb is an arm or a leg. It is a more formal or medical word.

forms.note: There is only the informal British phrase 'leg it' (run away fast): 'When the dog barked, we legged it.'

forms.definition: having long, thin body parts below the hips
forms.example: The leggy model walked across the stage.
forms.note: Usually about women, young animals or plants that grow tall and thin.

syn.note: Lanky means tall and thin, often moving in an awkward way.
Tall is about the whole body, not only the legs.

people.definition: tight, soft trousers that stretch and cover the whole body part from hip to ankle
people.example: She wore black leggings to the gym.

context.text: Aziz is a tall, leggy boy, so he is a great goalkeeper. Last week he hurt his leg playing football in Tashkent, and now he has to rest for two weeks.

reviewer_note: Verb 'leg' exists only in informal 'leg it' and is not in the gate dictionary, so it is a no_form note. -legged adjectives are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: A written message on paper sent to someone.

forms.definition: a written message on paper that you send to someone, usually by post
forms.example: She wrote a long letter to her grandmother in Khiva.
forms.note: The same word also means a sign of the alphabet, like A or B.

syn.note: A note is a short written message, often not sent by post.
A message can be written or spoken, on paper or on a phone.
Mail means all the letters and parcels that come by post. American English; British English often says 'post'.
Formal: all the letters a person sends and receives.

forms.definition: to write or paint words on a sign or other surface
forms.example: The name of the shop was lettered in gold.
forms.note: Belongs to letter = a sign of the alphabet (A, B, C), not a message sent by post.
Literate and literary come from the same old Latin root, but they are not made from 'letter'.

people.definition: written or painted words, and the style they are drawn in
people.example: The lettering on the old shop sign was beautiful.
people.note: Belongs to letter = a sign of the alphabet, not a message sent by post.

context.text: My grandmother in Khiva still writes letters by hand. Last week I got a long letter from her, and I wrote back the same day.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: alphabet letter vs message; verb 'letter' and 'lettering' belong to the alphabet sense. literate/literary and 'let' (allow) marked not_family; let is a different word.

corpus_definition: To move your body into a flat, horizontal position.
particle_note: Not separable and takes no object: 'I want to lie down.' Forms: lie down, lay down (past), lain down; lying down. Don't confuse with 'lay something down' (put something down).

relations.note: Rest means to relax or sleep; you often lie down to rest.
Formal: to lie or lean back, often in a chair.
Informal British: a short rest lying on a bed or sofa.
To stand up again after lying or sitting.
To move your body so that you are on your feet.

context.text: After a long day at the bazaar, my mother likes to lie down for an hour. Yesterday she lay down on the sofa and fell asleep.

reviewer_note: Trap: past of lie is lay (lay down), which looks like the verb 'lay' (put down); particle_note explains it.

corpus_definition: To pay attention to sounds being made.
particle_note: Not separable: 'listen to music', 'listen to him' (never 'listen music'). Without an object, use only 'listen': 'Please listen!'

relations.note: Hear means sounds come to your ears; listen to means you try to hear them.
Wider: you can pay attention to things you see or think about too.
To listen to a radio programme or show.
To pay no attention to someone or something on purpose.

context.text: Every morning on the bus I listen to Uzbek music. My teacher always says, 'Listen to the question carefully before you answer.'

reviewer_note: Prepositional verb; key learner error is dropping 'to' (listen music). hear vs listen to explained.

corpus_definition: To turn your eyes toward an object or person.
particle_note: Not separable: 'look at the picture', 'look at me' (never 'look the picture'). Without an object, use only 'look': 'Look!'

relations.note: See means something comes into your eyes; look at means you choose to turn your eyes to it.
Watch is for things that move or change, like TV or a football match.
To look at something very quickly.
To look at something for a long time without moving your eyes.
Formal: to look at something, often carefully.
To turn your eyes away from something.

context.text: Look at this old photo of Registan Square. My grandfather looked at it for a long time and smiled.

reviewer_note: Prepositional verb; trap is dropping 'at'. see/watch/look at distinction in notes.

corpus_definition: A meal eaten in the middle of the day.

forms.definition: the meal you eat in the middle of the day
forms.example: Let's go out for lunch on Friday.
forms.note: Usually no 'a' or 'the': 'have lunch', 'after lunch'. The old, very formal word is 'luncheon'.

syn.note: Usually the evening meal, but in some parts of Britain dinner is the meal in the middle of the day.
Any time you eat food: breakfast, lunch or dinner.
A late morning meal instead of breakfast and the midday meal.

forms.definition: to eat the midday meal, often at a restaurant
forms.example: The director lunched with the guests at a hotel in Tashkent.
forms.note: In everyday English people usually say 'have lunch'.

syn.note: General word for putting food in your mouth, at any time.
Formal: to eat a meal, usually the evening one.

context.text: In Uzbekistan, many families eat plov for lunch on Thursdays. Today my boss is lunching with guests from Samarkand, so the office is quiet.

reviewer_note: luncheon is the older full word, not a derived form, so it is only mentioned. lunchtime/lunchbox are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: Having a husband or wife.
usage_note: be married to + person: 'She is married to a doctor.' Use 'to', not 'with' or 'on'. Get married to someone = the wedding day; be married to = the state.

relations.note: Formal or old-fashioned; today it more often means strongly liking an idea.
Engaged to means you have promised to marry someone but are not married yet.
No longer married to someone because the marriage has legally ended.
Not married and not in a relationship.

context.text: My cousin Dilnoza is married to a teacher from Andijan. They have been married to each other for ten years and have three children.

reviewer_note: kind_hint was phrasal; corrected to phrase (adjective + preposition). Trap for Russian/Uzbek speakers: 'married on/with' instead of 'married to'.

corpus_definition: The food that you eat at a specific time.

forms.definition: the food you eat at one time, such as breakfast, lunch or dinner
forms.example: Lunch is my favourite meal of the day.

syn.note: Food is anything you eat; a meal is the food you eat at one time.
A dish is one kind of cooked food; a meal can have several dishes.
A very big meal for a special day, like a wedding.
Dinner is one kind of meal, usually in the evening.

forms.note: Mealy (dry and soft, like flour) comes from a different old word 'meal' meaning ground grain.

context.text: Plov is the most famous meal in Uzbekistan. In my family, we always eat our evening meal together at seven.

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: 'mealy' belongs to meal = ground grain, marked not_family. mealtime is a compound, left out. Snack is not a true opposite.

corpus_definition: A short note or words sent to another person.

forms.definition: a short piece of writing or words you send to another person
forms.example: I sent a quick message to my friend.
forms.note: Also means the main idea of a film or book: 'the message of the story'.

syn.note: A text is a written note sent by phone.
A short written note, often on paper.
A short written note sent inside an office or company.
A longer written note, usually on paper and sent by post.

forms.definition: sending short written notes by phone or computer
forms.example: Text messaging is the cheapest way to stay in touch.

forms.definition: to send someone a short note by phone or computer
forms.example: Message me when you get to Bukhara.

syn.note: Same meaning when you use a phone; very common in everyday English.
To get in touch in any way: call, write or visit.
To send someone a written note, often a letter or email.

people.definition: a person who takes notes or news from one person to another
people.example: In the past, a messenger carried news from Bukhara to Samarkand on horseback.
people.note: Also the name of some phone apps for sending notes.

context.text: Did you get my message? I messaged you twice this morning. My sister prefers messaging to phone calls because it is cheaper.

reviewer_note: GATE? 'text' is a verb in Oxford/Cambridge learner dictionaries (text someone = send a text); WordNet 3.1 just lacks it. messenger: no affix claimed because removing -er leaves 'messeng' (extra n). Verb 'message' is a real conversion in learner dictionaries.

gate_overrides.reason: text is a verb in modern English (to text someone); WordNet 3.1 predates it

corpus_definition: A small telephone that you can carry with you.
usage_note: British English; often shortened to 'mobile' or just 'phone'. American English says 'cell phone' or 'cell'. Verbs: call someone on their mobile phone, charge your mobile phone.

relations.note: The American English word for the same thing.
Everyday short word; it can also mean a phone at home.
A mobile phone that can use the internet and apps; most mobiles today are smartphones.
A phone connected by a wire, usually at home or in an office.

context.text: My mobile phone is out of battery, so I can't call a taxi. Can I use your mobile phone for a minute?

reviewer_note: British vs American: mobile phone vs cell phone. landline used as the contrast term.

corpus_definition: the coins or paper notes used to buy things

forms.definition: the coins and paper notes that you use to buy things
forms.example: I need some money to buy lunch.

syn.note: Cash is money in coins and notes, not on a card. Very common and easy.
Formal: money that is ready to be used for something.
The kind of money one country uses, like the Uzbek som.
Small coins, or the money you get back after you pay.

forms.note: No common verb is made from money. Monetize comes from the same old Latin root but is not made from money.

forms.definition: having a lot of riches; wealthy
forms.example: Only moneyed families could buy a car in those days.
forms.note: Rare and formal; also spelled monied. Monetary (about a country's money) is not made from money.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning; moneyed is formal and rare.
A little more formal than rich.

ant.note: Having very little to live on.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: My brother saves money every month for a new phone. He says only moneyed people can buy a new one each year, but he will get one by summer.

reviewer_note: Monetary/monetize share a Latin root but are not made from money: kept out. Moneyed is rare/formal but a real learner-dictionary word, so it is not hidden.

corpus_definition: A period of about four weeks.

forms.definition: one of the twelve parts of a year, about four weeks long
forms.example: My birthday is in one month.
forms.note: A magazine that comes out every month is called a monthly (noun).

syn.note: About the same length of time, but a month can have 28 to 31 days.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: happening or paid once every four weeks or so
forms.example: Our monthly rent is two million som.

forms.definition: once every four weeks or so
forms.example: The magazine is published monthly.

syn.note: Easy everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Easy everyday phrase with the same meaning.

context.text: I pay my internet bill monthly. The monthly cost is not high, and it is cheaper than last month.

reviewer_note: Monthly is both adjective and adverb (and also a noun for a magazine, mentioned in a note). Monthly is -ly on a noun, so it is not a manner adverb.

corpus_definition: A very high piece of land that is taller than a hill.

forms.definition: a very high area of land, much taller than a hill
forms.example: We climbed the big mountain.

syn.note: The pointed top of a mountain, or a mountain with a pointed top.
Used mostly in names, like Mount Everest; written as Mt.
A hill is lower and smaller than a mountain.

ant.note: The low land between mountains or hills.

forms.definition: the sport or activity of climbing high peaks
forms.example: Mountaineering in the Chimgan area is popular in summer.

forms.note: Some big dictionaries list mountaineer as a verb, but learner dictionaries (Oxford, Cambridge, Longman) show it only as a noun. People say 'go climbing'.

forms.definition: having a lot of very high land
forms.example: The east of Uzbekistan is more mountainous than the west.

syn.note: Hilly land has hills, which are lower.

ant.note: Flat land has no hills or high parts.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

people.definition: a person who climbs high peaks as a sport
people.example: The mountaineer reached the top before sunrise.

context.text: Our village is in a mountainous area near Chimgan. Every weekend tourists come to climb the mountain, and some are serious mountaineers.

reviewer_note: GATE? verb mountaineer is not in Oxford/Cambridge/Longman learner dictionaries (noun only), so no_form per rule 5. Mountaineering is the activity (noun slot); mountaineer is the person (People). No -ing affix claimed since the base is mountaineer, not mountain.

corpus_definition: Sounds made by voices or instruments that are pleasant to hear.

forms.definition: pleasant sounds made by voices or instruments
forms.example: I love listening to soft music in the evening.

syn.note: A melody is one tune inside a piece; music is the whole thing.
A tune is a short piece you can sing or remember; easy word.
A song is music with words that someone sings.

forms.note: No common verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: connected with sounds made by voices or instruments; good at playing or singing
forms.example: She plays three musical instruments.
forms.note: Musical is also a noun: a play or film with a lot of singing and dancing, e.g. 'We watched a musical.'

syn.note: Melodic means having a nice tune.
Tuneful means pleasant to listen to.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with sounds, songs or instruments
forms.example: Musically, the concert was excellent.

people.definition: a person who plays an instrument or sings, often as a job
people.example: My cousin is a musician and plays the dutar.

context.text: My sister is very musical. She listens to music all day and wants to become a musician.

reviewer_note: GATE? unmusical is a real word in Oxford and Cambridge learner dictionaries (adjective), the true opposite of musical. The noun musical (a show) is in the adjective's note because the gate does not allow repeating a form in People & things.

corpus_definition: The part of the face used for breathing and smelling.

forms.definition: the part of the face that you breathe and smell with
forms.example: The cold wind made my nose turn red.

syn.note: One of the two holes in your nose.
The long nose of some animals, like a pig.

forms.definition: to look around in a place to find out private things
forms.example: He was nosing around in my room.
forms.note: Belongs to nose = being too curious about other people. Usually 'nose around' or 'nose about'.

forms.definition: too interested in other people's private lives
forms.example: Our nosy neighbour always asks where we are going.
forms.note: Belongs to nose = being too curious, not the body part. Also spelled nosey. Nasal (about the nose) is not made from nose.
Nosily exists but is very rare; it goes with nosy, not the body part.

context.text: I hurt my nose playing football yesterday. Now I can't smell my mother's cooking.

reviewer_note: Nasal comes from Latin, not made from nose: kept out. Nosy and verb nose are other_meaning (curiosity), not the body part.

corpus_definition: a hard-shelled seed that people eat

forms.definition: a dry fruit or seed with a hard shell that you can eat
forms.example: She put a nut in her mouth.

syn.note: A seed is the small part a new plant grows from; many nuts are seeds.
The soft part inside the shell of a nut.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: tasting of or full of the small hard-shelled foods
forms.example: This cake has a nice nutty taste.
forms.note: In informal English, nutty also means a bit crazy.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: In autumn my grandmother buys walnuts at the bazaar. She cracks every nut and bakes a cake with a nutty taste.

reviewer_note: Other noun meanings of nut (metal piece for a bolt; a crazy fan) are not shown. Nutrition/nutrient look similar but come from a different root.

corpus_definition: a place where people sit at desks and do business

forms.definition: a room or building where people work at desks
forms.example: She arrives at the office by nine.

syn.note: Any place where people work, not only rooms with desks.
Usually a government department or a company office.
A room at home where you read or work.

forms.definition: to lead a ceremony or be the judge in a sports game
forms.example: A local imam officiated at the wedding.
forms.note: Belongs to office = an official job or duty, not a room with desks. Formal.

forms.definition: connected with the government or people in power
forms.example: English is not an official language in Uzbekistan.
forms.note: Belongs to office = a position of power (hold office), not a room with desks. Official is also a noun: a person with an important job.

forms.definition: in a way that is approved by people in power
forms.example: The new bridge will officially open next week.
forms.note: Belongs to office = a position of power, goes with official.

people.definition: a person with a high rank in the army or police
people.example: The police officer asked to see my passport.
people.note: Belongs to office = a position of authority, not a room with desks.

context.text: My father works in an office in the centre of Tashkent. His office is on the fifth floor and has a view of the park.

reviewer_note: Office (room) vs office (position of power): official, officially, officiate and officer all belong to the power sense, so they are other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Taking a break from work or school to relax and enjoy life.
usage_note: be on holiday / go on holiday (to + place). British English; American English says 'on vacation'. Do not say 'in holiday' or 'on holidays'.

relations.note: The same meaning in American English.
Away means not at home; it does not say why.
Not working today, but you may stay at home.
At your job, not taking a break.

context.text: My teacher is on holiday in Samarkand this week. Next summer we will go on holiday to the mountains.

reviewer_note: Phrase, not a word; British vs American (on vacation) noted.

corpus_definition: having no mistakes or flaws of any kind.

forms.definition: the state of having no mistakes or problems at all
forms.example: She practises every day, but she does not expect perfection.

syn.note: Very high quality, but not always without any mistakes.

ant.note: A small mistake or problem in something.

forms.definition: to make something as good as it can be, with no mistakes
forms.example: He spent a year in London to perfect his English.
forms.note: Stress changes: the adjective is PER-fect, the verb is per-FECT.

syn.note: Easy word: make better, but not always the very best.
Make small changes so that something is better.
Learn a skill completely.

forms.definition: with no mistakes or problems; as good as it can be
forms.example: The weather was perfect for our picnic.

syn.note: Without any problems or mistakes; a bit more formal.
The best possible for a certain purpose.
Very, very good, but there can still be small problems.

ant.note: Having some small mistakes or problems.
Having a mistake or weakness.

forms.definition: in a way that has no mistakes; also 'completely'
forms.example: She speaks English perfectly.

syn.note: Without any mistakes; more formal.
Easy phrase; a little weaker.
In 'perfectly happy' or 'perfectly fine', perfectly means completely.

ant.note: Not completely or not correctly.
In a poor way, with many mistakes.

people.definition: a person who wants everything to be done without any mistakes
people.example: My boss is a perfectionist and checks every report twice.

context.text: Malika's plov was perfect. She cooked it perfectly because she wanted to perfect her grandmother's recipe.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR A1). Verb perfect is a conversion with a stress shift. Grammar 'perfect tense' not shown.

corpus_definition: A conversation between two people using a mobile device.
usage_note: make a phone call (to someone); get / have / take a phone call; give someone a phone call. Often just 'a call'.

relations.note: The short, everyday way to say it: 'I got a call from Mum.'
British and informal: 'Give me a ring tonight.'
A call where you can also see the other person.
A written message on a phone, not a spoken talk.

context.text: I need to make a quick phone call to my brother. He was waiting for a phone call from the bank all morning.

reviewer_note: Two-word noun; treated as phrase with no forms.

corpus_definition: A soft object you put your head on when sleeping.

forms.definition: a soft bag full of feathers or soft material for your head in bed
forms.example: I need a soft pillow for a good sleep.

syn.note: Related: a cushion is for a chair or sofa; the one for your head in bed has its own name.

forms.definition: to rest your head on something soft
forms.example: She pillowed her head on her arms and fell asleep.
forms.note: Literary and rare; in everyday English say 'rest your head on'.

syn.note: Everyday word: 'She rested her head on her arms.'
Related: to put something down gently.

forms.note: No learner-dictionary adjective. 'Pillowy' (soft like a pillow) exists but is rare.
No adverb exists for this word.

context.text: Aziz was so tired after the long drive from Bukhara that he pillowed his head on his jacket. At home his mother gave him a big soft pillow.

reviewer_note: Compounds (pillowcase, pillow fight) left out for the Compounds branch. Verb 'pillow' is literary but in OALD.

corpus_definition: A living thing that grows in the earth.

forms.definition: a living thing with leaves and roots that grows in soil
forms.example: Water the plant every morning.

syn.note: Related: a flower is one kind of this, or its coloured part.
Related: all the green growing things in an area; formal and uncountable.
Related: a small one used in cooking or medicine, like mint or basil.
Related: a very big one with a wooden trunk.

forms.definition: the act of putting seeds or young trees into the ground
forms.example: Spring is the best time for planting in Fergana.

forms.definition: to put seeds or young trees into the ground so they grow
forms.example: We planted three apple trees in the garden.
forms.note: Other meanings: plant a bomb, plant evidence (put secretly). The noun 'plant' can also mean a factory: a power plant.

syn.note: Only for seeds: 'sow wheat'.
Related: to look after something until it is big.

ant.note: To take something out of the ground.

forms.note: No common adjective. Learners can say 'plant-based' (a compound) for food made from these living things.
No adverb exists for this word.

people.definition: a large pot or box for growing flowers in
people.example: We put a wooden planter with roses by the door.
people.note: Also: a person who owns a big farm in hot countries (old use).

people.definition: a large farm in a hot country where tea, cotton or coffee is grown
people.example: He worked on a tea plantation in Sri Lanka.

context.text: My grandmother loves her garden in Samarkand. In spring she is busy with planting tomatoes and herbs, and she waters each plant every morning.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: plant = factory and plant = put secretly are other meanings; map keeps the living-thing sense.

corpus_definition: To do something for fun or enjoyment.

forms.definition: activities that children do for fun
forms.example: Children learn a lot through play.
forms.note: Other meaning: a story acted in a theatre ('a play by Shakespeare').

syn.note: Fun is the good feeling; this noun is the activity itself.
Related: organised activities with rules.
Formal word for things you do to relax.

ant.note: Work is what you must do; this is what you do for fun.

forms.definition: to do things for fun, especially games or with toys
forms.example: Children like to play in the park.
forms.note: Other meanings: play football (a sport), play the guitar (music), play a role (acting).

syn.note: Easy phrase about enjoying yourself, not only with games.
Related: about being happy, not about the activity.
Informal British: to do silly things for fun.

ant.note: 'All work and no play' means only working, no fun.

forms.definition: liking to have fun and joke, not serious
forms.example: Our kitten is very playful in the morning.

syn.note: Related: happy and positive.
Related: full of energy.

ant.note: Thinking carefully, not joking.

forms.definition: in a way that is fun and not serious
forms.example: She playfully threw a snowball at her brother.

syn.note: Close: in a way that is not meant seriously.
Related: in a happy way.

ant.note: In a way that is not joking.

people.definition: someone who takes part in a game or sport
people.example: He is the youngest player on the team.

context.text: After school my little brothers play in the yard for hours. They are very playful and always laugh when they play hide-and-seek.

reviewer_note: Compounds (playground, playmate, playtime, playwright) left out. Theatre/sport/music senses noted, not mapped.

corpus_definition: Someone who takes part in a sport or activity.

forms.definition: a person who takes part in a game or sport
forms.example: She is the best tennis player on the team.
forms.note: Other meanings: a person who plays music ('a piano player') or a machine ('a DVD player').

syn.note: A person in a race or competition; more formal.
A man who does sport; sportswoman for a woman.
Related: a person who is good at sport, often running or jumping.
Related: one person in a group that plays together.

ant.note: A person who watches the game but does not take part.

forms.definition: the action of a game or sport while it is going on
forms.example: Rain stopped play for an hour.

syn.note: Related: the whole match, not the action in it.

forms.definition: to take part in a game or sport
forms.example: My brother plays football every Saturday.

syn.note: Easy phrase: 'take part in a match'.
Related: to try to win against others.

ant.note: To not take part in a game or dance.

forms.definition: liking to have fun and joke, not serious
forms.example: The puppy was very playful.
forms.note: Belongs to play = have fun and joke, not taking part in a sport.

forms.definition: in a way that is fun and not serious
forms.example: He playfully pulled his sister's hat.
forms.note: Belongs to play = have fun and joke, not taking part in a sport.

context.text: Uzbekistan's football players train hard before every big match. The team plays in Tashkent next week, and all the players are ready.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun (rule 6): stays main noun entry; no other person nouns in family except compounds (playmate, playwright), left out.

corpus_definition: Water that falls from the clouds in small drops.

forms.definition: water that falls in drops from the clouds
forms.example: Take an umbrella because of the heavy rain.

syn.note: Related: a short time of light falling water.
Related: very light, fine drops.
Related: a lot of heavy falling water in a short time.
Related: bad weather with strong wind, often thunder.

ant.note: Bright light from the sun, dry weather.

forms.definition: when water falls in drops from the clouds
forms.example: It rained all day in Tashkent yesterday.
forms.note: Used with 'it': it rains, it is raining.

syn.note: Related: to come down very heavily: 'It's pouring.'
Related: to come down lightly in very small drops.

forms.definition: having a lot of water falling from the sky
forms.example: April is often a rainy month.

syn.note: Easy word for weather with lots of falling water.
Related: with short periods of light falling water.

ant.note: With no water falling.
With a lot of bright sun.

forms.note: No adverb exists for this word.

context.text: It was a rainy morning in Samarkand. It rained for three hours, and the rain made the old streets shine.

reviewer_note: Compounds (rainbow, raincoat, raindrop, rainfall) left out for the Compounds branch.

corpus_definition: To produce a loud sound like a bell.

forms.definition: the sound a bell or phone makes
forms.example: There was a ring at the door.
forms.note: Other noun 'ring' (a circle, jewellery) is a different word with a different history.

syn.note: Related: a soft musical bell sound.
Related: a low electric sound, like a doorbell or phone on silent.

forms.definition: to make a loud, clear sound like a bell
forms.example: Did you hear the phone ring?
forms.note: Irregular: ring, rang, rung. British English also uses ring = phone someone: 'I'll ring you later.'

syn.note: Used mostly for bells and clocks.
Related: 'The alarm sounded.'
Related: a low electric sound.

forms.definition: loud and clear, like a bell
forms.example: He spoke in a ringing voice.

syn.note: Very loud, often used for success too.
Related: easy general word.

ant.note: Quiet and not clear, as if covered.

forms.note: No adverb in learner dictionaries ('ringingly' is extremely rare).

context.text: The school bell rang at eight o'clock. A moment later my phone started ringing in my bag, and the teacher looked at me.

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: ring (circle/jewellery) is a separate word, not a form of ring (sound). 'ringer' (bell-ringer) is rare; left out. ring/rang/rung irregular.

corpus_definition: A long line of water that flows into the sea.

forms.definition: a long natural line of water that flows to the sea or a lake
forms.example: The river flows through the city.

syn.note: Related: a small, narrow one.
Related: a very small one; a bit old-fashioned or literary.
Related: made by people, for boats or farms.

forms.note: No verb exists for this word.
No learner-dictionary adjective. 'Riverine' is a rare technical word.
No adverb exists for this word.

context.text: The Amu Darya is the longest river in Uzbekistan. Farmers use water from the river for their cotton fields.

reviewer_note: Compounds (riverbank, riverside, riverbed) left out for the Compounds branch. Only one existing form.

corpus_definition: feeling afraid of someone or something
usage_note: be scared of + noun / -ing: 'scared of spiders', 'scared of flying'. Also 'scared to do something' and 'scared stiff' (very scared, informal).

relations.note: Same meaning; a little more neutral.
Same meaning; common in British English.
Much stronger: very, very afraid.
Related: a little worried, not really afraid.
Not afraid of danger or pain.

context.text: My little brother is scared of spiders. I was scared of the dark when I was small, but now I'm not scared of anything!

reviewer_note: kind_hint said phrasal, but this is adjective + preposition, so kind = phrase.

corpus_definition: The large area of salt water that covers most of the Earth.

forms.definition: the large area of salt water that covers much of the Earth
forms.example: The children played by the sea.

syn.note: Very close; ocean is bigger. In American English 'the ocean' is common for the beach too.
Related: water with land all around it, usually not salty.

ant.note: The part of the Earth that is not covered by water.

forms.note: No verb exists for this word.

forms.definition: going or facing towards the open water, away from land
forms.example: The hotel is on the seaward side of the road.
forms.note: For 'connected with the sea' English uses marine or maritime, which come from a different root.

syn.note: Related: in the water, not far from the coast.

ant.note: Away from the coast, in the middle of a country.

forms.definition: towards the open water, away from the land
forms.example: The boats sailed seawards at sunrise.
forms.note: American English usually says seaward.

syn.note: Easy, common phrase: 'The boat went out to sea.'

ant.note: Away from the coast, towards the middle of a country.

context.text: Uzbekistan has no coast, so many families fly to the sea in summer. From our hotel we watched the fishing boats sail seawards at sunrise.

reviewer_note: marine/maritime are not family (Latin root). Compounds (seaside, seafood, seaman) left out. seaward/seawards are OALD entries.

corpus_definition: To look for something carefully.

forms.definition: an attempt to find someone or something by looking carefully
forms.example: The search for the lost child lasted all night.
forms.note: 'Research' is not made from this word in modern English; it means careful study.

syn.note: Close, a little informal: 'a hunt for a new flat'.
Related, informal: 'have a look for my keys'.
Related: a long, hard journey to find something; literary.

forms.definition: to look carefully in a place to find something
forms.example: I need to search for my keys.
forms.note: search a place (search the room); search for a thing (search for my keys).

syn.note: Easy and very common with the same meaning.
Close: 'hunt for a job'; a little informal.
Formal: to try to find or get something.
Related: to check many things one by one.

forms.definition: looking closely to find out the truth
forms.example: She gave me a long, searching look.

syn.note: Close: trying to find out hidden facts.
Related: careful and complete.

ant.note: Not careful or close.

forms.definition: possible to look through on a computer to find information
forms.example: The library catalogue is fully searchable online.

forms.definition: in a way that looks closely to find out the truth
forms.example: He looked at me searchingly before he answered.

syn.note: Related: very carefully.
Related: easy general word.

people.definition: a person who is trying to find someone or something
people.example: The searchers found the lost hiker near the river.

context.text: I searched the whole flat for my phone. My mother gave me a searching look and asked where I last used it. After a long search, my sister found it in the kitchen.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows have the same meaning; merged, lowest CEFR A1. research is not a re- + search split. 'search engine' is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: To cause something to go from one place to another.

forms.note: No common noun for the act itself; the person is 'sender' (see People & things). 'Send-off' (a goodbye party) comes from the phrasal verb send off.

forms.definition: to make a letter, message or parcel go to someone
forms.example: I will send you the photos tonight.

syn.note: British English for sending by mail: 'post a letter'. American English says mail.
Send by post, or by email; common in American English.
Formal, used by shops and companies: 'Your order was dispatched today.'
Send on something you received, like an email, to another person.
Send a signal or information, by radio or the internet; technical.

ant.note: One person sends, the other receives.
Everyday word: you get what someone sends you.

people.definition: the person who posts a letter or writes a message
people.example: Write the sender's address on the back of the envelope.

context.text: Every month I send money to my brother in Samarkand. The bank always shows the sender's name, so he knows it is from me.

reviewer_note: GATE? sender is a person noun, so by rule 8 it is in People & things, not the noun slot; no learner noun names the act of sending. Irregular verb: send, sent, sent.

corpus_definition: a group of words that makes a full statement or thought

forms.definition: a group of words with a subject and verb that expresses a full idea
forms.example: Write one sentence about your best friend.

syn.note: A clause is a part of a sentence with its own subject and verb; a sentence can have one or more clauses.
A statement is something you say or write as a fact; it is usually one sentence.
A phrase is a small group of words without a full subject and verb, like 'in the morning'.

forms.definition: to say officially in court what punishment someone will get
forms.example: The judge sentenced him to two years in prison.
forms.note: Belongs to sentence = a punishment given by a court, not a group of words.
'Sentential' exists only in linguistics books; not a learner word.

context.text: Our English teacher asked us to write five sentences about Tashkent. My first sentence was short: 'Tashkent is a big city.'

reviewer_note: GATE? sentential is a linguistics-only term, not in learner dictionaries, so rule 5 keeps it as no_form with a note. Verb sentence (court) shown as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To give a portion of something to another person.

forms.definition: the part of something that one person gets or gives
forms.example: Everyone paid their share of the bill.
forms.note: In business, a share is also one of the equal parts a company is divided into.

syn.note: A part of something; a bit more formal than share.
Easy, general word for a piece of a whole.
Informal, usually about money: 'He wants his cut.'

forms.definition: to give part of what you have to other people
forms.example: Please share your cake with your brother.
forms.note: Also 'share a room' = use it together with someone.

syn.note: Divide something between people: 'Let's split the pizza.'
Cut or separate into parts; you can divide something without giving it away.
Easy, general word; share means you keep some and give some.

ant.note: If you keep something, you do not give any of it to others.

forms.definition: used, owned or done by two or more people together
forms.example: We have a shared kitchen in our student flat.

syn.note: Belonging to a group: 'a common room', 'a common goal'.
Done or owned together: 'a joint bank account'.
Felt or done by both people: 'mutual respect'.

ant.note: Belonging to one person only, not shared.
For one person, not for a group.

forms.note: No adverb exists for this family.

context.text: My little sister always shares her sweets with me. Today she gave me a big share of her chocolate. We have a shared room, so we share everything.

reviewer_note: Shareholder is a compound (left out by rule 7). Shared kept as a participial adjective; no affix claimed for -ed.

corpus_definition: Very easy to understand or do.

forms.definition: the quality of being easy to understand or do
forms.example: I like the simplicity of this recipe.

syn.note: The fact that something is not difficult: 'with ease'.
Being clear and easy to understand; used about writing or explanations.

ant.note: The quality of having many parts and being hard to understand.
Being hard to do or understand.

forms.definition: the act of making something easier to understand or do
forms.example: This map is a simplification of the real city.

forms.definition: to make something easier to understand or do
forms.example: Can you simplify the instructions for the children?
forms.note: British and American spelling are the same.

syn.note: Easy everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Make something clearer; it does not always make it shorter or easier.

ant.note: To make something more difficult to understand or do.

forms.definition: easy to understand or do, not difficult
forms.example: This is a very simple task.

syn.note: Very close and very common: 'an easy test'.
Easy to do, with no problems; a bit more formal.
At the first, easiest level: 'basic English'.

ant.note: Hard to do or understand.
Having many parts, so hard to understand.
Having many connected parts; more formal than complicated.

forms.definition: making a problem seem easier than it really is
forms.example: His answer was too simplistic for such a big problem.
forms.note: Negative word: it means 'too simple', not just 'easy'.

forms.definition: in a way that is easy to understand
forms.example: The teacher explained the rule simply and clearly.
forms.note: Simply also often means 'only' or 'just': 'It's simply too expensive.'

syn.note: In a way that is easy to see or understand.
In a simple, clear way, without extra details.

context.text: My grandfather likes a simple life in the village. He explains things simply, and he says simplicity is the key to happiness.

reviewer_note: Spelling changes (simple to simply, simplicity, simplify) make suffix splits unclean, so only -ation on simplification is claimed. Simply's 'just' meaning noted, not split.

corpus_definition: To make musical sounds with your voice.

forms.definition: the activity of making music with your voice
forms.example: Her singing filled the whole room.

syn.note: The singing part of a recorded song: 'She did the vocals.'

forms.definition: a short piece of music with words that people perform with their voice
forms.example: We sang an old Uzbek song at the wedding.
forms.note: Song comes from sing by a vowel change, like sing, sang, sung.

forms.definition: to make music with your voice, often using words
forms.example: She likes to sing in the shower.
forms.note: Irregular verb: sing, sang, sung.

syn.note: Make music with your mouth closed, without words.
Sing or say words again and again, often in a group.
Sing, dance or act for an audience.

forms.note: No adjective for this family in learner dictionaries.

people.definition: a person who makes music with their voice as a job
people.example: Sevara Nazarkhan is a famous singer from Uzbekistan.

context.text: My sister sings every morning in the kitchen. Her singing is beautiful, and she wants to become a singer one day.

reviewer_note: Irregular verb sing/sang/sung. Song included as a noun extra (ablaut derivation); songwriter left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: A person who performs sounds using their voice.

forms.definition: a person who makes music with their voice, often as a job
forms.example: The famous singer gave a wonderful concert.

syn.note: A singer, especially in a band; a bit more formal.
Anyone who entertains an audience: singers, dancers, actors.
Used in the music business for a singer or band.

forms.definition: the activity of making music with your voice
forms.example: We could hear singing from the next room.

forms.definition: a short piece of music with words that people perform with their voice
forms.example: The singer finished with her most famous song.

forms.definition: to make music with your voice, often using words
forms.example: He sings at weddings every weekend.
forms.note: Singer is made from sing + -er. Irregular verb: sing, sang, sung.

syn.note: Make music with your mouth closed, without words.
Sing, dance or act for an audience.

context.text: My cousin is a singer in a small band in Bukhara. She sings at weddings, and people love her songs.

reviewer_note: Rule 6: singer stays main noun. No other person nouns in the family (songwriter is a compound).

corpus_definition: The time when you rest with your eyes closed.

forms.definition: the natural rest of the body at night, with your eyes closed
forms.example: You need enough sleep to feel refreshed.

syn.note: Time when you relax or stop working; you can rest without sleeping.
A short sleep, usually in the day.
Old-fashioned or literary word for sleep.

forms.definition: to rest with your eyes closed and your mind not awake
forms.example: I usually sleep for eight hours.
forms.note: Irregular verb: sleep, slept, slept.

syn.note: Relax and not work; you may or may not sleep.
Sleep lightly for a short time.
Sleep for a short time in the day.

ant.note: To stop sleeping.

forms.definition: tired and wanting to rest with your eyes closed
forms.example: The baby is sleepy after her bath.

syn.note: Very common; you can be tired without wanting to sleep.
Almost asleep; often used about medicine.

ant.note: Not sleeping.
Fully awake and paying attention.

forms.definition: not awake; in the state of resting at night
forms.example: The children are asleep upstairs.
forms.note: Used after a verb: 'She is asleep', not 'an asleep girl'.

ant.note: Not sleeping.

forms.definition: without any rest at night
forms.example: I had a sleepless night before the exam.

forms.definition: in a tired way, as if you want to rest
forms.example: He sleepily opened his eyes.

syn.note: In a tired way; you may be tired without wanting to sleep.

people.definition: a person who rests at night in a particular way
people.example: My brother is a heavy sleeper; nothing wakes him.
people.note: Also a train with beds: 'the night sleeper to Moscow'.

context.text: After a long day I always feel sleepy. Last night I fell asleep at nine, and I slept very well. Good sleep is important.

reviewer_note: Asleep (a- prefix, not in affix table) listed as an adjective extra; sleepover left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: Having or showing a quick, clever mind.

forms.definition: the quality of looking clean, neat and well dressed
forms.example: The school is known for the smartness of its uniform.
forms.note: Belongs to smart = neat and well dressed (mainly British). For a clever mind, say intelligence or cleverness.

forms.definition: to make a person or place look neater and cleaner
forms.example: He smartened himself up for the interview.
forms.note: Belongs to smart = neat and well dressed, not clever.

forms.definition: to feel a quick, sharp pain, or to feel upset
forms.example: My eyes were smarting from the smoke.
forms.note: Belongs to a different meaning of smart = sharp pain, not clever.

forms.definition: quick to learn and understand things; clever
forms.example: That was a very smart thing to say.
forms.note: In British English smart also means 'neat and well dressed'.

syn.note: Very close; British English uses clever more, American English uses smart more.
Same meaning, a little more formal.
Clever and quick to learn, often about children.

ant.note: Not clever; can be rude about a person.
Not sensible; a bit more formal.
Informal and rude, mainly American English.

forms.definition: in a neat, clean and fashionable way
forms.example: She was smartly dressed for the meeting.
forms.note: Belongs to smart = neat and well dressed. To say 'in a clever way', use cleverly.

context.text: Aziz is a very smart boy. He always finds a smart answer to difficult maths questions.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: smartness, smarten, smartly mostly belong to smart = neat/well dressed; verb smart = sharp pain. Smartphone left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: Soft white flakes that fall from the sky in winter.

forms.definition: soft white pieces of frozen water that fall from the sky when it is cold
forms.example: The ground is covered in deep white snow.

syn.note: A mix of rain and snow.
Frozen water; hard, not soft like snow.
A thin white layer of ice on the ground on cold mornings.

forms.definition: when white frozen flakes fall from the sky
forms.example: It snowed all night in Tashkent.
forms.note: Used with 'it': 'It is snowing.'

syn.note: When rain and snow fall together.

forms.definition: with a lot of white frozen flakes falling or on the ground
forms.example: We had a snowy winter this year.

syn.note: Typical of winter: cold, often with snow.

forms.note: No adverb exists for this family.

context.text: It snowed all night in Chimgan. In the morning the mountains were white with snow, and the children played outside all snowy day.

reviewer_note: Snowman, snowflake, snowball are compounds and left out (rule 7). No people nouns.

corpus_definition: A short piece of sounds meant to be performed by voices.

forms.definition: a short piece of music with words that people perform with their voice
forms.example: This is my favorite song on the radio.
forms.note: American spelling 'favorite', British 'favourite'.

syn.note: The music of a song; a tune can have no words.
One song on an album or playlist.
The main musical line of a song; a bit more formal.

forms.definition: the activity of making music with your voice
forms.example: There was a lot of singing and dancing at the party.

forms.definition: to make music with your voice, often using words
forms.example: Let's sing a song together.
forms.note: Song comes from sing by a vowel change. Irregular verb: sing, sang, sung.

syn.note: Make music with your mouth closed, without words.
Sing, dance or act for an audience.

forms.note: No adjective for this family in learner dictionaries.

people.definition: a person who makes music with their voice as a job
people.example: The singer forgot the words of her new song.

context.text: My grandmother knows many old Uzbek songs. She sings them to us in the evening, and her singing always makes us happy.

reviewer_note: Family is built on sing (song is an ablaut form of it). Songwriter and songbird left out as compounds.

corpus_definition: To move from sitting to being on your feet.
particle_note: Not separable and usually no object: 'Please stand up.' 'Everyone stood up.' Also 'stand up straight'. Careful: 'stand someone up' (not come to meet them) is a different meaning.

relations.note: Very close and common in everyday English: 'He got up from his chair.' Get up also means leave your bed.
Formal or written: 'The audience rose to their feet.'
To move from standing to sitting on a chair or the floor.

context.text: When the teacher came into the classroom, all the students stood up. She smiled and said, 'Thank you. You can sit down now, but stand up again when I call your name.'

reviewer_note: Kept only the 'get on your feet' sense; 'stand someone up' and 'stand up for' are mentioned as different meanings only.

corpus_definition: a piece of kitchen equipment used for cooking food with heat

forms.definition: a kitchen machine with hot rings or flames on top for cooking
forms.example: She put the soup pot on the stove to heat up.
forms.note: Stove is the usual word in American English; British English often says cooker. In both, a stove can also be a heater that burns wood.

syn.note: British English word for the same kitchen machine.
American English, a large stove with an oven; less common for learners.
Related: the oven is the closed box for baking; the stove top is where pots go.
British English: only the flat top part where you put pots.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family. 'Stove' as a past form of 'stave' is very rare and unrelated.

context.text: My grandmother cooks plov on an old gas stove in her kitchen in Bukhara. She says food tastes better when it is made slowly on the stove.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; stovetop is a compound and left out.

corpus_definition: A thin tube used for drinking liquid.

forms.definition: a thin plastic or paper tube that you drink through
forms.example: She used a straw to drink her juice.
forms.note: Straw also means dry yellow stems of wheat, used for animals. That is a different meaning.

syn.note: Related: any long hollow pipe; a straw is a small tube for drinks.

forms.note: In 'a straw hat', straw is a noun used before another noun and belongs to the 'dry stems' meaning.

context.text: In summer, cafes in Tashkent sell cold lemonade with a paper straw. Many people now choose paper straws because plastic is bad for nature.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: drinking straw vs straw = dried stems; map keeps only the drinking tube.

corpus_definition: To wash your body under falling water.
usage_note: take a shower (common in American and British English); British English also says 'have a shower'. Past: 'I took a shower.' Often with before/after: 'take a shower after the gym'.

relations.note: Same meaning, more common in British English.
The verb alone means the same: 'I showered and got dressed.'
Related: general word for cleaning yourself with water, not only under a shower.
Related: you wash while sitting in a bath full of water, not under falling water.

context.text: After football practice, Jasur always takes a shower before dinner. His sister prefers to take a shower in the morning to wake up.

reviewer_note: Fixed verb phrase; British 'have a shower' listed as synonym.

corpus_definition: A set of players working together in a game.

forms.definition: a group of players who play together against another group
forms.example: Our football team is the best in town.

syn.note: British English, very common in sport: 'Uzbekistan has a strong side this year.'
All the players a club can choose from, not only the ones playing today.
Related: the whole organisation; a club can have several teams.
Related: any number of people together, not only players.

forms.definition: to join with another person or group to work together
forms.example: Two local companies teamed up to build the new stadium.
forms.note: Belongs to team = any group working together, not players in a game. Mostly used as 'team up (with)'.

context.text: Our school has a basketball team and a football team. On Friday the football team will play against a team from Samarkand.

reviewer_note: teammate and teamwork are compounds and left out; verb 'team (up)' is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To keep someone or something in your mind for a while.
particle_note: Not separable: 'think about your offer', 'think about it' (never 'think it about'). Often + -ing: 'I'm thinking about moving to Tashkent.'

relations.note: More formal; often used for decisions: 'consider an offer'.
Think carefully before deciding; separable: 'think it over'.
Formal: think deeply and seriously about something.
Related: bring something from the past into your mind.
To stop keeping someone or something in your mind.

context.text: My friend asked me to join his business, and I said I would think about it. I thought about his offer all night before I decided.

reviewer_note: Kept the 'keep in your mind / consider' sense; think of is a near-neighbour, not listed.

corpus_definition: The hours, minutes, and days that pass.

forms.definition: the hours, minutes and days that pass, measured by clocks
forms.example: Do you have the correct time?

syn.note: Related: one length of time with a start and an end.
Related: a very short point in time.

forms.definition: the choice of the exact moment when something happens
forms.example: The timing of the concert was perfect, just after sunset.

forms.definition: to measure how many seconds or minutes something takes
forms.example: The coach timed each runner with a stopwatch.

syn.note: Informal, often in sport: 'She clocked ten seconds.'
Related: find the size or amount of anything, not only how long.

forms.definition: not changing or getting old-fashioned as the years pass
forms.example: Her songs have a timeless beauty that young people still love.

syn.note: Good and popular for a long time; used for clothes, books and films.
Never seeming to get older; a little literary.
Related: lasting forever, stronger than timeless.

ant.note: Looking old-fashioned because it belongs to the past.

forms.definition: happening at exactly the right moment
forms.example: Thanks to a timely warning, nobody was hurt.
forms.note: Belongs to time = the right moment for something. False friend: timely is an adjective, not an adverb.
timelessly exists but is very rare; learners use phrases like 'on time' and 'in time' instead.

people.definition: a small device that measures minutes and rings when they end
people.example: Set the timer for ten minutes so the rice does not burn.

context.text: Time goes fast when you are on holiday in Samarkand. Before our trip, my brother timed the drive from Tashkent: it took four hours. The old city has a timeless beauty.

reviewer_note: GATE? adverb slot: the gate links 'timely' as an adverb (WordNet), but Oxford, Cambridge and Longman list timely only as an adjective; it is shown as an adjective other_meaning (right moment), and calling it an adverb would mislead learners. timetable/timekeeper are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: To go from one place to another over a long distance.

forms.definition: the activity of going to other places, especially far away
forms.example: Air travel is getting cheaper in Central Asia.
forms.note: Usually uncountable: say 'a trip' or 'a journey', not 'a travel'. 'My travels' (plural) means many trips.

syn.note: Related: travel for holidays, and the business around it.
Related: one trip from one place to another; countable.

forms.definition: to go from one place to another, often a long way
forms.example: I love to travel to new countries.
forms.note: British spelling doubles the l: travelled, travelling. American: traveled, traveling.

syn.note: Easy, general word: 'We went to Istanbul by plane.'
Literary verb for a long trip.
Related: travel around a place and visit many parts of it.
Related: go to see a place or person for a short time.

ant.note: To remain in the same place, for example at home.

forms.definition: moving from place to place, not staying in one town
forms.example: A travelling circus came to our town last summer.
forms.note: American spelling: traveling.

syn.note: Used for shows and bands that go from city to city.
Related: able to move easily, e.g. a mobile library.

people.definition: a person who is going to other places or does so often
people.example: Many travellers stop in Khiva on the Silk Road route.
people.note: American spelling: traveler.

context.text: My cousin loves to travel. Last summer he travelled from Tashkent to Khiva by train, and in Khiva he watched a travelling puppet show with other travellers.

reviewer_note: Trap: noun travel is uncountable ('a travel' is wrong). British double-l spellings used, American noted.

corpus_definition: A tall plant with a hard trunk and many branches.

forms.definition: a tall plant with a hard wooden trunk, branches and leaves
forms.example: Birds live in that big tree.

syn.note: Related: any living thing that grows in the ground; trees are big plants.
Related: a smaller plant with many branches but no tall trunk.

forms.definition: with no tall woody plants growing on it
forms.example: The road crossed a dry, treeless plain near the Aral Sea.

syn.note: Related: with nothing growing or covering it.
Related: land where almost nothing can grow.

ant.note: Covered with many tall woody plants.

context.text: In spring, the apricot trees in Fergana are full of white flowers. Further west, the land becomes dry and treeless.

reviewer_note: treetop/tree house are compounds, left out. treeless is in Longman/Oxford but less common; kept so no real word is hidden.

corpus_definition: A visit to a place for work or fun.

forms.definition: a short visit to a place and back, for work or fun
forms.example: He is away on a business trip.
forms.note: British English also has tripper (a person on a day out), but it is rare and often a bit unkind.

syn.note: Journey is the act of travelling, often long; trip includes the stay and coming back.
A short trip by a group, often for sightseeing; a bit formal.
A short trip for fun, often for one day.
Related: focuses on the time you spend at the place or with a person.
Related: a trip that visits several places.

forms.definition: to hit your foot on something and almost fall
forms.example: I tripped on the stairs and dropped my phone.
forms.note: Belongs to trip = catch your foot and fall, not a visit to a place.

context.text: Next week our class is going on a trip to Samarkand. It is a short trip, only two days, but we will see the Registan.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: verb trip (fall) is other_meaning; day-trip is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: To stop a machine or light from working.
particle_note: Separable: 'turn off the light' or 'turn the light off'. With a pronoun the particle goes last: 'turn it off', never 'turn off it'.

relations.note: Same meaning, very common in British English, especially for electric things.
Often used for water, gas or engines: 'shut off the water'.
Only for lights: 'turn out the lights before bed'.
General word; turn off means you use a switch or button to stop it.
To start a machine or light: 'turn on the TV'.
Same as turn on, common for electric things.

context.text: Before Aziz goes to bed, he turns off the TV and the kitchen light. His mother always says, 'Turn your phone off too!'

reviewer_note: Only the 'stop a machine' sense; 'turn off' = make someone lose interest and 'turn off' a road are other meanings, not covered.

corpus_definition: To go see a person or a place for a while.

forms.definition: a time when you go to see a person or place for a short time
forms.example: We had a short visit to Bukhara last summer.
forms.note: Common phrases: 'pay a visit to', 'on a visit'.

syn.note: Related: a trip is the journey to a place and back; a visit is the time you spend there.
Related: a stay is usually longer, often with nights away from home.
A short visit to someone's home; a bit old-fashioned in this meaning.

forms.definition: to go and see a person or a place for some time
forms.example: I want to visit my grandmother this weekend.

syn.note: Easy everyday words with the same meaning.
Easy and common for people: 'I saw my aunt on Sunday.'
A short visit to a person; a bit formal or old-fashioned.
Related: you visit and also sleep at their home.
A short visit without planning it.

forms.definition: staying in a place for a short time, not living or working there
forms.example: A visiting teacher from London gave a lesson at our school.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: 'a visiting professor', 'the visiting team'. Also 'visiting hours' in a hospital.

syn.note: In sport, the team playing in the other team's city: 'the away team'.

ant.note: In sport, the team playing in its own city: 'the home team'.
Living or working in this place, not just here for a short time.

forms.note: There is no adverb from visit.

people.definition: a person who comes to see a place or a person
people.example: Samarkand has thousands of visitors every summer.

context.text: Every spring my cousins visit us in Tashkent. During their visit we go to the mountains, and the visiting children love the cool air there.

reviewer_note: visitation left out: formal and rare for A1-B2. visiting kept as a participle adjective (visiting professor/team).

corpus_definition: To stay in a place until someone or something comes.
particle_note: Not separable: 'wait for the bus', 'wait for her' (never 'wait the bus for'). Also wait for + someone + to do: 'We waited for the rain to stop.'

relations.note: Same idea, but formal and used without 'for': 'We await your answer.'
Informal: wait for a short time: 'Hang on, I'm coming.'
Wait for a short time, often on the phone: 'Hold on, please.'
Related: you think someone will come, but you are not staying in one place for them.
To go away from a place before someone comes.

context.text: I waited for my friend outside Chorsu Bazaar for twenty minutes. When she came, she said, 'Thanks for waiting for me!'

reviewer_note: Verb + preposition kept as phrasal (like 'take part in'); inseparable.

corpus_definition: to stop sleeping and become aware of your surroundings
particle_note: Without an object: 'I wake up at seven.' With an object it is separable: 'wake up the baby' or 'wake the baby up'; with a pronoun: 'wake me up', never 'wake up me'. Past: woke up, woken up.

relations.note: Same meaning without 'up'; a little more formal or written.
Literary verb with the same meaning; more common as an adjective: 'I am awake.'
Related but different: you wake up first, then you get up out of bed.
To start sleeping: 'I fell asleep in front of the TV.'
Easy, everyday: to start sleeping.

context.text: On school days I wake up at half past six. My little brother never hears the alarm, so I have to wake him up too.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows mean the same thing (stop sleeping), merged into one map.

corpus_definition: The clear liquid that we drink and use for washing.

forms.definition: the clear liquid in rivers, lakes and rain that people drink
forms.example: I drink plenty of water every single day.
forms.note: Uncountable: 'some water', 'a glass of water', not 'a water'.

syn.note: Related: any substance that flows, like milk, oil or juice.
Related: water that falls from the sky.

forms.definition: to pour liquid on plants or the ground to help them grow
forms.example: My grandfather waters the tomatoes every evening.
forms.note: Also: 'my eyes are watering' = tears are coming, and 'my mouth is watering' = I want to eat something.

syn.note: Formal; used for fields and farms, often with pipes or canals.
