Related: to drop small amounts of liquid over something.
Related: to make something not dry.

forms.definition: with too much liquid in it, so it is thin and has little taste
forms.example: The soup was cold and watery.
forms.note: Also 'watery eyes' = eyes with tears in them.

syn.note: Easy word for soup or sauce that is not thick.
More liquid than it should be: 'runny eggs'.
Related: for tea or coffee with too much liquid and little taste.

ant.note: Not flowing easily: 'thick soup'.

forms.note: There is no adverb from water.

context.text: In summer, Grandma waters her garden in Namangan early in the morning. She always tells me to drink more water, but she hates watery tea.

reviewer_note: Compounds (waterfall, watermelon, waterproof) left out for the Compounds branch. No people/thing noun made from water.

corpus_definition: A period of seven days.

forms.definition: a period of seven days, often from Monday to Sunday
forms.example: I will see you next week.

syn.note: Same length of time, said in a different way.
British English for two weeks; not common in American English.

forms.note: There is no verb from week.

forms.definition: happening or made once every seven days
forms.example: We have a weekly English test on Fridays.
forms.note: Used before a noun: 'a weekly meeting'. As a noun, a weekly is a magazine that comes out once every seven days.

syn.note: Related: happening again and again at the same times, not only every seven days.

forms.definition: once every seven days
forms.example: The magazine comes out weekly.

syn.note: Easy, everyday words; more common in speaking.
Easy, everyday words with the same meaning.

context.text: Our class has a weekly quiz. The teacher checks our homework weekly too, and next week we start a new book.

reviewer_note: weekly is both adjective and adverb (same spelling). weekend and weekday are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: The natural movement of air outdoors.

forms.definition: air that moves outside, often strongly
forms.example: The strong wind blew my hat away.
forms.note: Said /wɪnd/. Common phrases: 'a strong wind', 'a cold wind', 'the wind is blowing'.

syn.note: Related: a light, pleasant movement of air.
Related: a sudden, short, strong movement of air.
Related: a very strong movement of air, often at sea.
Related: very bad weather with strong air movement and often rain.

forms.definition: to hit someone so that for a short time they cannot breathe
forms.example: The ball hit him in the stomach and winded him.
forms.note: Belongs to wind = breath, not moving air; said /wɪnd/. Don't confuse with wind /waɪnd/ (wind a clock, a winding road), which is a different word.

forms.definition: with a lot of strong moving air
forms.example: It was too windy to have a picnic by the lake.

syn.note: With light, pleasant air movement; less strong.
Same meaning, informal British English.
Related: very bad weather, often with rain too.

ant.note: With no strong air movement: 'a calm day'.
With no air moving at all: 'The air was still.'

forms.note: There is no common adverb from wind (windily is very rare).

context.text: Spring in Tashkent can be very windy. Yesterday the wind was so strong that it blew the washing off the line.

reviewer_note: Homograph trap: wind /waɪnd/ (to turn, wind a clock) is a different word, not in this family. Verb slot is wind /wɪnd/ = make breathless (other meaning). Compounds (windmill, windscreen) left out.

corpus_definition: The hard stuff that comes from inside a tree.

forms.definition: the hard material that trees are made of, used for furniture and fires
forms.example: This table is made of dark brown wood.
forms.note: Uncountable in this meaning. 'A wood' or 'the woods' is a different meaning: a small forest.

syn.note: Wood used for building; mainly British English.
Wood cut for building; American English.
Related: a thick piece cut from a tree, often for a fire.

forms.note: There is no verb from wood in learner English.

forms.definition: made of the hard material that comes from trees
forms.example: We sat on a wooden bench in the park.
forms.note: Also means stiff and not natural: 'a wooden smile'.

forms.definition: smelling, tasting or feeling like the material from trees
forms.example: This perfume has a warm, woody smell.
forms.note: Also 'a woody stem' (hard, not soft) and, less often, 'covered with trees'.

forms.definition: in a stiff way, without showing any feeling
forms.example: The young actor spoke his lines woodenly.
forms.note: Belongs to wooden = stiff and not natural (a wooden smile), not wooden = made from trees. Rare.

context.text: My uncle in Kokand makes wooden doors. He chooses the wood carefully, and his workshop always has a nice woody smell.

reviewer_note: -en in wooden is not in the affix table, so no affix row. Compounds (woodwork, woodland, woodcutter) left out. 'the woods' = forest noted, not a separate form.

corpus_definition: tasks that you do to earn money

forms.definition: the job you do to earn money, or the place where you do it
forms.example: I go to work every morning.
forms.note: Uncountable: 'I have a lot of work', not 'a work'. 'Works' (a writer's works) is a different meaning.

syn.note: Countable: 'a job'; work is uncountable.
Formal word for having paid work.
Related: hard work, often with your body. American spelling: labor.
Formal: the kind of job you do, used on forms.

ant.note: Free time when you are not at your job.
Time when you relax or sleep and do nothing tiring.

forms.definition: to do a job, especially to earn money
forms.example: My father works in a hospital in Andijan.
forms.note: work as + job: 'She works as a nurse.' work for + company.

syn.note: Formal way to say you have a job.
Related: to get the money you need to live.
Related: to do hard work, often with your body. American spelling: labor.

ant.note: To stop doing things and relax.
To rest and enjoy yourself.

forms.definition: having a paid job, or connected with your job
forms.example: Working parents often need help with their children.
forms.note: Common phrases: 'working hours', 'working day', 'working conditions'. Also 'a working phone' = one that is not broken (another meaning).

syn.note: Having a paid job; more formal.

ant.note: Without a paid job.

forms.definition: possible to use or do in a practical way
forms.example: We need a workable plan before Monday.
forms.note: Belongs to work = function or succeed (the plan works), not work = a job.
There is no adverb from work.

people.definition: a person who does a job, especially with their hands
people.example: The factory has more than two hundred workers.

context.text: My sister works in a bank in Tashkent. Her working day starts at nine, and she gets home from work at six.

reviewer_note: Sense: work = paid job (noun). workable belongs to work = function, so other_meaning. Compounds (workplace, workshop, homework, hardworking) left out.

corpus_definition: A period of twelve months.

forms.definition: a period of twelve months, often from January to December
forms.example: It has been a long year.
forms.note: Common phrases: 'last year', 'next year', 'every year', 'ten years old'.

syn.note: Same length of time, said in a different way.
Very formal, mostly in 'per annum' about money: '$5,000 per annum'.

forms.note: There is no verb from year. (yearn = want very much is not related.)

forms.definition: happening once every twelve months
forms.example: The yearly music festival in Samarkand is very popular.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common, especially in writing.

forms.definition: once every twelve months
forms.example: The festival is held yearly in August.

syn.note: Same meaning, a bit more formal.
Easy, everyday words.
Easy, everyday words with the same meaning.

context.text: Our school has a yearly sports day in May. This year my brother won the running race.

reviewer_note: yearly is both adjective and adverb. yearn is not family. yearbook is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: Someone who admires or follows a person or group.
usage_note: be a fan of + person / team / band / thing: 'I'm a big fan of Pakhtakor.' Often with big or huge. Also: 'I'm not a fan of spicy food' = I don't like it much.

relations.note: Used most for sports teams and political groups: 'a Pakhtakor supporter'.
More formal; often for a person you like or respect, such as a writer or artist.
Someone who follows a person on social media or follows a leader's ideas; not always a big fan.
Only in phrases like 'a music lover' or 'a book lover'; on its own it means a romantic partner.
A critic says bad things about a person or their work; a fan says good things.

context.text: My brother is a huge fan of Real Madrid and watches every match. I'm not really a fan of football, but I am a fan of Uzbek pop music.

reviewer_note: Phrase kept as 'a fan of'; noted the common negative use 'not a fan of' = don't like much.

corpus_definition: A match where you compete with another person or team.
usage_note: a game against + team / person: 'We have a game against Bunyodkor on Sunday.' Also play against, win / lose a game against.

relations.note: The same meaning; match is very common in British English for football and tennis.
Also possible, but careful: 'a game with my friends' can mean playing together, not against each other.
More formal; a contest can be any competition, not only sport.

context.text: Our school team has a game against a team from Samarkand next week. Last year we lost the game against them, so we are training hard.

reviewer_note: Phrase kept as noun + preposition; no true antonym. 'a game with' can also mean playing together, noted as weaker.

corpus_definition: A particular kind or group of items.
usage_note: a type of + noun (usually no 'a' after 'of'): 'a type of fruit', not 'a type of a fruit'. Plural: 'different types of bread'.

relations.note: The same meaning and very common in speaking.
The same meaning; a little more informal, common in British English.
Often used for sports, art, energy or transport: 'a form of exercise'.
Careful: 'a variety of fruit' usually means many different kinds, not one kind.

context.text: Plov is a type of rice dish that is popular in Uzbekistan. There are many different types of plov, and each region cooks it in its own way.

reviewer_note: Noted the 'a type of a fruit' learner error and the variety of = many kinds trap.

corpus_definition: The skill or power to perform an action.

forms.definition: the skill or power to do something
forms.example: She has a great ability to paint well.

syn.note: A skill is usually learned through practice; ability can be natural or learned.
More formal; often used about machines, companies or armies.
A talent is a natural ability you are born with, like singing or drawing.
Power is about having the strength or control to do something.

ant.note: The fact that you cannot do something: 'his inability to swim'.

forms.definition: to make it possible for someone to do something
forms.example: The new bridge will enable people to cross the river quickly.
forms.note: Pattern: enable someone to do something. A little formal.

syn.note: Very close: allow someone to do something.
Easy and informal; no 'to': let someone do something.
Help makes something easier; enable makes it possible.

ant.note: To stop something from happening or someone from doing something.
Easy word: stop someone from doing something.

forms.definition: having the skill or power to do something
forms.example: Will you be able to come to the party on Friday?
forms.note: Most common in 'be able to + verb'. Ability is made from this word.

syn.note: Same meaning; pattern: capable OF doing something.
Skilled means you have learned to do something well.

ant.note: Not having the skill or power to do something: 'I was unable to sleep.'

forms.definition: in a skilful way; very well
forms.example: The team was ably led by its young captain.
forms.note: Not very common; usually in writing.

syn.note: Same meaning. American spelling: skillfully.
The easy everyday word.

ant.note: In a way that is not good or not skilful.

context.text: Aziza has a real ability to explain hard ideas. Because of her, our whole class was able to pass the exam. Her lessons enabled us to understand grammar at last.

reviewer_note: Ability is made from able (stem change), so no -ity split is claimed; inability/unable are kept as antonyms, not forms. disability left out (other sense, health).

corpus_definition: on or onto a ship, train, or aircraft

forms.definition: the act of getting onto a plane, ship or train
forms.example: Boarding starts thirty minutes before the plane leaves.
forms.note: Common at airports: boarding pass, boarding gate. In other contexts it can mean living at a school (boarding school).

syn.note: Formal word used for ships and planes.

forms.definition: to get onto a plane, ship, train or bus
forms.example: We boarded the train to Bukhara at seven o'clock.
forms.note: Aboard is made from a- + this word. Board is also a noun with other meanings (a piece of wood, a group of managers).

syn.note: Easy everyday phrasal verb with the same meaning.
Formal; used mostly for ships.
Used for cars and taxis rather than planes and trains.

ant.note: To leave a bus, train, plane or ship.
Formal: to leave a ship or plane.

forms.note: No adjective in this family; people say 'on board' instead.

forms.definition: on or onto a ship, plane or train
forms.example: All passengers must be aboard before the ship departs.
forms.note: Also used as a preposition: 'aboard the ship'. 'Welcome aboard!' is a friendly greeting to new passengers or new team members.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday speech.

ant.note: On or onto land from a ship.

context.text: At Tashkent airport, boarding began at nine. We boarded the plane quickly, and soon everyone was aboard.

reviewer_note: a- is not in the affix table, so no prefix is claimed on aboard. boarder (lodger / boarding-school pupil) left out: other sense and not common at A2.

corpus_definition: In or to a foreign country.

forms.note: No noun in this family. 'from abroad' uses the adverb after a preposition: 'students from abroad'.
No adjective form; use 'foreign' or 'overseas' (not the same family).

forms.definition: in or to a foreign country
forms.example: He often travels abroad for his work.
forms.note: No 'to' before it: 'go abroad', not 'go to abroad'. Broad (= wide) is a different word today, even though the history is shared.

syn.note: Same meaning; in British English it suggests across the sea.
General: not at home, but not always in another country.

ant.note: In your own country: 'Do you work at home or abroad?'

context.text: Many young people from Uzbekistan want to study abroad. My cousin went abroad last year and now studies in Korea.

reviewer_note: Common learner error 'go to abroad' noted. broad listed as not_family: same old root but a different meaning.

corpus_definition: A record of money that you keep in a place.

forms.definition: an arrangement with a bank to keep your money there
forms.example: She opened a new savings account today.
forms.note: Also used for websites and apps: an email account, an Instagram account.

syn.note: The full phrase; same meaning when we talk about money.
The money you keep, not the arrangement with the bank.
The amount of money that is in the account now.

forms.definition: the fact of being responsible for what you do
forms.example: People want more accountability from the government.
forms.note: Goes with accountable; belongs to account = explaining your actions.

forms.definition: to explain why something happened (always followed by 'for')
forms.example: How do you account for the missing money?
forms.note: Belongs to account = explanation or reason, not a bank account. Also 'account for' = make up a part: 'Students account for half the town.'

forms.definition: responsible for your decisions and actions
forms.example: Managers must be accountable for their mistakes.
forms.note: Belongs to account = explaining what you did, not a bank account.
accountably exists but is very rare.

people.definition: a person whose job is to keep or check money records
people.example: Our company accountant prepares the tax papers every year.

people.definition: the job or subject of keeping and checking money records
people.example: She studied accounting at university in Tashkent.
people.note: British English also uses accountancy.

context.text: I opened an account at a bank in Tashkent last month. My sister is an accountant, so she helped me choose the best one.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows are the same bank sense, merged. Verb account (for) and accountable/accountability belong to the 'explanation' sense and are other_meaning.

corpus_definition: The process of doing something to reach a goal.

forms.definition: the process of doing something to deal with a problem or reach a goal
forms.example: We need quick action to solve this.
forms.note: Common phrase: take action. Also countable: 'Your actions have consequences.'

syn.note: One action in a plan: 'take steps to fix the problem'.
Formal; an official action to deal with a problem.
Something you do to get a result, often in business or politics.
An old or literary word for something someone does, often good or bad.

ant.note: Doing nothing when you should do something.

forms.definition: something that people do, or a situation where a lot is happening
forms.example: There are lots of activities for children at the summer camp.

forms.definition: to do something to deal with a situation
forms.example: The police acted quickly to stop the fight.
forms.note: Action is made from this word. Act also means 'to perform in a play or film' and 'to behave'.

syn.note: Easy everyday phrase: 'We must do something now.'
More formal: do things to deal with a problem.
To act because something has happened.

ant.note: To do nothing until something happens.

forms.definition: to make a machine or system start working
forms.example: Press this button to activate the alarm.
forms.note: Belongs to the 'start working' idea (active machines), not people taking action.

forms.definition: doing things and taking part, not just watching
forms.example: My grandmother is still very active in our neighbourhood.

syn.note: Busy means you have a lot to do; active means you like to do things.
Having a lot of energy to do things.
Taking part in something: 'involved in the project'.

ant.note: Not doing anything or not taking part.
Letting things happen without trying to change them.

forms.definition: in a way that involves doing things and taking part
forms.example: She actively helps old people in her mahalla.

syn.note: With a lot of energy.
While doing many things.

ant.note: Without trying to do or change anything.

people.definition: a person who works hard to bring social or political change
people.example: Young activists cleaned the river bank on Saturday.

people.definition: a person who performs in films, plays or TV shows
people.example: The actor won a prize for his new film.
people.note: Belongs to act = perform in a play or film, not doing something to reach a goal.

people.definition: a woman who performs in films, plays or TV shows
people.example: She became a famous actress in Uzbek cinema.
people.note: Belongs to act = perform. Many people now use actor for women too.

context.text: The town had a lot of rubbish in the streets, so the mayor decided to act. He took action and asked active young people to help. Now the students actively clean the park every week.

reviewer_note: Actor/actress are other_meaning (perform). inaction/inactive kept as antonyms, not forms. act (noun) not added separately: same spelling as the verb.

corpus_definition: A message designed to sell products to people.

forms.definition: a picture, film or short text that tries to make people buy something
forms.example: I saw an advertisement for new shoes.
forms.note: Short forms: ad (common everywhere) and advert (British). Pronunciation differs: British /ədˈvɜːtɪsmənt/, American /ˌædvərˈtaɪzmənt/.

syn.note: Short, informal form of the same word; very common.
An advertisement on TV or radio only.
A large printed picture on a wall; it may or may not sell something.
Any activity to make a product popular, such as special prices.

forms.definition: to tell people about a product so that they buy it
forms.example: The new cafe advertises on Instagram and Telegram.
forms.note: Always spelled -ise, even in American English. Advertisement is made from this word.

syn.note: To help something sell or become popular, in many ways.
To make many people know about something. British spelling: publicise.

forms.note: No common adjective; 'advertised' is only a participle ('the advertised price').

people.definition: the business of making ads and showing them to people
people.example: My brother works in advertising in Tashkent.

people.definition: a person or company that pays to show ads
people.example: Many advertisers pay to use this website.

context.text: Our family shop wants more customers, so we decided to advertise online. My sister made a short advertisement for Telegram, and many people saw it.

reviewer_note: ad/advert are clipped forms of advertisement, listed as a synonym (not a separate family form) because learners need them; check this is acceptable. -ise spelling note added.

corpus_definition: To have the same opinion as someone else.
particle_note: Not separable: 'agree with someone / something' (agree with you, agree with your idea). Use 'agree that + clause' without 'with': 'I agree that it's expensive.' Not 'I am agree'.

relations.note: To support one person in an argument.
Informal idiom: to have the same opinion as someone.
To say you like an idea or plan and want it to succeed.
To say yes to an idea, even if you don't fully share the opinion.
To have a different opinion from someone.
To speak angrily with someone because you think differently.

context.text: My father thinks we should visit Khiva in spring, and I agree with him. My mother doesn't agree with us, because she wants to go in autumn.

reviewer_note: Prepositional verb treated as phrasal (inseparable). Common Uzbek/Russian-speaker error 'I am agree' noted.

corpus_definition: in a voice that others can hear, not silently

forms.definition: how strong or big a sound is
forms.example: The loudness of the music woke up the baby.
forms.note: Made from loud, the word that aloud comes from.

syn.note: Volume is the everyday word for how strong a sound is: 'turn the volume down'.
Noise is a sound, often unpleasant; loudness is how strong a sound is.

ant.note: Quietness is when there is little or no sound.
Silence is when there is no sound at all.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family. Use 'read out' or 'say out loud'.

forms.definition: making a strong sound that is easy to hear
forms.example: My neighbour has a very loud voice.
forms.note: Aloud is made from a- + loud. Aloud only means 'so people can hear'; loud means 'with a lot of sound'.

syn.note: Noisy is often about a place or people making too much sound.
Formal: possible to hear, but not always strong.

ant.note: Making little sound.
A soft voice or sound is gentle and not strong.

forms.definition: speaking so that other people can hear you, not silently
forms.example: Please read the passage aloud to the class.
forms.note: Common phrases: read aloud, think aloud, laugh aloud.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday speech: 'read it out loud'.
Formal: in a way people can hear.

ant.note: Without making any sound: 'read silently'.
With very little sound.

forms.definition: with a strong sound that is easy to hear
forms.example: The children laughed loudly in the garden.
forms.note: Don't confuse: aloud = not silently; loudly = with a lot of sound.

syn.note: Making a lot of noise, often too much.

ant.note: With very little sound.
Gently, without a strong sound.

context.text: In our English lesson in Bukhara, the teacher asked Dilnoza to read the story aloud. She was nervous, so she did not speak very loudly at first.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: aloud (not silently) vs loudly (with a lot of sound); aloud is a- + loud, but a- is not in the affix table, so no affix is claimed for aloud.

corpus_definition: Used to show that something is different than expected.
usage_note: although + clause: 'Although it was cold, we went out.' It can start the sentence or join two parts in the middle, but it can't go at the end (use though there).

relations.note: Same meaning and a little more informal; only though can go at the end of a sentence.
Stronger: the surprise is bigger. 'Even though he was ill, he came to work.'
Also shows contrast, but joins the ideas the other way round: 'It was cold, but we went out.'
Formal, used to compare two facts: 'While some people like tea, others prefer coffee.'

context.text: We went to the park although it was cold in Tashkent. Although the wind was strong, the children played outside for an hour.

reviewer_note: Function word (conjunction): simple map with no word forms. Though is a synonym here, not a form.

corpus_definition: very good or surprising in a pleasant way.

forms.definition: a feeling of great surprise
forms.example: She looked at the mountains in amazement.

syn.note: Easy, general word; amazement is a very strong surprise.
Very close, a little more formal.
Wonder is surprise mixed with admiration for something beautiful.

forms.definition: to surprise someone very much
forms.example: Her beautiful singing always amazes me.

syn.note: Easy, general word; amaze is stronger.
Very close in meaning.
To make someone admire you; not always a surprise.
Stronger: so surprised that you can't speak.

ant.note: To make someone feel tired and not interested.

forms.definition: very good, or surprising in a nice way
forms.example: That movie was absolutely amazing.
forms.note: Use 'absolutely amazing', not 'very amazing'.

syn.note: Very close: very good and pleasant.
Very close, a little informal.
Very good, or so surprising it is hard to believe.
Easy, everyday word, a little weaker.
Stronger on surprise, not always good.

ant.note: Very bad.
Not interesting or surprising at all.
Normal, not special in any way.

forms.definition: feeling very surprised
forms.example: I was amazed by how fast he learned Russian.
forms.note: Amazed = how you feel; amazing = the thing that causes the feeling.

syn.note: Easy, general word; amazed is stronger.
Very close in meaning.

forms.definition: very, or in a very surprising way
forms.example: The food in the new cafe was amazingly cheap.

syn.note: Very close: 'incredibly cheap'.
Weaker: just more than you expected.
Always positive: in a very good way.

context.text: We visited Samarkand last summer, and the old buildings were amazing. I was amazed by the blue tiles, and the food was amazingly cheap.

reviewer_note: -ing/-ed trap: amazing (causes the feeling) vs amazed (has the feeling); both shown in the adjective slot.

corpus_definition: A thought or belief that you hold.
usage_note: have / give / ask for an opinion about + noun or -ing: 'What is your opinion about the movie?' Also 'an opinion on' (a little more formal) and 'in my opinion' to give your own view.

relations.note: Very close, a little more formal: 'What's your view on the new rules?'
The same meaning; 'on' is common in more serious topics.
Friendly and everyday: 'What are your thoughts on the plan?'
The way one person sees a situation.
Stronger: something you feel sure is true, often about religion or values.

context.text: My friend Aziz always has an opinion about football. When I asked for his opinion about the new coach, he talked for an hour.

reviewer_note: Noun phrase; 'fact' is not a true antonym, so none listed.

corpus_definition: the yearly return of the date of a special event

forms.definition: the same date each year as an important event in the past
forms.example: They celebrated their wedding anniversary with dinner.
forms.note: Common phrases: wedding anniversary, 10th anniversary. A person's birth date is a birthday, not an anniversary.

syn.note: A special anniversary, often 25 or 50 years, usually for a king, queen or organisation.
Only for the day a person was born.
A party or special event; you often have one on an anniversary.

forms.note: No verb. Use 'celebrate an anniversary'.
No adjective made from anniversary.
No adverb made from anniversary.

context.text: Next week is my parents' 30th wedding anniversary. We are planning a big dinner for the whole family in Andijan.

reviewer_note: annual/annually share the Latin root annus (year) but are not made from anniversary, so they are not_family.

corpus_definition: To speak loudly and angrily with someone about a disagreement.
usage_note: argue with + person + about + noun / -ing: 'She argues with her brother about money.' Use 'about' (or 'over') for the topic and 'with' for the person.

relations.to: have an argument with sb about
relations.note: The same meaning, using the noun argument.
Very close, more common in British English and a little old-fashioned.
Informal: an angry argument, not always with hitting.
You have a different opinion, but you may not be angry or loud.
To have the same opinion as someone.

context.text: My brothers often argue with each other about football. Last night they argued with my dad about which team is the best in Uzbekistan.

reviewer_note: sb = somebody; context replaces it with a real person.

corpus_definition: To reach a large place like a city or country.
particle_note: Not separable: 'arrive in Tashkent', never 'arrive Tashkent in'. Use 'arrive in' for cities and countries, 'arrive at' for buildings, airports and stations, and no preposition with home, here and there.

relations.note: Everyday English: 'We got to London at 9.'
No preposition after it: 'We reached London at 9.'
Only when you arrive by plane.
To go away from a place.
Formal, used for trains and planes.

context.text: We arrived in Samarkand late at night. Our cousins were waiting for us, because we always call them when we arrive in a new city.

reviewer_note: Verb + preposition, kept as phrasal; key learner trap is in vs at, explained in particle_note.

corpus_definition: Objects like paintings or statues made to look beautiful.

forms.definition: paintings, drawings and statues that people make to be beautiful
forms.example: I love looking at modern art in the gallery.
forms.note: Usually uncountable: 'a lot of art', not 'many arts'. 'The arts' means music, theatre, painting and so on together.

syn.note: A single piece of art, or art in general.
Only one kind of art, made with paint.
Art made from stone, metal or wood, like a statue.

forms.definition: great skill in making or doing something creative
forms.example: Everyone admired the artistry of the carpet makers.
forms.note: Belongs to art = skill, not the objects themselves.
No verb in this family. Use 'make art', 'paint' or 'draw'.

forms.definition: connected with paintings, music and other creative work
forms.example: Bukhara has a rich artistic history.
forms.note: Also means 'good at drawing or painting': 'She is very artistic.'

syn.note: Easy word: good at making new and beautiful things.
About art, music and traditions of a group of people.

ant.note: Useful in real life, not made just to look beautiful.

forms.definition: clever at getting what you want, often by tricking people
forms.example: He gave an artful answer and avoided the real question.
forms.note: Belongs to art = clever skill or tricks, not paintings and statues.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with painting, music and other creative work
forms.example: The new hotel is artistically decorated with local pottery.

syn.note: In a way that shows new and interesting ideas.
Only about how it looks.

people.definition: a person who paints, draws or makes statues
people.example: The artist sells her paintings near the Registan.

people.definition: a person who makes things by hand with great skill
people.example: Local artisans make silk scarves in Margilan.
people.note: Belongs to art = skill or craft, not paintings and statues.

context.text: There is a new art gallery near our school in Tashkent. My sister is very artistic, and she wants to be an artist one day.

reviewer_note: artificial and artefact/artifact share the old root (art = skill) but are not learner-transparent family here; artistry/artful/artisan kept as other_meaning (art = skill). Compounds (artwork) left out of forms.

corpus_definition: feeling embarrassed or guilty about something you did

forms.definition: the bad feeling you have when you know you did something wrong
forms.example: He felt deep shame after he lied to his friend.
forms.note: 'What a shame!' / 'It's a shame' means 'What a pity!', a different meaning.

syn.note: Guilt is knowing you did wrong; shame is more about how others see you.
Weaker: you feel silly, not always because you did something wrong.
Losing other people's respect.

ant.note: The good feeling about something you did well.

forms.definition: to make someone feel bad about something wrong they did
forms.example: His parents tried to shame him into telling the truth.

syn.note: Easier word, a little weaker.
Stronger: to make someone feel stupid in front of others.
To make people lose respect for you or your family.

ant.note: To say good things about what someone did.

forms.definition: feeling bad and guilty because of something wrong you did
forms.example: He was ashamed of lying to his best friend.
forms.note: ashamed of + noun / -ing; ashamed to + verb. Used after the noun, not before it: 'He was ashamed', not 'an ashamed boy'.

syn.note: Weaker: you feel silly, not always guilty.
You know you did something wrong.
Easy word: you feel bad and wish you hadn't done it.
Stronger: very ashamed because others saw it.

ant.note: Feeling happy about something you or others did.
Not feeling ashamed, even when others think you should.

forms.definition: so bad that people should feel guilty about it
forms.example: Leaving the dog without water was shameful.
forms.note: Ashamed = how a person feels; shameful = the bad action.

syn.note: Very close in meaning.
Weaker: makes you feel silly.

ant.note: Good and deserving respect. American spelling: honorable.

forms.definition: not feeling bad when you do something wrong
forms.example: It was a shameless lie, and everyone knew it.

syn.note: Doing something bad openly, without caring.

forms.definition: in a very bad way that should make you feel guilty
forms.example: The old workers were treated shamefully.

syn.note: Very close in meaning.
Easy, general word, much weaker.

ant.note: In a good way that deserves respect. American spelling: honorably.

forms.definition: in an open way, without feeling bad about doing wrong
forms.example: He shamelessly copied his friend's homework.

syn.note: So that everyone can see; not always bad.

context.text: Jasur told his teacher a lie about his homework. Later he felt ashamed, and he said sorry because he knew his lie was shameful.

reviewer_note: ashamed = a- + shamed (a- not in affix table, no affix claimed). Feeling vs action trap: ashamed (person) vs shameful (action). unashamed is the opposite of ashamed, so it is in ashamed's ant list, not in forms.

corpus_definition: To tell someone you want something.
particle_note: Not separable: 'ask for water', never 'ask water for'. The person goes after ask: 'ask the waiter for the bill'. Common: ask for help, ask for advice.

relations.note: Formal, no 'for' after it: 'request information'.
Only for food, drinks or things you buy: 'order a pizza'.
Stronger: you ask in a strong way and expect to get it.
To ask in a very strong, emotional way.
To say you will give something to someone.

context.text: At the restaurant in Namangan, I asked for a glass of green tea. When I didn't understand the menu, I asked the waiter for help.

reviewer_note: Pattern trap: ask + person + for + thing; request takes no 'for'.

corpus_definition: Something or someone that looks very nice or pleasant to see.

forms.definition: the quality of looking nice and pleasant to see
forms.example: The attractiveness of the old city brings many tourists to Bukhara.

syn.note: Very close and much more common in everyday English.
Charm is about a pleasant, friendly quality, not only about looks.
Appeal is the quality that makes people want something or like it.

ant.note: The quality of looking bad or unpleasant.

forms.definition: a feeling of liking someone or something, often because of their looks
forms.example: There was a strong attraction between them from the first day.
forms.note: Also means an interesting place to visit: 'The Registan is the main tourist attraction in Samarkand.'

syn.note: Interest is weaker: you want to know more, but you may not like it.
Informal: the power that makes you want to go somewhere or be near someone.

forms.definition: to make people like someone or something, or want to come closer
forms.example: Bright flowers attract bees and butterflies.

syn.note: Used with crowds and people: 'The concert drew a big crowd.'
To be interesting or pleasant to someone.
To make someone want to know more; not always about looks.

ant.note: To make people or animals stay away. Formal.

forms.definition: looking nice and pleasant, so people like to see it
forms.example: She wore an attractive dress to the party.
forms.note: Also used for ideas and offers: 'an attractive price'.

syn.note: Easy word, used mostly for women, girls, places and small things.
Easy and very close, used for people.
Stronger: very attractive.
Very general and easy; nice can be about anything pleasant.
Pleasant and interesting; often used for ideas or food.

ant.note: The direct opposite, a little more polite than ugly.
Strong and not polite when used about a person.

forms.definition: in a way that looks nice and pleasant
forms.example: The cakes were attractively arranged in the shop window.

syn.note: Easy and common in everyday English.
Stronger: in a very nice way.

context.text: The new cafe in Chilonzor is very attractive. The owners painted it in bright colours to attract young people, and the cakes are attractively arranged on the shelves.

reviewer_note: attraction kept as a same-meaning noun (liking someone); its 'tourist attraction' use is a note, not a separate entry, to avoid repeating the form in People & things.

corpus_definition: A person who writes books or stories as their job.

forms.definition: a person who writes books or stories, usually as a job
forms.example: The author signed copies of her new book.

syn.note: Easy and very close; writer is more common in everyday speech.
A person who writes novels (long stories) only.
A person who writes poems, not books of stories.

forms.definition: the fact of being the person who wrote a book or text
forms.example: Nobody knows the authorship of this old poem.

forms.definition: to write a book, article or report
forms.example: She has authored three books about the history of Khiva.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Literary or used in newspapers: 'He penned a letter.'

forms.definition: connected with the person who wrote a book or text
forms.example: The novel has a strong authorial voice.
forms.note: Rare and formal; you will mostly see it in book reviews. Authoritative looks similar but comes from authority (power), not from writing books.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My favourite author lives in Tashkent. She has authored five books for children. Her authorship of a famous fairy tale book is still a surprise to many people.

reviewer_note: Person-noun headword kept as main noun entry; author is not author + -or (no 'auth'), so no affix claimed. Authorial is author + -ial (not in the affix table), so no affix claimed there either. Authoress is old-fashioned and left out.

corpus_definition: Something that is very good or impressive.

forms.definition: a feeling of great respect mixed with wonder or a little fear
forms.example: We looked up at the mountains in awe.
forms.note: Belongs to awesome = so big or powerful that it fills you with respect (the older meaning), not the informal 'very good'.

forms.definition: to fill someone with great respect and wonder
forms.example: The children were awed by the size of the old city walls.
forms.note: Belongs to the older meaning (great respect and wonder), not the informal 'very good'. Mostly used in the passive: be awed by.

forms.definition: very good, exciting or impressive
forms.example: That concert was truly awesome!
forms.note: Very common in American English, especially among young people.

syn.note: Very close and easy; a little less informal.
Easy everyday word, a little weaker.
Very close, used in both British and American English.
Informal, often used by young people.
Makes you admire it; more neutral and can be used in formal English.

ant.note: Very bad; easy everyday word.
Very bad; a little stronger and more British than terrible.

forms.definition: very bad or unpleasant
forms.example: The weather was awful, so we stayed at home.
forms.note: Comes from awe too, but today it means very bad: almost the opposite of awesome. A false friend inside the family.

forms.definition: in a very good or impressive way
forms.example: Our team played awesomely in the second half.
forms.note: Not very common; people often say 'really well' instead.

syn.note: In a very clever or very good way; common in British English.
In a very surprising and good way.

ant.note: In a very bad way: 'He played terribly.'

forms.definition: very, or very much
forms.example: I'm awfully sorry I'm late.
forms.note: Comes from awful, not from the 'very good' meaning. It just makes words stronger: awfully sorry, awfully kind.

context.text: We went to a football match in Tashkent last night, and it was awesome! Our team played awesomely in the second half and won three to one.

reviewer_note: False-friend trap: awful/awfully come from awe but mean 'very bad'/'very', shown as other_meaning; awe noun and verb belong to the older 'respect and wonder' meaning. -some is not in the affix table, so no affix on awesome.

corpus_definition: a heavy tool with a sharp blade used for cutting wood

forms.definition: a heavy tool with a sharp metal blade for cutting wood
forms.example: He used an ax to chop firewood in the yard.
forms.note: American spelling. British English: axe. Plural: axes.

syn.note: A small one with a short handle, used with one hand.
A heavy knife for cutting meat; also an informal word for a helicopter.

forms.definition: to suddenly end a plan or service, or get rid of jobs
forms.example: The company axed 200 jobs last year.
forms.note: Belongs to ax = cutting jobs, plans or costs (common in news), not the tool. British spelling: axe.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandfather keeps an old ax in the shed. Every autumn he uses the ax to chop wood for the winter.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: American ax vs British axe noted; the verb (cut jobs) is a different meaning.

corpus_definition: The things that are behind the main subject in a picture.

forms.definition: the part of a picture or view that is behind the main thing
forms.example: The mountain is visible in the background of the photo.
forms.note: It also means a person's family, education and experience: 'She comes from a farming background.' Used before nouns too: background music, background noise.

syn.note: Often the painted cloth behind actors, or a view behind an event.
The place where something happens, not only what is behind it.
Natural views like hills and fields, or the painted pictures in a theatre.

ant.note: The part of a picture that is nearest to you, at the front.

forms.note: There is no common verb in this family.
No adjective. The noun is used before other nouns instead: background music, background colour.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: In this photo of the Registan, you can see a blue sky in the background. For a passport photo, you need a plain white background.

reviewer_note: Compound word (back + ground); no family forms or affixes. The 'family and education' sense is noted on the base entry, not mapped here.

corpus_definition: Moving toward the direction that is behind you.

forms.definition: the state of being less developed than other places or people
forms.example: The report spoke about the backwardness of some village schools.
forms.note: Belongs to backward = less developed, not moving toward the back. It can sound rude about people.
There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: directed toward the back or toward where you started
forms.example: She gave a quick backward look before leaving the room.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: a backward step. It can also mean less developed than others, but that use can sound rude.

syn.note: Going the opposite way: 'in reverse order'.
At the back of something: 'the rear door'.

ant.note: Directed toward the front: 'a forward movement'.

forms.definition: toward the direction that is behind you
forms.example: She walked backwards toward the exit.
forms.note: American English often uses backward as the adverb too.

syn.note: Easy and common: 'Step back, please.'
Used for cars and for doing things in the opposite order.

ant.note: Toward the front. American English usually says forward.

context.text: The little boy walked backwards so he could wave to his grandmother. She gave a quick backward look from the bus window and smiled.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: backward (adjective, and US adverb) vs backwards (adverb); -ward(s) is not in the affix table, so no affix claimed.

corpus_definition: A person whose job is making bread or cakes.

forms.definition: a person whose job is making bread and cakes
forms.example: The baker makes fresh bread every single morning.
forms.note: The baker's (with 's) means the shop: 'I'm going to the baker's.'

syn.note: A cook who makes cakes and sweet food, often in a restaurant.
A person who makes any kind of food.

forms.definition: the activity of making bread, cakes and biscuits in an oven
forms.example: My mother loves baking on Sunday mornings.

syn.note: Making any kind of food, not only bread and cakes.

forms.definition: to cook bread, cakes or other food in an oven
forms.example: We bake non in a tandoor at my grandmother's house.

syn.note: Cook is general; this word is only for food cooked in an oven with dry heat.
Also in an oven, but used for meat and vegetables.

forms.definition: cooked in an oven
forms.example: I'd like baked potatoes with my fish, please.

syn.note: Also cooked in an oven, usually meat, nuts or vegetables.

ant.note: Not cooked at all.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a shop or place where bread and cakes are made and sold
people.example: There is a small bakery next to our school.

context.text: The baker on our street gets up at four o'clock to bake fresh non. His baking is famous in the whole mahalla.

reviewer_note: Person-noun headword kept as main noun entry; bakery goes in People & things as a place. No -y affix claimed on bakery (the ending is really -ery).

corpus_definition: A shop where you can buy bread and cakes.

forms.definition: a shop where bread and cakes are made and sold
forms.example: We bought a cake at the local bakery.

syn.note: Easy and clear, but a cake shop may sell only cakes.
Sells mostly cakes and sweet things, not bread.
A French word for a shop selling fine cakes and pastries.

forms.definition: the activity of making bread, cakes and biscuits in an oven
forms.example: The smell of fresh baking filled the street.

syn.note: Making any kind of food, not only bread and cakes.

forms.definition: to cook bread, cakes or other food in an oven
forms.example: They bake fresh samsa here every morning.

syn.note: Cook is general; this word is only for food cooked in an oven with dry heat.
Also in an oven, but used for meat and vegetables.

forms.definition: cooked in an oven
forms.example: This shop sells freshly baked bread.

syn.note: Also cooked in an oven, usually meat, nuts or vegetables.

ant.note: Not cooked at all.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person whose job is making bread and cakes
people.example: The baker gave us a warm loaf of bread.

context.text: There is a small bakery next to our school. Every morning the baker gets up early to bake warm non and samsa.

reviewer_note: Place-noun headword kept as main noun entry (like rule 6); baker goes in People & things. No -y affix claimed on bakery.

corpus_definition: a tall, fast-growing grass with a hard, hollow stem

forms.definition: a tall plant with hard, hollow stems that grows very fast
forms.example: The panda sat quietly, chewing on a bamboo stalk.
forms.note: Used before nouns for things made from it: a bamboo chair, a bamboo basket.

syn.note: The hard, hollow stem of some plants, used to make furniture.
A tall, thin grass that grows near water; softer and smaller.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
No adjective. The noun is used before other nouns instead: a bamboo table.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Bamboo can grow almost a metre in one day. In many Asian countries, people use bamboo to make chairs, baskets and even houses.

reviewer_note: Leaf-type word: no family forms, no people, no affixes.

corpus_definition: an official rule that stops something from being done

forms.definition: an official rule that says people must not do something
forms.example: The government introduced a ban on plastic bags.
forms.note: Usually: a ban on + noun / -ing.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
A rule that limits something but may not stop it completely.
An official ban on trade with another country.

ant.note: When someone in charge says you can do something.

forms.definition: to officially say that something must not be done or used
forms.example: Many cities ban cars from the centre on Sundays.
forms.note: Past forms double the n: banned, banning.

syn.note: Very close; often used for parents and rules at home too.
Same meaning, more formal; common on signs.
Easy word, but more general: you can stop something without a rule.
To make something illegal by law.

ant.note: To let people do something; easy everyday word.
Same as allow, but more formal.

forms.definition: not allowed by an official rule or law
forms.example: Some players took banned drugs before the race.

syn.note: Very close, a little stronger.
Formal, often on signs: 'Smoking prohibited.'
Against the law; a school or club rule is not a law.

ant.note: OK to do or have.
Allowed by the law.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Our city has a ban on smoking in parks. Smoking is also banned near schools, and people who break the rule must pay a fine.

reviewer_note: Banner looks like ban + -er but is a different word (a long sign or flag), so it sits in people_not_family.

corpus_definition: a strip of cloth used to cover and protect a wound

forms.definition: a long piece of cloth that you wrap around a cut or injury
forms.example: The nurse wrapped a bandage around his injured hand.

syn.note: Used by doctors and nurses: a cover put on a wound. It can be a pad, not only a long strip.
British English: a small sticky piece you put on a small cut. American English says Band-Aid.

forms.definition: to wrap a strip of cloth around an injured part of the body
forms.example: The doctor cleaned the cut and bandaged my knee.

syn.note: Medical use: to clean and cover a wound. 'The nurse dressed the wound.'
General word: to put cloth or paper around anything, not only an injury.
To tie something tightly; a little formal or old-fashioned for wounds.

ant.note: To take the cloth off again.

forms.definition: covered with a strip of cloth because of an injury
forms.example: He came to school with a bandaged arm.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Aziz cut his finger while cooking plov. His mother washed the cut and bandaged it carefully. The next day he went to work with a white bandage on his hand.

reviewer_note: Noun and verb are the same spelling (conversion); no affix claimed. Band-Aid is a brand name, kept only in a note.

corpus_definition: A sudden loud noise.

forms.definition: a sudden, short and very loud noise
forms.example: The door shut with a loud bang.

syn.note: A loud noise, often when something falls or hits something and breaks.
A deep loud noise that lasts a little longer, like thunder or a big gun.
General word for any sound, loud or not.
The loud noise and force when something like a bomb blows up.

forms.definition: to hit something hard or close it so that it makes a loud noise
forms.example: Please don't bang the door when you leave.

syn.note: Used mostly for doors and windows: to shut them hard and loudly.
To hit something, often a door, but usually more quietly.
General word; it doesn't always make a loud noise.
To hit something with a lot of force, often causing damage.

forms.note: No adjective for the noise meaning. 'Banging' (= excellent) is informal British slang and not for learners.

forms.definition: exactly, completely (informal): right in the middle, right on time
forms.example: The train arrived bang on time.
forms.note: Belongs to bang = exactly, an informal British use, not the loud noise.

context.text: Late at night we heard a loud bang in the kitchen. My little brother had dropped a pot. Then the wind started to bang the window, so Dad closed it.

reviewer_note: Noun, verb and informal adverb all share one spelling; the adverb (bang on time) is other_meaning. 'Bangs' (US hair fringe) is not this family and left out.

corpus_definition: an arrangement with a financial firm to keep your money safe
usage_note: Countable noun: open / close / have a bank account; put money into or take money out of your bank account; pay something into someone's bank account.

relations.note: Shorter and very common when the topic is clearly money: 'I paid it into my account.'
One kind of bank account for keeping money you don't spend; the bank often pays you extra.
British English: the everyday bank account for your salary and payments. American English says checking account.

context.text: When Malika got her first job in Tashkent, she opened a bank account. Now her salary goes straight into her bank account every month.

reviewer_note: Noun phrase; no forms. Current account (UK) vs checking account (US) noted.

corpus_definition: the loud sharp sound a dog makes

forms.definition: the short loud sound that a dog makes
forms.example: The dog's bark woke everyone in the house.
forms.note: A different word with the same spelling means the hard outside covering of a tree.

syn.note: Informal, often used with children or to copy the sound: 'woof woof'.
A short high sound a dog makes when it is hurt or excited.
A low angry sound a dog makes in its throat.
A long loud cry, like a wolf at night.

forms.definition: (of a dog) to make short loud sounds
forms.example: Our neighbour's dog barks every time someone walks past.
forms.note: Also used for a person who shouts an order angrily: 'He barked at the children.'

syn.note: Used for small dogs making high, annoying sounds.
To make a low angry sound, not a sharp loud one.
To make a long loud crying sound.

forms.note: No adjective for the dog-sound meaning. 'Barky' belongs to the other word bark (tree covering), not this one, and is rare.
No adverb exists for this meaning.

context.text: Every evening the dog next door starts to bark at the cats. Its bark is so loud that my baby sister can't sleep.

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: bark (tree covering) is a separate word, mentioned only in a note. 'Barker' is rare and not added.

corpus_definition: A room or floor located below the ground level.

forms.definition: a room or floor of a building that is under the ground
forms.example: We keep old boxes in the basement.

syn.note: An underground room, usually used for storing things like food or wine, not for living in.
Used in British shops, hotels and flats for a floor that is partly under the ground.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.
No adjective exists in this family.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Our building in Chilonzor has a basement. In summer it stays cool, so my grandmother keeps jars of jam in the basement.

reviewer_note: Historically base + -ment, but learners don't see 'base' inside basement and no form of base belongs to this meaning, so no affix and no family forms are claimed.

corpus_definition: a round open container used for washing or holding liquids

forms.definition: a large round bowl, or a fixed sink in a bathroom, for washing or holding water
forms.example: She washed her hands in the basin.
forms.note: In geography the same word also means a large area of land around a river: the Aral Sea basin.

syn.note: The fixed bowl with taps in a kitchen or bathroom. More common in everyday speech.
A round open dish; usually smaller and used for food.
A large open container, often for washing clothes or for a bath.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.
No adjective exists in this family.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: At my grandmother's house in the village, there is a metal basin outside. We fill the basin with water and wash our faces in the morning.

reviewer_note: Single-form family. Washbasin is a compound and left for the Compounds branch; river-basin meaning only noted.

corpus_definition: to win against another person or team in a game

forms.definition: a big loss in a game or competition
forms.example: Our team took a real beating in the final, 5-0.
forms.note: Often in 'take a beating'. It can also mean hitting someone many times, so be careful with it.

syn.note: Neutral word for losing a game or fight; a beating is a big, heavy defeat.
Common in sports reports: 'their third loss this season'.
Informal: a very heavy defeat.

ant.note: Winning a game, fight or competition.
Everyday word for a victory in a game.

forms.definition: the regular rhythm in music
forms.example: I love the beat of this song.
forms.note: Belongs to beat = rhythm or a regular sound like a heartbeat, not winning a game.

forms.definition: to win against someone in a game or competition
forms.example: Our team beat theirs in the final.
forms.note: Irregular: beat, beat, beaten. Beat the other team, but win the game.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal; common in news reports.
Easy phrase with the same meaning. Don't say 'win them'; say 'beat them'.
Informal: to beat someone very easily, by a lot.
To beat a problem or a difficult enemy after a hard fight.

ant.note: If A beats B, B loses to A.

forms.definition: having lost a game, fight or competition
forms.example: The beaten players sat quietly on the bench.

syn.note: Same meaning, more common in writing.

ant.note: Never lost a game: 'They are unbeaten this season.'
The team or player that won: 'the winning team'.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

people.definition: a kitchen tool for mixing eggs or cream quickly
people.example: Mix the eggs with a beater until they are light.
people.note: Belongs to beat = mix food quickly, not winning a game.

context.text: Pakhtakor beat Navbahor 3-1 on Sunday. The beaten team went home quietly, but their coach said one beating would not stop them.

reviewer_note: Many-sense word: map keeps only 'win against'. Rhythm noun and kitchen beater are other_meaning; unbeaten is an antonym, not a form. beating also means hitting a person, noted.

corpus_definition: A person who is just starting to learn or do something.

forms.definition: a person who has just started to learn or do something
forms.example: This book is perfect for a beginner.
forms.note: Common in 'a beginners' class' and 'beginner level'.

syn.note: Anyone who is learning; a learner is not always new to it.
Same meaning, more formal.
A person who is new to a place or group, not only to a skill.

ant.note: A person who knows a lot and is very good at something.
A person with a lot of skill, often who does it as a job.

forms.definition: the first part of something, or the time when it starts
forms.example: At the beginning of the course, I didn't know any English.

forms.definition: to start doing something
forms.example: I began learning to swim last summer.
forms.note: Irregular: begin, began, begun.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday speech.
To start a new hobby or activity: 'She took up tennis.'

ant.note: To come to the end of something.
To not continue doing something.

forms.note: No adjective. English uses the noun before another noun instead: 'a beginner course', 'beginners' level'.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Dilnoza began guitar lessons in September. She was a complete beginner, and at the beginning she could only play two notes.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); People & things is empty because no other person/thing noun is made from begin. Double n spelling: beginner, beginning.

corpus_definition: The first part of an event or time period.

forms.definition: the first part of an event, story or period of time
forms.example: I liked the beginning of the movie.
forms.note: Common phrases: at the beginning of, from beginning to end.

syn.note: Same meaning, very common: 'at the start of the film'.
The first part of a film, book, speech or event.
Where something first came from, not just its first part.

ant.note: The last part of something: 'at the end of the movie'.
The last part of a story or film.

forms.definition: to start, or to start doing something
forms.example: The concert will begin at seven o'clock.
forms.note: Irregular: begin, began, begun.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday speech.
Very formal; used in official writing.

ant.note: To finish or come to the last part.
To complete something or come to the end.

forms.note: No adjective in learner dictionaries; 'beginning' before a noun (beginning students) is mainly American and rare for learners.
No adverb exists in this family.

people.definition: a person who has just started to learn or do something
people.example: This dance class is for beginners.

context.text: The film festival in Tashkent begins on Friday. At the beginning of each film, the director says a few words to the audience.

reviewer_note: Double n spelling (beginning, beginner). Separate corpus entry from 'beginner'; maps share the begin family but keep their own headword.

corpus_definition: To be the property of a specific person.
particle_note: Not separable: 'belong to + person': 'This bag belongs to Sardor.' Not used in continuous tenses: say 'it belongs to me', not 'it is belonging to me'. The thing is the subject, the owner comes after 'to'.

relations.note: Same meaning, passive form: 'The house is owned by my uncle.'
Easy everyday way: 'Is this pen yours?' = 'Does this pen belong to you?'
The opposite direction: the owner is the subject. 'I own this car' = 'This car belongs to me.'

context.text: I found a blue phone on the bus. I asked everyone, 'Does this phone belong to you?' In the end it belonged to the driver.

reviewer_note: Phrasal with fixed preposition 'to'; owner/thing word order reversed compared with 'own', explained in the note. No antonym exists.

corpus_definition: A document showing how much money you must pay.

forms.definition: a piece of paper that shows how much you must pay
forms.example: Did you pay the electricity bill yet?
forms.note: Other meanings of the same spelling: a bird's beak, a plan for a new law, and (American English) a paper banknote.

syn.note: A bill from a company for goods or work, used in business.
American English for the bill in a restaurant: 'Can we have the check, please?'
Informal: the money you owe in a bar or cafe, often paid at the end.
Careful: you get a bill BEFORE you pay and a receipt AFTER you pay.

forms.definition: to send someone a paper saying how much they must pay
forms.example: The hotel will bill you after your stay.

syn.note: Very close: ask someone to pay money for something.
Business word: send a written request for payment.

forms.note: 'Billable' (work you can charge money for) is a business word, not common for learners.

context.text: Our gas bill was very high this winter. The company bills us every month, so I always check the numbers carefully.

reviewer_note: Kept the payment sense only; beak, law and banknote senses noted on the noun. Billable left as rare.

corpus_definition: Having no writing or pictures on it.

forms.definition: an empty space on a page where you write a missing word
forms.example: Fill in the blanks with the correct words.

syn.note: Very close in exercises: 'fill in the gaps' is common in British English.
General word for an empty place on a page or form.

forms.note: Common in exercises: 'Fill in the blanks.'

forms.definition: to ignore someone on purpose, or to suddenly forget something
forms.example: I said hello, but she blanked me. / My mind blanked in the exam.
forms.note: Belongs to blank = ignore or forget (informal), not an empty page. Also 'blank out' = cover writing so it can't be read.

forms.definition: with nothing written, drawn or printed on it
forms.example: Please sign your name on the blank page.

syn.note: Easy and very close, but empty is more general: an empty box, an empty page.
Used for paper: 'a clean sheet of paper' has not been used.
Not used yet; blank is about having no writing or pictures.
Plain paper has no lines or pattern, but it may still have writing.

ant.note: A full page has writing all over it.

forms.definition: without showing any feeling or understanding on your face
forms.example: He looked at me blankly when I asked the question.
forms.note: Belongs to blank = a face showing no feeling or understanding ('a blank look'), not an empty page.

context.text: The teacher gave us a blank sheet of paper. On the test, there were ten blanks to fill in, but I left two of them empty.

reviewer_note: Noun 'blank' (gap in an exercise) kept as same meaning; verb blank (ignore) and blankly (no expression) are other meanings.

corpus_definition: to lose blood from the body through a cut or wound

forms.definition: the losing of the red liquid from a cut or wound
forms.example: Press hard on the cut to stop the bleeding.

syn.note: Same meaning; used more by doctors and in the news.
Medical word for very heavy, dangerous loss of red liquid from the body. American spelling: hemorrhage.

forms.definition: the red liquid that moves around inside your body
forms.example: There was blood on his knee after he fell.
forms.note: The verb bleed comes from this noun (blood → bleed, with a vowel change, like food → feed).

forms.definition: to lose the red liquid from your body because of a cut
forms.example: His knee was bleeding after he fell off his bike.
forms.note: Irregular: bleed – bled – bled.

syn.note: The same meaning in easy words.

forms.definition: losing the red liquid from a cut or wound
forms.example: She held a tissue to her bleeding nose.

syn.note: Related: hurt by a cut or a weapon; a wounded person may or may not be losing much liquid.
Related: 'a cut finger' has a small opening in the skin.

forms.definition: covered in red liquid from a cut or wound
forms.example: He came home with a bloody nose after the football match.
forms.note: In British English 'bloody' is also a rude word used to make speech stronger. Be careful.

syn.note: Showing a lot of injury and violence, often in films.

context.text: Jamshid cut his finger while cooking, and it started to bleed. His mother put a cloth on it, and soon the bleeding stopped.

reviewer_note: bleed comes from blood (vowel change), so blood and bloody are family. Bloody's swear-word use is noted.

corpus_definition: Having hair that is light yellow or gold in color.

forms.definition: a person, usually a woman, with light yellow hair
forms.example: The blonde in the photo is my cousin.
forms.note: Can sound rude or like a stereotype. It is often better to say 'a woman with blonde hair'.

ant.note: A woman with dark brown hair.
A person with red or orange hair.

forms.note: There is no verb; people say 'dye your hair blonde' or 'bleach your hair'.

forms.definition: with hair that is light yellow or gold
forms.example: The girl with blonde hair is my sister.
forms.note: Also spelled 'blond'. In British English 'blonde' is often used for women and 'blond' for men; American English usually uses 'blond' for both.

syn.note: Very close and common: 'fair hair' means light-colored hair.
Describes a warm yellow color, often used in stories about hair.
Light hair can be blonde or light brown.

ant.note: Dark hair is black or dark brown.
Having dark brown hair.

context.text: My little brother has blonde hair, which is rare in our family. Everyone else is dark, so people ask if the blonde boy is really ours.

reviewer_note: Spelling blond/blonde noted. Person noun 'blonde' kept as a conversion in the noun slot with a politeness note.

corpus_definition: The red liquid inside your body.

forms.definition: the red liquid that the heart sends around your body
forms.example: The doctor took some of my blood.
forms.note: Uncountable: 'a lot of blood', not 'bloods'. Blood test, blood group and blood pressure are common partners.

syn.note: Blood from a bad injury, especially in violent films.

forms.definition: the losing of the red liquid from a cut or wound
forms.example: The nurse stopped the bleeding quickly.

forms.definition: to lose the red liquid from your body through a cut
forms.example: Your finger is bleeding. Let me get a plaster.
forms.note: Irregular: bleed – bled – bled. Vowel change like food → feed.

syn.note: The same meaning in easy words.

forms.definition: covered in red liquid from a cut or wound
forms.example: The player left the field with a bloody knee.
forms.note: In British English 'bloody' is also a rude word used to make speech stronger. Be careful.

syn.note: Showing a lot of injury and violence, often in films.

forms.definition: without any killing or fighting; or very pale
forms.example: It was a bloodless revolution: nobody died.
forms.note: Belongs to blood = killing and violence ('a bloodless revolution'), or to a very pale face; not the liquid in your body.

context.text: Before his operation, Bobur gave blood for a test. The next day his arm was still bleeding a little where the needle went in.

reviewer_note: bleed comes from blood by vowel change (like food → feed), so it is a family form, not a separate root.

corpus_definition: to send out air from the mouth

forms.definition: the act of pushing air out of your mouth or nose
forms.example: Give your nose a good blow.
forms.note: The common noun 'a blow' usually means a hard hit ('a blow to the head') or a shock ('the news was a blow'). That is a different word with the same spelling.

syn.note: A short, quick push of air or smoke from the mouth.

forms.definition: to push air out of your mouth
forms.example: The child will blow out the birthday candles.
forms.note: Irregular: blow – blew – blown. Also used for the wind: 'The wind is blowing.'

syn.note: Close, but you breathe out all the time; you blow with force, often on purpose.
Formal and medical: let air out of your body.
Blow in short, quick pushes: 'puff on a cigarette'.

ant.note: Take air into your body.
Formal: take air into your body.
Pull air or liquid into your mouth.

forms.definition: with a lot of wind
forms.example: It was a cold, blowy day by the lake.
forms.note: Belongs to blow = the wind moving (informal, British English), not air from your mouth. 'Windy' is more common.

context.text: Aziza blew out all the candles on her birthday cake. Her little brother tried too, but his blow was too weak to put out even one.

reviewer_note: Noun blow = the act of blowing (Oxford) kept; the 'hard hit' noun is a separate word, mentioned only in the note.

corpus_definition: A fun activity played on a flat surface with pieces or cards.
usage_note: Countable noun: a board game, two board games. Usually with 'play': 'play a board game'. Examples: chess, backgammon (nardi in Uzbekistan), Monopoly.

relations.note: General word: any game, including sports and video games.
Close: any game played on a table, including card games and board games.
Related: played only with cards, not on a board.

context.text: On cold winter evenings my grandfather loves to play board games. His favorite board game is nardi, and he almost always wins.

reviewer_note: Compound noun treated as a phrase; no forms. Video game is a different kind of game, not an antonym.

corpus_definition: A weapon that explodes and causes great damage.

forms.definition: a weapon that explodes and causes great damage
forms.example: The police safely removed the live bomb.
forms.note: The final b is silent: /bɒm/ (UK), /bɑːm/ (US).

syn.note: A substance or object that can explode; a more technical word.
Used in the news: 'an explosive device' means a bomb.
Related: a weapon that flies through the air to its target.

forms.definition: an attack in which a weapon explodes
forms.example: Many buildings were destroyed in the bombing.

syn.note: General word for any violent action against people or places.
An attack by planes dropping explosive weapons.

forms.definition: to attack a place by dropping or exploding weapons
forms.example: The planes bombed the bridge during the war.
forms.note: Informal other meanings: 'bomb' can mean to fail badly ('the film bombed') or to go very fast.

syn.note: Destroy something with an explosion.
General word; bomb is one way to attack.
Attack with big guns, not with dropped weapons.

forms.note: 'Bombed' (informal: very drunk) and 'bombed-out' (destroyed) exist but are not common for learners.

people.definition: a person who attacks people or places with explosive weapons
people.example: The bomber was caught by the police.
people.note: Also a plane that carries and drops explosive weapons.

context.text: The old bomb from the war was found under a road. Experts say it is from a bombing in 1944, and it is safe now.

reviewer_note: 'bombard' is from an older French root and is not made from bomb in English, so it is listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: A hard, white part that forms the structure of the body.

forms.definition: one of the hard white parts inside the body of a person or animal
forms.example: Milk is good for making every bone strong.

syn.note: Related: the skeleton is all of these hard parts together.

forms.definition: to take the hard parts out of fish or meat before cooking
forms.example: Ask the shop to bone the chicken for you.

syn.note: Very close for fish: cut the meat away from the hard parts.

forms.definition: very thin, with almost no fat or meat on the body
forms.example: The old horse was tired and bony.
forms.note: Also used for fish that have many small hard parts: 'This fish is very bony.'

syn.note: Informal and easy: very thin, often in a bad way.
Easy, general word; bony is much stronger.

ant.note: A little fat in a pleasant way.
Having too much fat on the body.

forms.definition: with all the hard parts taken out
forms.example: We bought boneless chicken for the plov.

context.text: My grandmother broke a bone in her arm last winter. She says she is too bony and needs to eat more, so we cook her boneless chicken soup.

reviewer_note: bony drops the e (bone → bony). Compounds like backbone are left out.

corpus_definition: To reserve a place for a future time.

forms.definition: an arrangement to have a room, seat or ticket later
forms.example: I made a booking for two nights at a hotel in Bukhara.
forms.note: More common in British English.

syn.note: The same meaning; reservation is more common in American English.

ant.note: When you say you no longer want the room, seat or ticket.

forms.definition: a set of printed pages fixed together inside a cover
forms.example: I am reading a good book about Samarkand.
forms.note: Belongs to book = something you read. The verb 'book' (reserve) first meant writing a name in a book of orders.

forms.definition: to arrange to have a room, seat or ticket at a later time
forms.example: I need to book a flight tonight.

syn.note: The same meaning; a little more formal.
Same meaning, common in hotels and restaurants.
Related: you order food or things to buy, but you book places, rooms and tickets.

ant.note: Say you no longer want the room, seat or ticket.

forms.definition: already arranged for someone, with no free places
forms.example: Sorry, the restaurant is fully booked tonight.
forms.note: Often 'fully booked' or 'booked up'.

syn.note: Very close: a reserved table is kept for someone.
Easy word: no free places.

ant.note: Free for someone to take.
Not taken by anyone.

forms.definition: that can be arranged in advance
forms.example: Seats on this train are bookable online.

context.text: Dilnoza booked a train ticket to Samarkand for Friday. When she called the hotel, it was fully booked, so she made a booking at a guesthouse instead.

reviewer_note: Reserve sense only; the reading noun 'book' is other_meaning. Bookable kept (Oxford learner entry).

corpus_definition: Feeling unhappy because you have nothing interesting to do.
usage_note: be/get bored with + noun or -ing: 'I'm bored with this game.' 'bored of' is also common in informal British English; 'bored by' is used for the thing that makes you bored. Don't confuse with boring: the film is boring, so I am bored.

relations.note: Very close and informal; you have had enough and feel a bit angry.
Close: you don't want any more of something because you have done it too long.
Stronger and informal: you really don't want it any more.
You want to know more and pay attention.
You feel happy and full of energy about something.

context.text: After two hours of homework, Aziz got bored with his maths exercises. He was bored with sitting at the desk, so he went outside to play football.

reviewer_note: Adjective + preposition pattern, so kind phrase, not phrasal. Trap: bored (feeling) vs boring (cause) is flagged in the usage note.

corpus_definition: To take something temporarily and return it later.
particle_note: Pattern: borrow + thing + from + person/place: 'borrow a pen from you', 'borrow books from the library'. The thing usually comes between borrow and from. Never 'borrow someone something'; for that use lend: 'lend me a pen'.

relations.note: General word: take does not say you will give it back.
Used for money from a bank or person: 'get a loan from the bank'.
Related: you use something that belongs to someone else for a short time.
The other side: the owner lends something to you, and you borrow it from them.

context.text: Dilnoza forgot her calculator, so she borrowed one from her friend. Next week she will borrow some books from the school library too.

reviewer_note: Verb + preposition kept as phrasal like 'ask for' and 'agree with' in earlier batches. Main learner trap borrow vs lend is in particle_note and the antonym.

corpus_definition: the person in charge of a group or a place of work

forms.definition: the person who is in charge of you at work
forms.example: My boss told me to work faster today.

syn.note: Close, more formal; a manager runs one part of a company.
A person who watches and checks other workers' work.
