The most important person in a group: the head of the department.
The person with the highest rank, in a company or the police.
Related: the person or company that pays you to work.

ant.note: A person who works for someone else and gets paid.
A person who does the work, not the one in charge.

forms.definition: the habit of always telling other people what to do
forms.example: Her bossiness made the other students angry.

syn.note: Related: thinking you are better than others.

forms.definition: to tell people what to do in an unpleasant way
forms.example: Stop bossing your little brother around!
forms.note: Usually 'boss someone around' (American) or 'boss someone about' (British).

syn.note: Same idea: give people orders all the time. British English also says 'order about'.
Related: treat someone badly because you are stronger.
Related and formal: have strong control over someone.

forms.definition: always telling other people what to do
forms.example: My older sister is very bossy.

syn.note: Close: wanting to control what other people do.
Stronger and more formal than bossy.
Related: trying too hard to get what you want.

ant.note: Relaxed and happy to let others decide.

forms.note: Bossily is very rare; most people say 'in a bossy way'.

context.text: My boss in Tashkent is kind, but she is a little bossy. She likes to boss everyone around in meetings.

reviewer_note: Bossy and the verb boss come from the 'person in charge' meaning, so they are existing, with a negative feeling. Adjective use 'boss' = excellent (US slang) left out.

corpus_definition: To jump back after hitting a solid object.

forms.definition: the movement of something going up again after hitting the ground
forms.example: Catch the ball after one bounce.

syn.note: Close; used a lot in sports.
Related: a quick movement up into the air.

forms.definition: to go up or away again after hitting the ground or a wall
forms.example: Watch the ball bounce on the floor.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal; common in sports.
Related: move up quickly and suddenly.
Related: easy word; people and animals jump, balls bounce.
Related: move up and down on water.

forms.definition: able to go up again easily after hitting something
forms.example: Children love bouncy balls.
forms.note: Also used for lively, happy people: 'a bouncy puppy'.

syn.note: Close: quickly goes back to its shape when pressed.
Related: can stretch and go back to its shape.

forms.note: Bouncily exists but is very rare; not in learner dictionaries as a separate entry.

people.definition: a person whose job is to stop trouble at the door of a club
people.example: The bouncer did not let him into the club.
people.note: Belongs to bounce = throw someone out (informal), not a ball jumping back.

context.text: The boys in our mahalla play with a bouncy ball. It bounces off the wall and they try to catch it after one bounce.

reviewer_note: Bouncer kept as other_meaning (club security). Bouncily left as no_form with note per rule 5.

corpus_definition: A male person that someone is having a romantic relationship with.

forms.definition: a man or boy that someone is in a romantic relationship with
forms.example: She went to the cinema with her boyfriend.

syn.note: Close; can be a man or woman, often for people living together or married.
Related and old-fashioned; also used to speak lovingly to someone.
Related: a man someone has promised to marry. Also written fiancé.
Related: the word for a woman or girl in the same kind of relationship.

context.text: Malika introduced her boyfriend to her parents last weekend. Her boyfriend brought flowers and some sweets for her mother.

reviewer_note: Compound noun (boy + friend); no forms. Girlfriend listed as related, not antonym or form.

corpus_definition: A piece of jewelry worn around the arm or wrist.

forms.definition: a piece of jewelry that you wear around your wrist
forms.example: She wore a gold bracelet on her wrist.

syn.note: Close: a hard round bracelet with no clasp.
Related: a band of cloth or plastic worn on the wrist, often for sport or events.
General word for all rings, necklaces and bracelets. British spelling: jewellery.

context.text: My grandmother gave me a silver bracelet for my birthday. I wear the bracelet every day on my left wrist.

reviewer_note: No family forms. American 'jewelry' vs British 'jewellery' noted in syn.

corpus_definition: The organ inside your head that helps you think.

forms.definition: the organ inside your head that controls thinking and the body
forms.example: Exercise is good for your brain health.

syn.note: Related: your mind is your thoughts and feelings; the brain is the organ.
Related: the part of the body where the brain is.
Informal name for the brain or for intelligence. American spelling: gray matter.

forms.note: The verb 'brain' (to hit someone hard on the head) is rare and informal. Brainstorm and brainwash are compounds.

forms.definition: clever and good at studying
forms.example: My cousin is really brainy; he always gets top marks.
forms.note: Belongs to brain(s) = intelligence, not the organ. Informal.

forms.definition: very stupid; not thinking at all
forms.example: That was a brainless thing to do.
forms.note: Belongs to brain(s) = intelligence, not the organ. Informal.

context.text: The brain uses a lot of energy when you study. Sleep, water and good food help your brain work well before exams.

reviewer_note: Both rows are the organ, merged; cefr A2. Cerebral is the medical adjective from Latin, not made from brain, so not listed as a form.

corpus_definition: Showing no fear when dealing with difficult or dangerous things.

forms.definition: the quality of not being afraid in danger or difficulty
forms.example: The firefighter got a medal for his bravery.

syn.note: Same meaning; very common.
Close: being confident and not afraid to take risks.
Related: very great courage, often to save others.

ant.note: Being too afraid to do the right or difficult thing.

forms.definition: to face something unpleasant or dangerous without fear
forms.example: Thousands of fans braved the cold to watch the match.
forms.note: Usually with weather or danger: brave the cold, brave the storm.

syn.note: Close: deal with something difficult.
Related and formal: suffer something for a long time.

forms.definition: not afraid when doing something difficult or dangerous
forms.example: It was very brave to help the cat.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Close: confident and ready to take risks.
Close: having no fear at all.
Related: very brave, like a hero.

ant.note: Too afraid to do something difficult or dangerous.
Shy and easily frightened.

forms.definition: in a way that shows no fear
forms.example: The little girl bravely jumped into the cold water.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Close: in a confident way, ready to take risks.

ant.note: In a shy, frightened way.

context.text: My brother was very brave when he had to speak in front of the whole school. Everyone clapped for his bravery, and he spoke bravely about his dream.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed for bravery: -ery is not in the affix table. Old noun 'a brave' (warrior) left out as offensive and outdated.

corpus_definition: To take air into your body and let it out.

forms.definition: the air that goes into and out of your lungs
forms.example: Take a deep breath and relax.
forms.note: Spelling and sound trap: breath /breθ/ is the noun; breathe /briːð/ is the verb.

syn.note: Related: what you take in when you breathe.
Related: a quick, loud breath in, from surprise or pain.

forms.definition: the action of taking air in and out of your body
forms.example: Slow breathing can help you feel calm.

syn.note: Same meaning; scientific or medical word.

forms.definition: to take air into your body and let it out again
forms.example: It is hard to breathe in the dusty room.

syn.note: Easy phrase for one breath in.
Technical word used in biology.
Related: only taking air in.
Related: only letting air out.

forms.definition: not able to get enough air, for example after running
forms.example: She was breathless after climbing the stairs.

syn.note: Same meaning; very common in speaking.
Related: breathing quickly and loudly.
Informal British word for the same feeling.

forms.definition: letting air pass through easily, used about cloth
forms.example: Cotton is a breathable fabric for hot summers.

syn.note: Related: light and letting air move through.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you can hardly get enough air
forms.example: He ran in and breathlessly told us the news.

syn.note: Related: often people speak this way when they are excited.

context.text: After running up the hill in Chimgan, I was breathless. I stopped, took a deep breath and tried to breathe slowly.

reviewer_note: Main trap: breath (noun) vs breathe (verb). Breathtaking is a compound, left out. Breathless kept as -less from breath.

corpus_definition: A hard, rectangular block used to build walls and houses.

forms.definition: a hard block of baked clay used to build walls
forms.example: The house is made of red brick.

syn.note: Related: any solid piece with flat sides, e.g. a concrete block.
Related: a natural hard material also used for building.

forms.definition: to close or fill a space with a wall of hard blocks
forms.example: They bricked up the old window.
forms.note: Almost always 'brick up' or 'brick in'.

syn.note: Same idea: close an opening with a wall.
Related: close something completely.

forms.note: 'brick' is used before nouns like an adjective (a brick wall, a brick house), but it is a noun here.

context.text: My grandfather built his house in Bukhara from brick. Later he bricked up one small window to keep the house warm in winter.

reviewer_note: Both rows are the building block, merged; cefr A2. Bricklayer and brickwork are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: very clever, impressive, or full of light

forms.definition: great cleverness or skill, or very strong bright light
forms.example: Everyone was amazed by the brilliance of her idea.

syn.note: Very great cleverness or talent; a little stronger.
The general ability to think and learn; less strong.
Use it for the light meaning: the brightness of the sun.

ant.note: Lack of good sense or cleverness.

forms.definition: very clever, very good, or shining with strong light
forms.example: She had a brilliant idea for the project.
forms.note: In British English, 'Brilliant!' is also an informal way to say 'Great!'

syn.note: Easy word for a smart person or idea; brilliant is stronger.
Very good; brilliant is a little more excited.
Easy, everyday word for very good.
For light: very bright and shining. Also for a smart student.
About a person's mind only, not ideas or light.
Makes people admire it; not always clever.

ant.note: Not clever; the opposite of a brilliant idea.
Not bright (light) or not interesting.
Very bad; the opposite of 'That's brilliant!'

forms.definition: in a very clever or skilful way, or with very bright light
forms.example: He played brilliantly and his team won the match.

syn.note: Easy phrase with almost the same meaning.
In a smart way; less strong.
For light: The sun shone brightly.

ant.note: In a poor way; the opposite of playing brilliantly.

context.text: Madina is a brilliant student at her school in Bukhara. She answered the hardest question brilliantly, and her teacher praised the brilliance of her thinking.

reviewer_note: One map for clever/impressive/bright since the corpus definition joins them; no -ance affix claimed for brilliance (no clean split).

corpus_definition: A brush with a long handle used for cleaning floors.

forms.definition: a brush with a long handle for sweeping floors
forms.example: I used the broom to sweep the kitchen floor.

syn.note: Any tool with hairs or bristles; a broom is a big brush with a long handle.
Also has a long handle, but cleans floors with water.

forms.note: We use 'sweep' as the verb: sweep the floor with a broom.

context.text: My grandmother cleans the yard with a big broom every morning. She says a good broom is better than any machine.

reviewer_note: Leaf noun; broomstick is a compound, left out. Sweep is the verb but not family.

corpus_definition: To make something by joining different parts together.

forms.definition: a structure with walls and a roof, like a house or school; also the work of making one
forms.example: The new school building has three floors.

syn.note: Anything built, such as a bridge or tower; a bit more formal.
The work of building; also a large built thing.
One kind of building where people live.

forms.definition: the size and shape of a person's body
forms.example: He has a strong build, like a wrestler.
forms.note: Belongs to build = body shape, not making houses. Same spelling as the verb.

forms.definition: to make a house, road or other thing by putting parts together
forms.example: They want to build a new school here.
forms.note: Past forms: built, built.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Easy general word; build is for big things like houses and roads.
Informal: build a wall, fence or tent quickly.
Put parts together, like furniture; usually smaller things.

ant.note: Break something so badly that it cannot be used.
Break a building so it falls: They knocked down the old house.
Formal: pull down a whole building on purpose.

forms.definition: to make something again after it was damaged or destroyed
forms.example: After the earthquake, people rebuilt their homes.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Make an old thing look like new again.

forms.note: 'Built' appears mainly in compounds such as well-built and built-in.

people.definition: a person whose job is making houses and other buildings
people.example: The builder finished our new kitchen in two weeks.

context.text: The builders are working on a new building near our house in Tashkent. They want to build five floors before winter.

reviewer_note: Noun build (body shape) kept as other_meaning; rebuild is a real same-sense verb, not an opposite.

corpus_definition: the glass part of a light that produces light when switched on

forms.definition: the glass part of a lamp that gives light
forms.example: Please change the bulb, this lamp is broken.
forms.note: Another meaning: the round root of some plants, like tulips and onions.

syn.note: The full name; same meaning.
The whole light you put on a table; the bulb is inside it.

forms.definition: round and fat in a way that does not look nice
forms.example: The clown had a big bulbous red nose.
forms.note: Belongs to bulb = the round root of a plant (shape), not a light. Not common; mostly used for noses.

context.text: The bulb in our kitchen stopped working last night. My brother bought a new bulb that uses less electricity.

reviewer_note: Plant-bulb meaning noted on the noun; bulbous shown as other_meaning (shape sense).

corpus_definition: a small metal object fired from a gun

forms.definition: a small piece of metal that comes out of a gun
forms.example: The bullet hit the target exactly.

syn.note: The act of firing a gun, or (old use) the bullet itself.
Used by soldiers and police: one bullet for a gun.
The case with the bullet and powder inside.

context.text: In the film, the hero stopped a bullet with his shield. The police found the bullet near the car.

reviewer_note: Leaf noun; bulletproof and bullet point are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: To treat someone badly because they are smaller or weaker.

forms.definition: hurting or frightening weaker people again and again
forms.example: Our school has strict rules against bullying.

syn.note: Bothering or threatening someone again and again; often used at work.
Making people afraid so they do what you want.

forms.definition: to hurt or frighten someone who is smaller or weaker
forms.example: It is wrong to bully your classmates.
forms.note: Past forms: bullied, bullied. 'Bully someone into doing something' = make them do it by threats.

syn.note: Informal and very common for children: treat one person badly again and again.
Make someone afraid; more formal.
Informal: tell someone what to do in a rude, unkind way.
Laugh at someone; can be friendly, so it is weaker.
Say you will hurt someone; bullying often includes this.

ant.note: Keep someone safe from harm.
Act or speak to keep a weaker person safe.

forms.definition: hurt or frightened by stronger people again and again
forms.example: The bullied boy did not want to go to school.

syn.note: Informal; same idea.

people.definition: a person who hurts or frightens weaker people again and again
people.example: The bully was taking lunch money from younger kids.

context.text: A bully in our class used to take other children's phones. When the teacher learned about the bullying, she talked to his parents, and he stopped bullying the younger kids.

reviewer_note: Merged verb row (B2) and person-noun row (A2): same meaning, so one map at A2; person 'bully' in People & things like cook/cook.

corpus_definition: a group of things of the same kind held or tied together

forms.definition: a group of flowers, keys, fruit and so on, held or tied together
forms.example: She bought a bunch of fresh flowers at the market.
forms.note: Informal: 'a bunch of' can also mean a lot of: a bunch of people.

syn.note: Things tied together, often papers or clothes.
Only for flowers, often a nice gift.
A small group growing or standing close together, like grapes.
Easy general word; not tied together.

forms.definition: to come or put things close together in a tight group
forms.example: The children bunched together at the door.
forms.note: Usually with up or together: bunch up, bunch together.

syn.note: Come or bring together in one place.
Stand or grow close together.
Put in groups; more neutral.

ant.note: Move apart so there is space between.

forms.definition: pressed or pulled together into a tight group
forms.example: His shirt was bunched up under his jacket.

syn.note: Pulled together, often about cloth.

context.text: At the Chorsu bazaar, my mother bought a bunch of grapes and a bunch of fresh herbs. The tourists bunched together to take photos of the colourful fruit.

reviewer_note: Verb bunch (up/together) is a real conversion in the same 'close group' meaning.

corpus_definition: To put something deep in the ground.

forms.definition: the act of putting a dead body into the ground
forms.example: The burial took place in the village where he was born.

syn.note: The whole ceremony for a dead person; the burial is one part.

forms.definition: to put something in a hole in the ground and cover it
forms.example: The dog likes to bury its bone.
forms.note: Pronounced like 'berry': /ˈberi/. Past forms: buried, buried. Also used for dead people: bury someone.

syn.note: Put something where people cannot see it; not always in the ground.
Put something over a thing; bury means cover with earth.
Easy phrase with the same meaning.

ant.note: Take something out of the ground: The dog dug up the bone.
Formal: find something by digging.

forms.definition: put under the ground or hidden under something
forms.example: The children read a story about buried treasure.

syn.note: Easy word: put where people cannot see it.
Under the ground, but not always put there.

context.text: Last summer my little brother buried a box of toys in our garden. Years later, he found the buried box when he dug up the ground to plant trees.

reviewer_note: Burial kept (same family, -al with y to i). Pronunciation trap noted.

corpus_definition: Without help from any other person.
usage_note: by + myself / yourself / himself / herself / ourselves / themselves: 'I fixed it by myself.' Also means 'alone': 'She lives by herself.'

relations.note: Same meaning and very common: 'Did you do it on your own?'
Means 'with nobody else'; by yourself often means 'with no help'.
More formal: without help or control from others.
Formal: without any help.
Someone else helped you do it.

context.text: Aziz is only eight, but he made breakfast by himself today. His mother asked, 'Did you really do it by yourself?'

reviewer_note: Reflexive changes with the subject (by myself, by herself); both 'without help' and 'alone' uses noted.

corpus_definition: Not feeling worried, angry, or excited.

forms.definition: the state of not being worried, angry or excited
forms.example: Her calmness helped everyone during the storm.

syn.note: Easy word: a quiet, relaxed feeling.
Formal: control of your feelings in a hard moment.

ant.note: A sudden strong fear that stops clear thinking.
A worried feeling before something happens.

forms.definition: a quiet and peaceful state or time
forms.example: We enjoyed the calm of the mountains after the busy city.
forms.note: Fixed phrase: the calm before the storm.

syn.note: No noise or trouble.
Easy word, very close.

ant.note: A time of strong fear and confusion.

forms.definition: to make someone stop feeling worried, angry or excited
forms.example: The teacher calmed the children before the exam.
forms.note: Very often 'calm down': Calm down, everything is OK.

syn.note: Make someone feel calmer, often gently.
Make someone quiet and still.
Make or become less worried.

ant.note: Make someone worried or unhappy.
Make someone feel strong, often happy, emotions.

forms.definition: not worried, angry or excited
forms.example: Please stay calm during the test.
forms.note: The l is silent: /kɑːm/. Also used for weather and the sea: a calm day.

syn.note: Easy word: not worried or tense.
Quiet and calm, also about places.
Informal: calm in a hard situation.
Formal: in control of your feelings.
Not noisy; a quiet person may not be calm inside.

ant.note: Worried and a little afraid.
Feeling strong anger.
Very worried about what may happen.

forms.definition: in a quiet way, without worry or anger
forms.example: He answered the angry customer calmly.

syn.note: Without much noise; close but not the same.
In a quiet, relaxed way.
Calm, sometimes in an unfriendly way.

ant.note: In a worried way.
In an angry way.

context.text: Before the football final, the coach told us to stay calm. He spoke calmly, and his calmness helped us play well.

reviewer_note: Silent l noted; noun calm and calmness both real, same meaning.

corpus_definition: To decide that a planned event will not happen.

forms.definition: a decision that a planned event will not happen
forms.example: The cancellation of the concert made many fans sad.
forms.note: American English also writes cancelation (one l).

syn.note: Everyday phrase for the same idea.
Related, but different: the event moves to a later date, it is not stopped.

forms.definition: to decide that a planned event will not happen
forms.example: They had to cancel the meeting today.
forms.note: British English: cancelled, cancelling. American English: canceled, canceling.

syn.note: Very close and very common in speaking: call off a match.
Informal: stop a plan completely.
Easy word, but more general: you can stop something that has already started.
Related, but different: you move the event to a later time.

ant.note: The planned event happens as planned: The match will go ahead.

forms.definition: that will not happen any more, though it was planned
forms.example: We waited at the airport because of a cancelled flight.
forms.note: American spelling: canceled.

syn.note: Same meaning, more informal.

context.text: Our flight to Tashkent was cancelled because of the snow. The airline said sorry for the cancellation and gave us a new ticket.

reviewer_note: British double l (cancelled, cancellation) vs American single l noted. Map keeps only the 'event will not happen' sense, not cancel = stop an order or cancel out.

corpus_definition: The act of protecting something or someone.

forms.definition: looking after someone or something so they are safe and well
forms.example: He takes good care of his plants.
forms.note: Common phrases: take care of, in someone's care, health care.

syn.note: Protection is about keeping safe from danger; care also means helping and feeding.
Related: giving time and thought to someone or something.
Related: watching children or workers to keep them safe.

ant.note: Not giving someone or something the attention they need.

forms.definition: to look after someone who is ill, very old or very young
forms.example: She cares for her grandmother every evening.
forms.note: In this meaning it is used with for: care for someone. 'Care about' is a different meaning.

syn.note: Easy, very common: look after a baby.
Same meaning, very common.
Related: look after someone who is ill.

ant.note: Not look after someone or something properly.

forms.definition: thinking about what you do so that nothing bad happens
forms.example: Be careful with that hot tea.

syn.note: Careful because you want to avoid danger or risk.
Related: watching and listening closely.

ant.note: Not thinking enough about what you do, so mistakes or accidents happen.

forms.definition: kind and wanting to help and look after others
forms.example: My aunt is a very caring person.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Related: showing love to family and friends.
Related: thinking about what other people need.

ant.note: Not kind; not interested in how others feel.

forms.definition: in a way that avoids mistakes, damage or danger
forms.example: Please carry the eggs carefully.

syn.note: Slowly and carefully because of possible danger.
Related: softly, without hurting or breaking anything.

ant.note: Without enough thought, so mistakes happen.

people.definition: a person who looks after someone who is ill or old
people.example: Her carer visits every morning to help her get dressed.
people.note: British English. American English says caregiver.

context.text: My grandmother needs a lot of care now. My mother cares for her every day and is very careful with her medicine. She is such a caring daughter.

reviewer_note: GATE? carer is a real British noun (Oxford, Cambridge: a person who looks after a sick or old person); the gate dictionary lacks it. Verb 'care' kept in the 'care for = look after' meaning; 'care about' is its own corpus item. Opposites careless/carelessly/uncaring are ant, not forms; caregiver/caretaker left out as compounds.

corpus_definition: To think that something or someone is very important.
particle_note: Not separable: 'care about your future', never 'care your future about'. Patterns: care about + noun / -ing / wh-clause ('I don't care about what they say'). Very common with negatives: I don't care about it.

relations.note: Related: you want to know about it, but it may not be very important to you.
Think something is important; a bit more formal.
Related: you care so much that you feel nervous about it.
Related, mostly in questions and negatives: 'I don't mind' means it is not a problem for me.
Pay no attention to something, as if it is not important.

context.text: My parents really care about my education. They don't care about expensive clothes, but they always buy me good books.

reviewer_note: Kept apart from 'care for' (look after / like); separability stated as non-separable.

corpus_definition: a person whose job is making things from wood

forms.definition: a person whose job is making and fixing things from wood
forms.example: The carpenter built a beautiful wooden table.

syn.note: Anyone who makes things from wood, as a job or a hobby.
British English: a carpenter who makes doors, windows and furniture.
Related: a person who builds houses, often using many materials.

people.definition: the work or skill of making things from wood
people.example: My uncle learned carpentry from his father in Bukhara.

context.text: Our neighbour in Andijan is a carpenter. He made our kitchen table, and he wants to teach carpentry to his son.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the noun-slot main entry (rule 6); carpentry goes to People & things as a field. No -er split: 'carpent' is not a word.

corpus_definition: a small worm-like creature that turns into a butterfly or moth

forms.definition: a small soft creature with many legs that later becomes a butterfly
forms.example: A green caterpillar was eating a leaf in the garden.

syn.note: Scientific word for a young insect before it changes form.
Related, but different: a worm has no legs and never becomes a butterfly.

context.text: My little sister found a caterpillar on the apple tree. She watched the caterpillar every day until it became a butterfly.

reviewer_note: Single-form word; no family forms. 'Caterpillar' as a brand of machines/tracks left out.

corpus_definition: To have a fun event for a special day.

forms.definition: a party or special event for an important day or success
forms.example: There was a big celebration in our street for Navruz.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word for a social event with food and music.
Formal; often plural: the New Year festivities.
Related: a special day or several days of events, often for a whole town.

forms.definition: to do something fun and special because of an important day
forms.example: We will celebrate my birthday on Sunday.

syn.note: Easy way to say it in everyday speech.
Do something to show a day is important: mark an anniversary.
Informal verb: have fun with friends, often with music and dancing.

ant.note: Feel and show deep sadness, for example after someone dies.

forms.definition: done or used for a happy special day or success
forms.example: After the match, the team had a celebratory dinner.

syn.note: Happy and bright, like a holiday.

forms.definition: famous and admired by many people
forms.example: Alisher Navoi is a celebrated poet.
forms.note: Belongs to celebrate = praise publicly, so 'celebrated' means famous, not 'having a party'.

context.text: Next week we will celebrate my grandfather's 80th birthday. The whole family is coming to the celebration, and my mother is cooking a celebratory plov.

reviewer_note: Celebrated (= famous) marked other_meaning. Celebrity is not made from celebrate in English (Latin celeber root), so it is in people_not_family.

corpus_definition: Food made from grain, often eaten with milk for breakfast.

forms.definition: a breakfast food made from grain, usually eaten with milk
forms.example: I like to eat cold cereal for breakfast.
forms.note: Sounds the same as serial (a story in parts). Cereal also means a grain plant such as wheat or rice.

syn.note: Related: a crunchy mix of baked oats, nuts and honey, eaten like cereal.
Related: a mix of oats, nuts and dried fruit.
Related: oats cooked with hot milk or water.

forms.note: Grain is a separate word (wheat, rice, oats), not made from cereal.
Grainy and granular come from grain, not from cereal.

context.text: My brother eats cereal with milk every morning. I prefer bread and tea, but sometimes I have a bowl of cereal too.

reviewer_note: Homophone trap cereal/serial noted. Grain-crop sense mentioned only in a note.

corpus_definition: an official document proving a fact or qualification

forms.definition: an official paper that shows a fact or that you finished a course
forms.example: She received a certificate after finishing the course.

syn.note: A certificate from a school, college or university.
Related: what you have after passing an exam or course; the paper proves it.
Related: an official paper that lets you do something, like drive. American spelling: license.
Related: any official paper.

forms.definition: the official process of giving someone a qualification
forms.example: Teachers need certification before they can work in this school.

syn.note: Formal: official approval for a school, course or person.

forms.definition: to say officially that something is true or correct
forms.example: The doctor certified that he was fit to work.

syn.note: Easier word: say that something is true.
Related: check that something is true.

forms.definition: officially shown to have the right training or quality
forms.example: We hired a certified translator for the documents.

syn.note: Has the right training or exams for a job.
Has official permission to do a job.

ant.note: Without the right training or exams for a job.

forms.note: Certainly shares an old Latin root through certain, but is not made from certificate.

context.text: After the IELTS course in Tashkent, every student got a certificate. Now Dilnoza is a certified teacher, and the certificate helps her find work.

reviewer_note: certify/certified/certification included as family (certificate is historically made from certify); certain/certainly are not family.

corpus_definition: A specific frequency or station on a television.

forms.definition: a television or radio station that has its own programmes
forms.example: Change the channel to the sports station.
forms.note: Also a YouTube channel. Other meanings: a long passage of water (the English Channel).

syn.note: Very close; station is more common for radio.
Related: a big company that owns many channels or stations.

forms.definition: to send money, energy or ideas into one particular use
forms.example: She channels all her energy into her studies.
forms.note: Belongs to channel = a way or passage for something to go through, not a TV station.

context.text: My grandfather always watches the news channel in the evening. My little brother wants to change the channel to cartoons.

reviewer_note: TV sense only; verb 'channel' (direct energy/money) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: One of the parts into which a book is divided.

forms.definition: one of the main parts of a book, often with a number or title
forms.example: I finished the first chapter of the story.
forms.note: Also used for a period in someone's life: a new chapter in my life.

syn.note: A part of a book or document; often smaller than a chapter.
Easy, general word: one piece of a whole book.
Related: one part of a TV series, not a book.

context.text: Our teacher asked us to read chapter three of the book at home. It was the longest chapter, but the most exciting one.

reviewer_note: Single-form word; 'a new chapter in life' mentioned only as a note.

corpus_definition: The qualities that make a person who they are.

forms.definition: all the qualities that make a person different from others
forms.example: Honesty is a very important part of his character.

syn.note: Very close and easy; personality is more about how you behave with other people.
Close: the kind of person you are naturally, e.g. 'She is kind by nature.'
Related: mostly about your feelings and moods, e.g. calm or nervous.
Related: who you are, including your name, country and group.

forms.definition: a typical quality or feature of a person or thing
forms.example: Patience is his best characteristic.

syn.note: Close and easy: a good or bad part of a person.
Close, a little formal: one part of your personality.
Related: more often used for things and places.

forms.definition: the way a writer shows the people in a story
forms.example: The characterization in this novel is excellent.
forms.note: Belongs to character = a person in a book, film or play, not a person's qualities. British spelling: characterisation.

forms.definition: to describe the typical qualities of someone or something
forms.example: His friends characterize him as calm and generous.
forms.note: British spelling: characterise. Also means 'to be typical of something'.

syn.note: Easy and close; characterize focuses on the most typical qualities.
Related: show someone in a certain way, often in art or writing.

forms.definition: typical of a particular person or thing
forms.example: She answered with her characteristic smile.

syn.note: Very close and easy.
Related and easy: what normally happens.
Related: easy to recognise because it is different.

ant.note: Not typical of someone: 'It was uncharacteristic of him to be late.'

forms.definition: in a way that is typical of a person or thing
forms.example: Characteristically, Aziz arrived early and helped everyone.

syn.note: Very close and easy.

ant.note: In a way that is not typical of someone.

context.text: My grandmother has a strong character. Her most famous characteristic is honesty, and characteristically, she always says what she thinks.

reviewer_note: Both rows mean personality, so one map at A2. characterization kept as other_meaning (story-character sense); characteristic is both noun and adjective.

corpus_definition: To talk in a friendly and casual way with someone.
usage_note: chat to + person + about + topic: 'I chatted to Malika about the film.' 'Chat to' is mostly British; 'chat with' is common in both British and American English.

relations.note: Very close and easy; chat is more friendly and relaxed, about small things.
Same meaning, used as a noun phrase: 'I had a chat with my aunt.'
Related but more serious and formal; no 'about' after it: 'discuss the plan'.
Related: chat about other people's private lives.

context.text: After class, I usually chat to my friends about football. Yesterday I chatted to my teacher about the exam in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Verb + preposition pattern, treated as a phrase (not a phrasal verb); no true antonym.

corpus_definition: Feeling happy and showing it in your behavior.

forms.definition: the state of being happy and showing it to others
forms.example: Her cheerfulness makes everyone in the office smile.

syn.note: Easy and close; cheerfulness is happiness that other people can see.
Related: a happy feeling, often for a short time.

ant.note: The feeling of being unhappy.
A sad feeling with no hope.

forms.definition: a loud shout of happiness or support
forms.example: A big cheer went up when our team scored.
forms.note: Belongs to cheer = shouting for someone, not the happy feeling of a person.

forms.definition: to make someone feel happier or more hopeful
forms.example: The good news cheered her a lot.
forms.note: More common as 'cheer up': 'Cheer up!' Cheer also means 'shout to support someone': cheer for a team.

syn.note: Related: give someone hope or confidence.
Related: make a sad person feel better.

ant.note: To make someone sad.

forms.definition: happy and showing it in your face and behaviour
forms.example: She had a cheerful smile every morning.

syn.note: Easy and close; cheerful also shows the happiness to other people.
Close, a little old-fashioned: happy and friendly.
Related: lively and happy, e.g. 'a bright smile'.
Related: hopeful and confident about the future.

ant.note: Sad and without hope.
Very unhappy.
Easy opposite: not happy.

forms.note: upbeat means almost the same but is not made from cheer; it is a separate word.

forms.definition: happy and friendly in the way you behave
forms.example: He gave us a cheery wave from the bus.

forms.definition: in a happy and positive way
forms.example: He cheerfully helped his neighbour carry the bags.

syn.note: Easy and close.
Related: willingly and with pleasure.

ant.note: In an unhappy way.

context.text: Our neighbour Nodira is always cheerful. Every morning she cheerfully says hello, and her cheerfulness makes the whole street feel friendly.

reviewer_note: cheer (noun = shout) is other_meaning; cheer (verb = make happier) kept as existing with note about 'cheer up'. cheerless left out (rare antonym); cheerleader is a compound.

corpus_definition: a professional cook who works in a restaurant or hotel

forms.definition: a person whose job is to cook in a restaurant or hotel
forms.example: The chef prepared a delicious meal for us.
forms.note: Pronounced /ʃef/, with 'sh' at the start.

syn.note: Easy and close; a cook can be anyone who cooks, a chef is usually a trained professional.
Related: the most important cook in a kitchen.

forms.note: There is no learner-dictionary verb from chef. Use 'cook'.
There is no adjective from chef.
There is no adverb from chef.

context.text: My cousin works as a chef in a hotel in Bukhara. Every evening the chef cooks plov for the guests.

reviewer_note: Headword is a job noun, so it stays in the noun slot. chief shares the old French root but is not made from chef.

corpus_definition: a hollow pipe that carries smoke from a fire out of a building

forms.definition: a tall pipe on a roof that takes smoke out of a house
forms.example: Smoke rose slowly from the chimney.

syn.note: Related: a very tall pipe on a factory or ship.
Related: the place inside a room where the fire burns; the pipe goes up from it.

forms.note: There is no verb from chimney.
There is no adjective from chimney.
There is no adverb from chimney.

context.text: In winter, smoke comes out of every chimney in our village. My grandfather cleans the chimney before the cold weather starts.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; chimney sweep is a compound and is left out.

corpus_definition: The power or act of picking what you want.

forms.definition: the act of picking one thing from several things
forms.example: You have a difficult choice to make today.

syn.note: Easy and close; a decision can be about anything, a choice is between things.
Close: one of the things you can pick.
Close but more formal.
Related and informal: 'Take your pick.'
Related: another thing you can pick instead.

forms.definition: to decide which thing or person you want
forms.example: You can choose any dessert from the menu.
forms.note: Irregular verb: choose, chose, chosen.

syn.note: Very close and easy, a little informal.
Very close but more formal.
Related: decide is about making up your mind.
Close and formal: 'opt for the cheaper one'.

ant.note: To say no to something and not take it.

forms.definition: careful about what you take and difficult to please
forms.example: My little brother is very choosy about food.

syn.note: Very close and informal.
Close: difficult to please, often about small things.
Related and more positive: careful in choosing.

forms.definition: of very high quality, used about food
forms.example: The shop sells choice fruit from Fergana.
forms.note: Belongs to choice = very good quality, not the act of picking.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: At the bazaar in Samarkand there is a huge choice of melons. My mother is choosy, so it takes her an hour to choose the best one.

reviewer_note: choose is the base verb (choice made from it); adjective choice (= high quality) shown as other_meaning. chooser left out as rare outside the idiom.

corpus_definition: To cut food into smaller pieces using a knife.

forms.definition: a quick hard cut with a knife or an axe
forms.example: He split the log with one chop.
forms.note: Chop also means a thick slice of meat with a bone in it: a lamb chop.

syn.note: Easy and close: the act of cutting.
Related: a hard hit with a hand or tool.

forms.definition: to cut something into pieces with a knife or a heavy tool
forms.example: You should chop the onions for the salad.

syn.note: Easy and general; chop means cutting into pieces with quick hard movements.
Close: cut food into small square pieces.
Related: cut into thin flat pieces.
Related: cut meat into very small pieces, often with a machine.
Related: cut roughly and hard, often wood or plants.

forms.definition: cut into small pieces
forms.example: Add some chopped tomatoes to the soup.

syn.note: Close: cut into small squares.
Related: cut into thin flat pieces.

ant.note: Not cut into pieces.

forms.definition: with a lot of small waves, because of the wind
forms.example: The lake was too choppy for the boat.
forms.note: Belongs to a different meaning (rough, broken-up water or movement), not cutting food or wood.
There is no adverb from chop.

people.definition: a heavy knife or small axe for cutting meat or wood
people.example: The butcher used a chopper to cut the meat.
people.note: In informal English, chopper also means a helicopter.

context.text: My father chops wood for the stove every Saturday. Then my mother adds chopped onions and carrots to the plov.

reviewer_note: Both rows mean cutting into pieces (food with a knife, wood with an axe), so one map at A2. Meat chop mentioned in the noun note; choppy is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: a boring but necessary household task done regularly

forms.definition: a boring job you must do often, especially at home
forms.example: Washing the dishes is her least favourite chore.

syn.note: Close; a task is any piece of work, not always boring.
Easy and close: 'household jobs'.
Related: all the work of cleaning and cooking at home; it is uncountable.
Related: something you must do.

forms.note: There is no verb from chore.
There is no adjective from chore.
There is no adverb from chore.

context.text: In our family, everyone has a chore. My job is to sweep the yard, and my sister does the other chores in the kitchen.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; usually plural 'household chores'.

corpus_definition: Easy to understand or see through without confusion.

forms.definition: the quality of being easy to understand or see
forms.example: I liked the clarity of her explanation.
forms.note: Clarity comes from the same Latin word as clear; clearness also exists but is less common.

syn.note: Related: being easy and not complicated.
Related: being easy to see through, like glass.

ant.note: A state where you do not understand something.
Not being exact or detailed.

forms.definition: official permission, or removing things from a place
forms.example: We need clearance before the plane can land.
forms.note: Belongs to clear = remove things or allow, not easy to understand.

forms.definition: to make something easier to understand
forms.example: Can you clarify the last question, please?

syn.note: Easy and close: give more information so people understand.
Related: make something less difficult.

ant.note: To make something harder to understand.

forms.definition: to remove things from a place
forms.example: Please clear the table after dinner.
forms.note: Belongs to clear = make a place empty or tidy, not easy to understand.

forms.definition: easy to understand, see or hear
forms.example: The instructions were very clear and simple.

syn.note: Close: very easy to see or understand.
Close: simple and easy to understand.
Close: possible to understand.
Related and easy: not difficult.
Related: about glass or water you can see through.

ant.note: Not easy to understand.
Making you not understand.
Not exact or detailed.

forms.definition: in a way that is easy to see, hear or understand
forms.example: Please speak clearly so everyone can hear you.

syn.note: Close: in a simple, easy way.
Related: used to say something is easy to see as true.

ant.note: In a way that is not exact.

context.text: Our teacher always speaks clearly. When a rule is not clear, she gives an example to clarify it.

reviewer_note: clarity/clarify are learner-dictionary family of clear (Latin clarus); verb clear (= remove things) and clearance are other_meaning. No transparent affix split for clarity/clarify.

corpus_definition: To make a place tidy by removing things.
particle_note: Separable: 'clear up your room' or 'clear your room up'. Also used without an object: 'Let's clear up before we go.' 'Clear up after someone' = tidy their mess.

relations.note: Very close and easy.
Close; clean up also means washing and removing dirt.
Related: put things back in their places.
To make a place untidy.

context.text: After the party, we cleared up the living room together. My mother always says, 'Clear up your toys before dinner!'

reviewer_note: Tidy sense only; clear up also means 'weather gets better' and 'explain a problem', not in this map.

corpus_definition: Able to learn or understand things very quickly.

forms.definition: the quality of being quick to learn and understand
forms.example: Everyone was surprised by the cleverness of the young girl.

syn.note: Very close; intelligence is the more common, neutral word.
Related: used about children and students who learn fast.
Related: wisdom comes from experience and good judgement, not only fast thinking.

ant.note: The quality of not thinking well or being silly.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: quick to learn and understand things
forms.example: The clever student finished the exam early.
forms.note: In British English clever can also describe a good idea or a skilful thing: 'a clever plan'.

syn.note: Very close and easy; very common in American English.
Very close; a little more formal.
Used mostly about children and young people who learn fast.
Related: much stronger, very very clever.

ant.note: Not able to think well; can be rude about a person.
Not sensible; a little formal.

forms.definition: in a smart way that shows good, quick thinking
forms.example: She cleverly solved the problem in two minutes.

syn.note: Very close; a little more formal.
Related: in a way that shows good skill. American spelling: skillfully.

ant.note: In a way that shows bad thinking.

context.text: My little brother is very clever: he learned to read when he was four. He cleverly hides his sweets where our mother can't find them.

reviewer_note: No verb or people nouns exist; cleverness and cleverly are both real and kept.

corpus_definition: To press a button on a mouse to select something.

forms.definition: the act of pressing a button on a computer mouse
forms.example: With one click, you can buy a train ticket to Samarkand.

syn.note: The same action on a phone or touch screen with your finger.
Related: pushing any button or key.

forms.definition: to press a button on a mouse to choose something on a screen
forms.example: Click here to see the pictures.
forms.note: Common patterns: 'click on a link', 'click here', 'double-click', 'right-click'.

syn.note: The same action on a phone screen with your finger.
Related: to push a button or key; more general.
Related: to choose something on a screen, by clicking or in another way.

forms.definition: that you can press with a mouse to open or start something
forms.example: The words in blue are clickable links.
forms.note: Mainly used about links, buttons and pictures on websites.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: To buy the ticket, click the green button. One more click opens your ticket, and the clickable link takes you to the map of the station.

reviewer_note: Only the mouse sense; click = short sharp sound and click = suddenly understand/get on are other senses not mapped. Compounds (double-click) left out.

corpus_definition: The usual weather conditions in a specific place.

forms.definition: the usual weather that a place has over many years
forms.example: Uzbekistan has a dry climate with hot summers.
forms.note: Common phrases: 'climate change', 'a hot/cold/dry/wet climate'. Climate can also mean the general feeling in a place: 'the political climate'.

syn.note: Related but different: weather is what happens today or this week; climate is the usual pattern over many years.
Related: the weather at a certain time, often in 'weather conditions'.

forms.definition: to slowly get used to new weather or a new place
forms.example: It took us a week to acclimatize to the heat in Termez.
forms.note: British spelling: acclimatise. American English also says acclimate. Pattern: 'acclimatize to something'.

syn.note: More general: to change to fit a new situation.
Easy and very common phrase.

forms.definition: connected with the usual weather of a place over a long time
forms.example: Scientists study climatic changes in Central Asia.
forms.note: Mostly used in science and news. In everyday English people often use 'climate' before a noun: 'climate change'.

forms.definition: in a way connected with the usual weather of a place
forms.example: The two regions are climatically very different.
forms.note: Rare and technical; mostly used in science writing.

people.definition: the science that studies the usual weather of places over many years
people.example: He studied climatology at university in Tashkent.

people.definition: a scientist who studies the usual weather of places over many years
people.example: A climatologist explained why our summers are getting hotter.

context.text: The climate in Tashkent is hot and dry in summer. Scientists say climatic changes are making our summers longer every year.

reviewer_note: acclimatize shown as the verb (ac- + climate + -ize; no affix claimed since acclimat- is not a word). Three corpus rows share one 'usual weather' meaning; merged, lowest CEFR A2. Weather given as related, not a synonym (common learner confusion).

corpus_definition: A small room used for hanging your clothes.

forms.definition: a small room or tall cupboard where you hang clothes
forms.example: Hang your coat in the closet.
forms.note: Closet is American English; British English usually says wardrobe or cupboard. 'Walk-in closet' = a closet big enough to walk into.

syn.note: British English uses wardrobe for a tall cupboard for clothes.
British English: a piece of furniture or small space with doors for storing things.
Related: a small metal cupboard at school, work or a gym.

forms.note: The verb 'be closeted with someone' (to be in a private meeting) exists but is rare and formal.

forms.definition: secret, not told to other people
forms.example: He is a closet fan of romantic films.
forms.note: Belongs to closet = something hidden or secret, not a room for clothes. Only used before a noun.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: In our new flat there is a big closet in the bedroom. My sister put all her dresses in the closet on the first day.

reviewer_note: No real affix: -et is not a productive affix here. Adjective closet (= secret) kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A person who teaches players how to perform well in sports.

forms.definition: a person who trains players or a team in a sport
forms.example: Our coach tells us how to run faster.
forms.note: A coach can also help people with work or life skills: 'a life coach'.

syn.note: Very close; trainer is also used for gyms and animals.
A person who teaches a practical skill, such as driving or swimming.
Related: a teacher works at school; a coach works with sports players.
Related: in football, the manager runs the whole team and chooses the players.

forms.definition: the work of training people in a sport or skill
forms.example: The team got better after a year of good coaching.

forms.definition: to train a person or team in a sport
forms.example: He coaches the girls' football team on Saturdays.

syn.note: Very close and easy.
More general: teach is used for any subject; coach is mostly for sports and skills.
Formal: to teach a practical skill.

forms.note: No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My younger brother plays football in Namangan, and his coach is very strict. She coaches the team three times a week, and her coaching has helped them win many games.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows have different meanings (sports trainer vs bus); split into two maps. Here the headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry.

corpus_definition: A large vehicle that carries many passengers.

forms.definition: a big comfortable bus for long trips between cities
forms.example: We took a coach to the city center.
forms.note: Mostly British English; American English usually says bus. Coach is also a carriage of a train, and an old carriage pulled by horses.

syn.note: Very close; in British English a coach goes on long trips, a bus goes around the town.
Related: a small bus for about 10 to 20 people.

forms.definition: to train a person or team in a sport
forms.example: He coaches the school basketball team.
forms.note: Belongs to coach = a sports trainer, not the bus.
No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: We went from Tashkent to Bukhara by coach. The coach had big seats and air conditioning, so the long trip was easy.

reviewer_note: Only the vehicle sense; sports-coach sense is its own map and appears here only as other_meaning verb.

corpus_definition: A small round piece of metal used as money.

forms.definition: a small, flat, round piece of metal used as money
forms.example: He dropped a silver coin.
forms.note: Coins are metal money; paper money is called notes in British English and bills in American English.

syn.note: Related: coins you carry or get back in a shop: 'small change'.
Related: used with a value: 'a 500-som piece'.
Related: all money in coins and paper notes.

forms.definition: all the coins that are used in a country
forms.example: The museum shows the old coinage of Bukhara.
forms.note: It can also mean a new word that someone has invented.

forms.definition: to invent a new word or phrase
forms.example: Who coined the word 'selfie'?
forms.note: Belongs to coin = making something new (first, making metal money), not the piece of money itself.
No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandfather keeps old Soviet coins in a small box. He says the coinage of that time was made of heavier metal.

reviewer_note: Verb coin (= invent a word) kept as other_meaning. No affix claimed: -age is not in the affix table.

corpus_definition: To keep many things of the same type.

forms.definition: a group of similar things that someone has kept over time
forms.example: He has a big collection of old stamps.
forms.note: Collection also means taking things or money from people: 'rubbish collection', 'a collection for charity'.

syn.note: Related: a group of things that belong together, often a complete group.
Related: a secret store of things, often money or food.

forms.definition: to bring together and keep many things of the same type as a hobby
forms.example: I like to collect old coins.
forms.note: Collect also means to go and get someone or something: 'collect the children from school'.

syn.note: To bring things together; less about keeping them as a hobby.
Formal: to get more and more of something over time.
Related: easy and general; to have something and not give it away.
Related: to keep something to use later.

ant.note: To get rid of things you do not want.

forms.definition: worth keeping because many people want to own one
forms.example: Old Soviet toys are very collectable now.
forms.note: American spelling: collectible. Also a noun: 'collectables' = things people collect.

forms.definition: done or shared by all the people in a group
forms.example: It was a collective decision of the whole class.
forms.note: Belongs to collect = bring people together as a group, not keeping things as a hobby.

forms.definition: calm and in control of your feelings
forms.example: She stayed calm and collected during the exam.
forms.note: Belongs to collect = collect yourself (become calm). Often in 'calm and collected'.

forms.definition: together, as a group
forms.example: The students collectively decided to clean the park.
forms.note: Goes with collective (as a group), not with keeping things as a hobby.

people.definition: a person who keeps many things of one type as a hobby
people.example: My uncle is a stamp collector.

context.text: My cousin Aziz collects old coins from different countries. His collection now has more than three hundred coins, and some of them are very collectable.

reviewer_note: Hobby sense only. collective/collected/collectively kept as other_meaning so they are not hidden.

corpus_definition: To put two or more things together.

forms.definition: two or more things put or used together
forms.example: Plov is a combination of rice, meat and carrots.
forms.note: Also the numbers that open a lock: 'I forgot the combination'.

syn.note: Things mixed together, often food or liquids.
Easy and informal: 'a good mix of people'.
Related: a smooth mixture where the parts are hard to see.

forms.definition: to put or bring two or more things together
forms.example: Combine the flour and eggs to make the cake.
forms.note: Pattern: 'combine A with/and B'. Stress on the second part: com-BINE.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Used especially for food and liquids.
To connect things or people so they become one.
Related: used for companies, roads or files becoming one.

ant.note: To divide things that were together.
To split one thing into parts.

forms.definition: made by putting two or more things together
forms.example: The combined price of the two tickets is 200,000 som.

syn.note: Done or owned together by two or more people.
Related: when you add all the numbers together.

ant.note: Kept apart, not together.

forms.note: No adverb in this family.

context.text: To make the salad, combine tomatoes, cucumbers and onions in a bowl. This combination is very popular in Uzbekistan, and the combined taste is fresh and simple.

reviewer_note: Noun 'combine' (a farm machine, short for combine harvester) is a separate meaning with different stress; not mapped.

corpus_definition: a funny movie or play

forms.definition: a film, play or TV show that is made to make people laugh
forms.example: We watched a funny comedy last night.

syn.note: Related: a funny TV series about the same people every week.
Related: the quality of being funny. American spelling: humor.

ant.note: A serious play or film with a sad ending.
A serious film or play; often used as the opposite type of film.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: funny, or connected with funny films, plays and shows
forms.example: He is a famous comic actor in Uzbekistan.
forms.note: Comic is also a noun: a magazine with picture stories (a comic book).

syn.note: Very close and easy.
A little formal.
Funny in a quiet, pleasant way.

ant.note: Very sad, connected with tragedy.
Not funny or joking.

forms.definition: funny in a strange or silly way
forms.example: He looked comical in his father's huge hat.

forms.definition: in a funny or silly way
forms.example: The little dog ran comically after the ball.

syn.note: In a way that is meant to be funny; a little formal.
Related: mostly used in 'funnily enough' (= strangely).

ant.note: In a way that is not funny.

people.definition: a person whose job is to make people laugh
people.example: The comedian told jokes about life in Tashkent.

context.text: Last night we watched a comedy at the cinema. The main comic actor was so funny that everyone laughed for two hours.

reviewer_note: comic (adjective) and comical are related but differ: comical = funny in a silly way. Noun comic (comic book / comedian) not repeated in people.

corpus_definition: Providing a relaxed feeling without any pain or trouble.

forms.definition: a pleasant, relaxed feeling with no pain or worry
forms.example: I like to travel in comfort, so I take the fast train.

syn.note: A feeling of being relaxed with no problems: 'at ease'.
Related: resting and enjoying yourself.
Related: very great comfort that costs a lot of money.

ant.note: A feeling of slight pain or of not being relaxed.

forms.definition: to make someone feel less sad or worried
forms.example: She comforted her friend after the bad news.
forms.note: Belongs to comfort = help someone who is sad, not a soft chair or shoes.

forms.definition: making you feel relaxed, with no pain or trouble
forms.example: These shoes are very comfortable to wear.
forms.note: Pronunciation: often three syllables, /ˈkʌmftəbl/. Also used about people: 'I feel comfortable here'.

syn.note: Warm, soft and relaxing, often about rooms and homes. American spelling: cozy.
Related: helping you rest and feel calm.
Related: pleasant to touch or sit on.

ant.note: Making you feel pain or not relaxed.

forms.definition: pleasant to sit in or wear; soft and relaxing
forms.example: This old sofa is really comfy.
forms.note: A short, informal word for comfortable.

forms.definition: making you feel less sad or worried
forms.example: Her kind words were very comforting.
forms.note: Belongs to comfort = help someone who is sad, not about soft shoes or chairs.

forms.definition: in a relaxed way, with no pain or trouble
forms.example: The children were sitting comfortably on the sofa.
forms.note: Also 'easily': 'win comfortably', 'live comfortably' (have enough money).

syn.note: In a warm and relaxed way. American spelling: cozily.
Easy phrase with the same meaning.

ant.note: In a way that makes you feel pain or not relaxed.

context.text: My grandmother's old chair is very comfortable. She sits in it comfortably every evening and says nothing gives her more comfort after a long day.

reviewer_note: Headword made from noun comfort; verb comfort/comforting (help someone who is sad) kept as other_meaning. uncomfortable/discomfort placed in ant, not forms.

corpus_definition: Something that makes people laugh.

forms.definition: a magazine or book of funny stories told in pictures
forms.example: He likes reading a funny comic book on the bus.
forms.note: Also used for a person who tells jokes (= comedian). American English often says 'comic book'.

syn.note: Related: a funny drawing or a short animated film, not a whole magazine.
Related: a longer, more serious book told in pictures.
Related: a Japanese style of comic.

forms.definition: a funny film, play or TV show that makes people laugh
forms.example: We watched a comedy last night and laughed a lot.
forms.note: Comic comes from comedy.

syn.note: Related: the quality of being funny. American spelling: humor.

ant.note: A sad play or story, often with an unhappy ending.

forms.note: No verb comes from comic in learner dictionaries.

forms.definition: funny and making people laugh
forms.example: The film has some very comic moments.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
A little more formal; it makes you smile more than laugh.
Showing humour; common in writing.

ant.note: Very sad, often about death or disaster.
Not joking or trying to be funny.

forms.definition: funny, often in a strange or silly way
forms.example: He looked comical in his father's huge coat.

syn.note: Easy and general.
Related: funny in a foolish way.

forms.definition: in a way that makes people laugh
forms.example: The dog jumped comically at the snow.

syn.note: Related; more often used in 'funnily enough'.
In a way that makes you smile.

people.definition: a person whose job is to tell jokes and make people laugh

forms.example: The cat crept along the floor towards the bird.
forms.note: Irregular: creep - crept - crept. 'Creeped out' (= frightened) is informal and different.

syn.note: Very close for babies and animals; crawl is more about hands and knees, creep about moving quietly.
To move quietly so nobody sees you; you can sneak while walking.
To walk quietly on the front of your feet, not on hands and knees.

forms.definition: strange and a little frightening
forms.example: The old empty house at the end of the street is really creepy.
forms.note: Belongs to creep = a strange, frightening feeling, not moving slowly. Informal.
No common adverb. 'Creepily' exists but is rare and belongs to creepy (frightening).

people.definition: a plant that grows along the ground or up walls and trees
people.example: Green creepers covered the walls of the old house.
people.note: Belongs to creep = plants slowly spreading over a surface, not a baby moving on hands and knees.

context.text: The baby crept slowly across the kitchen floor. When her mother turned around, she was creeping under the table to find the cat.

reviewer_note: Irregular past crept handled. Noun creep and creepy are informal other_meaning (unpleasant/frightening); creeper (plant) other_meaning.

corpus_definition: an action that is against the law and punishable

forms.definition: an action that is against the law and that the police can punish
forms.example: Stealing a car is a serious crime.
forms.note: Uncountable for crime in general ('crime is falling'), countable for one act ('commit a crime').

syn.note: More formal and legal; American spelling is offense.
Formal word for bad or illegal actions.
Breaking a rule or law, often less serious than a crime.
Breaking a religious or moral rule, not a law of the country.

forms.definition: to make an action illegal by a new law
forms.example: Some people want to criminalize using a phone while driving.
forms.note: British spelling: criminalise.

syn.note: Very close: to make something illegal.
Easier word: to say that something is not allowed, by law or by a rule.

ant.note: To make something allowed by law.

forms.definition: connected with breaking the law, or against the law
forms.example: Driving without a licence is a criminal offence.
forms.note: Also a noun: a criminal is a person who has broken the law ('The police caught the criminal'). Common patterns: 'criminal record', 'criminal offence'.

syn.note: Easy and very common: not allowed by law.
Formal: against the law.
Formal: not allowed, often secret, like illicit drugs.
Easy but general: not right, not always against the law.

ant.note: Allowed by the law.
Formal: allowed by the law.

forms.definition: in a way that is against the law
forms.example: The driver was criminally responsible for the accident.

syn.note: Easy and common: in a way that the law does not allow.
Formal: in a way that is against the law.

ant.note: In a way that the law allows.

people.definition: the scientific study of why people break the law
people.example: He studies criminology at university in Tashkent.

people.definition: an expert who studies why people break the law
people.example: The criminologist explained why young people steal.

context.text: Crime in our town has gone down this year. The police say that most criminal cases are now about cheating on the internet, not stealing.

reviewer_note: Person noun criminal shown in the adjective note (gate does not allow repeating criminal in People & things). No affix split for criminal (crimin- is not a word).

corpus_definition: Full of many people or objects.

forms.definition: a large number of people together in one place
forms.example: A big crowd waited outside the stadium in Tashkent.
forms.note: Crowded is made from crowd.

syn.note: A large amount of people or things together, without clear shape.
A big crowd, used in writing.
Easy word, but a group can be small; a crowd is always big.
An angry or wild crowd that may be dangerous.

forms.definition: to come together in large numbers and fill a place
forms.example: People crowded into the small shop to buy cheap bread.
forms.note: Common patterns: 'crowd into', 'crowd around'.

syn.note: To fill a place very tightly with people or things.
To push too many people or things into a small space.
Easy word: come together in one place, not always a lot of people.

ant.note: When a crowd breaks up and people go in different directions.

forms.definition: full of many people or things, with little free space
forms.example: The bus to Chilonzor was very crowded this morning.

syn.note: Easy and common for streets, shops and places with many people.
Very full; used a lot in speaking.
Easy word; full of people or things.
Too full; people or things pushed tightly together.
Used about roads and cities with too much traffic.

ant.note: With nobody or nothing in it.
With no people at all, often a little sad or frightening.

forms.definition: with too many people or things for the space
forms.example: The hospital was overcrowded during the winter.
forms.note: Stronger than crowded: there are more people than there is room for.
No adverb is made from crowded.

context.text: On Saturdays the Chorsu bazaar is very crowded. A big crowd gathers at the bread stalls, and the small streets around the market become overcrowded.

reviewer_note: GATE? overcrowded is a real learner-dictionary adjective (Oxford, Cambridge: 'too many people in a place'); the gate's word list lacks it. Headword is a participle adjective; noun/verb crowd included as the family base. Overcrowded added as an extra adjective (over- is not in the affix table, so no affix row).

corpus_definition: a circular decoration worn on the head by a king or queen

forms.definition: a round gold or silver object that a king or queen wears on the head
forms.example: The queen wore a golden crown at the ceremony.
forms.note: Crown also means the top of the head or a hill, and a cover for a broken tooth.

syn.note: A small crown with jewels, worn by women at special events.
An old word for a crown or a band worn on the head.

forms.definition: to put the round gold object on someone's head to make them king or queen
forms.example: The prince was crowned king in 1953.
forms.note: Usually passive: 'be crowned king/queen'. Also used for winners: 'She was crowned champion.'

syn.note: To put a king or queen on the throne officially.

ant.note: To remove a king or queen from power.

forms.definition: being the best or most important part of something
forms.example: Winning the gold medal was the crowning moment of his career.
forms.note: Belongs to crown = the best part at the end of something, not a king's head decoration. Pattern: 'crowning achievement'.
No adverb is made from crown.

context.text: In the museum in Bukhara you can see the crown of the last emir. The guide told us how he was crowned in a big ceremony.

reviewer_note: coronation shares the old Latin root (corona) but is not made from crown, so it is listed as not_family. Crowning (best part) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: The shared beliefs and arts of a society.

forms.definition: the way of life, beliefs, art and customs of a group of people
forms.example: She is interested in Japanese culture and food.
forms.note: Uncountable for culture in general ('Uzbek culture'), countable for one group ('different cultures').

syn.note: Easy phrase for how a group of people usually live.
A large, developed society with its own culture, often in history.
Customs and beliefs passed from parents to children; one part of culture.
The culture and history of the past that a country keeps.
The usual ways of doing things in a society.

forms.note: No common verb. 'Culture' as a verb (grow cells in a lab) is a rare science word.

forms.definition: connected with the way of life, art and customs of a society
forms.example: Navruz is an important cultural event in Uzbekistan.

syn.note: Connected with customs that are old and passed down.
Connected with art, music or painting only.
Connected with a group of people who share a nation or race.

forms.definition: with people from many different countries and ways of life
forms.example: Tashkent is a multicultural city.

forms.definition: well educated and interested in art, music and books
forms.example: My grandfather was a cultured man who loved poetry.
forms.note: Belongs to culture = a person's good taste in art and books, not the way of life of a society.

forms.definition: in a way connected with the way of life and customs of a society
forms.example: The two countries are culturally very similar.

syn.note: In a way that follows old customs; narrower than culturally.

context.text: Samarkand is full of history and culture. Every year it holds a big cultural festival, and visitors from many countries make the city feel truly multicultural.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows (shared beliefs and arts / ways of life) are one meaning, merged. cultivate shares the root but is not made from culture (not_family); cultured is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A piece of furniture with shelves to store things.

forms.definition: a piece of furniture with a door and shelves to keep things in
forms.example: Please put the clean plates in the cupboard.
forms.note: Pronounced /'kʌbəd/: the p is silent. Made from cup + board long ago but now one word.

syn.note: Very close; common in American English and for kitchens and bathrooms.
American English: a small room or tall cupboard for clothes.
A tall cupboard for hanging clothes.
A small room or cupboard for keeping food.
A flat board on a wall for putting things on, with no door.

forms.note: No verb is made from cupboard.
No adjective is made from cupboard.
No adverb is made from cupboard.

context.text: In my grandmother's kitchen there is a big wooden cupboard. She keeps her best tea bowls in the cupboard and only takes them out for guests.

reviewer_note: Leaf word with no family forms; cup and board are not listed as family (old compound). Silent p noted.

corpus_definition: a smooth rounded line or shape that bends gently

forms.definition: a line or shape that bends smoothly, not straight
forms.example: The road has a sharp curve just after the bridge.

syn.note: Very close and easy, especially for roads and rivers.
Part of a circle, a curve with an even shape.
A place where a road changes direction.
A small round shape, like in hair.

forms.definition: the amount that something bends, how round it is
forms.example: Scientists can measure the curvature of the Earth.

forms.definition: to bend or move in a smooth round line
forms.example: The river curves around the old town.

syn.note: Very close and easy.
To move in a curved line through the air, like a ball.
Said of roads and rivers that bend many times.

ant.note: To make something straight, with no curves.

forms.definition: having a smooth round shape, not straight
forms.example: The old bridge has a beautiful curved roof.

syn.note: With a round shape, especially at the edges.
Changed from a straight shape, often by force.
Curved at the top, like a door or a bridge.

ant.note: Going in one direction, with no bends.
Level, with no curves or bumps.

forms.definition: having many curves
forms.example: We drove along a curvy mountain road to Chimgan.
forms.note: Informal. Also used about a woman's body shape.
No common adverb is made from curve.

context.text: The road to Chimgan curves around the mountains. It is very curvy, so drivers must slow down at every curve.

reviewer_note: Noun, verb conversion and participle adjective curved all in this meaning; curvature added as formal extra; no false affix claimed for curvature (-ure not in table).

corpus_definition: The things you usually do at the same time every day.
usage_note: Usually with a possessive: 'my/your daily routine'. Common patterns: 'part of my daily routine', 'follow / change your daily routine', 'a daily routine of + -ing'.

relations.note: Without 'daily' it means the same in most sentences.
A plan of times for things you must do; a routine is what you usually do.
One thing you do often without thinking; a daily routine is many things.
Everyday activities in general, not a fixed order.

context.text: My daily routine is simple. I wake up at six, have tea with my family and take the metro to work. Going to the gym is now part of my daily routine too.

reviewer_note: Noun phrase; routine (one-word near synonym) listed as relation since the phrase is fixed.

corpus_definition: Foods made from the milk of cows or other animals.

forms.definition: food made from milk, such as cheese, butter and yogurt
forms.example: I try to eat less dairy because it makes me feel heavy.

syn.note: Same meaning, in very easy words.
Related: milk is one kind of dairy food.
Related: cheese is one example of dairy.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: made from milk, or connected with producing milk
forms.example: Yogurt and cheese are dairy products.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: dairy products, dairy farm, dairy cows.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My doctor says I eat too much dairy. Now I buy fewer dairy products like cheese and butter at the bazaar.
