reviewer_note: GATE? dairy as adjective (only before a noun: dairy products, dairy cattle) is listed as an adjective in Oxford Learner's; WordNet lacks it. Noun and before-noun adjective use (dairy products) share one spelling; dairy farmer is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: A small garden flower with white petals and a yellow center.

forms.definition: a small flower with white petals and a yellow middle
forms.example: The children made a chain of daisies in the park.

syn.note: Related: a daisy is one kind of flower.
Related: daisies often grow wild in grass.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: In spring, little daisies grow in the grass near our school. My sister picked a daisy and put it in her hair.

reviewer_note: Simple leaf word; no family forms. Plural daisies (y to ies).

corpus_definition: the part of the day when it is light outside

forms.definition: the time between morning and evening when it is light
forms.example: Most people work in the daytime and sleep at night.
forms.note: Often used before another noun: daytime TV, daytime temperatures.

syn.note: Very close and easier: 'during the day' = 'in the daytime'.
Related: the light of the sun during the day.

ant.note: Night is the dark part of the day.
The time when it is dark. American English often writes nighttime.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
No separate adjective; daytime is used before nouns (daytime temperatures), but it is still the noun.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: In Tashkent, daytime temperatures in July can reach 40 degrees. That is why many people stay inside in the daytime and go out in the evening.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a compound (day + time); no forms built on it. Attributive use noted, not given an adjective entry.

corpus_definition: Unable to hear anything.

forms.definition: the state of not being able to hear
forms.example: His deafness started after a serious illness.

syn.note: Close; hearing loss can be partial, deafness is often total.

forms.definition: to make someone unable to hear, usually for a short time
forms.example: The loud music deafened us for a few minutes.

forms.definition: not able to hear, or not able to hear well
forms.example: She has been deaf since she was a child.

syn.note: Polite phrase for people who can hear a little, but not well.
Formal and polite; used in official writing.

ant.note: Hearing people can hear: 'deaf and hearing students study together'.

forms.definition: so loud that you cannot hear anything else
forms.example: The noise of the crowd was deafening.

syn.note: Easy phrase with almost the same meaning.
Related but weaker: full of noise.

ant.note: Making little or no noise.

forms.note: No common adverb; deafeningly (deafeningly loud) is rare and used almost only with loud.

context.text: My grandfather is a little deaf, so we speak loudly to him. The music at my cousin's wedding was deafening, and for once he said his deafness was useful!

reviewer_note: deafen/deafening kept as same-meaning hearing family; 'the deaf' is not a separate noun entry.

corpus_definition: To be changed or decided by something else.
particle_note: Not separable: 'depend on the weather' (never 'depend the weather on'). Often 'It depends on + noun / wh- clause': 'It depends on how much it costs.' 'It depends.' can stand alone. Also spelled depend upon (more formal).

relations.note: Easy phrase with almost the same meaning.
More formal, common in writing.
Close, but used for one very important thing: 'Everything hinges on the exam result.'
Related, but a different meaning of depend on: to need or trust someone or something.

context.text: Will we go to the mountains on Sunday? It depends on the weather. The price of the trip also depends on how many people come.

reviewer_note: Kept only the 'be decided by' sense; rely on/trust sense noted as related only.

corpus_definition: A dry area with very little rain and few plants.

forms.definition: a large, dry area of land with very little rain and few plants
forms.example: It is very dry in the desert.
forms.note: Stress on the first part: DE-sert. Don't confuse with dessert (sweet food), stressed on the second part.

syn.note: Related: wild land where nobody lives; it may be wet or dry.
Related: many deserts are covered with sand.

forms.definition: the act of leaving a person, place or the army without permission
forms.example: He was punished for desertion from the army.
forms.note: Belongs to the verb desert = leave someone or something, not the dry land.

forms.definition: to leave a person or place and not come back
forms.example: He deserted his family and moved to another city.
forms.note: Belongs to desert = leave or abandon, not the dry land. Stress on the second part: de-SERT.

forms.definition: empty and quiet, with no people in it
forms.example: At night the streets were completely deserted.
forms.note: Belongs to desert = leave; a deserted place is one that people have left. It does not mean dry.
No adverb in this family.

people.definition: a soldier who leaves the army without permission
people.example: The deserter was caught near the border.
people.note: Belongs to desert = leave or abandon, not the dry land.

context.text: The Kyzylkum Desert covers a large part of Uzbekistan. In summer the desert is very hot in the day and cold at night.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: desert (DE-sert, dry land) vs desert/deserted/desertion/deserter (leave). Spelling trap with dessert noted. Desertification is rare (C2), left out.

corpus_definition: to draw a plan for how something should look or work

forms.definition: a drawing or plan that shows how something will look or work
forms.example: The architect showed us the design for the new school.
forms.note: Also: the subject of design ('She studied design') and a pattern ('a flower design').

syn.note: Easy and very close; plan is wider.
Related: a picture made with a pen or pencil.
Related: the way the parts of something are arranged.

forms.definition: to decide and draw how something will look or work before it is made
forms.example: She will design a new house for her family.

syn.note: Easy and close; design is more about how something looks or works.
Related: to make something new.
Related: to prepare a plan or document.

forms.definition: to change the plan or look of something and make it again
forms.example: The company redesigned its website last year.

forms.note: No adjective in this family. Before a noun, designer works like one: designer clothes (see People & things).
No common adverb; designedly is very rare.

people.definition: a person whose job is to plan how clothes, buildings or objects look
people.example: My cousin is a fashion designer in Tashkent.

context.text: My sister wants to design clothes, so she studied design at college. Now she works as a designer, and last month she redesigned the uniform for her old school.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows (A2 and B1) mean the same thing; merged, lowest CEFR kept. designate shares the Latin root but is not made from design.

corpus_definition: a sweet food eaten at the end of a meal

forms.definition: sweet food eaten after the main part of a meal
forms.example: We had ice cream for dessert.
forms.note: Spelling trap: dessert has double s (sweet food); desert has one s (dry land).

syn.note: British English, a little informal: 'What's for sweet?'
British English; can mean any dessert, not only a soft one.

forms.note: No verb in this family.
No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: After plov, my mother always brings a dessert to the table. Tonight the dessert was fresh melon and honey cake.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap with desert noted; no family forms.

corpus_definition: a small machine or tool created for a special purpose

forms.definition: a small machine or tool made to do one special job
forms.example: My phone is a very useful device.

syn.note: Informal; often a small, clever or new electronic thing.
Related: usually something you hold in your hand to do work.
Related: usually bigger, with moving parts.
Related: a machine used at home, like a fridge or washing machine.

forms.definition: to think of a new plan, method or system
forms.example: The teachers devised a new way to help weak students.
forms.note: Belongs to device = a plan or method; devise is about inventing ideas, not machines. Note the spelling: devise (verb, with s), device (noun, with c).
No adjective in this family.
No adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandmother does not like modern devices. Her only device is an old phone, and she uses it just to call us.

reviewer_note: devise placed as other_meaning (plan/method sense) with c/s spelling note.

corpus_definition: the food that a person usually eats every day

forms.definition: the food that a person or animal usually eats
forms.example: A healthy diet includes a lot of fruit and vegetables.
forms.note: Also means a special plan of eating less to lose weight: 'I'm on a diet.'

syn.note: Very close; the usual way a person eats.
Related: everything that people eat.
Related and more formal: the food your body needs to be healthy.

forms.definition: to eat less food, or only some kinds of food, to lose weight
forms.example: She is dieting before her sister's wedding.
forms.note: Belongs to diet = a special eating plan to lose weight, not the food you usually eat.

forms.definition: connected with the food that people eat
forms.example: Beans are a good source of dietary fiber.
forms.note: British spelling: dietary fibre.

syn.note: Close; nutritional is about what food gives your body.

forms.definition: having fewer calories or less sugar than the normal kind
forms.example: He always drinks diet cola.
forms.note: Belongs to diet = eating less to lose weight. Used only before a noun: diet cola, diet drinks.
No common adverb; dietarily is very rare.

people.definition: an expert who advises people about healthy eating
people.example: The dietitian told me to eat more vegetables.
people.note: Also spelled dietician.

people.definition: a person who is eating less to lose weight
people.example: Many dieters stop eating bread.
people.note: Belongs to diet = eating less to lose weight.

context.text: A good diet includes fruit, vegetables, bread and some meat. My dietitian says I need more dietary fiber, so now I eat more beans and lentils.

reviewer_note: GATE? diet adjective (only before a noun: diet cola, diet drinks) is an Oxford Learner's adjective entry; WordNet lacks it. Sense trap: corpus sense is usual food; the weight-loss verb, diet cola adjective and dieter are other_meaning. -ary and -itian not in affix table, so no affixes.

corpus_definition: Not being the same as another object.
usage_note: be different from + noun / pronoun / -ing: 'My phone is different from yours.' British English also says 'different to'; American English also says 'different than'.

relations.note: Easy and means exactly the same.
A preposition: 'Unlike my brother, I love maths.' You don't use 'be' before it.
Formal and not common in speaking.
Two things that are equal in every way.
Almost the same, with only small differences.

context.text: Life in Tashkent is very different from life in a small village. My new school is also different from my old one: the classes are bigger.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; BrE 'different to' and AmE 'different than' mentioned in usage note.

corpus_definition: The path or way that someone or something is moving.

forms.definition: the way that someone or something is going or facing
forms.example: We walked in the direction of the river.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word: 'Which way is the park?'
Used for ships, planes and planned routes.
A route is the full road or path you take from one place to another.
A path can be the line something moves along, or a small road.

forms.note: The plural 'directions' often means instructions for getting somewhere: 'Can you give me directions to the station?'

forms.definition: to tell or show someone how to get to a place
forms.example: A police officer directed us to the hospital.

syn.note: Easy phrase with almost the same meaning.
Guide often means you go with the person.
You show the way with your finger or a sign.

forms.note: Direct also means to manage something or to be in charge of a film; that is a different meaning.

forms.definition: going straight from one place to another without stopping
forms.example: There is a direct flight from Tashkent to Istanbul.

syn.note: Easy word for a line or path with no turns.
Used for trains and roads that go all the way without changing: 'a through train'.

ant.note: Going a longer way, with turns or stops.

forms.definition: giving orders or instructions about what to do
forms.example: The new manager has a very directive style.
forms.note: Belongs to direct = manage or control, not the way something is moving. Formal; more common as a noun (an official order).

forms.definition: in a straight line, without stopping or going anywhere else
forms.example: After school, go directly home.

syn.note: Easy and very common: 'Go straight home.'
Used before words like 'to' or 'into': 'right to the door'.

ant.note: In a way that is not straight or not simple.

forms.note: 'direct' can also be an adverb: 'This bus goes direct to the airport.'

people.definition: a person who manages a company or tells actors what to do in a film
people.example: The director of the film is from Uzbekistan.
people.note: Belongs to direct = manage or control, not the way something is moving.

context.text: Excuse me, which direction is Chorsu Bazaar? A kind woman directed us to the metro, and we went directly there.

reviewer_note: direct (verb) and direct (adjective) listed in this 'way' sense; director kept as other_meaning (manage).

corpus_definition: A serious sickness that affects a body or plant.

forms.definition: an illness of people, animals or plants, often serious
forms.example: Heart disease is a common problem in many countries.

syn.note: Very close; illness is often used for a person's period of being ill.
A little more general and less formal.
An illness caused by bacteria or a virus that gets into the body.
A health problem that lasts a long time; more polite and medical.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: sick or damaged because of an illness
forms.example: The farmer cut down the diseased trees.

syn.note: Easy word; diseased is used more for body parts and plants.
Infected means germs have got into it.

ant.note: Not sick; in good condition.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandfather grows apple trees near Fergana. Last year a disease attacked them, and he had to cut off all the diseased branches.

reviewer_note: False-prefix trap: dis- + ease is old history, not a clear split for learners; no affix claimed.

corpus_definition: Something that is very unpleasant and makes you feel sick.

forms.definition: a strong feeling of not liking something that seems dirty or wrong
forms.example: She looked at the dirty kitchen with disgust.

syn.note: Stronger and formal.
Much weaker: you simply don't like something.
Horror is mostly a feeling of fear and shock.

forms.definition: to make someone feel sick or very angry because something is so bad
forms.example: The smell of old fish disgusts me.

syn.note: Very close; often about bad actions.
Shock is about surprise and upset, not feeling sick.

ant.note: To make someone feel very happy.

forms.definition: so bad or dirty that it makes you feel sick
forms.example: The toilet at the old station was disgusting.

syn.note: Easy and common, but a little weaker.
Very common in speaking, especially with young people.
Same strength, a bit more British.
Easy word; very unpleasant.
Very bad, but not always about feeling sick.

ant.note: For food: tasting very good.
Very nice and pleasant.

forms.definition: feeling very upset and sick because of something bad
forms.example: I was disgusted by the way he spoke to his mother.

syn.note: Shocked because something is very wrong.

forms.note: Disgusted is how you feel; disgusting is the thing that makes you feel this way.

forms.definition: in a way that is very unpleasant
forms.example: The bin smelled disgustingly bad.

syn.note: Easy and close in meaning.

forms.note: Also used to mean 'very, too much', often jokingly: 'disgustingly rich'.

context.text: The food at that cafe was disgusting, and the tables were dirty. I was so disgusted that I left without paying.

reviewer_note: False-prefix trap: disgust is not dis- + gust; no dis- claimed. -ing vs -ed pair (disgusting/disgusted) shown.

corpus_definition: Not telling the truth and often trying to cheat people.

forms.definition: behaviour where a person lies, cheats or steals
forms.example: He lost his job because of his dishonesty.

syn.note: Close; behaviour that hides the truth.
Only about not telling the truth.
Breaking rules to win or get something.

ant.note: Always telling the truth and not cheating.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family; use 'lie' or 'cheat'.

forms.definition: not telling the truth, or trying to cheat people
forms.example: The dishonest seller sold us an old phone as new.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Easy word; describes someone who says things that are not true.
Tries hard to make people believe false things.
Informal: dishonest, often in business or money.

ant.note: Always telling the truth.
Telling the truth.

forms.definition: in a way that is not truthful or fair
forms.example: She got the money dishonestly.

syn.note: Not fair, but not always about lying.

ant.note: In a truthful way.

context.text: It is dishonest to sell old fruit as fresh. People in our mahalla stopped visiting the shop after they learned about the owner's dishonesty.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged; cefr A2 (lowest). honest/honesty/honestly listed as antonyms, not forms.

corpus_definition: far away in space or time from where you are

forms.definition: the amount of space between two places or things
forms.example: The distance from Tashkent to Samarkand is about 300 kilometres.

syn.note: Easy, in phrases: 'It's a long way.'
Length is how long one thing is, not the space between two things.
Space is the empty area between things.

forms.definition: to become less friendly or less involved with someone or something
forms.example: After the argument, he distanced himself from his old friends.
forms.note: Belongs to distant = not friendly or close, not far away in space. Usually 'distance yourself from'.

forms.definition: far away in space or time
forms.example: We could see distant mountains from the plane.

syn.note: Easy word; often in 'far away'.
Same meaning; used before a noun.
Far from towns and other people.
Same meaning, a little literary.

ant.note: A short distance away.
Not far.
Near the place you are.

forms.definition: in a way that is not close, for example in family relationships
forms.example: We are distantly related through my grandmother.
forms.note: Belongs to distant = not close in family or feelings (a distant cousin), not far away in space.

context.text: My aunt lives in a distant village in the mountains. The distance is not great, but the road is very bad, so the trip takes six hours.

reviewer_note: No -ant/-ance split claimed (dist- is not a word). distance verb and distantly kept as other_meaning (relationships).

corpus_definition: To move digital content from the web to your device.

forms.definition: a file or program that you copy from the internet
forms.example: This free download is only 20 megabytes.

syn.note: A file is any document, picture or program on a computer.

ant.note: A file that you send from your device to the internet.

forms.note: Also the act of copying: 'The download took five minutes.'

forms.definition: to copy files or programs from the internet onto your phone or computer
forms.example: I downloaded a new game last night.

syn.note: You keep a file on your device; you can save without the internet.
General word for making the same file in another place.
Easy, informal: 'I got the app yesterday.'

ant.note: To send files from your device to the internet.

forms.definition: able to be copied from the internet
forms.example: The teacher made the worksheets downloadable.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: I downloaded the VIRORA app on my phone last night. The download was quick, and all the lessons are downloadable, so I can study on the bus.

reviewer_note: download is not split into down + load (treated as one word, not a compound). upload as antonym.

corpus_definition: a sliding box built into a piece of furniture for storing things

forms.definition: a box in a desk or cupboard that you pull out to keep things in
forms.example: My passport is in the top drawer of my desk.

syn.note: A separate small space inside something, like a bag or car.
A flat board on a wall or in a cupboard, not a box that slides out.

forms.note: A piece of furniture with many drawers is called a 'chest of drawers'.

forms.definition: to pull something in a direction
forms.example: She drew the curtains and turned on the light.
forms.note: Drawer comes from draw = pull (draw the curtains). Most learners know draw = make a picture, which is a different meaning.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Mum always keeps spoons and forks in the kitchen drawer. When the drawer gets stuck, my brother has to pull it hard.

reviewer_note: Thing noun: stays main noun. drawer = 'thing you draw (pull) out'; verb draw shown as other_meaning (pull), not the picture sense.

corpus_definition: A picture made with a pencil or pen.

forms.definition: a picture made with a pencil or pen
forms.example: The children put their drawings on the classroom wall.

syn.note: A quick or simple drawing.
Easy, general word; a picture can also be a photo or painting.
A picture in a book or magazine.
A painting is made with paint, not pencil.

forms.note: Drawing is also the activity: 'She is good at drawing.'

forms.definition: a game in which both teams or players have the same score
forms.example: The match ended in a draw, 1-1.
forms.note: Belongs to draw = end a game with equal scores, not making a picture. American English often says 'tie'.

forms.definition: to make a picture with a pencil or pen
forms.example: Can you draw a cat?

syn.note: Draw quickly or simply.
To draw pictures for a book or magazine.
Paint uses paint and a brush, not a pencil.

forms.note: Irregular: draw, drew, drawn.

forms.definition: looking very tired, worried or ill
forms.example: She looked pale and drawn after the long night.
forms.note: Belongs to draw = pull (a face that looks pulled and tired), not making a picture.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a box in a desk that you pull out to keep things in
people.example: I keep my pens in the desk drawer.
people.note: Belongs to draw = pull, not making a picture.

context.text: My little sister loves to draw. For my birthday she gave me a drawing of our house in Bukhara.

reviewer_note: Several draw meanings (picture / pull / equal score) separated; drawer and drawn kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Expected to happen or arrive at a certain time.

forms.definition: money that you pay regularly to be a member of a club or group
forms.example: All members must pay their dues by January.
forms.note: Belongs to due = owed or right to pay, not expected to happen. Always plural in this meaning.
There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: expected to happen or arrive at a certain time
forms.example: The next bus is due in ten minutes.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Planned for a time in a timetable or plan.

forms.note: 'due to' is a different meaning: 'because of'. 'The train was late due to snow.'

forms.definition: late; not done, paid or returned at the expected time
forms.example: My library books are two weeks overdue.

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
Made late by something.

ant.note: At the expected time, not late.

forms.definition: more than is right or needed
forms.example: Don't put undue pressure on the children.
forms.note: Belongs to due = right or proper. Formal; not the opposite of 'expected'.

forms.definition: at the expected time or in the expected way
forms.example: The taxi was ordered for eight, and it duly arrived.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same idea.
In the correct way.

context.text: The train from Samarkand is due at six o'clock, and it duly arrived on time. Sadly, my library books are now overdue!

reviewer_note: Only the 'expected' sense mapped; due to (because of), dues and undue kept as other meanings. overdue kept as a family form (over- prefix, not a compound).

corpus_definition: To get money by doing work.

forms.definition: the money that you get for the work you do
forms.example: His earnings went up after he got a new job in Tashkent.
forms.note: Almost always plural: earnings.

syn.note: Very close; income can also come from things like rent, not only work.
Related: money paid every month for a job, usually in an office.
Related: money paid for work, often every week, for physical jobs.
Easy, everyday word for the money you get for working.

forms.definition: to get money because you do a job or work
forms.example: I earn more money now than last year.

syn.note: Easy, everyday: 'make money'. Earn sounds a little more serious.
Easy phrase: you get paid for your work.
Easy phrase with the same idea: 'She is paid well.'
Related: to get something useful, not only money.

ant.note: You earn money by working and spend it by buying things.
To have less money than before, for example in business.

forms.note: No common adjective made from earn. 'Hard-earned' (hard-earned money) is a compound.
No adverb made from earn.

people.definition: a person who gets money for the work they do
people.example: My father was the only earner in our family.

context.text: My sister earns good money as a nurse in Samarkand. Her earnings help the whole family, and she saves a little every month.

reviewer_note: Earnings is plural-only and listed as the noun; earner sits in people. No adjective or adverb exists.

corpus_definition: The process of learning things at school or university.

forms.definition: the process of teaching and learning at school or university
forms.example: Free education is important for every child.

syn.note: Close, but usually only about school, not university.
Related: getting knowledge in any way, not only at school.
Related: what teachers do; education is the whole process.
Related: learning practical skills for a job.

forms.definition: to teach someone, usually at a school or university
forms.example: She was educated at a university in Tashkent.
forms.note: Often passive: 'be educated at/in'.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word; educate sounds more formal and covers a long time.
Formal: teach a skill or give clear information.
Related: teach practical skills for a job or sport.

forms.definition: connected with teaching and learning, or helping you learn
forms.example: We watched an educational film about space.

syn.note: Formal: giving useful knowledge.
Related: giving a lot of useful information.
Related: connected with schools and universities, often studying and exams.

forms.definition: having learned a lot at school or university
forms.example: Her parents are both highly educated people.

syn.note: Formal and old-fashioned: knowing a lot after long study.
Related: knowing a lot about a subject, not only from school.

ant.note: Having had little or no teaching at school.
Not knowing things you should know; can sound rude.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with teaching and learning
forms.example: The game is fun and educationally useful.

syn.note: Related: in a way connected with study and exams.

people.definition: a teacher or a person whose job is teaching people
people.example: Many educators came to the conference in Bukhara.
people.note: More common in American English; British English usually says teacher.

context.text: In Uzbekistan, education is free in state schools. My grandfather was educated in Moscow, and he still loves watching educational programmes on TV.

reviewer_note: Educated (participle adjective) kept as an extra; uneducated is its antonym, not a form.

corpus_definition: the joint in the middle of your arm that allows it to bend

forms.definition: the part in the middle of your arm where it bends
forms.example: She hurt her elbow when she fell off her bike.

syn.note: Related: any place where two bones meet, like the knee or elbow.
Related: the whole arm; the elbow is one part of it.

forms.definition: to push someone with the bony part of your arm
forms.example: He elbowed his way through the crowd at the bazaar.
forms.note: Often: elbow your way through/past people.

syn.note: Easy, general word; elbowing is pushing with that part of your arm.
Informal: push hard and roughly.
Related: a small, gentle push, often to get attention.

forms.note: No adjective made from elbow.
No adverb made from elbow.

context.text: Aziz fell during the football match and hurt his elbow. Later, at the busy bus stop, a man elbowed him, and it hurt again.

reviewer_note: Verb elbow (push with the elbow) kept as a same-meaning conversion. Compounds like elbow room left out.

corpus_definition: Messages sent from one computer to another over the web.

forms.definition: a message that you send from one computer or phone to another
forms.example: I got an email from my teacher this morning.
forms.note: Spelling: email or e-mail; email is more common now.

syn.note: Related: any written note you send, also by phone or app.
Related: in American English mail can mean emails; usually it means letters.
The same word, older spelling with a hyphen.

forms.definition: to send a message to someone by computer or phone
forms.example: Please email me the report before Friday.

syn.note: Easy: send a message, often by phone app.
Related: general word; you send an email.
Related: send someone a letter or email.

forms.note: No adjective made from email.
No adverb made from email.

context.text: I check my email every morning before work. Yesterday my boss emailed me a new plan for our office in Namangan.

reviewer_note: Verb email is a zero-change conversion. e-mail is the same word spelled differently, listed as a synonym with a note.

corpus_definition: a male ruler of a large empire or group of countries

forms.definition: a man who rules a very large group of countries
forms.example: The emperor lived in a huge palace.

syn.note: General word for a person who controls a country.
Related: rules one country; an emperor rules many lands.
Formal: a king, queen, emperor or empress.
Related: the title of the old Russian emperors.

forms.note: No verb made from emperor.
No adjective made from emperor. 'Imperial' (connected with an empire or emperor) has the same old Latin root but is not made from emperor.
No adverb made from emperor.

people.definition: a woman who rules an empire, or the wife of an emperor
people.example: The empress gave money to build a new school.

context.text: The emperor ruled many countries for thirty years. After he died, the empress ruled the land until their son was old enough.

reviewer_note: Empire and imperial share an old root with emperor but are not made from it; empire is in people_not_family, imperial in not_family.

corpus_definition: the power to do physical or mental activities

forms.definition: the power and strength you need to be active
forms.example: After a long day at work, I have no energy left.

syn.note: Related: the power of your body, especially your muscles.
Related: general word for the ability to do things.
Related: the energy to keep doing something for a long time.
Formal: being full of energy and life.

ant.note: The feeling of needing rest or sleep.
Formal: very great tiredness.

forms.definition: to make someone feel more active and full of power
forms.example: A short walk in the morning energizes me.
forms.note: British spelling: energise.

syn.note: Related: make you feel less tired, for example after rest or a drink.
Formal: make you feel healthy and full of energy.
Related: make someone feel strong again after being very tired.

ant.note: To make someone need rest.
To make someone very, very tired.

forms.definition: having a lot of power and wanting to be active
forms.example: My little brother is very energetic; he never sits still.

syn.note: Easy word: always moving or doing things.
Full of life and interest; also used about places and music.
Related: full of energy and new ideas, often about people at work.

ant.note: Not wanting to work or be active.
Needing rest or sleep.

forms.definition: in an active way, with a lot of power
forms.example: The children danced energetically at the wedding.

syn.note: Related: in a busy, active way.
With a lot of strength and force.
Related: with great interest and excitement.

ant.note: In a slow way, without wanting to do much.

context.text: Our football coach is always energetic and loud. He says a good breakfast gives you energy for the whole day, so we eat plov after training.

reviewer_note: Personal-energy sense only; the machine/electricity row is a separate map. No -ic/-ly affix claimed on energetic(ally) because the split is not clean.

corpus_definition: The power that makes machines work or keeps us active.

forms.definition: power from electricity, gas, oil or the sun that makes machines work
forms.example: Solar panels turn sunlight into energy.
forms.note: Common phrases: solar energy, save energy, energy bills.

syn.note: Very close: 'power stations make power'. Power often means electricity.
Related: one kind of energy, used for lights and machines.
Related: something like gas or oil that is burned to make energy.

forms.definition: to make someone feel more active and full of power
forms.example: Morning sport energizes me for the day.
forms.note: Belongs to energy = a person's strength, not power for machines. British spelling: energise.

forms.definition: having a lot of power and wanting to be active
forms.example: She is an energetic teacher who loves her job.
forms.note: Belongs to energy = a person's strength, not power for machines.

forms.definition: in an active way, with a lot of power
forms.example: They cleaned the house energetically before the guests came.
forms.note: Belongs to energy = a person's strength, not power for machines.

context.text: Uzbekistan is building new solar stations to make clean energy. We can all save energy at home by turning off lights we don't need.

reviewer_note: Row 2 example ('keep the lights on') is the machine/electricity sense, so it gets its own map; all other family forms belong to the personal sense.

corpus_definition: Including everything or everyone without any exceptions.

forms.definition: the whole of something, with no part missing
forms.example: Please read the contract in its entirety before you sign.
forms.note: Mostly in the phrase 'in its entirety'.

syn.note: Easy: 'the whole of the book'.
Very formal: all of something.

forms.note: No verb made from entire.

forms.definition: including every part or every person, with nothing missing
forms.example: We cleaned the entire house before the holiday.
forms.note: Used before a noun: 'the entire class'.

syn.note: Easy and almost the same: 'the whole day'.
With every part; also means finished.
Related: used about amounts: 'the total cost'.
Related: 'a full day' = the whole day.

ant.note: Only a part of something, not all of it.
Not having every part; not finished.

forms.definition: completely, in every way
forms.example: I entirely agree with you.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Very close and a little informal.
Close: 'fully understand'.
Formal: completely.

ant.note: Only a little, not completely.
Formal: only in part.

context.text: The entire family came to my cousin's wedding in Fergana. It was an entirely different experience from weddings in the city.

reviewer_note: Entirety is formal but in learner dictionaries; no verb exists.

corpus_definition: A paper cover used to hold a message inside.

forms.definition: a flat paper cover that you put a letter or card in
forms.example: Write the address on the envelope before you post it.

syn.note: Related: a small paper box or bag; not usually for letters.
Related: anything that goes over or around something.

forms.definition: to cover or surround something completely
forms.example: Thick fog enveloped the mountains in the morning.
forms.note: Belongs to the old meaning 'wrap or cover', not a paper envelope. Formal, often in stories. Say /ɪnˈveləp/; envelope is /ˈenvələʊp/.
No adjective made from envelope.
No adverb made from envelope.

context.text: My grandmother still sends letters to her friends in Khiva. She writes the address on the envelope very carefully and puts a stamp in the corner.

reviewer_note: Envelop (verb, no final e) is the source word but a different meaning, so other_meaning with a pronunciation note.

corpus_definition: A short piece of writing about a particular subject.

forms.definition: a short piece of writing about one subject, often for school
forms.example: We have to write an essay about our hometown.

syn.note: Close: a piece of writing done at school, often shorter and simpler.
Related: in American English, a long essay written for university.
Related: a piece of writing in a newspaper or magazine.
Related: any task given by a teacher, not only writing.

forms.definition: to try to do something
forms.example: He essayed a smile, but he still looked sad.
forms.note: Belongs to an old meaning of essay = an attempt. Very formal and rare; learners don't need to use it.
No adjective made from essay.
No adverb made from essay.

people.definition: a writer who is known for writing short pieces on one subject
people.example: Abdulla Qodiriy was a novelist and also an essayist.

context.text: Our English teacher asked us to write an essay about our favourite holiday. The best essay will be read in front of the whole class.

reviewer_note: Verb essay (= try) is very formal and rare but in learner dictionaries, so it is other_meaning, not hidden.

corpus_definition: And other things of a similar kind.
usage_note: Put etc. at the end of a list, after a comma in British English: 'fruit, bread, milk, etc.' It is short for Latin et cetera; say it /et ˈsetərə/. Don't use 'and etc.' and don't use it after 'such as' or 'for example'.

relations.note: Same meaning; easier to say in speech.
Same meaning, a little more formal.
Close: things similar to the ones in the list.
Related: there are more things, but not always of the same kind.

context.text: For the trip to Chimgan, bring warm clothes, water, snacks, etc. We will also need tents, blankets, etc., so let's go to the shop on Saturday.

reviewer_note: GATE? Context does use etc. twice; the gate's word-boundary regex can't match a headword ending in a full stop before a space or comma. Abbreviation used like an adverb at the end of lists; treated as a function item with no forms.

corpus_definition: Not including the thing or person mentioned.
usage_note: except (for) + noun/pronoun: 'Everyone came except (for) Aziz.' Often after all, every, everyone, nothing: 'I eat everything except fish.' Also except + that clause: 'The trip was fine, except that it rained.'

relations.note: Same meaning, very common in British English: 'Everyone apart from him was there.'
Same meaning; except for is needed at the start of a sentence: 'Except for Monday, I'm free.'
After words like all, nobody, everything: 'Nobody but Lola knew.'
More formal, often about prices and lists: 'The price is $50, excluding tax.'
Including adds the person or thing to the group; except leaves it out.

context.text: All my friends came to the party except Bobur. He was in Samarkand with his family, so everyone except him had a great time.

reviewer_note: Function word (preposition), kind_hint 'word' corrected. Family words exception/exceptional are not shown because function maps have no forms.

corpus_definition: costing a lot of money

forms.definition: the money that you spend on something
forms.example: A new car is a big expense for a young family.
forms.note: Often plural: 'travel expenses' = money spent on a work trip.

syn.note: Easy and very close: the money you pay for something.
The price is the amount a shop asks; an expense is money you actually spend.
All the money you spend, not one single cost.

ant.note: Income is money that comes in; an expense is money that goes out.

forms.note: There is no verb made from expensive. Expend (= spend, formal) comes from the same old Latin root but is not made from expensive or expense in English.

forms.definition: costing a lot of money
forms.example: That watch is too expensive for me.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal; often about mistakes too: 'a costly mistake'.
British English, a bit old-fashioned: 'Fruit is very dear in winter.'
Informal, used in conversation.
Says the price is high; used about goods and services.

ant.note: The easiest opposite: costing little money.
Not costing much; a polite word that sounds better than cheap.

forms.definition: in a way that costs a lot of money
forms.example: The hotel rooms were expensively decorated with silk and gold.

syn.note: Related: spending a lot to make something rich and beautiful.
Related: in a rich, beautiful way, not only about money.

ant.note: Costing little money: 'You can eat cheaply at the bazaar.'

context.text: Phones are very expensive in this shop. A new phone is a big expense for a student, so I bought mine at a cheaper market in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Inexpensive is listed as an antonym, not a form. Expend is same Latin root but not made from expensive: not_family.

corpus_definition: Knowledge or skill gained by doing or seeing things.

forms.definition: knowledge or skill you get from doing something for a long time
forms.example: She has much experience in teaching children.
forms.note: In this meaning it is uncountable: 'a lot of experience', not 'many experiences'. 'An experience' (countable) is something that happens to you.

syn.note: Informal: practical knowledge of how to do something.
More formal: a high level of special skill or knowledge.
Related: the ability to do something well; experience is how you get it.
Related: what you know, from study or from doing things.
Related: doing something again and again to get better.

ant.note: Not having enough knowledge or skill because you are new to something.

forms.definition: to have something happen to you, or to feel something
forms.example: Many tourists experience problems with the heat in summer.
forms.note: Belongs to experience = something that happens to you, not knowledge or skill you have.

forms.definition: having knowledge or skill because you have done something many times
forms.example: We need an experienced driver for the mountain roads.

syn.note: Good at a job because of training or practice.
Very skilled; knows a lot about one subject.
Has done something for many years: 'a seasoned traveller'.
Related: has passed the exams or training for a job, but may have little practice.

ant.note: Without much knowledge or skill because you are new to something.

forms.note: No common adverb. Experientially exists only in very formal or academic writing.

context.text: Dilnoza has five years of experience in teaching English. She is an experienced teacher, so new teachers at her school often ask her for help.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: verb experience (= undergo) belongs to the 'event' sense, marked other_meaning. Expert shares the Latin root but is not made from experience. No affix: experi- + -ence is not a real split.

corpus_definition: to burst suddenly with a loud bang and great force

forms.definition: a sudden loud burst of something, like a bomb, with great force
forms.example: We heard a loud explosion from the old factory.
forms.note: In another meaning it is a sudden big increase: 'a population explosion'.

syn.note: Very close; common in news reports.
Related: the loud noise only, not the force.
Related: a sudden breaking open, often smaller.

forms.definition: to burst suddenly with a loud noise and great force
forms.example: The old factory exploded in the middle of the night.

syn.note: Everyday phrasal verb with the same meaning; it can also mean to make something explode.
Used about bombs, guns and alarms: 'The bomb went off at noon.'
Break open suddenly, often without fire: 'The balloon burst.'
Formal and technical, about bombs.

forms.definition: able or likely to burst suddenly with a loud noise
forms.example: Gas is explosive, so be careful with the cooker.
forms.note: Also a noun: 'an explosive' = a substance like dynamite. Explosive can also describe a situation or a person who gets angry suddenly.

syn.note: Scientific: can easily burn or turn into gas.
Related: can hurt people; much more general.

forms.definition: suddenly and with great force or noise
forms.example: The tyre burst explosively on the hot road.

syn.note: Related: with great force.
Related: quickly and unexpectedly, without the force.

context.text: Last night a gas tank exploded near our street in Andijan. The explosion was so loud that everyone woke up. Firefighters said the gas was very explosive.

reviewer_note: Explosive (noun = a substance) mentioned in the adjective note, not repeated in People & things. No -ive affix: explos- is not a word.

corpus_definition: To not be successful in something you try to do.

forms.definition: a lack of success in something you try to do
forms.example: The plan ended in failure because nobody helped.
forms.note: Can also be a person or thing that is not successful: 'I felt like a failure.'

syn.note: Same meaning, a little formal.
Related: losing a game, fight or election.
Informal: a film, show or product that nobody likes.
Related: a very bad failure or a terrible event.

ant.note: Getting the result you wanted.

forms.definition: a result showing that someone did not pass an exam
forms.example: I got a fail in maths, so I have to take the test again.
forms.note: Mainly British English, about exam results. 'Without fail' = always.

ant.note: A result showing that you were successful in an exam.

forms.definition: to not be successful in something you try to do
forms.example: Did you fail the driving test?

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal.
Informal, mostly American, about exams: 'He flunked chemistry.'
Related: used about plans that don't happen.
Related: not win a game or competition.

ant.note: To get the result you wanted.
To be successful in an exam or test.

forms.definition: not successful in what it tried to do
forms.example: After two failed attempts, he finally passed the exam.

syn.note: Same meaning; can be used after the noun too: 'The attempt was unsuccessful.'

ant.note: Getting the result you wanted.

forms.note: No adverb in this meaning. Unfailingly (= always, every time) is rare and formal.

context.text: Akmal failed his driving test the first time. The failure made him sad, but he practised every day and passed a month later.

reviewer_note: Unfailing/unfailingly mean 'always', not an opposite of failed; noted as rare. No affix: -ure and -ed are not in the table.

corpus_definition: a small magical creature with wings in stories

forms.definition: a small magical creature like a tiny person with wings, in stories
forms.example: The fairy waved her wand and the frog became a prince.

syn.note: Related: a small magical creature with pointed ears, usually without wings.
Related: a small playful magical creature in old stories.
Related: a literary word for a small magical spirit, often of water or air.

forms.note: No adjective. 'Fairy' is used before nouns in compounds like fairy tale and fairy lights.

context.text: My grandmother tells my little sister a story about a kind fairy every night. In the story, the fairy helps a poor girl from a village near Bukhara.

reviewer_note: Leaf noun: no derived forms. Fairy tale, fairy lights and fairyland are compounds, left for the Compounds branch.

corpus_definition: not real or genuine; made to look like something it is not

forms.definition: a copy made to look real so that it tricks people
forms.example: The painting in the museum was a fake.

syn.note: Related: something made to look the same; a copy is not always meant to trick people.
A fake document, signature, painting or banknote.
A copy of something more expensive: 'imitation leather'.

ant.note: The real first one, not a copy.

forms.definition: to make a copy of something to trick people, or to pretend
forms.example: He faked his father's signature on the school report.

syn.note: To copy documents, money or signatures illegally.
To act as if something is true: 'She faked a smile' = she pretended to smile.
Related: make something the same; not always to trick.

forms.definition: not real; made to look like something it is not
forms.example: The police found a fake passport in his bag.

syn.note: Not true or not real: 'a false name'.
Fake money or brand goods made to trick people.
Used about fake documents and signatures.
Informal. American spelling: phony.
Related: made by people, not natural, but not made to trick: 'artificial flowers'.

ant.note: The easiest opposite: true and not a copy.
Really what it seems to be: 'genuine leather'.
Formal: truly from the time, place or person it says.

forms.note: There is no adverb. Say 'falsely' or 'in a fake way'.

context.text: At the bazaar a man sold my brother a fake watch. It looked like a famous brand, but it stopped after two days. Now my brother knows how to spot a fake.

reviewer_note: Same spelling in noun, verb and adjective (conversions). Faker is not in learner dictionaries, so People & things is empty.

corpus_definition: Known by many people because of a special thing.
usage_note: be famous for + noun / -ing: 'Samarkand is famous for its old buildings.' 'He is famous for telling jokes.' Use famous as (not for) for a job or role: 'famous as a singer'.

relations.note: Same meaning, a little weaker; very common.
Same meaning, everyday English.
Formal, always about something good.
Formal, often in writing.
Related: famous for something BAD: 'The road is notorious for accidents.'

context.text: Uzbekistan is famous for its plov and its old cities. Bukhara is famous for its beautiful buildings, and many tourists visit every year.

reviewer_note: Adjective + preposition pattern; famous as vs famous for explained. No true antonym phrase, so none listed.

corpus_definition: An emotion or state of mind.

forms.definition: an emotion, like happiness or fear, or an idea you have
forms.example: I have a good feeling about this year.
forms.note: 'Hurt someone's feelings' (plural) = make someone sad.

syn.note: Very close; a little more formal.
Formal: a feeling or opinion about something.
Related: 'a sense of pride / a sense that something is wrong'.
Related: how you feel for a period of time, like a good or bad mood.

forms.definition: to have a particular emotion or state of mind
forms.example: I feel very happy when my family is together.
forms.note: Irregular: feel, felt, felt.

syn.note: Related, more formal: 'experience fear'.
To feel something without seeing or being told: 'I sensed she was worried.'

forms.note: No common adjective. Unfeeling (= not caring about other people's emotions) is rare and is a negative form.

forms.definition: in a way that shows strong emotion
forms.example: She spoke feelingly about her grandmother at the wedding.
forms.note: Rare; in everyday English people say 'with feeling' or 'emotionally'.

syn.note: Showing emotion; the common everyday word.
Related: with very strong feeling and energy.

ant.note: Without showing any emotion or kindness.

people.definition: one of the two long thin parts on an insect's head
people.example: The ant touched the bread with its feelers.
people.note: Belongs to feel = touch something, not feel an emotion.

context.text: I feel nervous before every exam. It's a terrible feeling, but my teacher says it is normal and it helps me study harder.

reviewer_note: Headword is made from feel, so feel is the verb form. Feeler belongs to the touch sense: other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A collection of information stored on a computer.

forms.definition: a collection of information with a name, kept on a computer
forms.example: Save the file before closing the program.
forms.note: Also a box or folder for keeping papers.

syn.note: A file with text in it, like a letter or report.
Related: information kept about someone or something.
Related, but careful: a folder holds files; it is not a file itself.

forms.definition: the work of putting documents in order so you can find them later
forms.example: On Fridays the secretary does all the filing.

forms.definition: to put documents in the right place so you can find them later
forms.example: I file all my work emails in different folders.
forms.note: In another meaning: officially give a document, like 'file a complaint'.

syn.note: Related: keep something in a place to use later.
Related, for computers: keep a document so it isn't lost.
Related: put things in order. British spelling: organise.

context.text: My teacher sent me a file with the homework. I saved it on my laptop and filed it in a folder called 'English'. Good filing saves me a lot of time.

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: file = tool for nails or metal, and 'in single file' (a line), are different words, not this family. Compounds (filename, filing cabinet) left out.

corpus_definition: To write missing details into an empty space.
particle_note: Separable: 'fill in the form' or 'fill the form in'. With a pronoun, the pronoun goes in the middle: 'fill it in'.

relations.note: Same meaning, more common in American English: "fill out a form".
More formal; used in official instructions: "Complete the form in black ink."
Related: to write something in a space, but not always a whole form.
Related: to type or write information, often on a computer.

context.text: At the bank, the woman gave me a long form. I filled in my name, address and passport number. Then she checked that I had filled it all in correctly.

reviewer_note: Kept to the 'write details on a form' sense; 'fill in for someone' (replace a person) is a different meaning and is not used.

corpus_definition: To make a space full of something.
particle_note: Pattern: fill + object + with + noun: 'fill the bucket with water'. The object always comes between fill and with. Passive: 'The room was filled with smoke.'

relations.note: Very close, but fill up stresses that the space becomes completely full: "fill up the tank".
Related: used for putting things into a car, truck or machine: "load the car with bags".
Related: to put many things tightly into a box or bag: "pack the box with books".
Related and informal: to push a lot of things into something quickly.
To take everything out of a space: "empty the bucket".

context.text: Before the picnic, Dilnoza filled the bottles with cold water. Her brother filled a big bag with apples from the garden.

reviewer_note: Verb + preposition pattern kept as phrasal per hint; the object must sit between fill and with.

corpus_definition: Small objects that make loud bangs and colorful light in the sky.

forms.definition: small objects that explode in the sky with bright colours and loud bangs
forms.example: We watched the fireworks on New Year's Eve.
forms.note: Usually plural. The singular firework means one of them: 'a firework exploded'.

syn.note: Related: a small one that makes a loud bang but little light.
Related: a technical word for the art of making and showing them.
Related: a small one you hold in your hand that gives off bright sparks.

forms.note: There is no verb from fireworks.
There is no adjective from fireworks.
There is no adverb from fireworks.

context.text: On Navruz evening the whole family went to the park. At ten o'clock the fireworks began, and the children shouted every time the sky turned red and gold.

reviewer_note: fireworks is itself a compound (fire + works); no derived forms exist, so all other slots are no_form.

corpus_definition: to make something broken work again

forms.definition: a way of solving a problem, often quickly or for a short time
forms.example: The mechanic said the problem was an easy fix.
forms.note: Common in 'a quick fix'.

syn.note: Repair is about a broken object; this word is also used for problems in general.
Related: a way to deal with any problem, more formal.

forms.definition: a sports match on a planned date; or a thing fastened in a house
forms.example: Our team's next fixture is against Pakhtakor on Saturday.
forms.note: Belongs to fix = decide a date or fasten in place, not repairing. Mainly British for the sports meaning.

forms.definition: to make something that is broken work again
forms.example: Can you fix my broken computer, please?

syn.note: Same meaning; a little more formal.
Same meaning, more British; used for clothes, shoes and roads.
Related and informal: to deal with a problem, not only a broken object.
Related: to bring something old back to its first, good condition.

ant.note: To damage something so it stops working.
To harm something so it does not work well.

forms.definition: not changing; or firmly attached to something
forms.example: The shop has fixed prices, so you cannot bargain.
forms.note: Belongs to fix = decide or fasten firmly, not repairing. 'The car is fixed' (repaired) is just the past participle of the verb.
fixedly (stare fixedly) is rare and belongs to the 'not moving' meaning, not repairing.

people.definition: a person who arranges things for others, sometimes in dishonest ways
people.example: The journalist hired a local fixer to find people to interview.
people.note: Belongs to fix = arrange something, not repairing. A person who repairs things is a repairman or mechanic.

context.text: My phone stopped working, so my brother tried to fix it. It was an easy fix: he only needed to change the battery.

reviewer_note: Kept fixed, fixture and fixer as other_meaning (decide/fasten/arrange senses); fixable left out as not in learner dictionaries.

corpus_definition: a bright tongue of burning fire

forms.definition: the bright, hot, moving part of a fire
forms.example: Flames quickly spread through the old building.
forms.note: 'In flames' means burning strongly: 'The house was in flames.'

syn.note: Related: the whole burning thing; this word is one bright part of it.
Related: a big, strong fire, often one that is dangerous.
Related: a very small piece of fire that jumps out.

forms.definition: to burn with a bright light
forms.example: The logs flamed in the fireplace all evening.

syn.note: Easy, general word; this verb is more literary and stresses the bright light.
To burn very brightly and strongly.

ant.note: When a fire stops burning: "The fire went out."

forms.definition: burning with bright fire
forms.example: He ran into the street with a flaming torch.
forms.note: In informal British English it can also show anger: 'that flaming dog!'. flammable (easy to set on fire) comes from the same Latin root but is not made from this word.

syn.note: Same meaning, more common in everyday English.
Burning very strongly.
Related: like fire, very hot or bright; also used for strong feelings.

forms.note: There is no adverb from flame.

context.text: We sat around the campfire in the mountains near Chimgan and watched the flames. The flaming wood kept us warm until midnight.

reviewer_note: flammable/inflammable share the Latin root flamma but are not English derivations of flame, so they are only noted, not entries.

corpus_definition: A small lamp that you can hold in your hand.

forms.definition: a small electric lamp that you carry in your hand
forms.example: It is dark, so please use your flashlight.
forms.note: American English. In British English the usual word is torch.

syn.note: Same thing; the British English word.
Related: any light that uses electricity, oil or gas, often fixed in one place.
Related: a lamp in a metal or glass box with a handle, often for camping.

forms.note: There is no verb from flashlight. flash (to shine brightly for a moment) is the first part of this compound, not a form made from it.
There is no adjective from flashlight.
There is no adverb from flashlight.

context.text: The electricity went off in our village last night. My father found a flashlight in the kitchen drawer, and we used it to find candles.

reviewer_note: Compound noun (flash + light); no derived forms. AmE flashlight vs BrE torch flagged in the note.

corpus_definition: A set of rooms for living inside a larger building.

forms.definition: a set of rooms for living in, on one floor of a bigger building
forms.example: They live in a small flat downtown.
forms.note: British English. American English usually says apartment.

syn.note: Same meaning; the American English word, also common in Uzbekistan's English.
Related: a small one with only one main room.
Related: any place where you live.
Related: a whole building for one family, not part of a larger building.

forms.definition: to make something smooth and level by pressing it
forms.example: Flatten the dough with your hands before you bake it.
forms.note: Belongs to flat = smooth and level, not a home.

forms.definition: smooth and level, with no hills or high parts
forms.example: The land around Bukhara is very flat.
forms.note: Belongs to flat = level surface, not a home. Also: a flat tyre has no air in it.

forms.definition: in a firm way that does not allow discussion
forms.example: She flatly refused to lend him money.
forms.note: Belongs to flat = firm and definite, not a home. 'Lie flat' (level) is another adverb use.

context.text: Aziz rents a small flat near the metro in Tashkent. The flat is on the fifth floor, and from the window he can see the TV tower.

reviewer_note: Home sense only; adjective flat, flatten and flatly are other_meaning (level/firm). flatmate left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: A trip taken by an airplane.

forms.definition: a journey through the air in a plane
forms.example: My flight to London leaves at noon.

syn.note: Related: any journey; this word is only for travel by plane.
Related: travel from one place to another by any transport.
Related: travelling by plane in general, not one trip.

forms.definition: to travel through the air in a plane
forms.example: We fly to Istanbul next Friday.
forms.note: Irregular: fly, flew, flown. The noun flight is made from this verb.

syn.note: Same meaning, longer and more formal.
Related: to go from place to place in any way.

forms.definition: to run away quickly from danger
forms.example: Many people had to flee their homes because of the flood.
forms.note: Belongs to flight = escaping (take flight), not air travel. Irregular: flee, fled, fled.

forms.definition: not serious, often changing your mind or your feelings
forms.example: Her friends say she is too flighty to keep a job.
forms.note: Belongs to an old meaning of flight (quick, unsteady movement), not air travel. Not common.
There is no adverb from flight.

people.definition: a person who travels by plane
people.example: Frequent flyers can get free tickets with their points.
people.note: Also spelled flier. Also means a small paper advertisement.

context.text: Our flight to Istanbul was two hours late. We flew with Uzbekistan Airways, and the flyers next to us slept the whole way.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same air-trip meaning merged. fly treated as the verb the noun is made from (fly -> flight).

corpus_definition: a fine white powder made from grain, used in baking

forms.definition: a fine powder made from wheat or other grain, used to make bread and cakes
forms.example: Add two cups of flour to the mixture.
forms.note: Sounds the same as flower. Uncountable: 'some flour', not 'a flour'.

syn.note: Related: any very fine dry substance, not only from grain.
Related: the soft mixture you make from it with water.

forms.definition: to cover something with a thin layer of fine white powder from grain
forms.example: Flour the table before you roll out the dough.

syn.note: To cover lightly with any fine powder: "dust the cake with sugar".

forms.definition: covered with fine white baking powder; or soft and dry, like some potatoes
forms.example: Her hands were floury after making the bread.

syn.note: Related: like or covered with any fine powder.

forms.note: There is no adverb from flour. flower comes from the same old word but is a separate word today.

context.text: My grandmother floured the table before she made the dough for samsa. Soon her hands were floury, and there was flour on the floor too.

reviewer_note: Homophone trap flour/flower noted; flower listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: A common illness like a bad cold with a fever.

forms.definition: a common illness, like a bad cold, with a high temperature and pain
forms.example: I cannot go out because I have the flu.
forms.note: Often with 'the': 'have the flu', 'get the flu'.

syn.note: Related: a milder illness with a runny nose and no high fever.
Related: the very small living thing that causes this and other illnesses.
Related: any time you are sick.

forms.definition: the full medical name of this common illness with fever
forms.example: Doctors say influenza spreads quickly in winter.
forms.note: flu is the short form of this word.
There is no verb from flu.
There is no common adjective. flu-like (flu-like symptoms) is a compound.
There is no adverb from flu.

context.text: Half of my class has the flu this week. Our teacher says influenza spreads fast in winter, so we should wash our hands often.

reviewer_note: flu is a clipping of influenza, so influenza is shown as a formal extra noun, not as a synonym.

corpus_definition: to bend something over itself

forms.definition: a line or mark made where paper or cloth was bent over
forms.example: Cut the paper carefully along the fold.
forms.note: Also the parts of cloth that hang over each other: 'the folds of her dress'.

syn.note: A line on paper or cloth, often one you did not want: 'creases in my shirt'.
Related: any long thin mark; a fold is a line made by bending.

forms.definition: to bend paper or cloth so that one part lies on top of another
forms.example: Please fold your clothes and put them away.
forms.note: Also: fold your arms = cross them over your chest.

syn.note: Bend is more general: you can bend a stick or your knees, not only paper or cloth.
Fold something once so it has two layers.
Related: make a sharp line in paper or cloth, often by pressing.
Related: push the edge of cloth or paper into a small space.

ant.note: Open something so it is flat again: 'She unfolded the map.'
Open something so it covers a big flat area.

forms.definition: made so you can bend or close it to make it smaller
forms.example: We took two folding chairs to the picnic.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: a folding table, a folding bike.

syn.note: Same meaning, more formal; used in shops and instructions.

forms.definition: bent over so that one part lies on top of another
forms.example: There was a folded letter inside the book.

ant.note: Open and flat again.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family. The ending -fold in twofold or threefold (= two or three times as much) is a different use.

people.definition: a cardboard or plastic cover for keeping loose papers in
people.example: Put your homework in the blue folder.
people.note: On a computer, a folder is a place where you keep files.

context.text: Dilnoza folded the clean towels and put them in the cupboard. Then she opened the folding table, and we had dinner on the balcony.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Unfold/unfolded are opposites, so they sit in ant lists, not as forms.

corpus_definition: Lasting for a large number of hours, days, or years.
usage_note: Usually at the end of a clause: 'I waited for a long time.' Common with the present perfect: 'I have known her for a long time.' In questions and negatives people often say (for) long: 'Did you wait long?' 'I can't stay long.'

relations.note: Same meaning, informal and very common in speaking: 'I waited for ages!'
Used mostly in questions and negatives: 'I didn't stay for long.'
Related: a long time measured in years.
Related: for some time, not always long.
For a short time: 'We spoke briefly after class.'
Lasting only a few minutes, days or weeks.

context.text: We waited for the bus for a long time, but it didn't come. In the end we took a taxi. My uncle has lived in Andijan for a long time, so he knows every street.

reviewer_note: Fixed time phrase; for long vs for a long time explained (questions/negatives).

corpus_definition: Available to be purchased by any customer.
usage_note: be for sale or noun + for sale: 'That house is for sale.' 'a car for sale'. Also put something up for sale. Don't confuse with on sale (= in shops now, or sold at a lower price).

relations.note: Same meaning, often about houses and flats: 'Their flat is on the market.'
Same meaning; often used when the owner has just decided to sell.
Related: you can get or use it; not always by buying.
Careful: on sale means you can buy it in shops now, or (mostly American) it is cheaper than usual.
Someone has already bought it, so you cannot buy it now.

context.text: There is a sign on the old house next to ours: "For sale". My father wants to know the price. He says a house for sale in this street will not stay empty for long.

reviewer_note: Trap handled: for sale vs on sale.

corpus_definition: A large area covered with many trees.

forms.definition: a large area of land covered with many trees
forms.example: We went for a walk in the forest.

syn.note: Smaller than a forest, often near a town: 'a walk in the woods'.
Land with many trees; a little formal.
Related: a thick forest in a hot, wet country.

forms.definition: the cutting down of all the trees in a large area
forms.example: Deforestation is a serious problem for many animals.
forms.note: Common in news and texts about the environment.
No common verb. Deforest (= cut down all the trees) and reforest (= plant trees again) exist but are rare and formal; the noun deforestation is the common word.

forms.definition: covered with many trees
forms.example: The hills near Chimgan are thickly forested.

syn.note: Same meaning, very common: 'a wooded valley'.
Related: full of trees, grass and plants.

ant.note: Having no trees: 'a treeless desert'.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

people.definition: a person whose job is to look after a large area of trees
people.example: The forester showed us which trees were very old.

people.definition: the science and work of planting and caring for trees
people.example: He studied forestry and now works in the mountains.

context.text: The Chatkal mountains in Uzbekistan have old forests with many animals and birds. These forested hills need protection, because deforestation can destroy them quickly.

reviewer_note: Verb slot no_form: deforest/reforest are rare; deforestation kept as a noun entry because learners meet it often. Rainforest is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: To stop feeling angry at someone who did something wrong to you.

forms.definition: the act of stopping being angry with someone who did wrong
forms.example: He asked his mother for forgiveness.

syn.note: Formal; often an official decision not to punish someone.
Related: kindness to someone you could punish.
Related: being kind because you know why someone did something.

ant.note: A feeling of anger that stays because someone treated you badly.
Hurting someone because they hurt you.

forms.definition: to stop being angry with someone who did something wrong
forms.example: Please forgive me for being late today.
forms.note: Pattern: forgive someone (for something / for doing something). Past: forgave, forgiven.

syn.note: Used for small things: 'Excuse me for being late.'
Formal or legal: a president can pardon a prisoner.
Related, informal: not punish someone.
Related: become friends again after an argument.

ant.note: To keep feeling angry about something someone did.
To make someone suffer because they did something wrong.

forms.definition: ready to stop being angry when someone does something wrong
forms.example: My grandmother is very forgiving, even when we break things.

syn.note: Kind because you know why someone did something.
Formal: kind to someone you could punish.
Related: accepting other people's ideas and actions.

ant.note: Not willing to stop being angry.

forms.definition: not so bad, so people can stop being angry about it
forms.example: A small mistake on your first day is forgivable.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little formal.

ant.note: So bad that nobody can stop being angry: 'That was an unforgivable thing to say.'

forms.note: No common adverb. Forgivingly is very rare; unforgivably (= in a very bad way) is the opposite form.

context.text: Aziz broke his sister's phone and said sorry many times. She is a forgiving person, so she forgave him the same evening. In our family, forgiveness is more important than a phone.

reviewer_note: Three corpus rows with the same meaning merged, lowest CEFR A2 used. For- is not a prefix from the table, so no affix on forgive itself; unforgiving/unforgivable are in ant lists.

corpus_definition: a structure that shoots water high into the air

forms.definition: a structure in a park or square that sends water up into the air
forms.example: Children played near the fountain in the park.

syn.note: Related: a strong, thin stream of water coming out of a small hole.
Related: a place where water comes out of the ground naturally.

forms.note: No common verb. Using fountain as a verb (= flow up like a fountain) is rare and literary.
No adjective exists in this family.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: In summer, families in Tashkent like to walk near the big fountain in the evening. The fountain is lit with coloured lights, and children love to run around it.

reviewer_note: Leaf word: only the noun exists. Fountain pen and drinking fountain are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: feeling very cold.

forms.definition: the temperature at which water turns into ice, 0°C
forms.example: Last night the temperature fell below freezing.
forms.note: Used in above freezing and below freezing. Also called freezing point.

syn.note: Related: on the Celsius scale, water turns to ice at zero degrees.

forms.definition: a period of very cold weather when water turns to ice
forms.example: The big freeze lasted for two weeks in January.
forms.note: Also other meaning: a pay freeze or price freeze = they stay the same and do not go up.

forms.definition: to feel very cold; or, of water, to turn into ice
forms.example: We froze while we waited for the bus.
forms.note: Past: froze, frozen. 'I'm freezing!' = I feel very cold.

syn.note: Easy words with the same meaning.
Related: your body shakes because you are cold.
Related: make or become cold, not as strong.
Related: when water in a lake or river becomes covered with ice.

ant.note: To become warmer.
When ice or snow turns into water.

forms.definition: very cold, about a person, the weather or water
forms.example: It is freezing outside, please wear a coat.
forms.note: Often freezing cold: 'The water was freezing cold.'

syn.note: Easy words with the same meaning.
Very cold, like ice; also used for roads covered with ice.
Used about wind and weather: 'a bitter wind'.
Related: cold, but not as cold as freezing.
Related: freezing is much stronger than cold.

ant.note: Informal: very hot: 'It's boiling in here!'
Having a high temperature.

forms.definition: turned into ice; or feeling very cold
forms.example: My hands are frozen, can I sit near the heater?
forms.note: Also frozen food = food kept very cold so it stays fresh.
No real adverb. In freezing cold, freezing works like 'very'. Freezingly is very rare.

people.definition: an electric box or part of a fridge that keeps food very cold
people.example: There is ice cream in the freezer.

context.text: It was freezing in Tashkent last January, and the temperature stayed below freezing for a week. The water in our garden froze, so we stayed inside and drank hot tea.

reviewer_note: Headword is the -ing adjective; freeze (verb) is the root. Frost is related in history but not made from freeze, so it is left out.

corpus_definition: feeling fear because of someone or something
usage_note: be frightened of + noun / -ing: 'Are you frightened of the dark?' 'She is frightened of flying.' Compare frightened to + verb for one action: 'I was frightened to open the door.'

relations.note: Same meaning; afraid is not used before a noun (not 'an afraid child').
Same meaning, a little more informal; very common in speaking.
Much stronger: very, very frightened.
Formal, mostly in writing.
Related: a little worried or afraid about something that will happen.
Formal: not feeling fear about something.
Ready to do dangerous or difficult things without fear.

context.text: My little brother is frightened of the dark, so he sleeps with a small light on. When I was a child, I was frightened of big dogs too.

reviewer_note: kind_hint said phrasal, but this is adjective + preposition, so kind is phrase (like famous for).

corpus_definition: the state of being male, female, or another identity

forms.definition: being male, female or another identity, especially in society
forms.example: The form asks you to state your gender.
forms.note: Often used before another noun: gender equality, gender roles. In grammar it also means masculine, feminine or neuter (Russian has three).

syn.note: Often means the body (biology); gender is often about identity and society. On forms both are used.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: connected with one sex, or treating men and women differently
forms.example: Some people think pink and blue toys are too gendered.
forms.note: Advanced (B2+) word, used in discussions about society.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: The school form asks for your name, age and gender. Some parents say that toys for children are too gendered: pink for girls and blue for boys.

reviewer_note: GATE? 'gendered' is a real adjective in Oxford and Cambridge learner dictionaries (formal, about differences between men and women) but missing from WordNet; kept as an entry marked advanced. Gender vs sex explained neutrally; gender-neutral is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: To enter a car.
particle_note: Not separable. get in with no object: 'Get in, we're late!'; get into + vehicle: 'get into the car / a taxi'. Use get in(to) for cars and taxis; for buses, trains and planes say get on.

relations.note: More formal and general: you can enter a room, a building or a car.
Informal and friendly: 'Hop in, I'll drive you home.'
Related: get in with some effort, for example a big truck.
Related: used for buses, trains, planes and bikes, not cars.
To leave a car or taxi: 'Get out of the car carefully.'

context.text: Get into the car, we are leaving! Dad got in last, and we drove to Bukhara to visit our grandparents.
