reviewer_note: get in(to) vs get on handled: cars and taxis vs buses, trains and planes.

corpus_definition: To leave a car.
particle_note: Not separable. 'get out' alone, or 'get out of + vehicle/place': 'get out of the car / taxi'. For buses, trains and planes we usually say 'get off'.

relations.note: Easy and general: you can leave a car, a room or a city.
Formal, used on signs and in instructions.
Related: used for buses, trains, bikes and planes, not usually for cars.
To enter a car: 'Get in, I'll drive you home.' Also 'get into the car'.

context.text: The taxi stopped near Chorsu Bazaar and we got out. Always get out of the car on the side of the pavement, not the road.

reviewer_note: Car sense only; get off kept as related because it is used for public transport, not cars.

corpus_definition: a spicy root used to flavour food and drinks

forms.definition: a hot-tasting root that people use in cooking and tea
forms.example: My grandmother puts fresh ginger in her tea when she has a cold.

syn.note: Related: any dried part of a plant used to give food flavour; ginger is one kind.
Related: the part of a plant under the ground; ginger is a root we can eat.

forms.note: 'Ginger up' (to make something more lively) exists but is rare and informal.

forms.definition: of a bright orange-brown colour, used about hair or cats
forms.example: Their neighbour has a big ginger cat.
forms.note: Belongs to ginger = the colour (mainly British), not the spice you cook with.
Gingerly means 'slowly and carefully'. It looks like ginger but comes from a different old word, so it is not in this family.

context.text: In winter, Dilnoza makes hot tea with lemon, honey and ginger. The ginger gives it a strong, warm taste.

reviewer_note: Gingerly is a false friend (not from ginger) so not_family; gingerbread is a compound and left out; ginger (hair colour) kept as other_meaning adjective.

corpus_definition: A female person that someone is having a romantic relationship with.

forms.definition: a woman or girl that someone is in a romantic relationship with
forms.example: He bought flowers for his girlfriend on her birthday.
forms.note: Women also say 'my girlfriend' about a female friend, especially in American English.

syn.note: Close; can be a man or woman, often for people living together or married.
Related and old-fashioned; also used to speak lovingly to someone.
Related: a woman someone has promised to marry. Also written fiancée.
Related: the word for a man or boy in the same kind of relationship.

context.text: Sardor met his girlfriend at university in Tashkent. This weekend his girlfriend is visiting his family in Namangan.

reviewer_note: Compound noun (girl + friend); no forms. Boyfriend listed as related, not antonym or form (matches boyfriend map).

corpus_definition: To return something to the person who owned it.
particle_note: Separable: 'give back the book' or 'give the book back'; with a pronoun only 'give it back'. 'give something back to someone' or 'give someone back something'.

relations.note: Very close; a little more formal: 'return a library book'.
Very close; you give it back with your hand, often straight away.
Related: used for money you borrowed.
You do not give it back; it stays with you.
You take something for a short time; later you give it back.

context.text: Can I use your pen? I'll give it back after the lesson. Aziz always gives back the books he borrows.

reviewer_note: Borrow kept as antonym in the sense of the opposite half of the exchange; pay back as related (money only).

corpus_definition: Feeling happy or pleased about something.

forms.definition: the feeling of being happy and pleased
forms.example: There was real gladness in her voice when she heard the news.

syn.note: Very close and much more common in everyday English.
Stronger: great happiness.
Related: the good feeling when you enjoy something.

ant.note: The feeling of being unhappy.
Deep sadness; formal or literary.

forms.definition: to make someone feel happy
forms.example: The good news gladdened everyone in the village.

syn.note: Everyday phrasal verb: make someone feel happier.
Make someone feel happy or satisfied.
Stronger: make someone very happy.

ant.note: To make someone feel sad.

forms.definition: happy and pleased about something
forms.example: I'm so glad you came to my birthday party!
forms.note: Usually after a verb: 'I am glad', not 'a glad person'. Patterns: glad to + verb, glad (that) + clause, glad about something.

syn.note: Very close and easy; happy can also come before a noun.
Very close; a little more formal.
Stronger: very happy.
Related: glad and grateful that something happened.
Related: glad because a worry or problem has gone.

ant.note: Unhappy about something.
Sad about something bad that happened: 'I'm sorry to hear that.'
Not pleased or happy.

forms.definition: happily and willingly, without minding at all
forms.example: I would gladly help you move to your new flat.

syn.note: Close; 'I'll happily do it.'
Close: because you want to, not because you must.
Polite phrase, often used to say yes to a request.

ant.note: Doing something although you do not want to.
Not wanting to do it.

context.text: I'm glad you called me! Of course I can come to your wedding in Bukhara. I'll gladly help with the food too.

reviewer_note: Gladness and gladden marked literary; -en of gladden not in the affix table so not claimed. Glad is mostly predicative.

corpus_definition: A clear, hard substance used for windows and drinking cups.

forms.definition: a clear, hard material that breaks easily, used for windows and bottles
forms.example: Be careful, the glass in that window is broken.
forms.note: Uncountable in this meaning: 'some glass', 'a piece of glass'. Countable 'a glass' is a cup for drinking.

syn.note: Related: very clear, high-quality glass for expensive cups and lights.

forms.definition: two pieces of clear material in a frame that you wear to see better
forms.example: My grandfather needs his glasses to read the newspaper.
forms.note: Belongs to glass = things made of the material that you wear on your eyes. Always plural. Also called spectacles.

forms.definition: to fit clear sheets into a window or door frame
forms.example: The builders will glaze the new windows next week.
forms.note: Mostly used in the form 'double glazing' (windows with two layers). Glaze also means to cover pots or food with a shiny layer.

forms.definition: smooth and shiny, like a window
forms.example: In the morning the lake was glassy and calm.
forms.note: Also used for eyes that show no feeling: 'glassy eyes'.

syn.note: Related: bright because light falls on it.
Related: flat, with no rough parts or waves.
Related: smooth and shiny, often about paper, hair or paint.

ant.note: Not smooth: with waves or bumps.

forms.note: Glassily exists but is very rare.

people.definition: a person whose job is to fit clear sheets into windows
people.example: We called a glazier to repair the broken kitchen window.

context.text: The new school in Samarkand has big glass walls. Workers glazed all the windows twice to keep the classrooms warm in winter.

reviewer_note: Material sense only; drinking glass not given its own row (same noun); glasses (spectacles) as other_meaning. Glaze/glazier are historically from glass. Compounds (glassware, glasshouse) left out.

corpus_definition: A piece of clothing for your hand with separate fingers.

forms.definition: a piece of clothing that covers your hand and each finger
forms.example: I lost one glove on the bus, so my left hand was cold all day.
forms.note: Usually plural: 'a pair of gloves'.

syn.note: Related: it covers the hand but has one part for all four fingers and one for the thumb.
Related: a thick, soft hand cover, for example for cooking or baseball.

forms.definition: wearing something warm or protective on the hand
forms.example: She held the hot pot with her gloved hand.
forms.note: Used before a noun: 'a gloved hand'.

ant.note: With nothing covering it: 'with bare hands'.

context.text: It snowed in Tashkent last night, so put on your gloves before you go out. With gloved hands, the children made a big snowman.

reviewer_note: Compounds (boxing glove) left out; -ed of gloved not in the affix table, so no affix claimed.

corpus_definition: To leave a place.
particle_note: Not separable and takes no object: 'go away', not 'go away the house'. 'go away for + time / to + place' often means a trip or holiday. 'Go away!' is a rude way to tell someone to leave.

relations.note: Very close and easy; leave can also take an object: 'leave the room'.
Formal, used for trains, planes and official travel.
Related: leave a place, often to do something: 'He went off to work.'
To return to the place you left.
To not leave; to remain in a place.

context.text: We are going away for the weekend to the mountains near Chimgan. The neighbours will water our plants while we are away. When we come back, I'll call you.

reviewer_note: Leave sense; holiday/trip use and rude 'Go away!' covered in particle_note.

corpus_definition: Something that you try hard to reach or achieve.

forms.definition: something that you want and work hard to get in the future
forms.example: Her goal is to study medicine in Tashkent.
forms.note: Common patterns: 'set a goal', 'reach / achieve a goal', 'my main goal'.

syn.note: Very close and easy.
Often a clear number or result: 'a sales target'.
Formal, used in business and studies.
Related: a big goal for your life, like a career.
Related: the reason why you do something.
Related: something you hope for, maybe not realistic.

forms.definition: in which no team scores any points in football
forms.example: The match ended in a goalless draw.
forms.note: Belongs to goal = a point in football, not an aim in life.

context.text: Jasur's goal this year is to pass his IELTS exam. He studies every evening because he really wants to reach his goal.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Goalkeeper/goalpost are compounds (football sense) and left out; goalless kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: the group of people who lead and control a country.

forms.definition: the group of people who lead a country and make its laws
forms.example: The government is building new schools in every region.
forms.note: In British English it can take a plural verb: 'The government are...'.

syn.note: Close, especially in American English: 'the Biden administration'.
Related: the people with official power, often local or police.
Related: the country as a political system: 'state schools'.
Related: the small group of top ministers.

forms.definition: the way a country or organization is controlled and run
forms.example: Good governance helps a country grow.

forms.definition: to officially lead and control a country or city
forms.example: The party governed the country for ten years.

syn.note: Very close; often about a king or one person.
Everyday: 'run the country'.
Easy: be in charge.
Related: have power over something.

forms.definition: connected with the people who run a country
forms.example: The project needs governmental support.
forms.note: Often 'non-governmental organization' (NGO).

syn.note: Related: approved by people in power.
Related: for everyone, paid for by the country.

ant.note: Owned or run by people or companies, not by the country's leaders.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with the people who run a country
forms.example: The new clinic is governmentally funded.
forms.note: Rare; people usually say 'by the state' instead.

syn.note: Related: in a way approved by people in power.

ant.note: Paid for or done by people or companies, not by the country's leaders.

people.definition: a person who leads a region or state
people.example: The governor of the region visited the new hospital.

people.definition: a woman who lived with a rich family and taught their children
people.example: In the old story, the governess taught the girls French.
people.note: Belongs to govern = control and guide children, not running a country. Old-fashioned.

context.text: The government of Uzbekistan plans to build more roads. People hope the new leaders will govern well, and the governor of Fergana has promised to help.

reviewer_note: Headword is govern + -ment; govern listed as verb. Governess kept as other_meaning (old-fashioned teacher).

corpus_definition: feeling thankful for something kind someone has done

forms.definition: the feeling of wanting to thank someone for their kindness
forms.example: She wrote a letter to show her gratitude to the doctors.
forms.note: Gratitude comes from the same Latin root as grateful (gratus = thankful).

syn.note: Easy everyday word; gratitude is more formal.
Very close; also used for understanding the value of something.

ant.note: Not showing thanks when someone helps you; formal.

forms.definition: the state of feeling thankful to someone
forms.example: His gratefulness to his teachers never changed.
forms.note: Less common than gratitude.

syn.note: Very close in meaning; both are less common than gratitude.

forms.note: There is no verb made from grateful. To show this feeling, say 'thank' or 'appreciate'.

forms.definition: feeling thankful because someone was kind to you
forms.example: I am grateful to my parents for their support.
forms.note: Use grateful to someone FOR something: 'grateful to you for your help'.

syn.note: Very close. Thankful is often used for good luck too: 'thankful that nobody was hurt'.
A little more formal; shows you value what someone did.
Formal and old-fashioned: 'I'm much obliged to you.'
Easy word, but glad just means happy, not always thankful.

ant.note: Not showing thanks when someone helps you.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you feel thankful
forms.example: He gratefully took the cup of tea.

syn.note: Careful: thankfully usually means 'luckily' at the start of a sentence.
Formal; shows you value something.

context.text: Aziz helped his neighbour fix the roof, and she was very grateful. She gratefully gave him a box of fresh apricots to show her gratitude.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged. Gratify left out as not_family (different meaning: to please). Grateful is not grate + -ful, so no -ful affix claimed.

corpus_definition: To develop from a child into an adult.
particle_note: Not separable and takes no object: 'I grew up in Bukhara.' Common patterns: grow up in + place, when I grow up. Noun form: grown-up (an adult).

relations.note: Easy and very close in meaning.
More formal; also used for becoming wiser and more sensible.
Related: about how your parents raised you, not just getting older.
General word for growing or changing over time.

context.text: My father grew up in a small village near Fergana. He always told us stories about growing up with seven brothers and sisters.

reviewer_note: Intransitive phrasal verb; 'grow up' with an object is wrong. No true antonym, so none given.

corpus_definition: To give an answer without knowing all the facts.

forms.definition: an answer you give when you are not sure it is right
forms.example: My guess is that the bus will be late again.

syn.note: Used for numbers, prices or amounts: 'a rough estimate'.
A guess about the future.
A feeling that something is true without proof; informal.

forms.definition: to give an answer when you do not know all the facts
forms.example: Can you guess what I bought for you?
forms.note: In American English 'I guess' also means 'I think' or 'I suppose'.

syn.note: Used for numbers and amounts: 'estimate the cost'.
Say what will happen in the future.
Think something is probably true; 'I guess' and 'I suppose' are close in speech.
Find the answer by thinking carefully, not by guessing.

ant.note: You guess when you do not know the answer.

forms.note: No adjective in learner dictionaries is made from guess.
No adverb is made from guess.

context.text: Can you guess how much this carpet cost? Your guess is too low. It was made by hand in Samarkand.

reviewer_note: Only conversion noun/verb exist. Compound guesswork left out for the Compounds branch.

corpus_definition: A person who visits your home or stays at a hotel.

forms.definition: a person you invite to your home, or who stays at a hotel
forms.example: We had ten guests at our house for Navruz.

syn.note: A visitor may come without an invitation; a guest is usually invited.
Uncountable, informal: 'We have company tonight.'
Related: a person who pays in a hotel or shop.

ant.note: The host invites people; the guests come to the party.

forms.definition: to appear as a special visitor on a TV show or in a concert
forms.example: A famous singer guested on the show last night.
forms.note: Belongs to guest = a special performer on a show, not a visitor at your home. Mostly informal and journalistic.
No adjective. 'Guest' before a noun (guest room, guest speaker) is a noun used as a modifier.
No adverb is made from guest.

context.text: Uzbek families always welcome a guest with tea and bread. When guests arrive, the host puts the best food on the table.

reviewer_note: Verb 'guest' listed as other_meaning (appear on a show). Compounds guesthouse, guest room left out.

corpus_definition: something that you do very often, usually without thinking.

forms.definition: something you do very often, often without thinking
forms.example: Biting your nails is a bad habit.
forms.note: Also means special clothes worn by a nun or monk; that meaning is not shown here.

syn.note: A custom is usually shared by a group or a country; a habit belongs to one person.
Things you do in the same order every day.
Something done regularly; more formal.
Something you are likely to do, not always done.

forms.definition: to make someone become used to something
forms.example: The animals were slowly habituated to people.
forms.note: Rare and formal; usually passive: be habituated to something.

syn.note: Very close; also formal.
Easy everyday phrase: 'get used to the noise'.

forms.definition: done or doing something very often, as a habit
forms.example: He is a habitual liar, so nobody believes him.

syn.note: Easy word: what normally happens.
Happening often or at fixed times.
Formal: usual in a place or group.

ant.note: Happening only sometimes.

forms.definition: in a way that is usual for someone, as a habit
forms.example: She habitually drinks green tea after lunch.

syn.note: Easy and very common.
Often or at fixed times.
Stronger: every time.

ant.note: Only sometimes, not as a habit.

context.text: My grandfather has a habit of waking up at five. He habitually walks to the bazaar before breakfast. These habitual walks keep him healthy.

reviewer_note: No -al affix claimed on habitual (stem is habitu-). Habituate included as rare/formal verb; the nun's clothing sense noted only.

corpus_definition: A tool with a heavy head used to hit things.

forms.definition: a tool with a heavy metal head for hitting nails
forms.example: Pass me the hammer, please. I need to fix this chair.

syn.note: A hammer with a wooden or rubber head.
General word for things like hammers and saws.

forms.definition: to hit something with a heavy tool, or to hit it hard many times
forms.example: He hammered the nail into the wall.
forms.note: Also used for hitting hard many times: 'hammer on the door'.

syn.note: Hit hard many times.
Easy, general word.
Hit hard and make a loud noise.
Hit lightly, often a door.

forms.definition: very drunk after drinking too much alcohol
forms.example: He got hammered at the party.
forms.note: Belongs to an informal, slang meaning (drunk), not the tool. Mostly British English; avoid in polite speech.
No adverb is made from hammer.

context.text: My brother bought a new hammer at the bazaar. He spent the whole evening hammering nails into the fence.

reviewer_note: Compounds (sledgehammer, hammerhead) left out. 'hammered' = drunk kept as informal other_meaning.

corpus_definition: the state of feeling good and joyful

forms.definition: the feeling of being pleased and full of joy
forms.example: Money cannot buy happiness.

syn.note: Stronger and shorter: great happiness.
Great pleasure, often for a short time.
A happy feeling from doing or having something nice.
A calm feeling of being satisfied.

ant.note: The feeling of being unhappy.
The state of not being happy.
Great sadness or pain.

forms.note: There is no verb made from happy. Say 'make someone happy'.

forms.definition: feeling good and pleased about something
forms.example: The children were happy to see their grandmother.
forms.note: Happiness is made from happy (y changes to i before -ness).

syn.note: Easy; usually not before a noun: 'I'm glad you came.'
Happy about something that happened.
Looking or sounding happy.
Very happy; a little literary.

ant.note: Not happy.
Not happy, or not satisfied.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you feel good and pleased
forms.example: The children played happily in the park.
forms.note: At the start of a sentence, happily can also mean 'luckily': 'Happily, nobody was hurt.'

syn.note: In a happy, bright way.
Willingly, with pleasure: 'I'll gladly help.'
Very happily.

ant.note: In an unhappy way.
In a way that is not happy.

context.text: My grandmother says happiness comes from family. She is always happy when we visit, and she happily cooks plov for everyone.

reviewer_note: Headword is the derived noun; happy is its source adjective. Unhappiness kept as antonym, not a form.

corpus_definition: An internal organ that pumps blood throughout the entire body.

forms.definition: the organ in your chest that pushes blood around your body
forms.example: Exercise is good for your heart.
forms.note: The adjective for this meaning is cardiac (medical), which is not from the same English word.

syn.note: Informal and humorous word for the heart.
Related: the beat of your heart that you can feel in your wrist.

forms.definition: to make someone feel more hopeful and brave
forms.example: We were heartened by the good news.
forms.note: Belongs to heart = courage and feelings, not the body organ. Formal; often passive.

forms.definition: friendly and loud, or (of a meal) large and filling
forms.example: We ate a hearty breakfast before the long walk.
forms.note: Belongs to heart = warm feelings, not the body organ.

forms.definition: cruel and not caring about other people
forms.example: It was heartless to leave the dog out in the cold.
forms.note: Belongs to heart = kind feelings, not the body organ.

forms.definition: with a lot of energy and feeling
forms.example: Everyone laughed heartily at his joke.
forms.note: Goes with hearty; belongs to heart = feelings, not the body organ.

context.text: The doctor listened to my heart and said it was strong. She told me that walking every day keeps the heart healthy.

reviewer_note: Organ sense only; all other family words belong to the feelings/courage sense. Cardiac and cardiologist are not family (Greek root).

corpus_definition: a large group of animals moving or feeding together

forms.definition: a large group of animals of one kind that live or move together
forms.example: A herd of sheep was eating grass on the hill.

syn.note: Used for sheep, goats and birds; herd is for cows, horses and others.
Used for wolves and dogs.
Easy, general word.

forms.definition: to make animals or people move together as a group
forms.example: The boy herded the goats back to the village.

syn.note: Bring animals together into one place.
Make animals move in one direction.
Bring together into one group.

ant.note: To make a group move away in different directions.

forms.note: No adjective is made from herd.
No adverb is made from herd.

people.definition: a person whose job is to look after a group of animals
people.example: The herder walked his cows to the river every morning.

context.text: Every morning a herder takes a big herd of cattle to the fields. In the evening he herds them home again.

reviewer_note: Herdsman left out as a compound. Collective noun traps (flock vs herd vs pack) explained in syn notes.

corpus_definition: A person who is very brave.

forms.definition: a person who is admired for doing something very brave
forms.example: The firefighter was a hero because he saved three children.
forms.note: Plural: heroes. Also the main male character in a book or film.

syn.note: A person who wins or who fights for something.
A famous person whom people love and admire.
A very famous person, often from the past.

ant.note: A person who is not brave.
The bad person in a story or film.

forms.definition: very brave actions or behaviour
forms.example: The soldiers were given medals for their heroism.

syn.note: Easier, very close word.
The ability to do something dangerous or difficult.

ant.note: Lack of courage.

forms.note: There is no common verb made from hero. 'Heroize' exists but is very rare.

forms.definition: very brave and deserving to be admired
forms.example: Her heroic actions saved many lives.

syn.note: Easy and common.
A little more formal.
Not afraid to take risks.

ant.note: Not brave.

forms.definition: in a very brave way that people admire
forms.example: He fought heroically to protect his village.

syn.note: Easy and common.
A little more formal.

people.definition: a woman who is admired for being very brave
people.example: The young nurse became a national heroine.
people.note: Do not confuse with heroin, a dangerous drug; they sound the same.

context.text: Our teacher told us about a local hero who saved a family from a fire. Everyone talked about his heroic act, and the town gave him a medal for his heroism.

reviewer_note: Heroine (person) moved to People. Heroin (drug) warned in the note. Superhero left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: Something you enjoy doing in your free time.

forms.definition: an activity you enjoy doing in your free time
forms.example: My favorite hobby is reading books.

syn.note: Very close, a little more formal; often used for games and sports too.
Something you like to learn about or do: 'Her interests are music and art.'
Formal phrase for anything you do when you are not working.
Easy phrase with the same meaning.

people.definition: a person who does an activity for fun, not as a job
people.example: Many hobbyists build model planes at home.

context.text: My brother's hobby is fishing in the river near Chirchiq. My hobbies are simpler: I like reading and drawing.

reviewer_note: Only noun forms exist; hobbyist is a real learner-dictionary word, kept in People & things.

corpus_definition: a covering for the head attached to a coat or jacket

forms.definition: a soft cover for your head that is part of a coat or jacket
forms.example: He pulled his hood up when it started to rain.

syn.note: A large, loose hood, like the ones monks wear; much less common.
Also covers your head, but a hat is separate from your coat.
A soft hat with a hard part at the front; not attached to a coat.

forms.definition: the metal cover over a car's engine
forms.example: He opened the hood to check the oil.
forms.note: Belongs to hood = a cover over a machine (American English; British English says bonnet), not part of a coat.

forms.definition: having a soft cover for the head as part of it
forms.example: She bought a warm hooded jacket for the winter.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning: 'a coat with a hood'.

people.definition: a warm sweatshirt with a cover for the head
people.example: He wears a grey hoodie to the gym.

context.text: It was cold and windy in Tashkent, so I wore my hooded jacket. When the rain started, I put my hood up.

reviewer_note: GATE? hoodie is in Oxford and Cambridge learner dictionaries (informal sweatshirt with a hood); WordNet lacks it. Suffix trap: the word hood is not the suffix -hood (childhood). Car-engine hood kept as other_meaning; no affixes claimed.

corpus_definition: A curved metal piece used to catch or hang items.

forms.definition: a curved piece of metal or plastic for hanging things on or catching things
forms.example: Hang your heavy coat on the wall hook.

syn.note: A small piece of wood or metal on a wall for hanging coats; usually straight, not curved.
A curved frame you put clothes on to hang them in a cupboard.
A small sharp hook used only for catching fish.

forms.definition: to hang, attach or catch something using a curved piece of metal
forms.example: She hooked the bag onto the back of her chair.

syn.note: General word for putting something up so it does not touch the ground.
To join one thing to another; more general.
To close or join something so it stays in place.
Used for fish: 'He hooked a big fish' means he caught it.

ant.note: To take something off a hook or free it from one.

forms.definition: curved like the shape of the letter J
forms.example: The old man had a long, hooked nose.

syn.note: General word for not straight.
Not straight, often because something was pushed.

ant.note: Having no curve.

forms.definition: enjoying something so much that you cannot stop
forms.example: After one episode, I was hooked on the series.
forms.note: Belongs to hook = catch someone's interest, not a curved metal piece. Informal; 'hooked on something'.

context.text: Aziz hooked his school bag on the hook behind the door. Then he went fishing and hooked a small fish in the lake.

reviewer_note: hooked = curved (same meaning) vs hooked = addicted (other_meaning, informal). unhook in the verb's ant list.

corpus_definition: to jump on one foot or move in short small jumps

forms.definition: a short jump, especially on one foot
forms.example: With one hop, the bird was on the fence.

syn.note: General word; a hop is a small, light jump.
A light jump from one foot to the other, often while walking.
Going up and down again and again, like a ball.

forms.definition: to jump on one foot, or move in short small jumps
forms.example: The children hopped across the stepping stones.

syn.note: General word; hop means small jumps, often on one foot.
To move with light jumps, changing feet.
To move up and down again and again.
A long or high jump; bigger than a hop.

forms.note: 'hopping mad' (very angry) is an informal fixed phrase, not a normal adjective.

context.text: The little girl hopped on one foot all the way to the gate. Her brother tried too, but after ten hops he fell on the grass.

reviewer_note: Informal hop = go somewhere quickly ('hop on a bus') is a use of the same verb; hops (beer plant) is a different word and not shown.

corpus_definition: the line where the sky meets the land or sea

forms.definition: the line far away where the sky seems to meet the land or sea
forms.example: The sun slowly sank below the horizon.

syn.note: The shape of buildings or hills against the sky, often in a city.
Simple description of the same place; not a fixed word.

forms.definition: the limit of what you know, have seen or have done
forms.example: Travelling abroad really broadened my horizons.
forms.note: Belongs to horizon = limit of your experience, usually plural: 'broaden your horizons'.

forms.definition: flat and level, going from side to side, like the line of land and sky
forms.example: Draw a horizontal line across the page.

syn.note: Easy word; flat also means smooth with no high parts.
Not higher at one end than the other.

ant.note: Going straight up and down.

forms.definition: in a flat, level way, from side to side
forms.example: Fold the paper horizontally.

syn.note: Towards one side; not exactly the same as level.
Informal: 'lay it flat'.

ant.note: Up and down.

context.text: In the Kyzylkum desert, you can see the horizon in every direction. The land is so flat that it looks like one long horizontal line.

reviewer_note: horizontal is derived from horizon (parallel to it); no -al affix claimed because 'horizont' is not a word. Plural horizons = experience as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: extremely unpleasant or frightening

forms.definition: a very strong feeling of fear and shock
forms.example: She watched in horror as the car hit the wall.
forms.note: Also a type of film or book: 'a horror film'.

syn.note: Very great fear.
Easy, general word; horror is stronger and includes shock.
A sudden bad surprise.

forms.definition: to shock and frighten someone very much
forms.example: The news of the accident horrified everyone.

syn.note: Easy word; horrify is stronger.
To shock someone because something is very bad. American spelling: appall.
To make someone afraid.

forms.definition: very bad, unpleasant or frightening
forms.example: The weather was horrible on the day of the trip.

syn.note: Very close and very common.
Very close; common in speaking.
Very close; a little old-fashioned or British.
Unpleasant; often about people, smells or tastes.
Not nice, but much weaker than horrible.

ant.note: Very nice and pleasant.
Extremely good.
Nice and enjoyable.

forms.definition: extremely bad and shocking, often about violence or accidents
forms.example: There was a horrific crash on the motorway.

syn.note: Common word; horrific is stronger and more serious.
Making people very surprised and upset.

forms.definition: very shocked and frightened by something you see or hear
forms.example: She was horrified when she saw the broken window.

syn.note: Easy word; horrified is stronger.
Shocked because something is very bad.

forms.definition: in a very bad or unpleasant way; also used to mean 'very'
forms.example: The plan went horribly wrong.

syn.note: Very close; also used to mean 'very'.
Close, informal.
Weaker and more general.

ant.note: In a very good way.

context.text: The food at the new cafe was horrible, and the room smelled bad. We looked at the bill in horror, and the plan for a nice evening went horribly wrong.

reviewer_note: horror/horrify/horrific/horrified all share the Latin root of horrible; horrid (informal) left out. No affixes: horr- is not a word, so -fy/-ic/-ible are not transparent.

corpus_definition: To cause pain to someone physically or emotionally.

forms.definition: a feeling of sadness because someone was unkind to you
forms.example: She could not hide the hurt in her voice.

syn.note: Easy word; used for body pain and sad feelings.
A general feeling of being unhappy.
A feeling of being worried or unhappy.

forms.definition: to cause pain or harm to someone's body or feelings
forms.example: His cruel words hurt her deeply.
forms.note: Irregular: hurt - hurt - hurt. 'My leg hurts' means it is painful.

syn.note: Only for the body, often in accidents.
To damage someone or something; a little more formal.
To hurt the body with a weapon, or deeply hurt feelings.
To make someone unhappy; only for feelings.

ant.note: To make a body or feelings well again.
To make someone feel less sad or worried.

forms.definition: injured, or sad because of something someone did
forms.example: She felt hurt when nobody remembered her birthday.

syn.note: Only for the body.
Only for feelings; easy and common.

ant.note: Not injured at all after an accident.

forms.definition: unkind and making someone feel sad
forms.example: That was a very hurtful thing to say.

syn.note: Very close and easy.
Stronger: hurting people on purpose.
Informal: unkind.

ant.note: Nice and caring to other people.

forms.note: hurtfully exists but is rare; most people say 'unkindly' or 'in a hurtful way'.

context.text: Jasur fell off his bike, but he wasn't badly hurt. His sister laughed at him, and her hurtful words hurt more than his knee.

reviewer_note: hurt is noun, verb and adjective with the same spelling; unhurt kept as antonym, not a form.

corpus_definition: a very small, simple shelter or house made of basic materials

forms.definition: a very small, simple house or shelter, often made of wood
forms.example: The fisherman rested in a wooden hut by the lake.

syn.note: A small wooden house, often in the mountains or forest.
A small, badly built hut.
A small building in a garden for keeping tools, not for living in.
A small, nice house in the countryside; bigger and better than a hut.

context.text: In the mountains near Chimgan, the shepherd lives in a small hut in summer. The hut has one room and a stove.

reviewer_note: No family forms in learner dictionaries; hutch (rabbit cage) is not from hut.

corpus_definition: a small card showing who you are with your name and photo.
usage_note: Countable noun: 'show your identity card', 'an identity card'. Usually shortened to 'ID card' or just 'ID' in everyday English.

relations.note: The short form; much more common in speaking.
Very common and informal: 'Can I see some ID?'
Another official document that shows who you are, used for travel abroad.
A card that lets you drive and can also show who you are. American English: driver's license.

context.text: At the bank in Samarkand, the woman asked to see my identity card. I forgot my ID card at home, so I showed my passport instead.

reviewer_note: Fixed compound noun; no forms. Also called ID card.

corpus_definition: Not feeling well or having a sickness.

forms.definition: a disease or a period of being unwell
forms.example: She missed a week of school because of illness.

syn.note: Very close; a little more informal.
A particular, often serious, medical problem with a name.
A long-term health problem: 'a heart condition'.

ant.note: The state of being well, with no disease.

forms.definition: a problem or something bad, usually used in the plural
forms.example: Poverty is one of the ills of modern society.
forms.note: Belongs to ill = bad or harmful, not being sick. Formal, usually 'ills'.

forms.definition: not feeling well, or having a disease
forms.example: He feels too ill to go out.
forms.note: Usually after a verb: 'She is ill.' Before a noun, say 'a sick child', not 'an ill child'. Comparative: worse.

syn.note: Very close; more common in American English.
Close, a little formal and polite.
Informal British English, often about children.

ant.note: Healthy, not ill.
Strong and not ill.

forms.definition: badly or in an unkind way
forms.example: You should not speak ill of other people.
forms.note: Belongs to ill = bad, not being sick. Formal; in phrases like 'speak ill of' and 'ill-prepared'.

context.text: Malika was ill last week and stayed at home in bed. The doctor said her illness was not serious, and now she feels much better.

reviewer_note: ill = sick vs ill = bad (speak ill of, the ills of society) kept as other_meaning. Predicative-use note added.

corpus_definition: A picture or photograph of a person or object.

forms.definition: a picture or photo of a person or thing
forms.example: The image on the screen is blurry.
forms.note: Also means the idea people have of a person or company: 'The company wants a better image.'

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Only a picture taken with a camera or phone.
Full form of photo; a little more formal.
A drawing or picture in a book or magazine.
A picture made with a pencil or pen, not a camera.

forms.definition: pictures or photos, especially of one kind, seen together
forms.example: Satellite imagery shows how much the city has grown.
forms.note: Also used about language in poems and books that makes pictures in your mind.

syn.note: Easy everyday word.
Only pictures taken with a camera.

forms.definition: to make a picture of something, especially the inside of the body
forms.example: Doctors imaged his heart before the operation.
forms.note: Mostly used in medicine and science. In everyday English say 'take a picture of' or 'scan'.

syn.note: Common word for making pictures of the inside of the body.
To take a photo with a camera.

forms.note: No adjective is made from image. Imaginary and imaginative come from imagine, which has the same old Latin root but is a different family.
No adverb is made from image.

context.text: The museum in Tashkent shows old images of the city. Next to them, you can see satellite imagery that shows how big Tashkent is today.

reviewer_note: Imagine/imaginary/imagination kept out as a separate family (same Latin root, not made from image). Verb 'image' kept as formal/technical conversion.

corpus_definition: behaving in a rude or disrespectful way toward others

forms.definition: rude behaviour that does not show respect to others
forms.example: The teacher was surprised by the boy's impoliteness.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday English.
Easy phrase for behaviour that is not polite.
Not showing respect; often stronger.

ant.note: Behaviour that is kind and shows good manners.
Formal word for polite behaviour.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: rude, not showing good manners to other people
forms.example: It is impolite to talk loudly on your phone in public.

syn.note: Easy and very common; rude can sound stronger.
Same meaning: having bad manners.
Not showing respect, especially to older people.
Same meaning, very formal.
Rude in a funny or not serious way, often about children.

ant.note: Having good manners and showing respect.
Formal: polite and kind.
Showing respect to other people.

forms.definition: in a rude way that does not show good manners
forms.example: He answered impolitely and walked away.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common.

ant.note: In a way that shows good manners.

context.text: In Uzbekistan it is impolite to sit while an older person is standing. My grandmother does not like impoliteness, so we always greet guests at the door.

reviewer_note: Negative headword: polite/politeness/politely listed as antonyms, not as forms.

corpus_definition: Having strong romantic feelings for someone.
usage_note: be / fall in love with + person: 'He fell in love with her.' Also used about places and things: 'I'm in love with Samarkand.'

relations.note: Informal; very strong feelings for someone.
Informal, mostly British; very strong feelings.
Strong feelings that are often short and not serious.
Weaker: you like someone a lot, but it is not romantic love.
No longer having romantic feelings for someone.

context.text: Aziz has been in love with Malika since school. Last summer she told him that she was in love with him too.

reviewer_note: Adjective phrase used after be / fall; no forms.

corpus_definition: At a time that is coming later.
usage_note: Usually at the end or start of a sentence: 'I will travel more in the future.' British English also has 'in future' = from now on: 'In future, please be on time.'

relations.note: Easy word; often a shorter time from now.
At some time later, often about hopes and plans.
Same as one day; more common in American English.
In the end, after a long time.
At a time before now.
At this moment.

context.text: In the future, I want to study medicine in Tashkent. My brother says that in the future most cars will be electric.

reviewer_note: Note on British 'in future' (= from now on) added to avoid confusion.

corpus_definition: The point equally distant from the two ends or sides.
usage_note: in the middle of + noun: 'Sit in the middle of the sofa.' Without of at the end: 'The table is in the middle.' Also about time or activity: 'in the middle of the night', 'I'm in the middle of cooking.'

relations.note: Very close; American spelling: in the center (of).
At the same distance from two points, often on a road or journey.
In the space with one thing on each side.
With many people or things all around.
At the outside part of a place or thing.
At the last part of something.

context.text: There is a big fountain in the middle of the square in Tashkent. My little sister always wants to sit in the middle when we travel by car.

reviewer_note: Optional 'of' covered in usage_note; time/activity uses mentioned.

corpus_definition: Not right or containing errors.

forms.definition: the fact of being wrong or having mistakes
forms.example: The incorrectness of the address meant the parcel never arrived.
forms.note: Not common. In everyday English people say 'mistake' or 'error'.

syn.note: Close; the fact of not being exact or right.
Easy word for one wrong thing.

ant.note: The fact of being right.

forms.note: There is no verb from incorrect. To make something right is 'correct' (verb), from the opposite word correct.

forms.definition: wrong, or having mistakes in it
forms.example: Your answer to the question was incorrect.

syn.note: Easy and very common.
Not exact; often about numbers or facts.
About a person's idea or belief that is wrong.
Not true; often about information or statements.
Not true; about facts or stories.

ant.note: Right, with no mistakes.
Easy word: correct.
Exact and correct in every detail.

forms.definition: in a wrong way, or with mistakes
forms.example: He spelled my name incorrectly on the form.

syn.note: Same meaning.
Informal adverb use: 'You spelled it wrong.'
Not in an exact way.

ant.note: In the right way.
Informal: 'You did it right.'

context.text: Three of my answers on the test were incorrect. I wrote the dates incorrectly, so I lost points.

reviewer_note: Negative headword: correct/correctly/correctness listed as antonyms; verb 'correct' explained in verb note, not shown as a form.

corpus_definition: A small animal with six legs and often wings.

forms.definition: a very small animal with six legs and often wings
forms.example: An ant is a very common type of insect.

syn.note: Informal; in American English any small insect.
Informal, used with children; any small insect or spider.
An insect or animal that damages crops or food.
One kind of small insect with wings.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
No adjective for learners. 'Insectile' and 'insectival' exist but are very rare.
No adverb is made from insect.

people.definition: a chemical used to kill small animals that damage plants
people.example: Farmers in the Fergana Valley spray insecticide on their cotton.

context.text: In summer there are many insects in our garden. My father uses a safe insecticide so they do not eat the tomatoes.

reviewer_note: Two identical corpus rows merged; cefr A2 (lowest). Only one existing form; insecticide shown as a thing.

corpus_definition: having a high level of mental ability.

forms.definition: the ability to learn, understand and think well
forms.example: She showed great intelligence in solving the problem.
forms.note: Also means secret information about enemies, as in 'military intelligence'.

syn.note: Easy word; often about quick, smart ideas.
Formal: a person's ability to think.
Informal: 'She has brains.'
Good judgement that comes from experience, not only ability.

ant.note: Lack of ability to think and understand well.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: able to learn, understand and think quickly and well
forms.example: She is a very intelligent student.

syn.note: Easy and very common, especially in British English.
Easy and very common, especially in American English.
Often about children and young people.
Much stronger: extremely clever.
Making good decisions because of experience.

ant.note: Not able to think well; can sound rude.
Formal opposite; more polite than stupid.
Not showing good sense.

forms.definition: in a clever way that shows good thinking
forms.example: He spoke intelligently about the problem.

syn.note: Same meaning, easy word.
In a way that shows good judgement.

ant.note: In a way that shows bad thinking.

context.text: Dilnoza is the most intelligent girl in our class. Her teacher says her intelligence will help her win a place at university in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Unintelligent is an antonym, not a form. No -ence affix claimed (intellig- is not a word). Intellectual shares an old root but is not made from intelligent.

corpus_definition: Wanting to know or learn more about something.
usage_note: be interested in + noun / -ing: 'Are you interested in joining our club?' Not 'interested to' + noun. Don't confuse with interesting (the thing that makes you interested).

relations.note: Mostly British; you like something and want to do it.
You want to know more about something.
Informal: 'I'm into football.'
Much stronger: very, very interested.
Not interested because something is the same or dull.
Not wanting to know about something.

context.text: My cousin is interested in computers and wants to study IT. Are you interested in coming with us to the science fair?

reviewer_note: kind_hint was phrasal; corrected to phrase (adjective + preposition), not verb + particle.

corpus_definition: A formal meeting where someone is asked questions to get a job.

forms.definition: a formal meeting where someone asks you questions to decide if you get a job
forms.example: I have an interview for the job tomorrow.
forms.note: Also a meeting where a journalist asks a famous person questions.

syn.note: General word; an interview is one kind of meeting.
An arranged time to see someone, not only for a job.
A short performance to get a job as an actor, singer or musician.

forms.definition: to ask someone questions to decide if they are right for a job
forms.example: The manager interviewed five people for the position.

syn.note: To ask someone many questions; can sound like the police.
Easy, general phrase.

forms.note: There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: the person who asks the questions at a job meeting
people.example: The interviewer asked me about my last job.

people.definition: the person who answers the questions at a job meeting
people.example: Each interviewee had twenty minutes to talk.

context.text: Tomorrow I have an interview at a bank in Tashkent. Three managers will interview me, so I am practising my answers tonight.

reviewer_note: Two same-meaning corpus rows merged; cefr A2. No 'inter-' affix claimed (not in table).

corpus_definition: To tell two people each other's names for the first time.

forms.definition: the act of telling people each other's names when they first meet
forms.example: After the introductions, everyone sat down to eat.

syn.note: Related: a greeting is what you say when you meet someone, like 'hello'; an introduction also gives names.

forms.note: Also means the first part of a book or talk, and bringing in something new; those belong to other meanings.

forms.definition: to tell two people each other's names when they meet for the first time
forms.example: Let me introduce you to my sister Dilnoza.

syn.note: More formal: 'May I present my wife?' Used at official events.
Formal and less common: 'acquaint someone with someone' means help them get to know each other.
Related: when you introduce two people, they meet. 'Have you met my brother?' is a friendly way to start.

forms.definition: coming at the start and giving basic first information
forms.example: I took an introductory English course last summer.
forms.note: Belongs to introduce = start or present something new (the first part), not telling people each other's names.
No real adverb exists; 'introductorily' is not used.

context.text: Aziz introduced me to his cousin at the wedding in Bukhara. After the introductions, we all sat down and ate plov together.

reviewer_note: Map keeps only the 'people meeting' sense; introduce = bring in something new and introduction = first part of a book are other meanings. No affix: removing -ion leaves no real word.

corpus_definition: To run slowly for exercise.

forms.definition: a slow run that you do for exercise
forms.example: I go for a jog in the park every morning.

syn.note: A run can be fast or slow; a jog is always slow and easy.
Related: a slow, easy run, often used for horses or small children.

forms.definition: the activity of running slowly and steadily to stay fit
forms.example: Jogging is a cheap way to keep healthy.

syn.note: Running is the general word; jogging is slower and more relaxed.

forms.definition: to run slowly and steadily, usually for exercise
forms.example: She jogs around the lake every evening.

syn.note: Run is the general word; jog means running slowly to keep fit.
Easy everyday phrase: 'I go running on Sundays.'
Related: to run slowly with short steps.

forms.note: No real adjective exists. In 'jogging shoes', jogging is a noun used before another noun.

people.definition: a person who runs slowly for exercise
people.example: The park is full of joggers early in the morning.

context.text: My father jogs in the park near our house every morning. He says jogging helps him feel fresh before work.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR A2). Spelling trap: final g doubles in jogger, jogging, jogged. 'Jog someone's memory' is a different meaning, left out.

corpus_definition: Traveling from one place to another.

forms.definition: the act of travelling from one place to another, often a long way
forms.example: It was a long journey by train from Tashkent to Nukus.

syn.note: Trip is shorter and often for fun or work and back again; journey is the travelling itself.
Related: travel is the general activity; a journey is one time you go somewhere.
Related: a long journey by sea or in space.
Related: a trip where you visit several places.

forms.definition: to travel, usually a long way
forms.example: Traders journeyed across the desert on camels.

syn.note: The everyday word; journey as a verb sounds old or like a story.

context.text: Our journey from Tashkent to Khiva took two days by car. Long ago, traders journeyed along the Silk Road with their camels.

reviewer_note: Verb journey is literary; marked register. 'Journeyman' is a different meaning (a skilled worker) and left out. American spelling 'traveling' in the corpus definition; British 'travelling'.

corpus_definition: A group of tools or items needed for a specific task.

forms.definition: a set of tools or things that you need for a special job
forms.example: He carries a small first aid kit in his car.

syn.note: Easy word: a group of things that go together, like a set of tools.
Related: all the things you need for an activity; it is uncountable.
Related: equipment and clothes for a sport or activity.

forms.note: In British English kit also means sports clothes: 'football kit'.

forms.definition: to give someone the clothes or tools they need for an activity
forms.example: The club will kit the players out with new boots.

syn.note: More formal and used in both British and American English.
Related: to give people things they need.

forms.note: British English, usually 'kit out' or 'kit up', often passive: 'be kitted out'.

context.text: Before our trip to the Chimgan mountains, my brother checked the first aid kit. Then Dad kitted us out with warm boots and jackets.

reviewer_note: Verb 'kit out' is British and informal; marked. Spelling trap: kitted, kitting. Kitten is not in this family.

corpus_definition: The middle part of a person's limb where it bends.

forms.definition: the joint in the middle of your leg where it bends
forms.example: I hurt my knee when I fell on the grass.

syn.note: Related: a place in the body where two bones meet, like the elbow or the hip.

forms.definition: to go down so that your bent legs rest on the floor
forms.example: My grandmother kneels on a small cushion in the garden.

syn.note: Related: to bend your legs low, but your feet stay on the ground.
Related: to bend your head or body forward to show respect.

ant.note: To rise and be on your feet again.

forms.note: Past tense: knelt (British) or kneeled (American).

forms.definition: to hit or push someone or something with the middle of your leg
forms.example: The player kneed the ball into the goal.

syn.note: Related: you kick with your foot, not the middle of your leg.

forms.note: No real adjective; 'kneeling' in 'a kneeling man' is only a participle.

context.text: My grandmother kneels on a soft cushion when she works in her garden in Fergana. She says it is better for her knees.

reviewer_note: Kneel is historically made from knee (Old English cneow); included as a family verb. Compounds kneecap and kneepad left for the Compounds branch. Spelling: kneed (hit with the knee) vs knelt/kneeled.

corpus_definition: a structure with steps used for climbing up or down

forms.definition: a tool with steps between two long sides, used for climbing up and down
forms.example: He climbed the ladder to reach the roof.

syn.note: British English: a small folding ladder you stand inside the house is 'a pair of steps'.
Related: steps fixed inside a building between floors.
Related: a whole set of stairs with its rails.

forms.note: In British English it also means a long thin hole in tights (American: run).

forms.definition: if tights get a long thin hole in them
forms.example: My tights laddered when I caught them on the chair.
forms.note: Belongs to ladder = a long thin hole in tights (British English; American 'run'), not the climbing tool.

context.text: My father climbed the ladder to fix the roof after the storm. I held the ladder at the bottom so it did not move.

reviewer_note: Only one existing form; BrE verb 'ladder' (tights) is other_meaning. 'Stepladder' is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: A large area of water with land all around it.

forms.definition: a large area of water with land all around it
forms.example: We went swimming in the lake near the village.

syn.note: Related: a small area of still water, often in a garden or park.
Related: a lake made by people to store water for a city.
Related: a small area of water, or a place made for swimming.
Related: a very large area of salty water; the Aral Sea is really a big lake.

context.text: Every summer my family goes to Charvak Lake near Tashkent. The water in the lake is cold and very clear.

reviewer_note: Simple noun; no family forms. Lake names: 'Lake Issyk-Kul' or 'Charvak Lake'.

corpus_definition: A small portable computer that fits on your knees.

forms.definition: a small computer that you can carry and use on your knees
forms.example: I use my laptop for school work.

syn.note: Short for 'notebook computer'; less common than laptop today.
Related: the general word for all kinds, big or small.
Related: a computer that stays on a desk; the other main type.
Related: a flat computer with a touch screen and no keyboard.

context.text: My sister bought a new laptop for her university studies. She takes the laptop to the library every day.

reviewer_note: Laptop is itself a compound (lap + top); no further forms. Desktop listed as related, not antonym.

corpus_definition: Arriving after the time when you were supposed to be there.
usage_note: be late for + event or place: 'late for school', 'late for work', 'late for the bus'. With a verb use 'late to' only rarely; say 'I was late, so I missed the start.'

relations.note: Related: delayed is often about trains or planes that leave later than planned.
Related: later than the plan, used for work and projects.
Arriving at the right time: 'on time for class'.
Arriving before the time: 'early for the meeting'.

context.text: I was late for school today because the bus did not come. My teacher said, 'Please don't be late for the test tomorrow.'

reviewer_note: Fixed adjective + preposition pattern; no forms.

corpus_definition: to make sounds with your mouth because something is funny
particle_note: Not separable: 'laugh at a joke', 'laugh at him' (not 'laugh him at'). With a person it often means to make fun of them in an unkind way: 'Don't laugh at me.'

relations.note: Easy and close: you think something is funny, but you may not make a sound.
More formal: something makes you smile or laugh.
Related: to laugh at a person in an unkind way.
Related: to laugh quietly, often in a silly or nervous way.
To think something is important and not funny: 'Take the exam seriously.'

context.text: Everyone laughed at Grandpa's funny story about his first car. But my little sister was sad because some boys laughed at her new glasses.

reviewer_note: Corpus definition is the 'funny' sense but the example shows the unkind 'make fun of' sense; map anchors to the definition and explains the unkind use in particle_note.

corpus_definition: Clothes, sheets, or towels that need to be washed.

forms.definition: clothes, sheets and towels that need washing or have just been washed
forms.example: I need to finish the laundry before dinner.

syn.note: Same meaning, very common in British English: 'hang out the washing'.
Easy phrase, but only for clothes that are not clean yet.
Related: clothes in general, clean or dirty.

forms.note: Uncountable: say 'do the laundry', not 'a laundry'. A laundry is also a business that washes clothes.

forms.definition: to wash, dry and iron clothes or sheets
forms.example: The hotel launders all the towels every day.

syn.note: Everyday word; launder is formal and old-fashioned for clothes.
General word for making anything clean.

forms.note: Laundry comes from this verb. Today launder is used more for hiding illegal money: 'money laundering'.
There is no adjective from laundry. Use it before a noun: 'a laundry basket', 'laundry room'.
There is no adverb from laundry.

people.definition: a shop with washing machines that people pay to use
people.example: There is a launderette near the university dormitory.
people.note: British English. American English: laundromat.

context.text: On Sunday Dilnoza does the laundry for the whole family. The hotel next door sends its sheets away to be laundered.

reviewer_note: Kept launder (formal, wash clothes) as existing; money laundering only mentioned in the note.

corpus_definition: A rule made by a country to control behavior.

forms.definition: a rule made by a government that everyone must follow
forms.example: In Uzbekistan the law says you must wear a seat belt.

syn.note: Easy word; a rule can be made by anyone (a school, a family), a law only by the state.
An official rule, often about details of how something must be done.
A law that a parliament has passed: 'the Education Act'.
A group of laws, or the making of laws.

forms.note: Also uncountable: 'the law' = the whole system of rules; 'study law' = the subject.
There is no verb from law. To make laws is 'legislate' (formal) or 'pass a law'.

forms.definition: allowed or recognised by the rules of a country
forms.example: He is the lawful owner of the house.

syn.note: Same meaning and much more common.
Allowed by the rules and fair.

ant.note: Not allowed by the rules of the country; formal.
Everyday opposite: against the rules of the country.

forms.note: 'Legal' has the same meaning but comes from Latin, not from law.

forms.definition: without rules, or where people do not obey the rules
forms.example: After the war the region was lawless for many years.

syn.note: Completely without order.
Related: not controlled, informal use.

forms.definition: in a way that the rules of the country allow
forms.example: The money was lawfully earned.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common.

ant.note: In a way that breaks the rules of the country; formal.
Everyday opposite.

people.definition: a person whose job is to give advice about legal problems and speak in court
people.example: My cousin is a lawyer in Tashkent.

context.text: Every driver must follow the law. A lawyer can tell you if your business is lawful.

reviewer_note: legal/legislate listed as not_family (Latin lex). unlawful kept as antonym, not a form. lawmaker/lawsuit left out as compounds.

corpus_definition: Material made from animal skin.

forms.definition: the skin of an animal made soft and strong for shoes, bags and belts
forms.example: He bought a nice leather belt.

syn.note: The skin of a large animal, usually before it is made into this material.
A soft kind with a rough surface, used for shoes and jackets.
Easy word; leather is skin that has been treated.

forms.note: Uncountable. Before a noun it works like an adjective: 'a leather jacket'.
No common verb. 'To leather someone' (= hit hard) is old informal British slang and not for learners.

forms.definition: hard, dry and rough, like old animal skin
forms.example: The old farmer had leathery hands from working in the sun.

syn.note: Hard to cut or chew; also used for food.
Related: not smooth to touch.
Related: with many lines, for old skin.

ant.note: Soft and even to touch.

forms.note: There is no adverb from leather.

context.text: Bukhara is famous for its leather bags and shoes. After forty years in the fields, my grandfather's hands were brown and leathery.

reviewer_note: leather + noun ('leather belt') is noun-as-modifier, not an adjective form; leathery is the real adjective.

corpus_definition: To say something that is not true on purpose.

forms.definition: something you say that you know is not true
forms.example: He told a lie about where he was last night.

syn.note: Same meaning, but formal and polite.
A small lie that is not very important.
Related, informal: an invented excuse, 'Don't tell stories!'

ant.note: What really happened or is real.

forms.note: We say 'tell a lie', not 'say a lie'. A small kind lie is a 'white lie'.

forms.definition: to say something false on purpose so that people believe it
forms.example: Do not lie to your parents.

syn.note: Tell a small, unimportant lie.
Make someone believe something false, by words or actions.
Related: invent a story or an excuse.

ant.note: Say what really happened.

forms.note: Forms: lie, lied, lied, lying. Different from lie = be flat on a bed (lay, lain).

forms.definition: saying things that are not true on purpose
forms.example: Don't listen to that lying salesman.

syn.note: Easy word: not honest in words or actions.
Often trying to trick people.

ant.note: Always saying what is true.
Telling the truth.

forms.note: There is no common adverb. Use 'dishonestly' or 'falsely'.

people.definition: someone who often says things that are not true
people.example: Nobody believes him because he is a liar.

context.text: Akmal lied to his teacher about his homework. The teacher knew it was a lie and said, 'I don't want any lying students in my class.'

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: lie (say false things: lied/lied) vs lie (be flat: lay/lain). Only the 'untruth' word is mapped; the other lie is a different word, not a form.

corpus_definition: A bright flash of light in the sky during a storm.

forms.definition: a sudden bright flash of electric light in the sky in a storm
forms.example: Lightning struck the tall tree in the garden.

syn.note: One single flash: 'a bolt of lightning'.
A flash together with its noise; mostly in stories.
Any short bright light.
Related: the loud noise that comes after the flash.

forms.note: Spelling: lightning (storm), not lightening (making lighter). Before a noun it means 'very fast': 'lightning speed'.
No verb from lightning. Say 'there was lightning' or 'lightning struck'. 'Lighten' means make lighter or brighter.
No adjective. Use the noun before another noun: 'a lightning strike', 'at lightning speed'.
No adverb. Use 'as quick as lightning'.

context.text: During the storm last night, lightning lit up the whole sky over Samarkand. My little brother counted the seconds between the lightning and the thunder.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged (cefr A2). Spelling trap lightning/lightening noted; lightning rod/conductor left out as compounds.

corpus_definition: One of the two soft parts that form the opening of the mouth.

forms.definition: one of the two soft edges around the opening of your mouth
forms.example: She bit her lip because she was worried.

syn.note: Related: the whole opening in your face, including the lips.

forms.note: Usually plural: 'lips'. 'Upper lip' and 'lower lip'.
No verb for learners. 'Lip-read' and 'lip-sync' are compounds.
No common adjective. '-lipped' appears only in compounds: 'thin-lipped'.
There is no adverb from lip.

context.text: My lips get dry and cracked in the cold Tashkent winter. My sister always puts balm on her lips before she goes out.

reviewer_note: Leaf word: no real derived forms. lipstick, lip balm, lip-read left out as compounds.

corpus_definition: Books, poems, and plays that are considered to be art.

forms.definition: written works such as novels, poems and plays that are seen as art
forms.example: She enjoys reading classical English literature.

syn.note: Related: anything written; 'Uzbek writing' can mean its books and poems.
Related: only invented stories, like novels.
Related: only poems.
Easy word, but books also include textbooks and dictionaries.

forms.note: Uncountable. It can also mean printed information about a product: 'sales literature'.
There is no verb from literature.

forms.definition: connected with novels, poems, plays and the people who write them
forms.example: Alisher Navoi is the most famous literary figure in Uzbek history.

syn.note: Related: like poetry, beautiful in style.
Related: in written form, not spoken.

ant.note: Used in everyday talk: 'literary words' vs 'colloquial words'.

forms.note: Don't confuse with literate (able to read and write) or literal (the basic meaning of a word). They share an old Latin root but are not made from literature.
No common adverb. 'Literarily' is very rare; don't confuse with 'literally', which is from literal.

context.text: Our teacher loves Uzbek literature, especially the poems of Navoi. She also runs a literary club at the school library.

reviewer_note: False-family trap: literate/literacy/literal/literally share the Latin root but are not made from literature; listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: Relating to the area where you live.

forms.definition: a particular area or neighbourhood
forms.example: There are three schools in this locality.

syn.note: Easy and common word with the same meaning.
The streets around your home. US: neighborhood.
An official part of a city or country.

forms.note: 'Location' and 'locate' come from the same Latin root but are not made from local.

forms.definition: a person who lives in the area you are talking about
forms.example: Ask a local which bus goes to the bazaar.

syn.note: A person who lives in a place; more formal.
A person who was born in that place.

ant.note: A person who comes from somewhere else for a short time.
A person who travels for pleasure.

forms.note: Usually plural: 'the locals'. Informal in this sense. In British English 'the local' also means the nearest pub.

forms.definition: to change a product so it suits the people of one country or area
forms.example: The company localized its app for Uzbek users.

syn.note: Change something so it fits a new situation.
Related: only changing the language.

forms.note: British spelling: localise. In medicine 'localized' means only in one part of the body.

forms.definition: in or connected with the area where you live
forms.example: I buy bread at the local shop.

syn.note: Easy word; it only means close, not part of your community.
About a bigger area, like a region.

ant.note: For the whole country.
Between or for many countries.
From another country.

forms.definition: in or near the area where you live
forms.example: We try to buy fruit that is grown locally.

syn.note: Easy word: close to here.
Easy phrase with the same meaning.

ant.note: Across the whole country.
Across the whole world.

context.text: Our local market sells vegetables grown locally in Fergana. The locals say it is the best market in the city.

reviewer_note: local (noun, person) kept as a noun-slot conversion extra because the spelling already appears as the adjective base; location/locate listed as not_family.

corpus_definition: not tight or firmly fixed; having extra space or room

forms.definition: the state of not being tight or firmly fixed
forms.example: The looseness of the dress made it comfortable in summer.

syn.note: Used for ropes and wires that hang down.

ant.note: The state of being tight.

forms.definition: to make something less tight or less firmly fixed
forms.example: He loosened his tie after the meeting.

syn.note: Open a button, knot or belt completely.
Make a rope or belt less tight.
Make a muscle or your hold less tight.

ant.note: Make something tighter.

forms.definition: not tight, with extra space, or not firmly fixed
forms.example: These trousers are too loose around the waist.

syn.note: For clothes that are big and hang loosely; informal.
Easy word for clothes that are too large.
For a rope or wire that is not pulled tight.

ant.note: Fitting closely, with no extra space.
Fixed strongly so it does not move.

forms.note: Spelling trap: loose /luːs/ (not tight) vs lose /luːz/ (not find, not win). US: pants; UK: trousers.

forms.definition: in a way that is not tight or firmly fixed
forms.example: She tied the scarf loosely around her neck.

syn.note: Related: with little force.

ant.note: In a tight way.
Strongly, so it does not move.

context.text: After the holiday, my belt was loose, so I didn't need to loosen it at dinner. My mum wears her scarf loosely in summer.

reviewer_note: Two rows (clothes / not fixed) are one meaning; merged at A2. -en suffix not in the affix table, so no affix claimed for loosen.

corpus_definition: When you spend more than you earn.

forms.definition: money that goes out of a business when it spends more than it earns
forms.example: The company reported a loss this year.

syn.note: When more money goes out than comes in; used for governments and companies.
Related: money you owe to someone.

ant.note: Money you make when you earn more than you spend.
An increase in money or value.

forms.note: 'Make a loss' or 'run at a loss'. Loss also means losing something or someone, but this map is about money.

forms.definition: to have less money because you spend more than you get
forms.example: The small shop lost money last year.

syn.note: Related: use money badly, so it is gone.

ant.note: Easy word: 'make money'.
Get money for your work.

forms.note: Forms: lose, lost, lost. Spelling trap: lose /luːz/ vs loose /luːs/ (not tight).

forms.definition: not knowing where you are, or impossible to find
forms.example: We got lost in the old city of Khiva.
forms.note: Belongs to lose = not find something or someone, not losing money.
There is no adverb from loss.

people.definition: a person who does not win a game or competition
people.example: The loser of the match shook hands with the winner.
people.note: Belongs to lose = not win a game, not losing money.

context.text: Our shop lost a lot of money during the winter. We hope to turn this year's loss into a profit by summer.

reviewer_note: Corpus sense is business money loss; lost/loser kept as other_meaning (finding / games).

corpus_definition: Good things that happen to you by chance.

forms.definition: good things that happen to you by chance, not because of your effort
forms.example: Good luck with your exam tomorrow!

syn.note: More formal; also can mean a lot of money.
Related: chance is what happens without a plan, good or bad; luck is usually good.
Related: a fluke is one surprising lucky result.

ant.note: Bad things that happen to you by chance. Also: bad luck.

forms.note: No single-word verb for learners. Informal American English has the phrasal verb 'luck out' (= be lucky).

forms.definition: having good things happen to you by chance
forms.example: You are very lucky to have such kind neighbours.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Related: having something good in your life, often said with thanks.

ant.note: Having bad things happen to you by chance.

forms.definition: having no good chances; often having bad things happen
forms.example: The luckless team lost every game this season.

forms.definition: used to say that something good happened by chance
forms.example: Luckily, the bus was late too, so I didn't miss it.

syn.note: Same meaning, very common in speaking and writing.

ant.note: Used when something bad happened.
Used when something bad happened by chance; less common than unfortunately.

context.text: My brother found a cheap flat in Tashkent just by luck. He is lucky, because luckily the owner wanted a quiet student.

reviewer_note: Opposites unlucky/unluckily kept in ant lists, not as forms. 'Luck out' is phrasal and informal, so verb is no_form with a note.

corpus_definition: Having good things happen to you by chance.

forms.definition: good things that happen to you by chance, not because of your effort
forms.example: Good luck with your exam tomorrow!

syn.note: More formal; also can mean a lot of money.
Related: chance is what happens without a plan, good or bad; luck is usually good.
Related: a fluke is one surprising lucky result.

ant.note: Bad things that happen to you by chance. Also: bad luck.

forms.note: No single-word verb for learners. Informal American English has the phrasal verb 'luck out' (= be lucky).

forms.definition: having good things happen to you by chance
forms.example: You are very lucky to have such kind neighbours.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Related: having something good in your life, often said with thanks.

ant.note: Having bad things happen to you by chance.

forms.definition: used to say that something good happened by chance
forms.example: Luckily, the bus was late too, so I didn't miss it.

syn.note: Same meaning, very common in speaking and writing.

ant.note: Used when something bad happened.
Used when something bad happened by chance; less common than unfortunately.

context.text: Dilnoza was lucky to get the last ticket to Samarkand. Luckily, the train left late, and she said it was pure luck.

reviewer_note: Unlucky is the antonym of lucky, not a separate form. Rare 'luckless' only in the luck map.

corpus_definition: Bags and cases that you take on a trip.

forms.definition: the bags and cases you take with you when you travel
forms.example: We checked our heavy luggage at the airport counter.

syn.note: Same meaning; more common in American English and at airports.
Everyday word: 'Where are your bags?'
Related: one case with a handle; luggage means all your bags together.

forms.note: Uncountable: say 'a lot of luggage' or 'a piece of luggage', never 'luggages'.
No verb in this family. The old verb 'lug' (= carry something heavy with effort) is where the word came from, but learners don't treat it as a form of luggage.

context.text: At Tashkent airport we put our luggage on the scale. My mother had too much luggage, so she paid extra.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Uncountable trap noted. No affix: -age is not in the table and 'lugg' is not a word.

corpus_definition: The act of speaking words that are not true.

forms.definition: the act of saying things that are not true
forms.example: Lying makes it very hard to build trust.

syn.note: Wider: dishonesty also includes cheating and stealing.
Formal: trying to make people believe something false.

ant.note: Always telling the truth.
The quality of telling the truth; more formal.

forms.definition: something you say that you know is not true
forms.example: He told a lie about his homework.

syn.note: Formal and polite word.
Informal: a small lie that is not very serious.

ant.note: What is real and correct.

forms.definition: to say something that you know is not true
forms.example: Don't lie to me. Where were you?

syn.note: Related: make someone believe something false, not only by speaking.
Related: invent a story or excuse.

ant.note: Say what really happened.

forms.note: Forms: lie, lied, lied, lying. Don't confuse with lie = be flat on a bed (lay, lain, lying).

forms.definition: not telling the truth
forms.example: I won't listen to that lying salesman again.

syn.note: Very close; dishonest is more common.
Same meaning, more formal.
