ant.note: Always telling the truth.
Telling the truth; more formal.

forms.note: 'Lyingly' is very rare and not in learner dictionaries.

people.definition: a person who often says things that are not true
people.example: Nobody believes him because he is a liar.

context.text: My little brother lied about breaking the cup. Mum said lying is worse than breaking a cup, and told him a lie always comes out.

reviewer_note: Adjective 'lying' (a lying cheat) is a participial adjective in Oxford/Cambridge. Homonym trap: lying (not telling the truth) vs lying (lie = be flat, lay, lain); map keeps only the untruth sense. No affix: removing -ing leaves 'ly', and -ar is not in the table.

corpus_definition: A box where people put messages for a service worker to collect.

forms.definition: a public box in the street where you put letters to send them
forms.example: He dropped the cards into the blue mailbox.

syn.note: British English word for the same thing.

forms.note: American English. It also means a box at your house where letters arrive, and the place on a computer where your emails are kept.
Compound of mail + box; it has no verb form. 'Mail' (= send by post) is a separate word, not a form of mailbox.

context.text: I wrote a postcard to my grandmother in Fergana. On the way to school I put it in the mailbox near the bank.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a compound; no forms, people or affixes. British/American difference (postbox) noted.

corpus_definition: To check that something is true or done correctly.
usage_note: make sure + (that) + clause: 'Make sure (that) the door is locked.' Also make sure + to do: 'Make sure to call me.' Make sure of + noun: 'Make sure of the time.'

relations.note: Check is about looking; make sure is about being certain that something is done.
More formal, common in writing: 'Please ensure the form is signed.'
Means you take care that something happens: 'See to it that the door is locked.'
Related: find out or say that something is true, often by asking.

context.text: Make sure you lock the door when you leave. Before every trip to Bukhara, my father makes sure the car has enough petrol.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; no forms.

corpus_definition: A number or letter given to show how well someone did.

forms.definition: a number or letter that shows how good a student's work is
forms.example: She got a high mark on the test.

syn.note: Same meaning; the usual word in American English.
A number of points, in a test or a game.
Related: what you get at the end of an exam.

forms.note: British English; American English usually says 'grade'.

forms.definition: the work of checking students' tests and giving them numbers
forms.example: Our teacher has a lot of marking to do this weekend.
forms.note: Mainly British English; American English says 'grading'.

forms.definition: small spots or lines on a surface
forms.example: There are dirty marks on the wall.
forms.note: Belongs to mark = a spot or sign on something, not a school result.

forms.definition: to check students' work and give it a number or letter
forms.example: The teacher marked our essays very quickly.

syn.note: Same meaning; the usual word in American English.
Related: judge how good something is; more formal.
Related: find and fix the mistakes in someone's work.

forms.definition: clear and easy to notice
forms.example: There is a marked difference between the two cities.
forms.note: Belongs to mark = a sign that can be seen, not a school result.

forms.definition: in a way that is clear and easy to notice
forms.example: Prices have risen markedly this year.
forms.note: Goes with marked = easy to notice, not a school result.

people.definition: a pen with a thick tip, used for writing on boards
people.example: The teacher wrote the date with a red marker.
people.note: Belongs to mark = a sign or line you make, not a school result.

context.text: Our English teacher spent the evening on her marking. Aziz got the highest mark in the class, so he was very happy.

reviewer_note: Map keeps only the school-score sense; marked/markedly/marker belong to mark = sign. British mark/marking vs American grade/grading noted.

corpus_definition: the elected leader of a city or town

forms.definition: the person people choose to lead a city or town
forms.example: The mayor opened the new library yesterday.

syn.note: Related: a governor leads a state or region, which is bigger than a city.
Related: a member of the group that helps run a city. American spelling: councilor.

forms.note: In Uzbekistan the head of a city is called the hokim.

forms.definition: connected with the leader of a city or with that job
forms.example: The mayoral election will take place in May.

people.definition: a woman who leads a city, or the wife of the city leader
people.example: The mayoress welcomed the guests at the town hall.
people.note: British English and old-fashioned; today a woman is usually just called 'mayor'.

context.text: The mayor visited our school and planted a tree. Next year there will be a mayoral election, and many people want him to win again.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun so it stays in the noun slot (rule 6); mayoress goes in people. Affix -ess is not in the table, so not claimed.

corpus_definition: To find the exact size or amount of something.

forms.definition: the exact size or amount of something that you find
forms.example: Write down the measurements of the window.

syn.note: Related: everyday word for how big something is.
Related: the length, width or height of something.

forms.definition: an official action taken to deal with a problem
forms.example: The city took measures to stop the traffic jams.
forms.note: Belongs to measure = an action or plan ('safety measures'), not finding size. 'A measure of' (= an amount) is also another meaning.

forms.definition: to find the exact size, length or amount of something
forms.example: I need to measure the kitchen floor.

syn.note: Related: find a number using maths, not with a tool.
More formal; also used for judging feelings or opinions.
Related: measure how heavy something is.

forms.definition: big enough or clear enough to be counted or checked
forms.example: The new teacher made a measurable difference to our results.

syn.note: Related: easy to see or notice.

ant.note: Too big or too great to be counted.

forms.definition: slow, careful and calm
forms.example: He spoke in a measured voice.
forms.note: Belongs to measure = being careful and controlled, not finding size.

forms.definition: by an amount that can be seen or counted
forms.example: The air in the city is measurably cleaner this year.

syn.note: Related: in a way people can easily see.

context.text: Before buying a new carpet, my father measured the living room. He wrote the measurements in his notebook and took them to the bazaar.

reviewer_note: Map keeps the size sense; measure (noun) = official action and measured = careful are other meanings. Immeasurable kept as antonym, not a form. Tape measure is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: A substance taken to help someone recover from sickness.

forms.definition: something you take to help you get better when you are ill
forms.example: Take your medicine before you go to sleep.

syn.note: Also used for illegal substances, so 'medicine' is safer in everyday talk.
Often a simple or traditional cure: 'a home remedy for a cold'.
Related: a small hard piece of medicine you swallow.
Related: something that makes an illness go away completely.

forms.note: Also means the science and work of treating illness ('study medicine'); that is another meaning.

forms.definition: medicine that a doctor gives you, often for a long time
forms.example: My grandfather takes medication for his heart.

forms.definition: to give someone medicine
forms.example: The nurse medicated the patient every four hours.

syn.note: Related: give medical care to someone, not only medicine.

forms.definition: used to help cure illness
forms.example: Mint tea has some medicinal effects.

syn.note: Easier word with a similar meaning.
Formal word: helping to treat an illness.

forms.definition: connected with illness, injury and how doctors treat them
forms.example: She needs medical help right away.
forms.note: Belongs to medicine = the science and work of doctors, not the substance you take.

forms.definition: as a way to treat illness
forms.example: This plant has been used medicinally for hundreds of years.

forms.definition: in a way connected with doctors and medical science
forms.example: He is not medically fit to play football.
forms.note: Goes with medical = the work of doctors, not the substance you take.

people.definition: a doctor, a medical student, or a soldier who gives first aid
people.example: The medic helped the injured player on the field.
people.note: Belongs to medicine = the work of doctors, not the substance you take. Informal.

context.text: The doctor gave me some medicine for my cough. My grandmother prefers medicinal herbs from the bazaar, but she also takes her medication every morning.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged. Medical/medically/medic belong to medicine = the science. No affix claimed: removing -al or -ation leaves no clean word.

corpus_definition: a time when people talk about business together

forms.definition: a planned time when people come together to talk and decide things
forms.example: We have a meeting with the director at two o'clock.
forms.note: Common patterns: 'have / hold / attend a meeting', 'in a meeting', 'a meeting with someone'.

syn.note: A bigger and more formal meeting, often for many days or many people.
A meeting of a large group, for example all the students in a school.
A period of time for one activity: 'a training session'.
A group of people who come together, often for a social reason.
Formal discussions between groups or countries, often to agree on something.

forms.definition: to come together with someone at a planned time and place
forms.example: The team meets every Monday morning to plan the week.
forms.note: meeting is made from meet + -ing. Irregular verb: meet, met, met.

syn.note: Easy and informal: 'Let's get together after work.'
Many people come to one place.
Very easy and everyday: 'I'm seeing the manager tomorrow.'

forms.note: No adjective is made from meeting or meet in this meaning.
No adverb is made from meeting or meet.

context.text: Our team meets every Tuesday in a small room near the office. Today's meeting was short because the manager had to fly to Samarkand.

reviewer_note: meeting = meet + -ing (noun). Adjective and adverb slots honestly empty; no person noun (meeter is not a learner word).

corpus_definition: To turn into liquid because of heat.

forms.definition: the process of something solid becoming liquid because it gets warm
forms.example: The melting of snow in the mountains fills the rivers in spring.
forms.note: Also used as an adjective: 'melting snow'. 'Meltdown' is a compound with a different meaning (a nuclear accident or losing control) and is left out.

syn.note: Used for ice and snow when the weather gets warmer: 'the spring thaw'.

ant.note: Water turns into ice; the opposite process.

forms.definition: to change from solid to liquid when it gets warm
forms.example: The ice cream melted quickly in the hot sun.
forms.note: Also used for people: 'Her heart melted' = she felt love or pity suddenly.

syn.note: Used for ice, snow and frozen food: 'Thaw the chicken before you cook it.'
Related but different: sugar dissolves in water; it mixes into a liquid, it is not heat.
To become softer, like butter in a warm room, but not liquid yet.

corpus_definition: a building with machines for grinding grain into flour

corpus_definition: a person who has at least one million units of money

corpus_definition: Tissue in the body that helps you move by pulling.

forms.definition: making a lot of loud sounds
forms.example: The children were very noisy in the garden.

syn.note: Easy word, very close in meaning.
Related: loud and a little wild, about people.

ant.note: Making little or no sound.
Making no sound at all.

forms.definition: making no sound at all
forms.example: The new fridge is almost noiseless.

forms.definition: in a way that makes a lot of loud sounds
forms.example: The students ran noisily down the stairs.

syn.note: Easy word, very close in meaning.

ant.note: Making little sound.
Making no sound at all.

context.text: Our street is very noisy in the morning. Cars and buses go past noisily, and the noise wakes up the baby.

reviewer_note: noisy is made from noise (noun listed as derivational). noiseless kept as an extra adjective with opposite meaning via -less.

corpus_definition: to see or become aware of something

forms.definition: attention, when you see or think about something
forms.example: She took no notice of the noise outside.
forms.note: Common in 'take no notice of' and 'come to someone's notice'. Notice also means a written sign or a warning (a notice on the door; two weeks' notice): that is another meaning.

syn.note: Easy, general word: 'pay attention to'.

forms.definition: to see or become aware of something
forms.example: Did you notice the new sign on the door?

syn.note: Easy word; notice means you see something and it gets your attention.
To notice something that is hard to see. A little informal.
Related: to understand something that you did not know before. British: realise.
Related: to watch carefully; more formal.

ant.note: To not see or notice something.
To see something but choose not to pay attention.
To not notice something, often a mistake.

forms.note: Notify (to tell someone officially) shares an old Latin root but is not made from notice.

forms.definition: easy to see or become aware of
forms.example: There is a noticeable change in her English since summer.

syn.note: Related: easy to see or understand.
Very easy to see; stronger.
Related: can be seen with your eyes.

ant.note: Too small to be seen or felt.
Cannot be seen at all.

forms.definition: in a way that is easy to see
forms.example: The weather is noticeably colder this week.

syn.note: Easy word, close in meaning.
In a way you can see with your eyes.
Related: very clearly, often used for opinions too.

context.text: I noticed that my brother looked tired. He was noticeably thinner after his exams, but he took no notice when Mum told him to rest.

reviewer_note: Noun notice kept in the 'attention' sense (same meaning); sign/warning sense mentioned in note. noticeable keeps the e.

corpus_definition: not in any place; not anywhere at all
usage_note: Used with a positive verb: 'The keys were nowhere.' With a negative verb use anywhere: 'I can't find them anywhere.' Phrases: nowhere to be found, nowhere near, in the middle of nowhere, go nowhere.

relations.note: Same meaning; use it with a negative verb: 'It isn't anywhere.'
In every place.
In some place that you do not name.

context.text: I looked everywhere for my phone, but it was nowhere to be found. Then I saw it in my bag, of course!

reviewer_note: Kind corrected to function (adverb/pronoun of place like anywhere); no derived forms.

corpus_definition: The very large areas of salt water between continents.

forms.definition: one of the very large areas of salt water on Earth
forms.example: Whales live in the deep ocean.
forms.note: The five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern. In American English 'the ocean' often means the sea near the beach.

syn.note: Easy word; a sea is usually smaller and often partly closed by land.
Literary: the deep part of the ocean.

ant.note: The part of Earth that is not covered by water.

forms.note: No verb is made from ocean.

forms.definition: connected with the very large seas of the world
forms.example: Scientists study oceanic animals and plants.

syn.note: Connected with the sea; common in science.

forms.note: No adverb is made from ocean.

people.definition: the science that studies the seas of the world
people.example: She wants to study oceanography at university.

people.definition: a scientist who studies the seas of the world
people.example: The oceanographer measured the temperature of the water.

context.text: Uzbekistan has no ocean, so many people see one for the first time on holiday. My cousin loves oceanic animals and dreams of swimming with dolphins in the ocean.

reviewer_note: Ocean vs sea difference noted. oceanography/oceanographer are B2+ but clear derivations; no -er affix claimed (oceanograph is not a word).

corpus_definition: Traveling by using your legs instead of riding in a vehicle.
usage_note: go/come/travel + on foot: 'We went to school on foot.' Not 'by foot' in careful English; compare by car, by bus.

relations.note: Easy, close: 'We went walking' or 'I walk to school'.
Travelling in a car.
Travelling on a bus.

context.text: The old city of Khiva is small, so we explored it on foot. It took only an hour to see everything on foot.

reviewer_note: Contrasted with by + vehicle; 'by foot' noted as less correct.

corpus_definition: Located near the land where the ocean or sea meets the sand.
usage_note: be/live/stay + on the coast: 'They live on the coast.' Use on, not in: on the coast, on the beach, by the sea.

relations.note: Very close and easy.
British English, often about holidays.
Related: on the sand itself, not just near the sea.
Far from the sea, in the middle of a country.

context.text: Many Uzbek families take holidays on the coast in Turkey. My uncle has a small flat on the coast, and we visit him every summer.

reviewer_note: Preposition trap noted: on the coast, not in the coast.

corpus_definition: Alone or without needing help from others.
usage_note: on + my/your/his/her/our/their + own, after a verb: 'She lives on her own.' 'I did it on my own.' Add 'all' for emphasis: 'all on his own'.

relations.note: Very close. Alone can also mean lonely; on your own is more neutral.
Same meaning and very common: 'I did it by myself.'
More formal; stresses that you need no help from others.
Used for doing an activity alone, like a solo trip or a solo song.
With other people, not alone.
When other people help you do something.

context.text: Dilnoza moved to Tashkent and now lives on her own. She cooks, cleans and pays the bills on her own. Her brother still can't do his homework on his own!

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; the pronoun changes with the subject (on my/her/his own).

corpus_definition: Being connected to the internet.

forms.note: There is no noun from online. Use 'the internet'.
There is no verb from online. Use 'go online'.

forms.definition: connected to the internet or available on it
forms.example: Many students take online classes now.

syn.note: Connected means your device is linked to the internet; online is more general.
Digital is about computers and data in general, not only the internet.
Virtual means it exists on a computer, not in the real world.

ant.note: Not connected to the internet.

forms.definition: on the internet or using the internet
forms.example: We bought the tickets online last night.

syn.note: Same meaning, longer phrase.
Stresses that something travels through the internet, like a payment.

ant.note: Not using the internet.
Going there yourself, face to face.

context.text: Aziz is online every evening. He chats with friends online and buys books from an online shop.

reviewer_note: GATE? offline is a real adjective and adverb (Oxford, Cambridge) and the true opposite of online; the gate's WordNet lacks it. Same spelling for adjective and adverb; compound, so no affixes.

corpus_definition: weighing more than is considered healthy or normal

forms.note: There is no common noun for this state; learners say 'being overweight'. The base word weight (how heavy something is) has its own map.
There is no verb from overweight. The verb weigh belongs to the word weight.

forms.definition: too heavy, in a way that is not healthy for your body
forms.example: The doctor said he was slightly overweight for his age.

syn.note: Heavy is softer and more polite; it can describe things too.
Same idea but can sound rude when you say it about a person.
A little round and soft; sounds kinder than fat.
A medical word for someone who is very overweight.

ant.note: Weighing less than is healthy.
Having little fat on the body.
Thin in an attractive way.

forms.note: There is no adverb from overweight.

context.text: My uncle was overweight, so he started walking every morning in the park. Now he eats less plov and feels much better.

reviewer_note: over- is not in the affix table, so no affixes; weight/weigh treated as base word, noted in no_form notes.

corpus_definition: To put things into a bag.

forms.definition: the work of putting your things into bags or boxes
forms.example: I always leave my packing until the last minute.

syn.note: Preparation is any work you do to get ready; packing is only about bags.

forms.definition: a set of things in one box or paper cover; also a group of wild dogs or wolves
forms.example: I bought a pack of cards for the trip.
forms.note: Belongs to pack = a set or group (also a bag carried on the back), not the action of filling a bag.

forms.definition: a box or parcel that is sent by post
forms.example: A package arrived for you this morning.
forms.note: Belongs to pack = wrap things for sending or selling, not filling your own bag.

forms.definition: to put your things into a bag or suitcase for a trip
forms.example: I need to pack my suitcase for tomorrow.

syn.note: Load is for putting many things into a car, truck or machine.
Fill is more general: make something full of anything.
Simple and easy, but not only for bags.
Wrap means to cover something with paper or cloth.

ant.note: To take your things out of a bag or suitcase.

forms.definition: having all your things in bags, ready for a trip
forms.example: Are you packed and ready to go?

syn.note: Ready is more general: prepared for anything.

forms.note: There is no adverb from pack.

people.definition: a person whose job is putting goods into boxes
people.example: She works as a packer in a fruit factory.

people.definition: the boxes, paper and plastic around things you buy
people.example: Too much plastic packaging is bad for the planet.
people.note: Belongs to package/pack = wrapping goods for sale, not filling your own bag.

context.text: Malika is packing for her trip to Bukhara. Her packing takes all evening, but at last she is packed and ready.

reviewer_note: Noun pack (a set/group) and package are other meanings; unpack is the antonym, not a form; backpack is a compound and left out.

corpus_definition: A physical feeling of being hurt or sick.

forms.definition: the bad feeling you have in your body when you are hurt or ill
forms.example: I feel a sharp pain in my leg.

syn.note: An ache is a long, dull pain, like a headache or toothache.
Hurt as a noun is less common and often about feelings.
Soreness is a mild pain, often in muscles or the throat.
Discomfort is a weaker, unpleasant feeling, not a strong pain.

ant.note: A pleasant feeling of having no pain or worry.

forms.definition: to make someone feel sad or upset
forms.example: It pains me to see my friend so unhappy.
forms.note: Belongs to pain = sadness or hurt feelings, not body pain. Formal.

forms.definition: causing a strong bad feeling in your body
forms.example: My knee was very painful after the football match.

syn.note: Sore is about a part of the body that hurts a little, like a sore throat.
Aching means hurting with a long, dull feeling.
Simple and informal: 'My back is hurting.'

forms.definition: causing no bad feeling in your body
forms.example: The injection was quick and painless.

syn.note: Easy is more general: not difficult.

forms.definition: showing that you feel upset or annoyed
forms.example: She gave me a pained look when I was late again.
forms.note: Belongs to pain = sadness or hurt feelings, not body pain.

forms.definition: in a way that hurts your body
forms.example: He walked painfully to the car after the fall.

forms.definition: without causing any bad feeling in the body
forms.example: The dentist took out the tooth painlessly.

context.text: After the fall, Jasur had a pain in his arm. It was painful to lift his bag, so he walked painfully to the doctor.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows merged (same meaning). Verb pain and adjective pained are other meanings (emotional hurt). Painkiller is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: A colored liquid that you put on walls or pictures.

forms.definition: a coloured liquid you put on walls or pictures
forms.example: We need blue paint for the bedroom walls.
forms.note: American spelling: colored; British spelling: coloured.

syn.note: Dye is a liquid used to change the colour of cloth or hair.
Colour is more general; 'paint' is the liquid itself.
Ink is a coloured liquid for writing or printing.
Varnish is a clear liquid that makes wood shiny.

forms.definition: the activity of putting colour on walls or making pictures
forms.example: Painting is my favourite hobby.
forms.note: Also a picture made this way: 'a painting by a famous artist'.

syn.note: Drawing uses pencils or pens, not wet colour.
Decoration is making a room look nice in any way, not only with colour.

forms.definition: to put coloured liquid on a wall or make a picture with a brush
forms.example: We painted the kitchen yellow last summer.

syn.note: To colour is to add colour, often with pencils or pens.
Decorate is to make a room nicer with colour, paper or other things.
Draw is to make a picture with a pencil or pen.
Coat means to cover something with a thin layer of anything.

forms.definition: covered with coloured liquid, or made with a brush
forms.example: The old house has a painted blue door.

syn.note: Coloured means having colour, made in any way.

ant.note: Not covered with any colour; bare.

forms.note: There is no adverb from paint.

people.definition: a person who makes pictures or colours walls as a job
people.example: The painter finished our walls in two days.

context.text: Farrukh bought some green paint and painted the old gate. His daughter loves painting, so she helped him.

reviewer_note: Paintbrush is a compound, left out. Painter can be an artist or a house decorator; both fit this meaning.

corpus_definition: a public procession with people marching in celebration

forms.definition: a line of people walking through the streets to celebrate something
forms.example: The children watched the parade from the street.

syn.note: Very close; procession is more formal and can be slow and serious.
A march is often for soldiers or to protest, not only to celebrate.
A carnival is a big street party with music, dancing and costumes.
A festival is a whole celebration, often over several days.

forms.definition: to walk together through the streets in a celebration
forms.example: The dancers paraded through the centre of Tashkent.
forms.note: Also 'parade' = show something off proudly: 'He paraded his new car.'

syn.note: March is to walk in step, like soldiers.
Walk is general and easy; parade adds a public show.

forms.note: There is no adjective from parade.
There is no adverb from parade.

context.text: On Independence Day there is a big parade in the city. Musicians and dancers parade along the main street while families watch.

reviewer_note: Noun and verb share one spelling; no derivational forms exist.

corpus_definition: A person who shares in a business or activity.

forms.definition: a person who owns a business or does an activity together with you
forms.example: He is my business partner.
forms.note: Partner also means a husband, wife, boyfriend or girlfriend.

syn.note: Associate is a more formal word for someone you work with.
A colleague works in the same place, but does not share the business.
An ally helps you, often in politics or war.
A teammate plays or works in the same team.

ant.note: A person or company that competes against you.
Someone trying to win against you in business or sport.

forms.definition: the state of working together and sharing a business
forms.example: The two companies started a partnership last year.

syn.note: Collaboration is working together on a project.
Cooperation is helping each other, often for a short time.
An alliance is a formal agreement, often between countries.

ant.note: Trying to win against others, not working together.

forms.definition: to work together with someone in a business or activity
forms.example: Our school partnered with a company in Samarkand.
forms.note: Often used as 'partner with someone'.

syn.note: Informal phrasal verb: join with someone to do something.
Cooperate means to help each other and work together.
Join is more general: become part of a group.

ant.note: To try to win against someone.

forms.note: There is no adjective from partner.
There is no adverb from partner.

context.text: Sardor and his partner opened a small cafe. Their partnership is strong, and next year they will partner with a bakery.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the noun main entry (rule 6); spouse meaning only noted.

corpus_definition: An official document needed to visit other countries.

forms.definition: an official book that shows who you are when you travel abroad
forms.example: Do not forget to bring your passport.

syn.note: A general name for any paper that lets you cross a border.
An identity card shows who you are, but often only inside your country.
A visa is a stamp or paper that lets you enter a country; it goes in your passport.
Document is general: any official paper.

forms.note: There is no verb from passport.
There is no adjective from passport.
There is no adverb from passport.

context.text: Before her trip to Turkey, Nilufar checked her passport. It was still valid, so she did not need a new one.

reviewer_note: Compound of pass + port; no forms or affixes.

corpus_definition: A secret word used to enter a computer or private place.

forms.definition: a secret word or set of letters you type to open a computer or account
forms.example: Never share your password with anyone.

syn.note: A PIN is a short number for a bank card or phone.
Code is more general: secret numbers or letters.
A key opens a door; in computers, a key can be a secret code.

forms.note: There is no simple verb from password. People say 'password-protect' a file.
There is no adjective from password.
There is no adverb from password.

context.text: Bekzod forgot his email password again. He made a new, strong password and wrote it in a safe place.

reviewer_note: Compound of pass + word; no forms or affixes.

corpus_definition: A thick, soft substance used for sticking things together.

forms.definition: a thick, soft, wet substance used to stick paper together
forms.example: Use some paste to fix the paper to the wall.

syn.note: Very close and more common; glue is often stronger and used for wood or plastic too.
Formal or technical word for anything that sticks things together.
In British English, gum can mean a weak glue for paper; usually it means chewing gum.

forms.note: Paste also means any thick soft food mixture: tomato paste, toothpaste.

forms.definition: to stick something onto a surface using glue
forms.example: She pasted the photos into her school notebook.

syn.note: Same meaning; very common.
Easy, general word: stick a stamp on a letter.

ant.note: To pull something that is stuck away from a surface.

forms.note: On a computer, paste means to put copied text in a new place: copy and paste.

forms.definition: thick, soft and sticky, like wet flour mixed with water
forms.example: The mixture was pasty and hard to stir.

syn.note: Related: sticky things hold on to your fingers.
Related: not flowing easily, like honey.

forms.note: Pasty more often describes a face that is pale and looks unwell: 'a pasty face'. The noun pasty (a meat pie) is a different word.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: For the school poster, we mixed flour and water until it was thick and pasty. Then Dilnoza used the paste to stick photos of Samarkand onto the card.

reviewer_note: Noun pasty (pie) is a different word; adjective pasty kept with its 'like paste' sense and a note on the pale-face sense.

corpus_definition: a design or repeated shape on a surface

forms.definition: a design of lines, shapes or colours that repeats on a surface
forms.example: She likes the flower pattern on this rug.

syn.note: Very close; a design does not always repeat.
A pattern printed on cloth: a floral print.
One shape or picture that is repeated in a design.
Anything added to make something look nice.

forms.note: Pattern also means the usual way something happens: 'sleep patterns'. American spelling: color.

forms.definition: to cover a surface with repeated lines, shapes or colours
forms.example: Frost patterned the window glass with tiny white stars.

syn.note: Related: to make something look nicer by adding things to it.

forms.note: Not common in this meaning; more often used as 'be patterned on' = be copied from a model.

forms.definition: decorated with repeated lines, shapes or colours
forms.example: He wore a patterned shirt to the wedding.

syn.note: More general: with things added to look nice.
With a design printed on it, like cloth.

ant.note: Plain cloth has one colour and no design.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandmother has a patterned tablecloth from Bukhara. Every pattern on it is sewn by hand, and each flower pattern has a meaning.

reviewer_note: Kept design sense; verb noted as uncommon in this meaning (more often 'be patterned on'). No affix claimed for -ed.

corpus_definition: To give money to buy goods or services.
particle_note: Not separable: 'pay for the coffee', never 'pay the coffee for'. The amount goes after pay: 'pay 20,000 sum for the book'. You can also pay for another person: 'I'll pay for you.'

relations.note: Buy means you get the thing; pay for is about giving the money, sometimes for someone else.
Informal: pay for something for someone: 'I'll cover lunch today.'
Informal idiom: pay for something, often something expensive.
The shop charges for something; the customer pays for it.

context.text: Akmal paid for our lunch at the cafe today. Tomorrow it is my turn to pay for the plov.

reviewer_note: Prepositional verb, kept as phrasal. Also used for 'be punished for' (pay for a mistake); map keeps the money sense.

corpus_definition: A small round green vegetable that grows in a pod.

forms.definition: a small, round, green seed eaten as a vegetable
forms.example: He ate a small green pea from his plate.

syn.note: Related: another seed from a pod, usually bigger and not always round.
The general group that peas belong to.

forms.note: Usually plural: peas. Chickpeas and peanuts are different plants.
There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My mother always puts peas in her soup. Many children don't like peas, but my little brother eats them with everything.

reviewer_note: Only the noun exists; compounds like chickpea, peanut and pea-green are left out.

corpus_definition: a time when there is no war or violent conflict

forms.definition: a time when there is no war or fighting between groups
forms.example: We all want to live in world peace.

syn.note: Related: people living or working together without fighting.
Related: an agreement to stop fighting for a time; peace lasts longer.
Related: a quiet time without noise or trouble.

ant.note: Fighting between countries or groups.
A serious fight or disagreement, often with weapons.

forms.note: Peace also means quiet and calm: 'I want some peace and quiet.'
There is no verb made from this word. Pacify comes from the same old Latin root but is not made from peace.

forms.definition: without war, fighting or violence
forms.example: The protest in the city centre was peaceful.

syn.note: Very close: not using violence, often about protests.
Related: quiet and without trouble.

ant.note: Using force to hurt people.
Ready and wanting to fight wars.

forms.note: Peaceful also means quiet and relaxing: 'a peaceful village'.

forms.definition: not wanting to fight; living without arguments or violence
forms.example: The two countries found a peaceable answer to the problem.
forms.note: Less common than peaceful and a little formal.

forms.definition: in a way that does not involve force or fighting
forms.example: The two groups settled the problem peacefully.

syn.note: Very close: without using force.
Related: in a quiet way, without getting angry.

ant.note: Using force to hurt people.

context.text: After many years of war, the people of the region finally have peace. The talks were peaceful, and the leaders agreed to solve problems peacefully.

reviewer_note: No verb (pacify not made from peace). Compounds peacekeeper, peacemaker, peacetime left out.

corpus_definition: a small British or American coin of very low value

forms.definition: a small coin; in Britain, 100 of them make one pound
forms.example: It doesn't cost a penny to enter the park.

syn.note: The American name for this coin: 100 cents make one dollar.
Related: any piece of metal money.

forms.note: Plural: pennies (the coins) or pence (the amount): 'two pennies' but 'it costs 50 pence'.
There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: having no money at all; very poor
forms.example: He arrived in the city penniless and hungry.

syn.note: Easy, general word; penniless is stronger: no money at all.
Informal: having no money right now.

ant.note: Having a lot of money.
Rich; a little more formal.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: In London, Jasur saved every penny for a trip to Scotland. On the last day he lost his wallet and was penniless.

reviewer_note: Plural trap pennies vs pence noted. Compounds like penny-pinching left out.

corpus_definition: For every single item or unit.
usage_note: per + singular noun with no 'a' or 'the': per person, per hour, per kilo. Common with prices, speeds and amounts: '60 kilometres per hour'.

relations.note: Same meaning, more everyday: 'ten dollars for every person'.
Very common in speech: 'ten dollars a person', 'three times a day'.
Goes after the price: 'The tickets cost ten dollars each.'

context.text: The taxi costs 5,000 sum per kilometre. At the museum, tickets are 20,000 sum per person.

reviewer_note: Function word (preposition): kind corrected from word to function. Per cent/percent left out (compound).

corpus_definition: a pleasant liquid with a nice smell, worn on the body

forms.definition: a liquid with a nice smell that people put on their skin
forms.example: She sprayed perfume on her wrist before leaving home.

syn.note: Very close; scent can also mean any nice natural smell.
Same meaning, more formal and used in shops.
A lighter perfume, often for men.
General word for anything you notice with your nose, good or bad.

forms.note: Perfume can also mean any pleasant smell: 'the perfume of roses'.

forms.definition: to give something a pleasant smell
forms.example: Roses perfumed the air in the garden.

syn.note: Same meaning; also mostly written.

forms.definition: having a pleasant smell, often because one was added
forms.example: She washed her hands with perfumed soap.

syn.note: Same meaning; very common on shop labels.
Smelling nice, often naturally, like flowers.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person whose job is making or selling nice-smelling liquids
people.example: The perfumer mixed rose and lemon oils.

people.definition: a shop or place where nice-smelling liquids are made or sold
people.example: We bought a gift at the perfumery in the mall.

context.text: Madina bought a small bottle of perfume at the bazaar in Tashkent. She also got some perfumed soap, and now the whole bathroom smells of roses.

reviewer_note: Verb perfume marked literary. No affix claimed for perfumery (-ery not in table).

corpus_definition: Belonging to just one human and not for everyone else.

forms.definition: a human being; one man, woman or child
forms.example: Only one person can use this computer at a time.

syn.note: One person, separate from a group; a little formal.
Any man, woman or child, not an animal.
Used when we don't know or say which one.

forms.note: Plural: people (usually), persons in formal or legal English.

forms.definition: the character of someone, for example friendly, shy or funny
forms.example: My sister has a very friendly personality.
forms.note: Belongs to person = what someone is like inside, not things belonging to one person. Also means a famous person on TV.

forms.definition: to make or change something so it is right for one particular owner
forms.example: You can personalize your phone with your own photos.

syn.note: Very close; often about products, apps and cars.
Make something fit one person's needs exactly.

forms.note: British spelling: personalise. Common adjective: personalized (a personalized mug with your name).

forms.definition: belonging to or used by one particular human only
forms.example: This is my personal diary, please do not read it.

syn.note: Close; private stresses that others may not see or use it.
Easy: 'my own room' means it is mine only.
For one person, not a group: individual lessons.

ant.note: Open to and used by everyone.
Used by more than one person.
Not friendly and showing no human feeling: an impersonal letter.

forms.definition: made especially for one particular owner, often with their name
forms.example: She got a personalized cup with her name on it.
forms.note: British spelling: personalised.

forms.definition: by you yourself, not by someone else
forms.example: The director personally answered every letter.

syn.note: You go or do it yourself, face to face.
Without anyone in the middle.

forms.note: Personally also means 'in my opinion': 'Personally, I prefer tea.'

context.text: This is my personal phone, so please don't use it. The school director personally answered every letter, and each student got a personalized reply.

reviewer_note: Personality kept as other_meaning (character). Personnel left out: borrowed from French, not made from personal in English.

corpus_definition: a powerful ruler of ancient Egypt, treated like a god

forms.definition: a king of ancient Egypt, treated like a god
forms.example: The pharaoh ordered a great pyramid to be built.

syn.note: Easy, general word for a male ruler of a country.
Any person who controls a country.
Related: the ruler of a big empire, like Rome or China.

forms.note: Spelling trap: -aoh at the end. Pronounced /ˈfeərəʊ/.
There is no verb in this family.
No learner-dictionary adjective. Pharaonic exists but is very rare.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Tutankhamun was a young pharaoh who died at nineteen. Today tourists visit the tombs of the pharaohs in Egypt.

reviewer_note: Pharaonic is too rare for learners; noted in the adjective no_form.

corpus_definition: A shop where you buy medical items.

American English. A drugstore sells medicine but also sweets, drinks and makeup.
Related: a hospital is where doctors treat sick people; a pharmacy only sells medicine.

forms.note: No verb is made from pharmacy.

forms.definition: connected with making and selling medicines and drugs
forms.example: My cousin works for a big pharmaceutical company in Tashkent.
forms.note: Mostly used before a noun: 'a pharmaceutical company', 'the pharmaceutical industry'.

syn.note: Related: about medicine and treating illness in general.
Related: used as a medicine, for example medicinal plants.

forms.note: Pharmaceutically exists but is very rare and not in learner dictionaries.

people.definition: a person whose job is to prepare and sell medicines
people.example: The pharmacist told me to take the tablets after meals.

people.definition: the science that studies drugs and how they work in the body
people.example: He wants to study pharmacology after school.

context.text: There is a small pharmacy next to our house in Chilonzor. The pharmacist said the tablets come from a big pharmaceutical company in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: False friend: Russian/Uzbek 'apteka' is not English; British chemist's and American drugstore given as synonyms.

corpus_definition: To lift something from the floor.
particle_note: Separable: 'pick up the toys' or 'pick the toys up'. With a pronoun the particle goes after it: 'pick it up' (not 'pick up it').

relations.note: Very close; lift is about moving something up, from anywhere, not only from the floor.
Related: move something to a higher position, often a hand or a flag: 'Raise your hand.'
Related: pick up many things and put them together: 'gather the papers'.
Put something back on the floor or on a table.
Let something fall from your hand, often by accident.

context.text: My little brother never picks up his toys. Mum says, 'Pick them up now or they go in the box!' So he picked up every car and put it away.

reviewer_note: Only the 'lift from the floor' meaning; other meanings (collect someone, learn a language, answer the phone) are left for other maps.

corpus_definition: a group of things lying on top of one another

forms.definition: a group of things lying one on top of another
forms.example: There is a large pile of books on the desk.
forms.note: Informal: 'piles of work' = a lot of work.

syn.note: Very close; a heap is often untidy: 'a heap of dirty clothes'.
A neat pile of flat things of the same kind: 'a stack of plates'.
Related: a round pile, usually of earth, sand or stones.
Related, informal: 'piles of' and 'lots of' can both mean a large amount.

forms.definition: to put things one on top of another
forms.example: She piled the plates in the sink after dinner.
forms.note: Often with up: 'The dishes piled up.' 'pile up the boxes'.

syn.note: Put things on top of each other, usually in a neat way.
Very close; often for an untidy or very large pile.
Related: put a lot of things into or onto something: 'load the car'.

forms.note: No adjective is made from pile. 'Piled' is only a verb form: 'a plate piled high with plov'.
No adverb is made from pile.

context.text: After the wedding there was a huge pile of dishes in the kitchen. My aunts piled the clean plates on the table, and we carried them back to the neighbours.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR A2). Pile-up (a car crash) left out as a compound-like noun.

corpus_definition: A detailed set of steps for doing something in the future.

forms.definition: an idea or set of steps for something you want to do later
forms.example: We have a good plan for the weekend trip.
forms.note: Common patterns: 'make a plan', 'have plans for the weekend', 'go according to plan'.

syn.note: Related and easy: an idea can be a first thought; a plan has steps.
A careful, long plan to reach a big goal, often in business or sport.
British: an official plan. In American English it can sound dishonest.
Related: a plan about the time and place of something: 'travel arrangements'.
Related: a planned piece of work with a goal.

forms.definition: the work of deciding how you will do something
forms.example: The trip took weeks of careful planning.
forms.note: Double n: plan → planning.

syn.note: Getting ready for something; planning is deciding the steps.
Arranging things and people so an event works. British also: organisation.

forms.definition: to decide in detail what you are going to do
forms.example: We are planning a trip to Samarkand in May.
forms.note: Patterns: plan to do something; plan a party. Past: planned (double n).

syn.note: Make all the arrangements for an event. British also: organise.
Decide the time and place of something: 'arrange a meeting'.
Plan to do something; a little formal: 'I intend to study abroad.'
Related: get ready for something.

ant.note: Do something without planning, using what you have at the moment.

forms.definition: arranged or decided before it happens
forms.example: The planned visit to the museum was cancelled because of rain.

syn.note: Wanted and planned, often about a result.
Organized before: 'an arranged meeting'.
Related: done on purpose, not by accident.

ant.note: Not planned; it happens without anyone deciding it.
Happening by chance, not because someone planned it.

forms.note: No adverb is made from plan. Say 'as planned' or 'according to plan'.

people.definition: a person who decides how something will be done or built
people.example: The city planners want more parks in Tashkent.
people.note: Also a book or app where you write your plans: 'a weekly planner'.

context.text: My sister loves planning. She made a plan for every day of our holiday in Bukhara, and the trip went exactly as planned.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: double n in planning, planned, planner. Unplanned placed in the ant list of planned, not as a form.

corpus_definition: A large round object in space that orbits a star.

forms.definition: a large round object in space that moves around a star
forms.example: Earth is a beautiful planet.
forms.note: 'The planet' often means our Earth: 'save the planet'.

syn.note: Related: in stories and science, a world can mean a planet: 'life on other worlds'.
Related: the globe means our Earth, or a round map of it.
Related but different: a star, like the Sun, makes its own light; a planet does not.

forms.note: No verb is made from planet. The dictionary links 'earth' (to connect to the ground), but it is not made from planet.

forms.definition: connected with the large round objects that move around a star
forms.example: Scientists study the planetary system of a nearby star.

syn.note: Related, formal: connected with the sky or space.

forms.note: No adverb is made from planet.

people.definition: a building where you watch shows about stars on a round ceiling
people.example: We watched a show about Mars at the planetarium.

context.text: There are eight planets in our solar system. At the planetarium, my class watched a film about planetary scientists who study Mars.

reviewer_note: planetary (-ary) is not in the affix table, so no affix is claimed; planetarium listed as a thing.

corpus_definition: A light material made by humans used to make many objects.

forms.definition: a light, strong material made in factories, used for bottles and bags
forms.example: Plastic bottles are bad for the environment.
forms.note: Informal: 'plastic' can also mean credit cards: 'Can I pay with plastic?'

syn.note: Related: a thin, soft kind of this material used for bags. American English: polyethylene.
Related: one kind of this material, used for floors and old music records.
Related but different: rubber is soft and stretchy and can come from trees.

forms.note: No common verb is made from plastic. 'Plasticize' is technical and very rare.

forms.definition: made of a light material that factories produce
forms.example: Please don't use plastic bags at the bazaar.
forms.note: Another meaning: easy to bend and shape. In 'plastic surgery' it means changing the shape of the body.

syn.note: Related: made by people from chemicals, not natural.
Related and easy: made by people, not found in nature.

forms.note: No adverb is made from plastic in this meaning.

context.text: Many shops in Tashkent now sell cloth bags instead of plastic ones. Plastic takes hundreds of years to break down, so we try to use less of it.

reviewer_note: Noun and adjective are the same spelling (conversion). Plasticity is C2 and another meaning (easy to shape), so it is left out.

corpus_definition: The raised area beside train tracks where passengers wait.

forms.definition: the raised area next to the train tracks where people wait
forms.example: The train is waiting at platform five.
forms.note: Other meanings: a raised stage for speakers, a political plan, and a computer system or website (a learning platform).

syn.note: Related: the station is the whole building; the platform is one part of it.
Related: the metal rails the train runs on; American English also uses track for the platform number.
Related: another raised area, but for people who speak or perform.

forms.note: No verb is made from platform.
No adjective is made from platform.
No adverb is made from platform.

context.text: At Tashkent station, the fast train to Samarkand leaves from platform two. We waited on the platform with our bags for ten minutes.

reviewer_note: No derived forms exist; other meanings (stage, computer system) mentioned only in the note.

corpus_definition: to push someone or something with your finger or a stick

forms.definition: a quick push with your finger or a stick
forms.example: She gave me a poke in the ribs to wake me up.

syn.note: Almost the same: a short push with a finger or a stick.
A quicker and harder push, often with an elbow or a sharp thing.
Related: a gentle push, usually with your elbow.

forms.definition: to push someone or something quickly with your finger or a stick
forms.example: She poked him in the arm to get his attention.
forms.note: Phrases: poke fun at someone (laugh at them), poke your nose into something (ask about things that are not your business).

syn.note: Almost the same meaning.
Harder and quicker, sometimes to hurt.
Related and easy: push is general; poke is a small push with one finger or a thin thing.
Related: push gently, usually with your elbow.
Related: touch lightly, often to get attention, without pushing.

forms.definition: too small and not comfortable, used about a room or house
forms.example: They live in a poky little flat in the city centre.
forms.note: Belongs to an old meaning of poke = a small bag, not pushing with a finger. Informal, mostly British. American English also: pokey.
No adverb is made from poke.

people.definition: a metal stick for moving wood or coal in a fire
people.example: Grandfather moved the burning wood with a poker.

context.text: My little nephew poked the cat with a stick, and it ran away. I told him, 'Don't poke animals!' He said sorry and gave the cat a gentle pat.

reviewer_note: poker (fire tool) is from poke; poker the card game is not related, noted in people_not_family. poky shown as other_meaning (old 'small bag' sense).

corpus_definition: A small area of water that is smaller than a lake.

forms.definition: a small area of still water, smaller than a lake
forms.example: The ducks are swimming in the park pond.
forms.note: Informal British: 'the pond' can mean the Atlantic Ocean ('across the pond').

syn.note: A small area of water; often a swimming pool, but also natural water: 'a rock pool'.
Related: a lake is much bigger.
Related: a very small amount of water on the ground after rain.
Related: a big man-made lake that stores water for a city.

forms.note: No verb is made from pond.
No adjective is made from pond.
No adverb is made from pond.

context.text: In the centre of old Bukhara there is a famous pond called Lyabi-Hauz. People sit under the trees around the pond and drink tea.

reviewer_note: Simple noun with no derived forms.

corpus_definition: Liked or admired by many people in a group.
usage_note: be popular with + a group of people: 'popular with tourists', 'very popular with young people'. 'Popular among' is similar and a little more formal.

relations.note: Very close and easy: 'She is liked by everyone.'
Stronger: people like it very much.
Liked more than others in a group: 'This song is a favourite with children.' American spelling: favorite.
Liked by many people; used about people more than things.
Not liked by a group of people: 'The new rule is unpopular with students.'

context.text: Chorsu Bazaar is very popular with tourists. Our new English teacher is popular with the students because her lessons are fun.

reviewer_note: Fixed adjective + preposition phrase; antonym uses the family's negative form unpopular.

corpus_definition: the number of people who live in a specific place.

forms.definition: the number of people who live in a place
forms.example: Tashkent has a population of about three million people.

syn.note: The people who live in a place; a bit formal. Population is usually the number.
The people who live in a place, often a town or building.
Easy, general word; population is more exact and often a number.

forms.definition: to live in an area and fill it with people
forms.example: The valley is populated mainly by farmers.
forms.note: Most often used in the passive: 'be populated by'.

syn.note: Formal: to live in a place.
Easy everyday words with almost the same meaning.
To go and live in a place, often for the first time.

forms.definition: having people living in it
forms.example: Fergana Valley is the most densely populated area of Uzbekistan.
forms.note: Usually with an adverb: densely populated, thinly populated.

syn.note: Having people living there; a little formal.
Related: full of people in a small space, often too many.

ant.note: With no people in it.
With nobody living there.

forms.definition: with a lot of people living there
forms.example: China is one of the most populous countries in the world.

forms.note: No adverb in this family; use 'densely populated' or 'by population'.

reviewer_note: Kept 'popular' out: same Latin root but not made from population (popular = liked by many). populous added as formal extra.

corpus_definition: A town by the sea with a place for ships to dock.

forms.definition: a town or place by the sea where ships stop
forms.example: The ship arrived at the port early this morning.

The exact place where a ship is tied up and loaded.
A port by the sea; used to make clear it is not a river port or airport.

forms.note: The verb 'port' exists only in computing (to move software to another system), which is a different word history.

corpus_definition: a painting, drawing, or photo of a person

forms.definition: a painting, drawing or photo of a person

A picture made with paint; it may not show a person.
Formal: a picture that looks like a real person.

forms.definition: to show or describe someone in a picture, film or book

Easy everyday word.
To show something in a picture or as a sign.
Used for words, not pictures.

reviewer_note: portray/portrayal kept as family (same root, Oxford links them). portraitist and portraiture left out as rare for A1-B2.

corpus_definition: Having a good or happy view of things.

Believing something good may happen.

Happy and in a good mood; about mood more than views.

ant.note: Thinking mostly about the bad side of things.
Expecting bad things to happen.

reviewer_note: Map anchored to 'good attitude'; other senses (positive test result, positive number, certain) not used in examples.

corpus_definition: a large printed picture or notice put on a wall

forms.definition: a large printed picture or notice that you put on a wall

syn.note: A piece of paper with information for people to read.
A large sign, often carried at a protest.
A long piece of cloth with words on it.
A small printed paper given out to advertise something.

To show something so people can see it.

ant.note: To remove a notice or picture from a wall.

forms.example: Please write your postal address on the form.

corpus_definition: To speak to God or a spiritual power.

Easy phrase with the same meaning.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed: the -er in prayer is not the agent suffix (prayer is not a person here). Homophone trap pray/prey noted.

corpus_definition: To make a paper copy of a digital document.

Same meaning, more common in British English.

corpus_definition: a building where people are kept when they break the law.

Informal phrase.
To keep someone, often for a short time, at a police station.

To let someone go.

people.definition: a person who is kept in a building as punishment

corpus_definition: Only for one person or a small group, not everyone.

syn.note: Being alone, often by choice; a little formal.
Related: keeping something hidden from others.

ant.note: Attention from many people and the media.

forms.definition: a soldier of the lowest rank in the army

forms.definition: only for one person or a small group, not for everyone

corpus_definition: Feeling very happy about something good you or others did.

corpus_definition: Something bad given to someone who did wrong.

Related: one kind of punishment where you must pay money.

Related: punish someone by making them pay money.

corpus_definition: A small bag used by women to carry money.

Related: a bigger bag for many things; Americans call it a purse.
Related: the general word for any bag.

corpus_definition: to place things back in the correct storage spot after using them

Take something out of the place where it is kept.
Remove something from a box, bag or cupboard.

corpus_definition: To gain extra mass on your body.

Become thinner, often by eating less or exercising.

corpus_definition: a large farm, usually for raising cattle or horses
