Close; a ranch can also have horses or sheep.
Related: a large area of land with one owner.

forms.definition: the work or business of keeping animals on a very large farm
forms.example: Ranching is an important business in Texas.

syn.note: Close; ranching is on very large areas of land.
Related: the general word for working on a farm.

forms.definition: to keep animals on a very large farm as your job
forms.example: His family has ranched in Montana for a hundred years.
forms.note: Mainly American English and not very common; most people say 'run a ranch'.

syn.note: The general word for working on land with animals or crops.

people.definition: a person who owns or runs a very large farm for animals
people.example: The rancher had more than five hundred cows.

context.text: My cousin went to America and worked on a horse ranch for one summer. The rancher taught him how ranching works, from feeding the horses to fixing fences.

reviewer_note: Verb 'ranch' is mainly American and uncommon; kept as conversion with a note. Compounds (ranch hand, ranch house) left out.

corpus_definition: a narrow line of light coming from a bright source

forms.definition: a narrow line of light from the sun or a lamp
forms.example: A ray of sunshine came through the bedroom curtains.
forms.note: Also used in 'a ray of hope' (a small sign of hope).

syn.note: Very close; a beam can also be from a torch or car lights.
Close, more literary: 'a shaft of light'.
Related: a small, short shine of light.
Related: the general word.

forms.note: Radiate (send out light or heat) comes from the same old Latin root but is not made from ray.

context.text: In the morning, the first rays of the sun shine on the blue domes of Samarkand. Tourists stand in the square and take photos of them.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; radiate marked not_family. Other meanings (the fish, X-ray compound) left out.

corpus_definition: The cause or explanation for an event.
usage_note: the reason for + noun / -ing: 'the reason for the delay'. With a clause, use 'the reason why' or 'the reason (that)': 'the reason (why) I left'.

relations.note: Close; cause is often about what made something happen, especially a bad thing.
Close; an explanation is what you say to make the reason clear.
Formal: a good reason, often legal: 'grounds for divorce'.
Related: the reason a person does something, often a crime.
Related: a reason you give, which may not be true.

context.text: What is the reason for this delay? The driver said the reason for the late train was snow on the line.

reviewer_note: kind_hint said phrasal; corrected to phrase (noun + preposition). No true antonym, so none listed.

corpus_definition: a paper showing that you have paid for something

forms.definition: a piece of paper that shows you have paid for something
forms.example: Keep your receipt in case you want a refund.
forms.note: The p is silent: /rɪˈsiːt/. In formal English it also means the act of receiving: 'on receipt of your letter'.

syn.note: Formal phrase used in shops and online.
American English for a small shop paper.
Related, but careful: you get a bill BEFORE you pay and a receipt AFTER.
Related: a paper asking a company to pay; used in business.

forms.definition: the place in a hotel or office where visitors are welcomed
forms.example: Please leave your key at reception.
forms.note: Belongs to receive = welcome people (also a formal party), not a paper for payment.

forms.definition: to get something that someone gives or sends you
forms.example: The shop gives you a paper when it has received your money.
forms.note: Receipt is made from this verb: the paper shows the shop received your money.

syn.note: Everyday English; receive is more formal.
Easy, with the same meaning.
Formal: get something, often with effort.

ant.note: One person sends, the other receives.
One person gives, the other receives.

forms.definition: willing to listen to and accept new ideas
forms.example: The students were very receptive to the new teaching method.
forms.note: Belongs to receive = accept ideas or people, not a paper for payment.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you are willing to accept new ideas
forms.example: She listened receptively to every suggestion.
forms.note: Goes with receptive. Very rare; most people say 'with an open mind'.

people.definition: a person who gets something, such as money or a letter
people.example: The recipient of the payment must sign the form.

people.definition: a person who welcomes visitors at a hotel or office
people.example: The receptionist gave us the room key.
people.note: Belongs to receive = welcome guests (reception), not a paper for payment.

people.definition: the part of a phone that you hold to your ear
people.example: He picked up the receiver and said hello.
people.note: Belongs to receive = get a signal or call, not a paper for payment.

context.text: I bought new shoes in Tashkent and the shop assistant gave me a receipt. When I got home, I received a message from the shop with a discount code.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR A2). Silent p noted; re-ceive is not a real prefix split, so no affix. Rare verb 'to receipt (a bill)' left out.

corpus_definition: Happening only a short time ago.

forms.note: Recency exists but is rare and technical; learners do not need it.

forms.definition: happening or made only a short time ago
forms.example: Have you seen any recent movies?

syn.note: Easy and close; new can also mean 'not used before'.
Close: the newest one: 'the latest news'.
Related: the one just before now: 'last week'.
Related: new and not old, like fresh news or fresh bread.
Related: happening now, not just before now.

ant.note: Happening or made a long time ago.
From a time before now, often long ago.

forms.definition: not long ago
forms.example: We recently moved to a new flat in Tashkent.

syn.note: Close; used with the present perfect: 'I haven't seen him lately'.
Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Related: used before a past participle: 'newly built'.

ant.note: At a time far in the past.

context.text: I recently started a new job in Samarkand. In my most recent message, I told my friends about it.

reviewer_note: Recency is rare, so noun slot is no_form with a note. Lately is a synonym of recently (false-friend trap not relevant here).

corpus_definition: Instructions for cooking a specific dish.

forms.definition: a list of foods and steps that tell you how to cook a dish
forms.example: This cake recipe is very easy.
forms.note: Also used in 'a recipe for disaster' (something likely to go very wrong). Pronounced /ˈresəpi/.

syn.note: Related: steps that tell you how to do anything.
Related: steps to follow, for cooking or for using something.
Related: the part of a recipe that gives the cooking steps.
Related: a fixed list of things mixed in a certain way.

context.text: My grandmother has a secret recipe for plov. She never writes it down, so I watch her cook and try to remember every step.

reviewer_note: Single-form family. Recipe comes from the same Latin root as receive but is not made from it, so no links.

corpus_definition: To make something smaller in size, amount, or degree.

forms.definition: the act of making something smaller or less
forms.example: There has been a big reduction in the price of flights.

syn.note: Very common and easy, especially for money and prices: a cut in taxes.
Very close, a little more formal.
Related: a fall is when something gets smaller by itself; a reduction is often made by someone.
Related: a reduction in the price of something in a shop.

ant.note: Something gets bigger instead of smaller.
A rise is when an amount goes up.

forms.definition: to make something smaller in size, amount or level
forms.example: We must reduce the number of accidents on the roads.

syn.note: Easy and very common, especially for money: cut costs, cut prices.
Very close; used for prices, levels and temperatures.
Close, a little more formal; can also mean get smaller by itself.
Informal phrasal verb: cut down on sugar.
Formal; used for pain, risk or effects.

ant.note: To make something bigger in size or amount.
To make prices, levels or amounts higher.

forms.definition: made smaller or lower than before
forms.example: All winter coats are on sale at reduced prices.

syn.note: Easy word; reduced shows that someone made it lower.
Related: used for prices and money, as in cut prices.

forms.note: No common adverb exists for this family.

context.text: The city wants to reduce traffic in the centre of Tashkent. After the new metro line opened, there was a big reduction in cars, and buses now run at reduced prices.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR A2). No affix claimed: reduction minus -ion leaves 'reduct', not a word. reducible omitted as rare.

corpus_definition: To say no to something offered or asked.

forms.definition: the act of saying no to something that is offered or asked
forms.example: Her refusal to help surprised everyone in the office.

syn.note: Close; often used for plans, offers and job applications.
Related, informal: 'I got a no from the bank.'
Related: saying that something is not true or not allowing something.

ant.note: Saying yes to something that is offered.
Saying yes to a plan or request.

forms.definition: waste material that people throw away
forms.example: The city collects refuse from every street twice a week.
forms.note: A different word with the same spelling, said /ˈrefjuːs/. It means rubbish, not saying no. Formal.

forms.definition: to say no when someone offers or asks you something
forms.example: She had to refuse the invitation because she was ill.

syn.note: Easy and very common in speaking.
Very close phrasal verb: turn down an offer or invitation.
Polite and formal: 'I must decline your kind offer.'
Stronger: often for ideas, plans or applications.

ant.note: To say yes to something that is offered.
To say yes to what someone asks or suggests.

forms.note: No common adjective exists for this meaning.
No common adverb exists for this family.

context.text: Aziz invited me to his birthday party, and I could not refuse. My refusal would make him sad, so I said yes.

reviewer_note: Homograph trap: refuse /ˈrefjuːs/ = rubbish is shown as other_meaning so learners do not think it is the noun of 'say no'.

corpus_definition: A member of your family.

forms.definition: a person who is in your family, for example an aunt or cousin
forms.example: All my relatives are coming for the wedding.

syn.note: Very close and easy.
Old-fashioned or literary; usually 'next of kin' in forms.
Related: means the whole group of people, not one person.

forms.definition: the way two people are connected by family or marriage
forms.example: What is your relationship to the bride? I'm her cousin.

syn.note: Related: a link between people or things in general.
Formal word for family connection.
Related: usually plural, as in family ties.

forms.definition: to show or find a connection between two things
forms.example: It is hard to relate these two ideas.
forms.note: Belongs to relate = connect or understand; for family we use the adjective: 'We are related.'

forms.definition: in the same family, by birth or marriage
forms.example: Are you and Dilnoza related? You look very similar.
forms.note: Usually after a verb: 'We are related.' 'He is related to my mother.'

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.

ant.note: Not in the same family.

forms.definition: compared with something else
forms.example: The village lives in relative peace now.
forms.note: Belongs to relative = compared to other things, not a family member.

forms.definition: quite, when compared to other things
forms.example: The test was relatively easy.
forms.note: False friend: belongs to relative = compared to other things. It has nothing to do with family.

people.definition: a person who belongs to the same family as you
people.example: We have relations in Bukhara and Khiva.
people.note: Same meaning as relative in this sense, often plural.

context.text: Every summer our relatives come from Namangan to visit us. Some of them are related to my father, and some are from my mother's side.

reviewer_note: Family sense only. relative (adj) and relatively are false friends here (= compared with), shown as other_meaning. relate (verb) belongs to 'connect'.

corpus_definition: To rest and stop feeling busy or worried.

forms.definition: time spent resting and enjoying yourself without worry
forms.example: I listen to music for relaxation after work.

syn.note: Easy word; rest can also mean sleeping or not moving.
Related: free time when you are not working.
Related, formal: things you do for fun in free time.

ant.note: A feeling of worry because of problems or work.
A nervous feeling that stops you from feeling calm.

forms.definition: to rest and stop feeling busy, worried or nervous
forms.example: I like to relax on the beach in the summer.

syn.note: Easy; rest often means stopping work or activity.
Very close, used after a busy day: 'I need to unwind.'
Used when someone is angry, excited or nervous.
Informal phrase: rest and don't work too hard.
Very informal, common with young people.

ant.note: To keep thinking about problems and feel nervous.
To become stiff and nervous.

forms.definition: calm and not worried or nervous
forms.example: After the holiday, she looked happy and relaxed.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Related: feeling good and without pain or worry.
Related: describes a person who is usually calm, not one moment.

ant.note: Nervous and not able to relax.
Worried because of too much work or problems.
Worried and a little afraid.

forms.definition: making you feel calm and rested
forms.example: We had a relaxing weekend in the mountains near Chimgan.
forms.note: relaxed = how you feel; relaxing = what makes you feel that way.

syn.note: Close, a little more formal.
Close: something that makes you calm.
Related: quiet and calm, often about a place.

ant.note: Making you feel worried and tense.
Making you feel tired.

forms.note: No common adverb. 'relaxedly' is very rare; say 'in a relaxed way'.

context.text: On Sundays my father likes to relax in the garden. He says it is the most relaxing day of the week, and he always looks relaxed after it.

reviewer_note: -ed/-ing trap: relaxed (feeling) vs relaxing (cause) both shown with a note.

corpus_definition: The belief in one or more gods and organized worship.

forms.definition: belief in a god or gods and the ways people pray and worship
forms.example: Many people find comfort in their religion.

syn.note: Close; faith often means one person's strong belief, or one religion: the Muslim faith.
Related: anything you think is true, not only about God.
Related: the act of praying and showing love to God.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.

forms.definition: connected with belief in God, or believing strongly in God
forms.example: My grandmother is very religious and prays five times a day.

syn.note: Formal: believing very strongly and following all the rules.
Related: about the soul and deep feelings, not always a religion.
Related: connected with God and special, like a holy place.

ant.note: Not connected with religion, as in a secular school.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with belief in God
forms.example: The family celebrates the holiday religiously every year.
forms.note: Also used informally to mean 'very regularly': 'He goes to the gym religiously.'

syn.note: Formal: in a way that shows strong belief.

context.text: In Uzbekistan, many people visit religious places in Bukhara and Samarkand. People of every religion are welcome to see the old mosques and madrasas.

reviewer_note: No verb in this family. No -ous affix claimed (religi- is not a word). religiously has an informal extra meaning (very regularly), mentioned in a note.

corpus_definition: To put a new thing in place of an old one.

forms.definition: a new thing or person that takes the place of an old one
forms.example: My phone broke, so the shop gave me a replacement.

syn.note: Close; often something used for a short time instead of the usual thing.
Related: the act of making something different.

forms.definition: to put a new thing where an old or broken one was
forms.example: I need to replace my broken phone.

syn.note: Easy and common: change a light bulb, change the battery.
Related, informal: give one thing and take another.
Formal: use one thing instead of another.
Very close phrase.

ant.note: To continue to have the old thing.

forms.definition: possible to change for a new one
forms.example: The battery in this watch is replaceable.

ant.note: So special or valuable that nothing new can take its place.

forms.note: No common adverb exists for this family.

context.text: The old buses in our city are being replaced with new electric ones. The replacements are quiet and clean.

reviewer_note: No re- affix claimed: replace = substitute, not clearly 'place again'. irreplaceable is listed as the antonym of replaceable.

corpus_definition: A document giving information about a specific topic.

forms.definition: a written or spoken description of a topic or of events
forms.example: The students wrote a report about animals in the desert.

syn.note: Close: a description of what happened.
Related: a piece of writing in a newspaper or magazine.
Related: any official paper with information.
Related: something said or written officially.

forms.definition: to give people information about something that has happened
forms.example: Journalists report on daily events in the city.

syn.note: Easy and general: tell someone the news.
Related: say what something is like.
Related: tell many people officially.
Related, formal: give someone information.

ant.note: To keep information secret.
To stop people from learning about something bad.

forms.definition: said or written by someone as news or information
forms.example: There were twenty reported cases of the illness last month.
forms.note: Also used in grammar: reported speech.

syn.note: Formal: said to be true but not proved.

ant.note: Not told to the police, a newspaper or other people.

forms.definition: according to what people say or what news says
forms.example: The singer is reportedly coming to Tashkent next month.

syn.note: Easy and common in speaking.
Formal, often about crimes.
Related: shows you are not sure it is true.

people.definition: a person whose job is to find and write news
people.example: The reporter asked the minister a question.

context.text: A small fire at the bazaar was reported on the local news. The report said that nobody was hurt, and reportedly the shops will open again tomorrow.

reviewer_note: Noun row (document) and verb row (give information) are one meaning, merged; verb shown as conversion.

corpus_definition: What happens after an action or event.

forms.definition: something that happens because of an action or event
forms.example: The game ended with a good result for our team.

syn.note: Very close, a little more formal.
Close: a change that something causes.
Close; often about a bad or important effect.
Related: the points at the end of a game.

ant.note: The thing that makes something happen.

forms.definition: to happen because of something, or to cause something
forms.example: The heavy rain resulted in floods. The floods resulted from the heavy rain.
forms.note: Use 'result in' + effect and 'result from' + cause.

syn.note: Close to result in: 'Too much sugar can lead to health problems.'
Related: result in = cause.
Related: to happen after something.

forms.definition: happening because of something just mentioned
forms.example: The storm and the resulting damage closed the road.

syn.note: Formal and written.

forms.definition: caused by the thing that was just mentioned
forms.example: The factory closed, and the resultant job losses hurt the town.

forms.note: No adverb exists. Use the phrase 'as a result'.

context.text: Laziz studied hard all year, and the result was great. With the resulting grades, he got a place at a university in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: No adverb; the phrase 'as a result' is mentioned in the note only.

corpus_definition: To look at something again to give an opinion.

forms.definition: a careful look at something to judge it or check it
forms.example: The teacher did a quick review of the lesson before the test.
forms.note: Also: a piece of writing that gives an opinion about a book, film or product.

syn.note: Related, easy: a quick look to find mistakes.
Related, formal: judging how good something is.
Related, British: studying notes again before an exam.
Related: an official, careful look at a place or thing.

forms.definition: to look at something again carefully and judge it
forms.example: I need to review my notes before the test.

syn.note: Common phrasal verb: go over your answers.
Close; usually a quicker look.
Related, easy: look for mistakes.
British English for studying notes again before an exam.
Related, formal: judge how good something is.

ant.note: To pay no attention to something.

forms.note: No common adjective exists for this family.
No common adverb exists for this family.

people.definition: a person who gives an opinion about a book, film or product
people.example: The reviewer said the new film was boring.

context.text: Before the exam, Malika reviews her notes every evening. On Sunday she does a big review of everything she learned.

reviewer_note: re- + view = look again is transparent here. Book/film review sense mentioned in a note on the noun.

corpus_definition: when words end with the same sound, especially in a poem

forms.definition: a word with the same end sound as another word, as in 'cat' and 'hat'
forms.example: The children loved poems with a funny rhyme.
forms.note: The h is silent and 'y' sounds like 'i' in 'time': /raɪm/. Also: a short poem for children (nursery rhyme).

syn.note: Related: writing with a regular beat, often in a poem.
Related: a piece of writing in lines; many poems use rhyme.
Related: a short song with simple rhymes, often in ads.

forms.definition: to have the same end sound as another word
forms.example: 'Cat' rhymes with 'hat'.
forms.note: Pattern: X rhymes with Y.

syn.note: Related, easy phrase: but rhyme is only about the end of words.

forms.definition: having the same end sound, or using such words
forms.example: We played a rhyming game in English class.

forms.note: No adverb exists for this family.

context.text: Our teacher reads us a short poem every day. We have to find the words that rhyme, like 'day' and 'play'. Rhyming games help us remember new words.

reviewer_note: Don't confuse with rhythm (the beat), which is not in this family; not listed as not_family since it is not the same root.

corpus_definition: to cook food in an oven or over a fire with dry heat

forms.definition: a large piece of meat cooked in an oven, or a meal of it
forms.example: My grandmother made a big roast for the family on Sunday.

syn.note: British: a large piece of meat for cooking; it may not be cooked yet.

forms.definition: to cook meat or vegetables in an oven or over a fire
forms.example: We roasted a chicken for Sunday dinner.

syn.note: Also cooking in an oven, but we bake bread and cakes and roast meat.
Cooking with strong heat from above or below, often faster.
The general word for making food hot and ready to eat.
Making bread or nuts brown with dry heat.

forms.definition: cooked in an oven or over a fire, used before a noun
forms.example: We had roast beef with potatoes.

syn.note: Cooked in an oven; used for potatoes, bread and fish.
Cooked with strong direct heat.

ant.note: Raw food is not cooked at all.

forms.definition: cooked with dry heat until brown
forms.example: She bought a bag of roasted almonds at Chorsu Bazaar.
forms.note: Roast beef and roasted beef are both fine; roasted is more common for nuts, coffee and vegetables.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a pan or machine used for cooking meat or coffee beans
people.example: Put the chicken in the roaster and cover it.

context.text: On Navruz we roasted a whole lamb over the fire. The roast was ready in the evening, and the children ate roasted nuts while they waited.

reviewer_note: Roast is verb, noun and adjective with the same spelling; roasted kept as a participle extra.

corpus_definition: to take money or things from someone by force.

forms.definition: the crime of taking money or things from a person or place by force
forms.example: There was a robbery at the bank last night.

syn.note: Theft is any stealing; a robbery usually uses force or threats.
A robbery with a gun, for example in a shop or bank.
Going into a building to steal, often when nobody is there.
Robbing a person in the street.

forms.definition: to take money or things from a person or place, often using force
forms.example: Two men tried to rob the shop yesterday.
forms.note: You rob a person or a place, but you steal a thing: 'They robbed the bank' / 'They stole the money'.

syn.note: Very close: 'steal from a shop' = 'rob a shop'.
To rob someone in the street.
To go into a house to steal. American English: burglarize.
To rob a bank or shop using a gun.

forms.note: No adjective in this family; 'robbed' is only used as a past participle.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who takes money or things from others by force
people.example: The police caught the robber near the station.

context.text: Last night a man tried to rob a small shop in our street. The police caught the robber quickly, and the robbery was in the news this morning.

reviewer_note: Rob vs steal object trap explained in the verb note; robbery uses -ery, which is not in the affix table, so no affix is claimed for it.

corpus_definition: a long thin straight stick or bar made of wood or metal

forms.definition: a long, thin, straight stick or bar of wood or metal
forms.example: He sat by the river holding his fishing rod.

syn.note: Easy word; a stick is usually wood and not always straight.
A bar is usually metal and often thicker.
A pole is long and usually thicker and taller, like a flag pole.
A thin stick, for example for walking or from a plant.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My father bought a new fishing rod. On Saturday we took it to the lake, and he used a metal rod to hold the tent up.

reviewer_note: Leaf noun; fishing rod and lightning rod are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: not feeling smooth or flat to the touch

forms.definition: the quality of a surface that is not smooth
forms.example: You can feel the roughness of the old wall with your hand.

syn.note: A surface with high and low parts.
How any surface feels, rough or smooth.

ant.note: A surface with no bumps.

forms.definition: to make a surface less smooth
forms.example: Years of hard work had roughened his hands.

ant.note: To make a surface flat and even.

forms.definition: not smooth or flat when you touch it
forms.example: The wood felt rough before I sanded it.

syn.note: Not flat; with higher and lower parts.
Easy word, often for roads: with many small high parts.
Rough and thick, often for cloth, hair or sand.
Rough and rocky, used for land and mountains.

ant.note: Flat and even, with no bumps.

forms.definition: about; not exactly
forms.example: The trip from Tashkent to Samarkand takes roughly two hours by train.
forms.note: False friend: the common meaning is 'approximately', not 'in a not-smooth way'. It can also mean 'not gently': 'He pushed me roughly.'

context.text: The old table in my grandfather's house is very rough. You can feel the roughness when you touch it, so I want to make it smooth before I paint it.

reviewer_note: roughly is a false friend (approximately) so it is other_meaning; roughen is uncommon but in learner dictionaries; -en not in affix table.

corpus_definition: To remove pencil marks from paper using a small rubber tool.
particle_note: Separable: 'rub out the word' or 'rub the word out'; with a pronoun only 'rub it out'. Mainly British; American English says 'erase'.

relations.note: Same meaning; the usual word in American English.
General word for taking something away.
Used for words on a computer or phone, not pencil on paper.

context.text: I wrote the wrong answer, so I rubbed it out with my rubber. Our teacher says we should rub out mistakes neatly before handing in the test.

reviewer_note: British 'rubber' = American 'eraser'; no forms for a phrasal verb.

corpus_definition: to leave a place quickly to avoid someone or something
particle_note: Not separable: 'run away from the dog' (never 'run the dog away from'). Object always comes after 'from'. Also used for problems: 'run away from your problems'.

relations.note: Very close and also everyday English.
Often used when someone is trapped or kept somewhere.
Formal; used in news: 'flee the war'.
To stay away from something, without running.
To deal with a person or problem instead of running away.

context.text: The little dog ran away from the loud fireworks and hid under the car. My mother always says you can't run away from your problems.

reviewer_note: Three-part phrasal verb kept as phrasal; the antonym 'face' fits the 'problems' use.

corpus_definition: a period when shops sell items at lower prices

forms.definition: a time when a shop sells things at lower prices than usual
forms.example: I bought this dress in the summer sale.
forms.note: 'on sale' can mean 'cheaper than usual' (American English) or just 'available to buy' (British English).

syn.note: A sale to get rid of old goods: 'a clearance sale'.
The amount taken off the price, not the time period.
Something you buy cheaply, often in a sale.

forms.definition: to give something to someone and get money for it
forms.example: They sell fruit and vegetables at the bazaar.
forms.note: Belongs to sale = the act of selling something ('for sale'), not a period of low prices. The noun sale comes from sell.
'saleable' (able to be sold) exists but is rare and belongs to the selling meaning.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who offers things for money
people.example: The seller at the market gave me a good price.
people.note: Belongs to sale = the act of selling, not a discount period.

context.text: The big shopping centre in Tashkent has a sale every January. Last year I bought winter boots in the sale for half the price.

reviewer_note: Only the noun exists in the discount sense; sell and seller shown as other_meaning; salesperson/salesman are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: Having a strong flavor because of added table salt.

forms.definition: a white substance you put on food to give it flavour
forms.example: Can you pass me the salt, please?

ant.note: Sugar makes food sweet; salt makes it taste of the sea.

forms.definition: how strong the taste of the white food powder is in a dish
forms.example: I didn't like the saltiness of the soup.

ant.note: The taste of sugar.

forms.definition: to put a white food powder on food to give it flavour
forms.example: Don't forget to salt the water before you cook the pasta.

syn.note: To add salt, pepper or spices to food.

forms.definition: tasting strongly of the white powder added to food
forms.example: These potato chips are too salty for me.

syn.note: Not sweet; tasting of salt or spices. American spelling: savory.
Very salty, like sea water; less common.

ant.note: Tasting of sugar; in everyday talk the main contrast with salty.

forms.definition: with the white powder added to keep or flavour food
forms.example: I bought salted peanuts for the trip.

ant.note: With no salt added: 'unsalted butter'.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My aunt's plov was a bit too salty today. She says she put the salt in twice by mistake, so next time she will use less.

reviewer_note: Headword is made from salt, so salt (noun/verb) is a family base; salt shaker/salt cellar are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: to keep money to use later

forms.definition: money that you have kept and not spent
forms.example: She used all her savings to buy a car.
forms.note: Always plural in this meaning: 'my savings'.

syn.note: Money kept for the future.
Money kept for when you need it, often for a company or country.

ant.note: Money you owe to other people.

forms.definition: an amount of money that you do not have to spend
forms.example: Buying in the market gives you a saving of ten thousand sum.

forms.definition: to keep money so you can use it later
forms.example: I am trying to save for a new computer.

syn.note: Keep money for a special reason.
Same as put aside, a little more formal.
Keep money and not spend it.
Easy, general word: not give away or spend.

ant.note: To use money to buy things.
To use money badly or for nothing.

forms.note: There is no adjective in this meaning; 'safe' is not made from save.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who keeps money in a bank instead of spending it
people.example: Banks give savers more interest this year.

people.definition: a person who helps someone out of danger
people.example: The doctor was our saviour that night.
people.note: Belongs to save = keep someone safe, not keeping money. American spelling: savior.

context.text: Aziz saves part of his salary every month. His savings are in the bank, and he wants to buy a car next year.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows share the money meaning; save from (danger) is a separate group. saviour shown as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To help someone stay safe or avoid a bad situation.
particle_note: The object always comes between: 'save someone from something' (save the child from the fire). Also 'save someone from + -ing': 'save him from drowning'.

relations.note: Same meaning; often used for quick action in real danger.
Keep someone safe before the danger comes.
General easy word; not always about danger.
To make someone not safe.
Formal: to put someone or something in danger.

context.text: The lifeguard saved a boy from drowning in the pool. His parents thanked him for saving their son from danger.

reviewer_note: Corpus example is missing the object ('save from drowning'); the pattern needs 'save someone from'.

corpus_definition: To make someone feel afraid.

forms.definition: a sudden feeling of fear
forms.example: The loud bang gave me a real scare.

syn.note: Very close: a sudden feeling of fear.
Related: a sudden bad surprise, not always fear.
Fear is the general feeling; a scare is short and sudden.

forms.definition: to make a person or animal feel afraid
forms.example: The loud noise did not scare me.
forms.note: Often in the passive pattern 'be scared of' and the phrase 'scare someone away/off'.

syn.note: Same meaning; scare is a little more informal.
Much stronger: to make someone very, very afraid.
Related: to surprise someone suddenly so they jump.
Related: to make someone worried that something bad will happen.

ant.note: To make someone feel less afraid or worried.
To say or do things so someone stops feeling afraid or worried.

forms.definition: feeling afraid or worried about something
forms.example: My little brother is scared of dogs.
forms.note: scared = how you feel; scary = what makes you feel it.

syn.note: Same meaning; afraid is not used before a noun.
Same meaning, a little more formal.
Much stronger: very afraid.
Related: a little worried, not really afraid.

ant.note: Not afraid of danger.
Relaxed, not worried or afraid.

forms.definition: making you feel afraid
forms.example: We watched a scary film last night.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Much stronger: very frightening.
Related: strange and scary in a quiet way.

ant.note: Making you feel calm and safe.

forms.definition: in a way that makes you feel afraid or surprised
forms.example: The two sisters look scarily alike.
forms.note: Often used before an adjective to mean 'surprisingly': 'scarily good'.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Related: in a way that makes you worried.

context.text: Aziz is scared of the dark, so his sister never tells him scary stories at night. Once a loud noise from the street scared him so much that he could not sleep.

reviewer_note: scared (feel it) vs scary (cause it) trap explained; scarecrow left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: a list showing the time when things should happen.

forms.definition: a list or plan of things to do and the times they happen
forms.example: My schedule is very busy today.
forms.note: British /ˈʃedjuːl/, American /ˈskedʒuːl/. Phrases: on schedule, ahead of schedule, behind schedule.

syn.note: Very close; common in British English, especially for buses, trains and school lessons.
Related: a plan is what you want to do; a schedule adds the times.
Related: a list of things to discuss at a meeting.
Related: a list of events at a show or festival. American spelling: program.

forms.definition: to plan that something will happen at a certain time
forms.example: The meeting is scheduled for Monday morning.

syn.note: Close; plan is more general.
Close: to organize a time for something.
Related: to reserve a time, a table or a ticket.

ant.note: To decide that a planned event will not happen.

forms.definition: to change the time or date of a planned event
forms.example: Can we reschedule our lesson to Friday?

syn.note: Related: to move something to a later time only.
Everyday English: 'Can we move the meeting?'

forms.definition: planned to happen at a certain time
forms.example: The scheduled flight to Tashkent leaves at nine.

syn.note: Same meaning, everyday word.
Related: a scheduled bus or flight runs at regular times.

ant.note: Not planned: an unscheduled stop.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Dilnoza checks her schedule every morning. Her English lesson is scheduled for four o'clock, but today she had to reschedule it because of a doctor's visit.

reviewer_note: Both corpus rows mean the same 'list/plan of times'; merged into one map. British vs American pronunciation noted.

corpus_definition: A person who works in science.

forms.definition: a person who studies the natural world and does experiments
forms.example: The scientist discovered a new cure.
forms.note: Kinds of scientist: biologist, chemist, physicist.

syn.note: Close: a person who studies a subject to find new facts; not always in science.
Related: a person who knows a lot about any subject.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: connected with science or using its careful methods
forms.example: She reads scientific articles about the sea.

syn.note: Related: connected with special knowledge or machines.
Related: done carefully, step by step, like a scientist.

ant.note: Not done in a careful, scientific way.

forms.definition: in a way that uses the careful methods of science
forms.example: The new medicine was scientifically tested.

syn.note: Related: carefully and step by step.

people.definition: the study of the natural world through facts and experiments
people.example: Science is my favourite subject at school.

context.text: My cousin is a scientist in Tashkent. She does scientific work on water, and every result is scientifically checked before it is published.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, kept as main noun entry (rule 6); science goes in People & things as the field. No affixes claimed: science -> scientist/scientific changes the stem.

corpus_definition: The total number of points gained in a game.

forms.definition: the number of points or goals each player or team has in a game
forms.example: What is the final score of the match?
forms.note: Also used for tests: 'a high score in the IELTS exam'.

syn.note: Close: the final score at the end of a match.
Related: what you count to get the score.
Related: the number you get for a test at school. American English: grade.

forms.definition: to get a point or goal in a game or sport
forms.example: Bobur scored two goals in the second half.

syn.note: Everyday English: 'get a goal', 'get ten points'.
Related: you win a match or a prize, but you score a goal or a point.

ant.note: To let the other team score a goal or point against you.

forms.definition: with no goals or points for either team
forms.example: The game ended in a scoreless draw.

syn.note: Same meaning for football; common in British English.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a player who gets goals or points in a game
people.example: He was the top scorer in the league this year.

context.text: Our team scored three goals in the first half. At the end the score was 3-1. Last week's game was a boring scoreless draw.

reviewer_note: Corpus meaning is points in a game; the old meaning 'twenty' is not shown. Scoreboard left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: The flat part of a computer or phone that shows images.

forms.definition: the flat glass part of a phone, computer or TV that shows pictures
forms.example: The computer screen is very bright today.
forms.note: Also a big white surface in a cinema. Phrases: on screen, touch screen.

syn.note: Close; used more in technical English.
Related: the whole box with the screen that you connect to a computer.

forms.definition: a showing of a film; or a medical test to find illness early
forms.example: There is a free screening of the film tonight.
forms.note: Belongs to screen = show a film, or check people for illness, not the part of a phone.

forms.definition: to show a film or programme; or to check people for an illness
forms.example: The film will be screened on national TV next week.
forms.note: Belongs to screen = show a film, or test people for illness, not the flat part of a phone.
There is no common adjective in this meaning.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: I use my phone so much that the screen is always dirty. My brother bought a new laptop with a bigger screen for his studies.

reviewer_note: Verb screen and screening are other meanings (show a film / medical check). Compounds screenshot, touchscreen, screensaver left out.

corpus_definition: Something you do not tell other people.

forms.definition: something that you know and do not tell other people
forms.example: Keep this a secret, please.
forms.note: Phrases: keep a secret, tell someone a secret, in secret.

syn.note: Related: something nobody knows or understands.
Formal: something private that you tell someone you trust.

forms.definition: the state of keeping things hidden from other people
forms.example: The plans were made in complete secrecy.

syn.note: Related: being alone or away from other people's eyes.
Formal: keeping information private, often at work.

ant.note: Being honest and not hiding things.

forms.definition: to hide something in a secret place
forms.example: He secreted the letter inside an old book.
forms.note: Belongs to secret = hiding things, and is rare and formal. In biology, secrete also means 'to produce a liquid' (the body secretes sweat).

forms.definition: known by only a few people and hidden from others
forms.example: They have a secret plan for their mother's birthday.

syn.note: Close: not easy to see or find.
Related: only for you or a small group.
Formal: used for official information.

ant.note: Known by everyone.
Not hidden; done so everyone can see.

forms.definition: liking to hide your feelings, plans or information
forms.example: He is very secretive about his new job.

syn.note: Related: not wanting to share personal things.
Related: quiet and not showing feelings easily.

ant.note: Happy to share feelings and information.

forms.definition: in a way that other people do not know about
forms.example: She secretly saved money for a new phone.

syn.note: Same meaning, as a phrase.
Close: without other people there.

ant.note: In a way that everyone can see or know.
In front of everyone.

context.text: Madina told me a secret: she is planning a secret party for her friend. She has been secretly buying presents all week.

reviewer_note: Secretary is not listed as a family person (link is only historical). Secrete shown as other_meaning verb (rare, formal 'hide').

corpus_definition: Not funny or light; very important.

forms.definition: the quality of being not funny, or of being very important
forms.example: He did not understand the seriousness of the problem.

syn.note: Related: how much something matters.
Formal: how serious a bad situation is.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: not joking or funny; also important and needing attention
forms.example: He gave a serious look to me.
forms.note: Common phrases: Are you serious? = Are you joking? A serious problem/illness = a bad one.

syn.note: Close: very serious and quiet, for example at an important event.
Formal: very serious and worrying.
Related: easy word for the 'very important' meaning.

ant.note: Making people laugh.
Small and not very important.

forms.definition: in a way that is not joking, or very badly
forms.example: Please think seriously about your future.
forms.note: 'Seriously?' alone in speech means 'Really? Are you joking?'

syn.note: Close, a bit formal: really meaning it.
Related: for injuries and illness: 'seriously hurt' = 'badly hurt'.

ant.note: In a way that is not meant to be true.
Without thinking carefully.

context.text: Our teacher is usually funny, but today she was very serious. She spoke seriously about the exam and the seriousness of cheating.

reviewer_note: Corpus definition joins two meanings (not funny / important); both are covered in one map since all forms share them.

corpus_definition: to provide food or drinks to customers

forms.definition: the work of bringing food and drinks to customers
forms.example: The service in this cafe is very fast.
forms.note: A 10% service charge is often added to the bill in restaurants.

syn.note: Related: what staff do for customers in general.

forms.definition: an amount of food for one person
forms.example: This recipe makes four servings of plov.

syn.note: Same meaning.
Same meaning, a little informal.

forms.definition: to give food or drinks to people at a meal or in a cafe
forms.example: They serve breakfast until ten o'clock.
forms.note: Other meanings: serve in the army, serve the ball in tennis.

syn.note: Everyday word, but more general.
Related: to say someone can have something.
Close: to put food on plates for people.

forms.note: There is no common adjective in this meaning.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who brings food and drinks to tables in a restaurant
people.example: Our server brought the menu and some water.
people.note: Mostly American English; British English says waiter or waitress. Also a main computer in a network.

people.definition: a person who works in someone's house, cooking and cleaning
people.example: In the old film, the rich family had many servants.
people.note: Belongs to serve = work for someone, not serving food in a cafe.

context.text: At my uncle's cafe in Bukhara, the staff serve green tea with every meal. The service is quick, and one serving of plov is enough for two people.

reviewer_note: Service kept in the noun slot as the action of serving; server (job) in People. Servant marked other_meaning (work for someone).

corpus_definition: To join pieces of material using a thin string.

forms.definition: the activity of making or fixing clothes with a needle and thread
forms.example: My grandmother taught me sewing when I was ten.
forms.note: Also means the clothes you are working on: 'Put your sewing away.'

syn.note: Close: sewing and similar work with a needle.
Close: the lines of thread or the act of making them.

forms.definition: to join pieces of cloth with a needle and thread
forms.example: She learned to sew her own clothes.
forms.note: Pronounced /səʊ/ like 'so'. Past: sewed; past participle: sewn or sewed.

syn.note: Same meaning; stitch is about each small line of thread.
Related: to fix a hole in clothes, often by sewing.
Related: to sew pretty pictures onto cloth.

ant.note: To take out the threads that join pieces of cloth.

forms.note: There is no common adjective; 'sewn' is the past participle (hand-sewn).
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My mother can sew very well. On winter evenings she does her sewing by the window and makes dresses for my sisters.

reviewer_note: Sewer is listed as not family: the common word sewer (/ˈsuːə/) is a pipe for dirty water. Pronunciation of sew (so) noted.

corpus_definition: the physical form of an object

forms.definition: the outside form or outline of something
forms.example: The table has a round shape.
forms.note: Phrase: in good shape = healthy or fit.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Related: the line around the edge of something.
Related: the shape of a person's body.

forms.definition: to make something into a certain form
forms.example: She shaped the dough into small balls.

syn.note: Close: to make something have a shape.
Close: to press soft material into a shape. American spelling: mold.

forms.definition: having a certain form, often in compounds
forms.example: She bought a heart-shaped cake for her mother.
forms.note: Usually joined to a noun: star-shaped, egg-shaped.

syn.note: Related: made into a certain form.

forms.definition: without a clear or attractive form
forms.example: He wore an old, shapeless jumper.

syn.note: Related: for clothes that are too big and loose.

forms.definition: having an attractive form, often about a person's body
forms.example: She has long, shapely arms.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: The children shaped the clay into animals. My favourite was a star-shaped cookie with a funny shape.

reviewer_note: Shapely is an -ly adjective, not an adverb; adverb slot correctly empty.

corpus_definition: to cut the hair from your face or body with a blade

forms.definition: the act of cutting the hair off your face with a razor
forms.example: My father has a shave every morning before breakfast.

syn.note: A trim makes hair or a beard shorter; a shave takes all of it off.

forms.definition: to cut hair off your face or body with a razor
forms.example: He shaves his face every morning before work.
forms.note: Often 'shave off': 'He shaved off his beard.'

syn.note: Cut is general; shave means cutting the hair very close to the skin with a razor.
Trim means making hair a little shorter, not taking it all off.

ant.note: If you grow a beard, you let the hair get long instead of cutting it.

forms.definition: with the hair cut off very close to the skin
forms.example: The soldiers all had shaven heads.
forms.note: Most common in 'clean-shaven' (with no beard). 'Shaved' is also possible: 'a shaved head'. Old participle of shave, now used mainly as an adjective (a shaven head).

syn.note: Bald usually means hair does not grow there any more; shaven means it was cut off.

ant.note: Unshaven means a man has not shaved for some time, so he has short hair on his face.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: an electric tool for taking hair off your face
people.example: He bought a new electric shaver for his trip.

context.text: My grandfather shaves every morning with an old razor. He says a clean shave makes him feel young, but my brother keeps his head shaven all summer.

reviewer_note: GATE? shaven is the old irregular past participle of shave (Oxford lists it as an adjective: shaven head, clean-shaven); lemminflect only knows 'shaved'. unshaven placed as antonym, razor not family.

corpus_definition: a person whose job is to look after a flock of sheep

forms.definition: a person whose job is to look after sheep
forms.example: The shepherd guided his sheep down the hillside.

syn.note: A herder looks after any group of animals, such as sheep, goats or cows.
A man who looks after a group of animals; a little old-fashioned.
A farmer owns or works on a farm; a shepherd only looks after sheep.

forms.definition: to guide a group of people or animals carefully to a place
forms.example: The teacher shepherded the children onto the bus.

syn.note: Very close; shepherd suggests a group that you look after carefully.
Lead means going in front so others follow you.
Herd means moving animals or people together as a group, often with less care.

forms.note: There is no adjective in this family. 'Pastoral' (about country life and farm animals) is a different word.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a woman who looks after sheep
people.example: In the old story, a young shepherdess sang to her sheep.
people.note: Old-fashioned; today 'shepherd' is used for both men and women.

context.text: My uncle is a shepherd in the mountains near Jizzakh. Every evening he shepherds his sheep back to the village before it gets dark.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); shepherdess is literary.

corpus_definition: a law officer responsible for keeping order in a county or town

forms.definition: in the US, an elected officer who makes people obey the law in a county
forms.example: The sheriff rode into town to calm the situation.
forms.note: Mostly American. In Britain and Scotland the word names a different legal or ceremonial job.

syn.note: A police officer works for the police; a sheriff is elected and leads law work in a county.
A US marshal is also a law officer, but works for the national government.
A general word for a person with authority in the police or army.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: In old American films, the sheriff always catches the bad men. Today a sheriff is still an elected officer in many US counties.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; deputy is not made from sheriff, so People & things stays empty.

corpus_definition: very soon, in a short time from now

forms.definition: the quality of being small in length or height
forms.example: His shortness never stopped him from playing basketball.
forms.note: Belongs to short = not long or not tall, not the 'soon' meaning. Also in 'shortness of breath'.

forms.definition: a situation when there is not enough of something
forms.example: There is a shortage of water in the village this summer.
forms.note: Belongs to short = not having enough, not the 'soon' meaning.

forms.definition: to make something less long
forms.example: Can you shorten these trousers for me?
forms.note: Belongs to short = not long. You can also shorten a meeting or a trip.

forms.definition: lasting only a little time
forms.example: We only had a short wait for the bus.
forms.note: Shortly is made from short. Short also means 'not tall' and 'not long'.

syn.note: A little more formal: 'a brief meeting'.
Quick is about speed; short is about how long something lasts.

ant.note: A long time is the opposite of a short time.

forms.definition: in a little while from now; very soon
forms.example: The train will arrive shortly, so please be ready.
forms.note: False friend: shortly does NOT mean 'in a short way'. Also 'shortly before/after' = a little before/after. Rare: 'answer shortly' = answer rudely.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning; shortly is a little more formal.
Means the same; used more in stories and speech.
Suggests an even shorter time: a few seconds or minutes.

context.text: The doctor will see you shortly. It is only a short wait, so please sit down and fill in this form.

reviewer_note: False-friend trap: shortly = soon, not 'in a short way'; shortness, shortage and shorten belong to other meanings of short.

corpus_definition: The body part between your neck and your arm.

forms.definition: the part of your body between your neck and the top of your arm
forms.example: He put a hand on my shoulder.

forms.definition: to accept a difficult duty or a big responsibility
forms.example: After his father died, Aziz had to shoulder the costs of the family.
forms.note: Belongs to shoulder = carrying a heavy load (a responsibility), not the body part itself. It can also mean 'to push with your shoulder'.
No single-word adjective; '-shouldered' is used only in compounds like 'broad-shouldered'.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My school bag is heavy, so I carry it on my right shoulder. After the football match, both my shoulders hurt.

reviewer_note: Verb 'shoulder' marked other_meaning (take responsibility); compounds like shoulder bag and broad-shouldered left out.

corpus_definition: A short period of rain.

forms.definition: a short time when it rains, often not very hard
forms.example: We had a quick shower this morning.
forms.note: The same word also means washing your body under falling water: 'I'll have a shower.'

syn.note: Rain is the general word; a shower is a short time of rain.
Drizzle is very light rain in very small drops.
A downpour is a lot of heavy rain in a short time.

forms.definition: to wash your body while standing under falling water
forms.example: I usually shower before I go to bed.
forms.note: Belongs to shower = washing your body, not rain. It can also mean 'to give someone a lot of something': 'They showered her with gifts.'

forms.definition: with many short periods of rain
forms.example: The weather will be cool and showery all weekend.

syn.note: Easy, common word; rainy weather may have long rain, not only short times.
Wet weather is any weather with a lot of rain.

ant.note: Dry weather has no rain at all.
Sunny weather has bright sun and no clouds.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: The weather forecast for Tashkent says tomorrow will be showery. Take an umbrella, because a shower can start very suddenly.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: the map keeps rain only; the washing sense (verb and noun) is marked as other meaning.

corpus_definition: Feeling nervous around other people.

forms.definition: the feeling of being nervous and quiet with other people
forms.example: Her shyness made it hard for her to make new friends.

syn.note: Formal; it also means not being brave.
Nervousness can come from any worry, not only from meeting people.

ant.note: Confidence is feeling sure of yourself with other people.

forms.definition: to avoid something because you are nervous or afraid
forms.example: She never shies away from difficult questions.
forms.note: Almost always used as 'shy away from something'. A horse can also shy: move back suddenly in fear.

syn.note: Easy, general word; shy away from adds the idea of being nervous.
To move back from something because you are afraid.

ant.note: To face a problem is to deal with it bravely.

forms.definition: nervous and quiet when you are with other people
forms.example: The shy girl hid behind her mother.
forms.note: Comparative and superlative: shyer, shyest (sometimes shier, shiest).

syn.note: Timid also means easily frightened, not only with people.
A little old-fashioned; often used about children.
A quiet person does not talk much, but may not be nervous.
Nervous is about any worry, not only meeting people.

ant.note: Sure of yourself and not nervous with people.
Friendly and happy to meet and talk to new people.

forms.definition: in a nervous, quiet way, as when you meet new people
forms.example: The little boy smiled shyly at his new teacher.

syn.note: In a nervous way, without being brave.
In a worried way, for any reason.

ant.note: In a way that shows you are sure of yourself.
In a brave way, without fear.

context.text: At first, Malika was very shy at her new school in Namangan. She smiled shyly but did not speak. Her teacher slowly helped her lose her shyness.

reviewer_note: Verb shy kept as existing (shy away from = avoid out of nervousness); spelling shyly, not shily.

corpus_definition: Making absolutely no sound.

forms.definition: a time or state when there is no sound at all
forms.example: There was a long silence after the teacher asked the question.

syn.note: Easy word; quiet can mean only a little sound, not none.
Stillness means no movement and often no sound.
A sudden quiet, often when people stop talking.

ant.note: Noise is loud or unpleasant sound.
Any sound breaks the silence.

forms.definition: to make someone or something stop making any noise
forms.example: The teacher silenced the class with one look.

syn.note: British English; American English often says 'quiet': 'quiet the children'.
Often used about calming children or a crowd.

forms.definition: making no sound at all
forms.example: The house was completely silent at night.
forms.note: Also means 'not speaking': 'He stayed silent.' A silent letter is not spoken, like the k in 'know'.

syn.note: Easy word; quiet can mean making only a little sound.
Means exactly the same, but is less common.
Often used about machines or movements.
Still means not moving, and often quiet too.

ant.note: Making a lot of sound.
Making a strong sound that is easy to hear.

forms.definition: without making any sound
forms.example: The cat walked silently across the room.

syn.note: Easy word; quietly can mean with only a little sound.
Less common; often about movement.

ant.note: In a way that makes a strong sound.
In a way that makes a lot of noise.

people.definition: a part of a car exhaust that makes the engine quieter
people.example: The car was very loud because the silencer was broken.
people.note: British English; American English says 'muffler'. Also a device that makes a gun quieter.

context.text: The library in Samarkand was silent. Everyone was reading in silence, and even the children walked silently between the shelves.

reviewer_note: silence is both noun and verb (verb made from the noun, so relation derivational, not conversion of silent).

corpus_definition: looking or acting much like another person or thing.
usage_note: be similar to + noun/pronoun: 'My car is similar to yours.' Also 'similar in + size/colour/age'. Use 'similar to', not 'similar with'. Strong form: 'very similar to'.

relations.note: Easy and common: 'My car is like yours.' Like is a preposition, so no 'to'.
Used after the two things, with no object: 'Our cars are alike.'
More formal; often about size, price or quality.
The same as means there is no difference; similar to means there are only small differences.
Not like another person or thing: 'My car is different from yours.'
A preposition meaning not like: 'Unlike his brother, he is quiet.'

context.text: My sister's voice is very similar to mine, so people often confuse us on the phone. Her taste in music is similar to my father's.

reviewer_note: Fixed adjective + preposition pattern; common learner error 'similar with' noted.

corpus_definition: The act of using your voice to produce pleasant sounds.

forms.definition: the activity of making music with your voice
forms.example: Her singing voice is truly beautiful.

syn.note: Used in pop music for the singing part of a song: 'vocals by Dilnoza'.
Chanting is repeating words on one or two notes, often in a group.

forms.definition: a short piece of music with words, made for the voice
forms.example: We sang a traditional Uzbek song at the party.
forms.note: Same old family as sing (sing - sang - sung - song), but made by changing the vowel, not by adding an ending.

forms.definition: to make music with your voice
forms.example: My grandmother sings old songs while she cooks.
forms.note: Irregular: sing, sang, sung. Singing is the -ing form used as a noun.

syn.note: To make music with your mouth closed, without words.
To sing or say words again and again on one or two notes.

forms.note: No common adjective. 'Singable' (easy to sing) exists but is rare.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person who makes music with their voice, often as a job
people.example: Sevara Nazarkhan is a famous Uzbek singer.
people.note: Said /ˈsɪŋə/, with no hard g sound.

context.text: My cousin Dilnoza sings at weddings in Bukhara. Her singing is so beautiful that she wants to become a professional singer.

reviewer_note: song included as a family noun (vowel change from sing); reviewer may prefer not_family. Adjective slot no_form (singable is rare).

corpus_definition: Not married or having a romantic partner.

forms.definition: a person who is not married or in a relationship
forms.example: There is a dance evening for singles at the club on Friday.

syn.note: Related: only a man who has never married; a single can be a man or a woman.

forms.note: Usually plural: singles.

forms.definition: a record or song sold on its own, not in an album
forms.example: The band's new single is on the radio every day.
forms.note: Belongs to single = only one (one song), not 'not married'. In British English it is also a one-way ticket.

forms.definition: to choose one person or thing from a group
forms.example: The teacher singled out Dilnoza for special praise.
forms.note: Belongs to single = only one; used in the phrasal verb 'single out', not 'not married'.

forms.definition: not married and not in a romantic relationship
forms.example: My cousin is thirty and still single.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal; used on official forms.
Not in a romantic relationship; a bit formal.
Related but different: alone means without other people at this moment, not 'without a partner'.

ant.note: Has a husband or wife.
Informal: already in a relationship.

forms.definition: one at a time; not in a group
forms.example: The guests arrived singly or in pairs.
forms.note: Belongs to single = only one, not 'not married'. Quite formal.

context.text: My cousin Aziz is still single, and he is happy. On Fridays there is a tea evening for singles in his town, but he prefers to watch football.

reviewer_note: Kept the 'not married' sense; the record/ticket noun, single out and singly are other_meaning. Singular is a separate Latin word, not listed.

corpus_definition: all the things happening in a place at a certain time.

forms.definition: everything that is happening in a place at a particular time
forms.example: The situation on the roads is bad because of the snow.

syn.note: Usually plural; a little more formal: 'in these circumstances'.
Formal phrase with the same meaning.
Related: often the situation of one person: 'I'm in a difficult position.'
Related: the state something is in, often health or quality.
Related: one particular example or event: 'in that case'.

forms.definition: to build or put something in a particular place
forms.example: They decided to situate the new school near the park.
forms.note: Belongs to situation = the place where something is, not 'all the things happening'. Formal; mostly used as 'be situated'.

forms.definition: connected with a particular time, place and events
forms.example: We practise situational English, like ordering food in a café.

syn.note: Related: connected with the context around something; formal.

forms.definition: in a particular place
forms.example: The hotel is situated near the old city of Khiva.
forms.note: Belongs to situation = location of a place, not 'all the things happening'. Means the same as 'located'.
Situationally exists but is very rare; learners do not need it.

context.text: The traffic situation in Tashkent is bad every morning. Our teacher uses situational role plays, so we practise English for real life, like buying a train ticket.

reviewer_note: Situate/situated belong to the 'location' sense, so other_meaning. Situational kept as formal existing adjective.

corpus_definition: The ability to do a specific task well.

forms.definition: the ability to do something well because you have practised it
forms.example: Cooking is a useful life skill.

syn.note: Very close; ability can also be natural, without practice.
Formal: a lot of knowledge and skill in one area.
Related: a natural ability you are born with; a skill is often learned.
Informal: practical knowledge of how to do something.

forms.note: The verb deskill exists but is rare and technical.

forms.definition: trained and experienced, so able to do a job well
forms.example: Skilled workers can earn good money in Uzbekistan.

syn.note: You learned the job in a course or at work.
You have done the job for a long time.
Related: you have the official papers or exams for a job.
Very skilled; knows a lot about one area.

ant.note: No special training: unskilled work.
Has not done something much before.

forms.definition: good at doing something, especially with hands or the body
forms.example: He is a skillful driver and never has accidents.

syn.note: Good at something, often naturally.
Related: quick to learn and good with ideas or hands.
Easy everyday word: 'a good driver'.

ant.note: Often drops things or makes mistakes with the hands.

forms.note: British spelling: skilful.

forms.definition: in a way that shows great ability and practice
forms.example: She skillfully cut the bread into thin pieces.

syn.note: Same meaning: like an expert.
Easy, more general.
Related: in an intelligent or smart way.

ant.note: In a careless way, often dropping or breaking things.
Not well.

forms.note: British spelling: skilfully.

context.text: My grandmother is a skilled cook. She cuts onions skillfully and very fast, and she says cooking is a skill you only learn by practice.

reviewer_note: American spellings skillful/skillfully used, British skilful/skilfully in notes. Unskilled is in skilled's ant list, not a form.

corpus_definition: a small vehicle that slides over snow, used for fun or transport

forms.definition: a small vehicle for sliding over snow
forms.example: The children pulled their sled up the hill.

syn.note: British word for the same thing.
A long, light kind used for sliding down hills for fun.
Related: a bigger one pulled by horses or reindeer.

forms.note: American English; British English usually says sledge.

forms.definition: the activity of riding down snowy hills for fun
forms.example: Sledding is the children's favourite winter activity.

syn.note: Very close: riding a toboggan down a hill.

forms.note: British English: sledging.

forms.definition: to ride over snow on a small vehicle
forms.example: We sledded down the hill all afternoon.

syn.note: British word with the same meaning.
To slide down a hill on a toboggan.
Related: to move smoothly over a surface; more general.

forms.note: Usually used as 'go sledding'.

context.text: In January the children go sledding on the hill near our house in Chimgan. My little brother loves his red sled and never wants to go home.

reviewer_note: Sledge (British) listed as synonym, not form; sleigh is related but a different word.

corpus_definition: the part of a shirt that covers your arm

forms.definition: the part of a shirt or jacket that covers your arm
forms.example: He rolled up his sleeves before washing the dishes.

syn.note: Related: only the end part, near your hand.

forms.note: The verb is only technical (to fit a tube over something).

forms.definition: having no parts that cover the arms
forms.example: It was hot, so she wore a sleeveless dress.

context.text: It was very hot in Bukhara, so I wore a sleeveless shirt. My father wore a long shirt and simply rolled up his sleeves.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Long-sleeved/short-sleeved are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: A thin, flat piece of food cut from a larger one.

forms.definition: a thin flat piece cut from a larger piece of food
forms.example: Can I have another slice of bread?

syn.note: Easy and more general; any part of something.
A very thin, small piece.
Related: a thick, flat piece.
Related: the amount of food for one person.

forms.definition: to cut food into thin flat pieces
forms.example: Please slice the tomatoes for the salad.

syn.note: Easy and more general.
Related: to cut into small pieces, not thin flat ones.
Related: to cut cooked meat into pieces.

forms.definition: already cut into thin flat pieces

syn.note: Easy, more general.

ant.note: Not cut: a whole loaf or a whole melon.

people.definition: a tool or machine for cutting food into thin pieces
people.example: The shop uses a slicer to cut the cheese.

context.text: My mum bought sliced bread at the bazaar. Then she sliced a big melon and gave everyone a sweet slice.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. Slicer is a thing noun, in People & things.

corpus_definition: having a thin and attractive body shape

forms.definition: the quality of being thin in an attractive way
forms.example: She was proud of her slimness.

syn.note: Same meaning; more formal or literary.
Close, but can sound less positive.

forms.definition: to become thinner by eating less or exercising
forms.example: I'm trying to slim before the wedding.

syn.note: The most common everyday phrase.
Related: to eat less or only certain foods to lose weight.

ant.note: To become heavier.

forms.note: Mainly British; often 'slim down'.

forms.definition: thin in an attractive way
forms.example: She is slim because she walks a lot.

syn.note: Easy and common, but can sound negative (too thin).
Same meaning; a bit literary.
Related: thin and strong, with little fat.
Related: small and thin.

ant.note: Big and heavy; can be rude about people.
Heavier than is healthy; more polite than fat.

forms.definition: helping you lose weight or making you look thinner
forms.example: Dark colours are often slimming.

syn.note: Related: making you look good.

ant.note: Food that makes you put on weight.

forms.note: Mainly British.
Slimly exists but is very rare.

reviewer_note: Kept the body sense; 'a slim chance' (small) is a different meaning of the same adjective.

corpus_definition: Difficult to hold or walk on because it is smooth or wet.

forms.note: Slip is also a small mistake: 'a slip of the tongue'.

forms.definition: to slide by accident and lose your balance
forms.example: Be careful not to slip on the ice.

syn.note: Move smoothly over a surface; not always by accident.
Usually for cars or bikes.
Related: your foot hits something and you fall.
Related: easy, more general.

forms.definition: so smooth or wet that it is hard to hold or stand on

Related: covered with ice.
Related: covered with oil or fat.
Related: easy word; wet things are often hard to walk on.

ant.note: A rough surface is easy to stand on.

forms.definition: so smooth or wet that you can easily fall

Related: covered with ice.

forms.note: Informal British English.
Slipperily exists but is very rare.

people.example: My grandfather always wears slippers at home.

corpus_definition: A surface that is higher at one end than the other.

syn.note: Very close.
Related: sloping a lot.

ant.note: With no part higher than another.
Flat and even.

corpus_definition: having a flat surface with no lumps or marks

Related: soft things are often also even.

ant.note: The quality of not being flat or even.

forms.definition: to make something flat and even with your hands

syn.note: To make flat.
Related: only for clothes, with a hot iron.
Related: to make level or equal.

ant.note: To make lines or folds in cloth or paper.

Same height everywhere.
Related: soft and smooth like silk.
Related: made shiny and smooth by rubbing.

With many bumps, like a bad road.
Not flat or level.

forms.definition: without problems or sudden movements

corpus_definition: A topic that is being discussed or studied.

forms.definition: the thing that people are talking, writing or reading about

A situation or problem to think about: 'a private matter'.

A point that needs an answer or decision: 'the question of money'.

corpus_definition: Having the power or skill to do a task.

The exact meaning in plain English.

ant.note: To stop something from happening.

forms.definition: having the power or skill to do something

Formal: good enough at your job.
Easy: "good at maths" is about skill; "able to" is about what is possible.

ant.note: The direct opposite: "I was unable to sleep."
Formal and stronger: completely unable.

forms.definition: in a skilful way

corpus_definition: To do something.

corpus_definition: Doing many things or moving around a lot.

Simple, but start is used for many more things.

The easy opposite.

forms.definition: doing many things or moving around a lot
forms.example: Children are usually more active in the morning.

Full of energy, often about children and places.
Related: busy means you have a lot to do; it doesn't mean you move around.

Negative: you don't want to do things.

forms.definition: in a way that involves doing things, not just watching

Related: with interest and wanting to do it.

people.definition: a person who works hard to change society or politics

corpus_definition: Helpful words about what someone should do.
