ant.note: Take money out of a bank account.

forms.definition: likely to make money; that people can rely on
forms.example: She is one of the most bankable actors in Hollywood.
forms.note: Informal, from business English. Not about putting money in a bank.

people.definition: a person who owns a bank or has an important job in one
people.example: Her uncle is a banker in Tashkent.

people.definition: the business of keeping, lending and managing people's money
people.example: He wants to work in banking after university.

context.text: My father has banked with the same bank for twenty years. He says the staff know him by name.

reviewer_note: Two-meaning word: 'river bank' is a completely different sense and is left out of this map. Family members banker/banking exist but don't fit a slot.

corpus_definition: A short period of time to rest.

forms.definition: a short time when you stop working or studying to rest
forms.example: Let's take a ten-minute break before the next lesson.

syn.note: Rest is about relaxing your body; a break is stopping work for a while.
Informal: "Let's take a breather."
Related: shorter, sometimes just a few seconds.
Related: a break in the middle of a concert or play.

forms.definition: to stop working or studying for a short time
forms.example: We broke for lunch at one o'clock.
forms.note: Irregular verb: break, broke, broken. The verb also means to damage something; that is a different meaning.

syn.note: Easy: "Let's stop for lunch."
Related: stop for a very short time.

ant.note: To keep doing something.
Formal: start again after a break.

forms.definition: easy to break or damage
forms.example: Pack the breakable plates in paper.
forms.note: Belongs to break = damage something, not break = a short rest.

context.text: Our English lesson is ninety minutes long, so we always take a break in the middle. Yesterday we broke a little early because the teacher had a meeting.

reviewer_note: Two-meaning word: the common sense 'damage' (break a glass) is left out because the corpus row is the 'rest' sense. Adjective 'broken' belongs to the damage sense, so it is no_form here.

corpus_definition: Giving a lot of attention to avoid mistakes.

forms.definition: attention you give so that nothing is harmed or damaged
forms.example: Please handle these glasses with care.

syn.note: Easy and close: "Pay attention to the details."
Care to avoid danger: "Drive with caution."

ant.note: Not paying attention.
Formal: not giving something the care it needs.

forms.definition: to feel that someone or something is important to you
forms.example: I really care about my exam results.

syn.note: Related, mostly in questions and negatives: "I don't mind."
Related: easy, but weaker than care.

ant.note: To pay no attention to something on purpose.

forms.definition: giving attention to avoid mistakes or danger
forms.example: Be careful when you cross this road.

syn.note: Cautious is about avoiding danger or risk. Careful also covers avoiding mistakes.
Looking carefully so you notice problems early.
Related: careful and complete, checking every part.
Related: about listening and noticing, often to people.

ant.note: Same base, opposite suffix: -ful means full of, -less means without.
Stronger: not caring about danger at all.

forms.definition: in a way that avoids mistakes or danger
forms.example: Read the instructions carefully before you start.

syn.note: With care to avoid danger.
Related: with a lot of attention: "Watch closely."

ant.note: Without paying attention.

context.text: My grandmother always told me to take care of my things. She was a careful person, and she folded every shirt carefully before putting it away.

corpus_definition: To be very sure about something.

forms.definition: the feeling of being completely sure
forms.example: I can't say with certainty that he will come.

syn.note: Related: feeling sure about yourself or a result.
Related and formal: a strong belief.

ant.note: The feeling of not being sure.
Made with the prefix un-.

forms.note: Certify (to say officially that something is true) comes from the same old Latin root, but it isn't made from certain. Ascertain is formal and rare.

forms.definition: completely sure about something
forms.example: Are you certain that the shop is open today?

syn.note: The closest match and more common in speech.
Informal: "Are you positive?" means are you completely sure?
Related: trusting yourself or a result; certain is about knowing a fact.

ant.note: Made with the prefix un-.
A little more informal than uncertain.

forms.definition: without any doubt
forms.example: It will certainly rain later, so take an umbrella.

syn.note: Very close and common in speech.
Easy answer: "Can you help?" "Of course!"
Related: careful, surely often shows surprise: "Surely you're not leaving?"

ant.note: Not an exact opposite: possibly means maybe, not for sure.

context.text: I was certain that I had locked the door, but my sister wasn't. She said, "Certainty is good, but checking is better," and she was certainly right.

reviewer_note: Corpus definition 'To be very sure about something.' is written like a verb; certain is an adjective. Fix the corpus row.

corpus_definition: A very young person who is not yet an adult.

forms.definition: a young person who is not yet an adult
forms.example: Every child in the village goes to the same school.
forms.note: Irregular plural: children.

syn.note: Same meaning, but informal.
Usually an older child or teenager; slightly old-fashioned.
Related: a baby is a very young child, under about one year.

ant.note: A fully grown person.
Informal, often used by children.

forms.definition: behaving in a silly way, like a small child
forms.example: Stop being so childish and say sorry to your sister.
forms.note: Negative. For a positive meaning use childlike (innocent, like a child).

syn.note: More formal: behaving younger than your age.
Informal and strongly negative.
Related and easy: any foolish behaviour, not only like a child.

ant.note: Behaving like a sensible adult.
Informal: acting like an adult.

forms.definition: in a silly way, like a small child
forms.example: He childishly refused to talk to anyone after losing the game.

syn.note: Easy, with the same meaning: "He was acting like a child."
Related: in a silly way.

ant.note: In a sensible, adult way.

context.text: As a child, my father lived in a small village. He says the children there never had childish arguments because they were too busy helping their parents.

reviewer_note: Affix -hood refers to 'childhood', which is not one of the four slots. Test: should the gate accept an affix whose in_form is outside the slots?

corpus_definition: To pick one thing out of many different available options.

forms.definition: a decision to pick one thing from several things
forms.example: You made a good choice: this phone is cheaper and faster.

syn.note: Formal; also means a group to choose from: "a selection of cakes".
Related: about any question; a choice is picking between things.
Related: one thing you can choose; a choice is the act of choosing.

forms.definition: to pick one thing from several things
forms.example: I chose the blue shirt because it was on sale.
forms.note: Irregular verb: choose, chose, chosen.

syn.note: Very close and a little more informal: "Pick a card."
More formal, often in instructions and on websites.
"We decided on the blue one."
Informal: "I'll go for the chicken."

ant.note: To say no to something that is offered.

forms.definition: difficult to please because you only accept what you like
forms.example: My cat is very choosy about her food.

syn.note: British English, very common: "a fussy eater".
Informal, common in American English.

ant.note: Happy with most things; not difficult to please.

context.text: There were ten cakes in the shop, and my brother couldn't choose. He is so choosy! In the end, his choice was the smallest one.

corpus_definition: A person you know very well and like a lot.

forms.definition: a strong feeling of friendship or love between people
forms.example: There is a real closeness between the two sisters.

syn.note: Formal; can suggest a romantic relationship.
Related: a strong connection: "a strong bond between sisters".
Related: the relationship between friends.

ant.note: A feeling of not being close to someone.

forms.definition: to shut something
forms.example: Please close the window, it's cold.
forms.note: Same spelling, different word and sound: the verb is /kləʊz/, the adjective is /kləʊs/.

forms.definition: knowing someone very well and liking them a lot
forms.example: Aziz is my closest friend; we have known each other since school.

syn.note: Stronger and more private; it can suggest a romantic relationship.
Related: about love and value: "a dear friend".
Related and easy: "a good friend" is a little weaker than "a close friend".

ant.note: Not friendly or connected: "a distant relative".

forms.definition: in a way that involves a strong connection
forms.example: The two families have worked closely together for years.

syn.note: Idiom: work hand in hand means work closely together.
Related: next to each other, helping each other.

ant.note: Apart, not together.
"Loosely connected" means only a little connected.

context.text: Madina and I have been close friends since we were six. Our closeness means we can talk about anything, and we work closely on every school project.

reviewer_note: Corpus definition describes a person ('A person you know very well'), but close is an adjective. Fix the corpus row. Sense trap: close /kləʊz/ (shut) is a different word.

corpus_definition: A state of feeling relaxed and free from any physical pain.

forms.definition: a pleasant feeling of being relaxed and free from pain
forms.example: These shoes are made for comfort, not for style.

syn.note: More about having no difficulty: "live in ease".
Warm, soft comfort, especially at home.
Related: the activity of resting; comfort is the feeling.

ant.note: Made with the prefix dis-: a feeling of slight pain.
The strong opposite.

forms.definition: to make someone feel less sad or worried
forms.example: She comforted her friend after the bad news.
forms.note: Belongs to comfort = help with feelings, not physical comfort.

forms.definition: making you feel relaxed and free from pain
forms.example: This sofa is really comfortable.

syn.note: Informal and very common in speech.
Warm and comfortable, like a small room in winter.
Related: about how a person feels, not things.

ant.note: Made with the prefix un-.

forms.definition: in a relaxed way, without pain
forms.example: The baby was sleeping comfortably in her bed.

syn.note: In a warm, comfortable way.
Related: "We can comfortably fit five people" means easily.

ant.note: In a way that doesn't feel good.

context.text: After a long flight, all I wanted was comfort. The hotel bed was so comfortable that I slept comfortably for ten hours.

corpus_definition: to make something exist or come into being

forms.definition: the act of making something new, or the new thing itself
forms.example: The creation of the website took three months.

syn.note: Easy: "the making of the film".
Related: something new, often a machine or method.
Related: a piece of art: "his latest work".

ant.note: Destroying something completely.

forms.definition: to make something new exist
forms.example: The artist created a huge painting for the station.

syn.note: Make is everyday and general; create stresses that the thing is new.
Related: making things, often many of them.
Related: plan how something will look or work.
Related: make something with parts, like a house or an app.

ant.note: To damage something so badly that it no longer exists.

forms.definition: good at having new and interesting ideas
forms.example: She is very creative; she makes all her own clothes.

syn.note: Full of new ideas.
Good at thinking of new, clever ideas.
Related: good at art, music or design.
Related: new and different from others.

ant.note: Without new ideas.

forms.definition: in a way that uses new and interesting ideas
forms.example: Try to use the old boxes creatively.

syn.note: With new ideas.
Related and easy: "cleverly used the old boxes".

people.definition: the person who makes something new for the first time
people.example: Who is the creator of this popular game?

context.text: Our class created a short film for the school festival. The creation took weeks, but everyone said it was the most creative project of the year.

corpus_definition: The possibility of being hurt or killed.

forms.definition: the possibility that someone will be hurt or killed
forms.example: The sign says: Danger! Do not swim here.

syn.note: The chance something bad happens; also used for money and business.
Formal; used on signs and at work: "a fire hazard".
Related: a particular person or thing that could cause harm.

ant.note: The state of being safe from harm.

forms.definition: to put someone or something at risk of harm
forms.example: Driving too fast endangers everyone on the road.

syn.note: The same meaning in plain English.
Related: be a danger to something: "Pollution threatens the river."
Related: do something that might lose it: "risk your life".

ant.note: To keep someone or something safe.

forms.definition: likely to hurt or kill someone
forms.example: It is dangerous to walk on the ice.

syn.note: The same meaning, made with un-.
Easy and common, often about choices: "a risky plan".
Formal, used in rules and on signs.

ant.note: Not likely to cause harm.
Not able to hurt anyone.

forms.definition: in a way that could hurt someone
forms.example: The bus was dangerously close to the edge of the road.

syn.note: Literary: "perilously close to the edge".
Related: without caring about danger: "drive recklessly".

ant.note: Without danger.

context.text: The mountain road is dangerous in winter. Drivers who go too fast endanger other people, so the police put up signs warning of danger.

corpus_definition: To have a different opinion from someone else.

forms.definition: a situation where people have different opinions
forms.example: There was a small disagreement about where to eat.

syn.note: A polite way to say it: "We had a difference of opinion."
Related: usually with angry words.
Related but much stronger: a serious fight or war.

ant.note: A situation where people have the same opinion.

forms.definition: to have a different opinion from someone else
forms.example: I disagree with you: I think the film was great.

syn.note: Formal: "Experts differ on this question."
Related: you talk angrily about it; disagree can be calm.
Related: you say you are against something.

ant.note: Remove the prefix dis- and you get the opposite.

forms.definition: unpleasant or unfriendly
forms.example: The meeting was long and disagreeable.
forms.note: Not 'having a different opinion'. Formal.

forms.definition: in an unpleasant or unfriendly way
forms.example: The room smelled disagreeably of smoke.
forms.note: Goes with disagreeable (unpleasant). Rare.

context.text: My parents often disagree about holidays. Last year their disagreement lasted a week, until my mother finally said we could go to the mountains.

corpus_definition: The system of trade and industry within a country.

forms.definition: the system of trade, industry and money in a country
forms.example: Tourism is important for the economy of Uzbekistan.

syn.note: The market is where buying and selling happen; the economy is the whole system.
Finance is about managing money, for a person, company or country.

forms.definition: to save money by spending less
forms.example: We had to economize on food after I lost my job.
forms.note: Belongs to economy = being careful with money (like economical), not a country's economy. British spelling: economise.

forms.definition: connected with trade, industry and money
forms.example: The country has had strong economic growth this year.
forms.note: Don't confuse with economical, which means 'not using much money or fuel'.

syn.note: Related: about money for a person or company too; economic is about a whole country.
Related: about buying and selling.

forms.definition: not using much money, fuel or time
forms.example: This small car is very economical.
forms.note: Belongs to economy = being careful with money, not a country's economy. Don't confuse with economic.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with trade, industry and money
forms.example: The region is growing economically.

syn.note: Related: in a way connected with money.

people.definition: an expert who studies how money, trade and industry work
people.example: The economist said prices will rise next year.

people.definition: the subject that studies money, trade and industry
people.example: She is studying economics at university in Tashkent.

context.text: The government wants to grow the economy by building new factories. Experts say economic growth will be fastest in the cities, which are already doing well economically.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: economic (about the economy) vs economical (saving money). Map keeps only the 'system' sense.

corpus_definition: To teach someone at school or in a formal way.

forms.definition: the process of teaching and learning, especially at school
forms.example: Education is free for all children in the country.

syn.note: The education you get at school.
Related: the job or work of a teacher.
Related: the learner's side: "online learning".
Related: practice for a job or sport.

ant.note: Not knowing things.

forms.definition: to teach someone, especially at a school or university
forms.example: She was educated in Tashkent and London.

syn.note: Teach is everyday and can be one lesson; educate is a long, formal process.
Formal: teach someone how to do something.
Related: practical skills for a job or sport.
Related, formal and old-fashioned as a verb: "schooled in Paris".

forms.definition: teaching you something useful
forms.example: We watched an educational film about the ocean.

syn.note: Giving you useful facts.
Formal: teaching you something useful.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with teaching and learning
forms.example: The game is fun, but is it educationally useful?

syn.note: Related: about school and university studies.

people.definition: a person whose job is teaching people, often in schools
people.example: My mother has been an educator in Samarkand for twenty years.

context.text: My grandmother was educated in a small village school. She believes education changes lives, so she buys educational books for all her grandchildren.

reviewer_note: Deliberate gate test: 'school' is marked relation 'synonym' at 0.60, which the rules forbid.

corpus_definition: the natural world around us.

forms.definition: the air, water and land where people, animals and plants live
forms.example: Plastic bags are bad for the environment.

syn.note: The same meaning in plain words.
Plants, animals and landscapes; the environment includes air and water quality too.
Related: the place around you right now, like a room or a street.

forms.definition: connected with the natural world and how to protect it
forms.example: Air pollution is a serious environmental problem.

syn.note: Scientific: about how living things and their surroundings work together.
Informal: "green energy" means good for the environment.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with the natural world
forms.example: Cycling is an environmentally friendly way to travel.

syn.note: In a way connected with nature and how it works.

people.definition: a person who works to protect the natural world
people.example: Environmentalists are worried about the Aral Sea.

context.text: Our school started an environmental club this year. We plant trees, collect rubbish and teach younger students how to live in an environmentally friendly way that protects the environment.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows exist for 'environment' (duplicate). False-split test: 'environ' is not an English word, so -ment here is not a productive suffix.

corpus_definition: To discover information or facts.
particle_note: Separable: you can say 'find out the answer' or 'find the answer out'. With a pronoun it must go in the middle: 'find it out'.

relations.note: More formal, and often about something surprising or new.
"I learned that the shop was closed." Close, but learn is also about studying.
Realize is about understanding something suddenly, often without being told.

context.text: I want to find out what time the museum opens. Yesterday I found out that it is closed on Mondays.

corpus_definition: To travel through the air using wings or an airplane.

forms.definition: a journey in a plane
forms.example: Our flight to Istanbul takes three hours.

syn.note: Related: any trip; a flight is a trip by plane.
Related: a short journey for a visit or holiday.

forms.definition: to travel through the air
forms.example: We flew to Tashkent last summer.
forms.note: Irregular verb: fly, flew, flown.

syn.note: Easy, everyday English.
The same meaning, more formal; used in travel information.
Related: fly smoothly without effort, like a bird or a paper plane.
Related: fly high in the sky, usually birds.

ant.note: To come down to the ground at the end of a flight.

forms.definition: often changing your mind; not serious or reliable
forms.example: He was too flighty to keep a job for long.
forms.note: Comes from flight, but it's about personality, not travelling by air. Informal.

people.definition: a person who travels by plane
people.example: Frequent flyers often get free seats on long trips.
people.note: Also spelled flier. A flyer is also a small paper advertisement.

context.text: My aunt is afraid to fly, so she always takes the train. Last year she finally flew to Moscow, and she said the flight was easier than she expected.

reviewer_note: Irregular inflection test (flew, flown). Noun 'fly' (the insect) is a different word.

corpus_definition: very cold weather when water freezes, or ice on the ground

forms.definition: a thin white layer of ice that forms when it is very cold
forms.example: There was frost on the car windows this morning.

syn.note: Related: ice can be thick, like on a lake; frost is a very thin layer.

ant.note: Not an exact opposite: a thaw is when frost and ice melt.

forms.definition: to cover something with a thin layer of ice
forms.example: The cold night frosted the grass white.

syn.note: "The windows iced over in the night."
Related: become ice because of the cold.

ant.note: To melt after being frozen.

forms.definition: very cold, with ice on the ground
forms.example: It was a frosty morning, and the roads were slippery.

syn.note: Covered with ice; easy and common.
Very cold: "It's freezing outside!"
Related and easy, but weaker: frosty means cold enough for ice.
Related: a little too cold.

ant.note: Pleasantly hot.
Not very cold; used about weather.

forms.definition: in a cold, unfriendly way
forms.example: 'No, thank you,' she said frostily.
forms.note: Belongs to frosty = unfriendly, not frost on the ground. Rare.

context.text: In January we often wake up to frost. On frosty mornings my father has to clean the ice off the car before he drives to work.

corpus_definition: To enter a bus, train, or plane.
particle_note: Not separable: 'get on the bus', not 'get the bus on'. For cars and taxis use 'get in(to)'.

relations.note: Formal, used in airports and stations: "Passengers may now board."
To leave a bus, train or plane.

context.text: We got on the bus at the city centre. It was so full that the last people couldn't get on at all.

reviewer_note: Two-meaning phrasal verb: 'get on (with someone)' = have a good relationship is a different sense, left out.

corpus_definition: Stop doing something that you used to do regularly.
particle_note: Separable: 'give up sugar' or 'give sugar up'. Often followed by -ing: 'give up smoking'.

relations.note: Very close and a little informal, common in American English: "quit smoking".
Stop is general; give up suggests a habit you had for a long time.
To start a new hobby or habit: "She took up yoga."

context.text: My uncle gave up smoking three years ago. He says it was hard, but giving up was the best decision of his life.

corpus_definition: The condition of your body or mind.

forms.definition: the condition of your body or mind
forms.example: Sleep is very important for your health.

syn.note: Modern word, often in adverts: "a wellness centre".
Related: how strong your body is for exercise.
Related: includes feeling happy, not only a healthy body.

ant.note: The state of being ill.
Being ill; also feeling you want to vomit.

forms.note: 'Heal' comes from the same old root, but it means to become well again after an injury. It is a different word.

forms.definition: strong and not ill; good for your body
forms.example: Fruit and vegetables are part of a healthy diet.

syn.note: Easy: "I feel well" means not ill.
Strong because you exercise.
Related: about food that is good for your body.

ant.note: Made with the prefix un-.
Easy: not well.

forms.definition: in a way that is good for your body
forms.example: Since he started eating healthily, he has more energy.

syn.note: Related: "eat well" means eat healthily.
Related: in a wise, careful way.

ant.note: Easy: "He eats badly" means his food isn't good for him.

context.text: My doctor says my health is good, but I should eat more healthily. Now I try to have a healthy breakfast every day.

corpus_definition: Telling the truth and not cheating or stealing.

forms.definition: the quality of telling the truth
forms.example: Honesty is the most important thing in a friendship.

syn.note: Always telling the truth.
Related and easy: what is true; honesty is the habit of telling it.
Related: really meaning what you say.
Related: not hiding things.

ant.note: Lying or cheating.

forms.definition: telling the truth and not cheating or stealing
forms.example: Please give me your honest opinion about my essay.

syn.note: Truthful is about what someone says; honest is also about how they act.
Related: you really mean what you say or feel.
Related: treating people equally and correctly.
Related: ready to talk about things and not hide them.

ant.note: Made with the prefix dis-.
Formal and strong: tricking people.

forms.definition: in a truthful way
forms.example: Honestly, I didn't know about the test.

syn.note: In a truthful way.
Related: used before saying something people may not like: "Frankly, the food was bad."
Related: really meaning it.

ant.note: By lying or cheating.

context.text: The shop assistant was very honest: she told me the cheaper phone was better. I really respect her honesty, and I honestly think I'll shop there again.

reviewer_note: Deliberate gate test: the -y/-ty affix record is inconsistent (affix '-y' with meaning key '-ty').

corpus_definition: Facts or details about a person or event.

forms.definition: facts or details about something
forms.example: You can find more information on our website.
forms.note: Uncountable: 'some information' or 'a piece of information', never 'an information' or 'informations'.

syn.note: Informal and very common in speech.
Easy and close: information is made of facts.
Related: small, specific pieces of information.
Related: numbers and facts collected for study.

forms.definition: to tell someone facts, often officially
forms.example: Please inform the teacher if you will be absent.

syn.note: Easy and polite: "Please let me know if you are late."
Easy, everyday English.
Formal, used in emails and official letters.

forms.definition: giving you a lot of useful facts
forms.example: The museum tour was very informative.

syn.note: Teaching you something useful.
Related: helping you do something.
Related: making things easier for you.

ant.note: Giving you few useful facts.

forms.definition: in a way that gives useful facts
forms.example: The guide spoke clearly and informatively about the old city.
forms.note: Rare. Most people say 'in a very informative way'.

syn.note: Related and easy: in a way that helps.

people.definition: the study of how computers collect, store and use facts
people.example: My brother teaches informatics at a school in Bukhara.
people.note: Common school subject name in Uzbekistan and Russia; in English schools it is usually called computer science or IT.

context.text: The airport sent us an email to inform us about the new gate. The information was short but informative: gate 12, at 9:40.

reviewer_note: False-prefix trap: 'in-' in information is not the negative prefix. No in- affix is claimed.

corpus_definition: To make someone want to learn more about something.

forms.definition: the feeling of wanting to know more about something
forms.example: He has a strong interest in history.

syn.note: Wanting to know or learn something.
Related: strong interest and excitement.
Related: "My interests are chess and music." Here interest is close to hobby.

ant.note: Feeling tired and uninterested.
Formal: not caring at all.

forms.definition: to make someone want to know more
forms.example: Space has always interested me.

syn.note: Stronger: you are very, very interested.
"The job appeals to me" means it interests me.
Related: pull someone closer; interest makes them curious.

ant.note: To make someone feel tired and not interested.

forms.definition: making you want to know more
forms.example: That was a really interesting lesson.
forms.note: Interesting describes the thing; interested describes how you feel: 'I'm interested in this interesting book.'

syn.note: Stronger: extremely interesting.
Related: makes you feel happy and full of energy.
Related: so interesting you can't stop: "a gripping film".

ant.note: Not interesting at all.
Not interesting; a little more formal than boring.

forms.definition: used to say that something is surprising or worth noticing
forms.example: Interestingly, most of the students chose the harder test.

syn.note: Used the same way: "Curiously, nobody noticed."
Related: in a way you didn't expect.

context.text: Old maps have always interested me. My interest started when my grandfather showed me an interesting map of the Silk Road.

reviewer_note: Participial adjective test (interesting / interested). False-prefix trap: 'inter-' in interest is not the prefix meaning 'between'. The money sense (bank interest) is a different sense, left out.

corpus_definition: To create something that has never been made before.

forms.definition: something new that someone has made for the first time
forms.example: The telephone was one of the most important inventions in history.

syn.note: A new idea or method, often in business or technology.
Related: the act of making something new, or the thing itself.
Related: a machine or tool made for one job.

forms.definition: to make something new for the first time
forms.example: Who invented the first computer?

syn.note: Create is wider: you can create art. Invent is for new machines, methods or ideas.
Informal: think of a new idea: "She came up with a plan."
Related: plan how something new will look or work.
Common mistake: you discover something that already existed; you invent something new.

forms.definition: good at thinking of new and clever ideas
forms.example: My brother is very inventive; he built a robot from old toys.

syn.note: Good at having new ideas.
Full of new ideas.
Related and easy: "a clever idea".

ant.note: Without new ideas.

forms.definition: in a new and clever way
forms.example: The small kitchen was inventively designed.

syn.note: With new ideas.
Related: in a smart way.

people.definition: a person who makes something new for the first time
people.example: Thomas Edison was a famous American inventor.

context.text: Ulugh Beg did not invent astronomy, but his observatory was a great invention of its time. He was an inventive scientist who measured the year very accurately.

reviewer_note: Deliberate gate test: false split 'in-' + 'vent' is claimed. The gate must reject it.

corpus_definition: the flat green part of a plant that grows from a stem

forms.definition: a flat green part of a plant that grows from a stem
forms.example: In autumn the leaves turn yellow and red.
forms.note: Irregular plural: leaves.

syn.note: Related: all the leaves of a plant or tree together.
Related: a long thin leaf of grass.
Related: the coloured part of a flower, not a leaf.

forms.definition: to turn the pages of a book or magazine quickly
forms.example: I leafed through a magazine while I waited.
forms.note: Always with through: leaf through. Belongs to leaf = a page of a book.

forms.definition: having a lot of leaves or trees
forms.example: We live on a quiet, leafy street.

syn.note: Full of healthy green plants: "lush gardens".
Related and easy: "a green street" with many trees.
Related: with shade from trees.

ant.note: With no leaves: "bare trees in winter".

context.text: Our garden is very leafy in summer. In October my little sister collects the fallen leaves, and every leaf is a different colour.

corpus_definition: To keep someone safe and healthy.
particle_note: Not separable: 'look after the baby', not 'look the baby after'.

relations.note: The same meaning; take care of is a little more common in American English.
Often used for looking after someone who is old or ill.
Look after children for a few hours, often for money.
To not give someone the care they need.

context.text: When my parents travel, my grandmother looks after us. She looked after my father too when he was a boy.

corpus_definition: to be the same or look good together

forms.definition: something that looks good with another thing
forms.example: Those shoes are a perfect match for your dress.

syn.note: Related: two things that go together.
Related: things put together.

ant.note: Things that don't go together.

forms.definition: to be the same as something, or look good with it
forms.example: Your socks don't match!

syn.note: Everyday spoken English: "Does this tie go with my shirt?"
Used in fashion: "coordinate your colours".
Related: about looking good on a person: "Blue suits you."
Related: be the right size or shape.

ant.note: Colours clash when they look bad together.

forms.definition: having the same colour or style
forms.example: The twins wore matching jackets.

syn.note: Chosen to look good together.
Related: exactly the same.

ant.note: Not going well together.

context.text: I bought a scarf to match my new coat. The colours are a perfect match, and my sister bought matching gloves.

reviewer_note: Two-meaning word: 'a football match' and 'a match to light a fire' are different senses, left out.

corpus_definition: a group of people living together under one government in a country

forms.definition: a country and the people who live in it
forms.example: The whole nation watched the final on television.

syn.note: Country is the everyday word; nation stresses the people and their identity.
Related: stresses the government and laws.
Related and literary: "a beautiful land".
Related: "the Uzbek people": the population, not the country itself.

forms.definition: the official fact of belonging to a particular country
forms.example: Please write your nationality on the form.

syn.note: Citizenship is the legal status; nationality also means the group you belong to by birth.

forms.definition: when a government takes control of a company or industry
forms.example: The government nationalized the railways in 1948.
forms.note: About governments and companies, not the people of a country. British spelling: nationalise.

forms.definition: belonging to or connected with a whole country
forms.example: Navruz is a national holiday in Uzbekistan.

syn.note: Across the whole country.
Related: inside a country, not international: "domestic flights".

ant.note: Between countries.
Belonging to one small area, not the whole country.

forms.definition: in every part of a country
forms.example: The concert will be shown nationally on Saturday.

syn.note: Easy, with the same meaning.

ant.note: Only in one small area.
In many countries.

people.definition: a person who wants their country to be independent or strong
people.example: The nationalists wanted their country to be free from the empire.
people.note: Often negative: it can also mean someone who thinks their country is better than all others.

context.text: On Independence Day the whole nation celebrates. There is a national parade in Tashkent, and the fireworks are shown nationally on TV.

reviewer_note: Affix '-ity' points to 'nationality', which is outside the four slots (same test as child/-hood).

corpus_definition: To plan or arrange an event so it happens correctly.

forms.definition: the work of planning and arranging something
forms.example: The concert was a success thanks to good organization.
forms.note: Also means a company or group (the United Nations is an organization). British spelling: organisation.

syn.note: Related: the thinking and preparing part.
Related: the plans for an event: "travel arrangements".
Related: things in their correct place.

ant.note: No order or organization at all.
A lack of order; a little formal.

forms.definition: to plan and arrange an event
forms.example: Our class organized a party for the teacher.

syn.note: Often about details like time and place: "arrange a meeting".
Informal: "We set up a meeting for Friday."
Related: plan is the thinking part; organize includes doing the work.
Related and informal: put things in order or fix a problem.

forms.definition: well planned, or good at planning things
forms.example: She is very organized; she never forgets a deadline.

syn.note: Neat and well arranged.
Related and easy: about places and things being in order.
Related: working well without wasting time.

ant.note: Made with the prefix dis-.
Easy and informal: untidy.

forms.definition: in a way connected with how a company or group is run
forms.example: Organizationally, the school is very well run.
forms.note: Goes with organization = a company or group, not organizing an event. Formal.

people.definition: a person who plans and arranges an event
people.example: The organizers of the concert sold all the tickets in two days.
people.note: British spelling: organiser.

context.text: Every year my mother organizes a big family dinner. The organization takes a week, but she is so organized that nothing ever goes wrong.

reviewer_note: False-split test: 'organ' + '-ize' is technically a real split (organ is a word) but the meaning is unrelated. Should the gate flag a stem whose meaning isn't connected?

corpus_definition: Able to stay calm when you have to wait.

forms.definition: the ability to stay calm when you have to wait
forms.example: Learning a language takes a lot of patience.

syn.note: Related: accepting things you don't like.
Related: being calm.
Related: controlling your feelings.

ant.note: Not being able to wait calmly.

forms.definition: able to stay calm while waiting
forms.example: Please be patient; the doctor will see you soon.

syn.note: Related: not worried or excited; patient means calm while you wait.
Related: you accept other people's opinions or behaviour.
Related: kind when someone makes mistakes.

ant.note: Made with the prefix im-.

forms.definition: in a calm way, without getting angry
forms.example: We waited patiently for the bus.

syn.note: Easy and close.

ant.note: Without waiting calmly.

people.definition: a person who is getting treatment from a doctor or in hospital
people.example: The nurse checked on every patient twice a night.
people.note: Same spelling, different meaning: a person in hospital, not being calm while you wait.

context.text: Our teacher is very patient with beginners. She explains everything patiently, and her patience makes us feel relaxed.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: the noun 'patient' (a person in hospital) is a different word. The noun slot uses 'patience', not 'patient'.

corpus_definition: Behaving in a kind way that respects others.

forms.definition: behaviour that shows respect for other people
forms.example: In Uzbekistan, politeness to older people is very important.

syn.note: Easy and very common.
Formal.
Related: showing someone is important.

ant.note: Being rude.

forms.definition: behaving in a way that respects other people
forms.example: It is polite to say thank you.

syn.note: The same meaning: having good manners.
More formal: "The hotel staff were courteous."
Related: showing that someone is important, like a teacher.
Related and easy: kind is about caring; polite is about good manners.

ant.note: The common opposite.
Made with the prefix im-; softer than rude.

forms.definition: in a respectful way
forms.example: He politely asked the man to move his car.

syn.note: In a polite, formal way.
Related and easy: "Ask nicely!"
Related: in a way that shows respect.

ant.note: In a rude way.

context.text: My grandfather taught me to be polite to everyone. He always answers questions politely, and people remember his politeness.

corpus_definition: To make air, water, or land dirty and unsafe.

forms.definition: dirty or harmful things in the air, water or land
forms.example: Air pollution is a big problem in many cities.

syn.note: Harmful substances in something.
Related and easy, but dirt can be harmless mud or dust.
Related: polluted air you can see, common in big cities.

forms.definition: to make air, water or land dirty and harmful
forms.example: Factories should not pollute the river.

syn.note: Often about one harmful substance, like poison in water.
Related: everyday, and can be just mud; pollute means harmful.
Related and stronger: make something dangerous to life.

ant.note: "Volunteers cleaned the beach."
Formal: remove harmful things.

forms.definition: made dirty and harmful
forms.example: Don't swim there; the lake is polluted.

syn.note: Made harmful by a substance.
Related and easy.
Related: poisonous.

ant.note: Not dirty or harmful.
With nothing harmful mixed in.

people.definition: a substance that makes air, water or land dirty
people.example: Car fumes are one of the main pollutants in big cities.

people.definition: a person, company or country that makes air, water or land dirty
people.example: The new law makes big polluters pay for cleaning the river.

context.text: Old cars pollute the air in our city. On days when the air is very polluted, the government asks people to use buses, because pollution is worst in the morning.

corpus_definition: To like one thing more than another.

forms.definition: a feeling that you like one thing more than another
forms.example: Do you have a preference: tea or coffee?

syn.note: Related and easy: the thing you like best.
Related: the thing you choose.
Related: the kinds of things you like: "music taste".

ant.note: Something you don't like.

forms.definition: to like one thing more than another
forms.example: I prefer walking to taking the bus.
forms.note: Spelling: preferred, preferring (double r).

syn.note: Easy: "I like tea better than coffee."
Slightly formal: "Most students favour online classes."
"I'd rather walk." Followed by a verb without to.
Related: choose is the action; prefer is the feeling.

ant.note: Not liking something.

forms.definition: better or more suitable
forms.example: A short meeting is preferable to a long one.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Related and formal: sensible to do.

forms.definition: if possible; this would be best
forms.example: Call me tomorrow, preferably in the morning.

syn.note: The same meaning in plain words.
In the best situation: "Ideally, call before 10."

context.text: I prefer summer to winter. My preference is simple: I love long, warm evenings, preferably by the river.

reviewer_note: Deliberate gate test: 'choose' is also used as a synonym target by another headword in this batch (clue collision check).

corpus_definition: To decide to do something at a later time.
particle_note: Separable: 'put off the meeting' or 'put the meeting off'; 'put it off', not 'put off it'. Often followed by -ing: 'put off doing homework'.

relations.note: The same meaning, more formal.
Delay can also be something that just happens: "The train was delayed."
Common mistake: cancel means it will not happen at all.

context.text: We had to put off the trip because of the snow. My brother always puts off his homework until Sunday night.

reviewer_note: Two-meaning phrasal verb: 'put someone off' (make them dislike something) is a different sense, left out.

corpus_definition: To get something that is given or provided.

forms.definition: a piece of paper that shows you have paid for something
forms.example: Keep the receipt in case you want to return the shoes.
forms.note: The p is silent: /rɪˈsiːt/. In formal English it also means the act of receiving: 'on receipt of your letter'.

syn.note: Formal phrase used in shops and online.
Related, but careful: you get a bill BEFORE you pay and a receipt AFTER.

forms.definition: to get something that someone gives or sends you
forms.example: Did you receive my email?

syn.note: Everyday English; receive is more formal.
Easy, with the same meaning.
Formal: get something, often with effort.
Related: you agree to take it; you can receive something and not accept it.

ant.note: One person sends, the other receives.
One person gives, the other receives.

forms.definition: willing to listen to and accept new ideas
forms.example: The students were very receptive to the new teaching method.
forms.note: Belongs to receive = accept ideas or people, not getting a parcel. Same family: receive, reception, receptive.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you are willing to accept new ideas
forms.example: She listened receptively to every suggestion.
forms.note: Goes with receptive. Very rare; most people say 'with an open mind'.

context.text: I received a parcel from my aunt today. Inside there was a book and a receipt, so I can change it if I already have it.

reviewer_note: False-prefix trap: 're-' + 'ceive' is not a real split; no affix is claimed.

people.definition: the part of a phone or radio that gets the signal
people.example: He picked up the receiver and said hello.

people.definition: a person who gets something, such as a prize or letter
people.example: The recipient of the award was a young teacher.

people.definition: a person who welcomes visitors at a hotel or office
people.example: The receptionist gave us the room key.
people.note: Belongs to receive = welcome guests (reception), not getting a parcel.

corpus_definition: To process waste so it can be used again.

forms.definition: the process of making waste into something that can be used again
forms.example: Our street has a special bin for recycling.

syn.note: Related: using things again without changing them.

ant.note: Not a direct opposite: a place where rubbish is buried instead of recycled.

forms.definition: to treat waste so it can be used again
forms.example: We recycle all our bottles and paper.

syn.note: Technical: treat waste so it can be used again.
Related: use the same thing again without changing it.

ant.note: Put something in the rubbish.
Use something badly, so it is lost.

forms.definition: able to be used again after special treatment
forms.example: Is this cup recyclable?

syn.note: Related: can be used again without processing, like a cloth bag.

ant.note: Cannot be recycled.
Made to be thrown away after one use: "disposable cups".

reviewer_note: Real prefix test: 're-' + 'cycle' is a genuine split, so the gate should accept it (compare receive).

corpus_definition: A physical game or activity that people play for fun or competition.

forms.definition: a game or activity that needs physical effort and skill
forms.example: Football is the most popular sport in my country.

syn.note: Formal and wider: any activity that moves your body.
Related: a game can be chess or cards; sport needs physical effort.
Related: running, jumping and throwing sports.

forms.definition: to wear or show something proudly
forms.example: He was sporting a new pair of sunglasses.
forms.note: Informal. Nothing to do with games.

forms.definition: liking sport and good at it
forms.example: My sister is very sporty; she plays tennis and basketball.

syn.note: Strong and good at sport.
Related: doing many things and moving a lot.
Related: strong because you exercise.

forms.definition: in a fair and generous way
forms.example: He sportingly shook hands with the winner.
forms.note: Goes with sporting = fair and generous. Rare.

people.definition: a man who plays a lot of games like football or tennis

people.definition: a woman who plays a lot of games like football or tennis
people.example: She is the best sportswoman in our school.

corpus_definition: Achieving what you wanted to do or reach.

forms.definition: getting the result that you wanted

syn.note: Formal: something difficult you did well.

Related: winning a fight, game or election.

ant.note: Not getting the result you wanted.

Related: win is about beating others; you can succeed without beating anyone.

ant.note: Not do what you were trying to do.

forms.definition: having done or got what you wanted

syn.note: Related: "a winning team", about beating others.
Related and formal: rich and doing well, often about businesses or towns.
Related: works well and gets the result you want.

ant.note: Made with the prefix un-.

forms.definition: coming one after another

Related: in a way that works.

ant.note: Without getting the result you wanted.

people.definition: a person who takes a job or position after someone else

corpus_definition: When a plane starts to fly.

Come down to the ground at the end of a flight.

reviewer_note: Two-meaning phrasal verb: 'take off your shoes' and 'become successful quickly' are different senses, left out. Corpus definition is written as a 'when' clause; consider fixing.

corpus_definition: To practice a sport so you can get better.

forms.definition: practice to get better at a sport or job

Related: training given by a coach.
Related: getting ready for something.

forms.definition: to practise a sport so you get better

Related: get ready: "prepare for the match".

Doing something for fun, not as a job.

people.definition: a person who is learning the skills for a job

corpus_definition: Make the sound of a device quieter.

Make the sound louder.

reviewer_note: Two-meaning phrasal verb: 'turn down an offer' (refuse) is a very common different sense, left out.

corpus_definition: to bring separate groups or things together into one

syn.note: Common for countries and organisations: "the union of two states".
The everyday word for the same action.
Related: only for companies joining together.

Keeping or moving things apart.

forms.definition: to bring separate parts together into one whole

Easy, everyday English with the same meaning.

To keep or move things apart.

Not joined; existing apart.

corpus_definition: A large boat or a container used to hold liquids.

corpus_definition: The state of the sky like rain or sun.

forms.definition: how hot, cold, wet or windy it is outside

forms.note: Uncountable: 'bad weather', never 'a bad weather'.

syn.note: Related: used in reports: "weather conditions".

corpus_definition: To look at someone and feel deep liking and respect.

forms.definition: to like and respect someone or something very much

Informal phrasal verb, used for people only.
Easy but much weaker; there is no deep respect.
Related: you see the value of something, often with thanks.
Related but stronger: you love someone very much.

ant.note: To feel that someone is bad and deserves no respect.
To think that someone is less important than you.

forms.definition: deserving respect and praise because it is very good

Easy, but much weaker.

Very bad and deserving strong criticism.

forms.definition: showing that you like and respect someone

Related: polite and showing respect, but not always liking.

people.definition: a person who likes and respects someone very much
people.example: She has many admirers among the young singers in Tashkent.
